tools.name: Canvas Stretcher & Gallery Wrap Calculator
tools.description: Work out the canvas cut size for stretching over stretcher bars from the finished face, bar depth and fold-under, or find the largest face an existing canvas can cover.
tools.method: The canvas is cut as the finished front face plus the bar depth and fold-under on every side, so both cut dimensions grow by twice the sum of those two allowances; the same rule is solved backwards to give the largest face that a canvas of known cut size can cover. The bar depth becomes the visible wrap band on each side of a gallery wrap, while the fold-under is turned to the back and never shows, so an image that runs around the edge has to extend past the face by at least the bar depth. Measurements are entered in inches or centimetres and converted with the exact 2.54 centimetre inch; the arithmetic is linear, so the geometry is the same in either unit, and areas are reported in square inches and square feet or square centimetres and square metres. Values are refused outside 1 to 240 inches (2.5 to 600 centimetres) for the face size, 1 to 400 inches (2.5 to 1000 centimetres) for a canvas entered in fit mode, 0.25 to 4 inches (0.6 to 10 centimetres) for the bar depth and 0 to 12 inches (0 to 30 centimetres) for the fold-under, and a canvas that is not wider and taller than twice the bar depth plus fold-under is refused in fit mode. The page is pure arithmetic: it does not judge whether a bar profile suits a canvas size, assess stretcher strength, allow for squaring a stretched edge or model canvas weave direction, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A stretched canvas needs canvas on every side for the bar depth plus enough to turn under and staple to the back, so the cut size is the face size plus twice the bar depth and fold-under.
Stretcher bar depth is the profile thickness, and on a gallery wrap the image continues across that depth so the sides show the image rather than bare canvas.
One inch is exactly 2.54 centimetres, so converting a measurement between the two units leaves the geometry of the cut unchanged.

tools.name: Knife-Edge Diffraction Calculator
tools.description: Estimate the extra loss a single sharp obstruction adds to a radio path, with the Fresnel–Kirchhoff parameter, the first-zone clearance and the total path loss over both legs.
tools.method: A single sharp obstruction is reduced to the Fresnel–Kirchhoff parameter v = h × √(2/λ × (1/d1 + 1/d2)), where h is the obstruction height above the straight line between the antennas in metres and d1 and d2 are the two leg lengths in metres. The diffraction loss follows the ITU-R P.526 single-edge approximation L = 6.9 + 20 log10(√((v − 0.1)² + 1) + v − 0.1) dB, which gives 6.03 dB when the edge grazes the line at v = 0, and is taken as zero once v is at or below −0.78, so an edge that clears the path adds no loss instead of a small gain. The first Fresnel radius at the obstruction is r1 = √(λ d1 d2/(d1 + d2)) and the clearance is reported as −h/r1, which equals −v/√2; a positive clearance means the edge sits below the line. The free-space loss 20 log10(4π(d1 + d2)/λ) over the whole path is reported alongside the diffraction loss and their sum. Wavelength is λ = c/f with c = 299,792,458 m/s exactly, so 2400 MHz gives 0.1249 m. Values are refused outside 1 to 100,000 MHz for frequency, 0.01 to 500 km for each leg and −1000 to 1000 m for the edge height, and decimal commas are accepted. The page models one sharp edge over flat ground with no atmosphere, terrain profile, rounded-ridge correction, multiple edges, vegetation or ground reflection, it does not recommend antenna heights or judge whether a link will close, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A single knife-edge obstruction is characterised by the Fresnel–Kirchhoff diffraction parameter v, which grows with the obstruction height above the line of sight and with the square root of 2/λ × (1/d1 + 1/d2).
ITU-R P.526 approximates the loss of a single knife edge as 6.9 + 20 log10(√((v − 0.1)² + 1) + v − 0.1) dB, about 6 dB at grazing incidence, and treats edges well below the line as no loss.
The first Fresnel zone radius at the obstruction is √(λ d1 d2/(d1 + d2)), so clearance is commonly judged against that radius rather than against the geometric line alone.

tools.name: Anchor Rode & Swing Radius Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much rode a chosen scope asks for from the water depth and bow roller height, plus the swing circle the boat traces around the anchor.
tools.method: The vertical drop is the water depth plus the height of the bow roller above the waterline, both in metres. The rode to deploy is the scope multiplied by that drop, where the scope is the rode length divided by the drop, so 5 means 5:1. With the rode straight and taut the bow sits a horizontal distance √(rode² − drop²) from the anchor, which is the swing circle radius, and twice that is the diameter; the rode's angle below horizontal at the bow is asin(drop/rode). The extra rode each extra metre of depth needs is the scope itself, which is what a falling or rising tide adds. A slack chain hangs in a catenary and reaches less than the taut figure, so the radius is the room the boat can use rather than a guaranteed position. Values are refused outside 0.5 to 100 m of depth, 0 to 10 m of bow roller height and a scope of 1.5 to 20, and decimal commas are accepted. The page does not model holding ground, weather, anchor type, chain size, snubbing or local rules, it makes no claim about whether an anchorage is safe, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Anchoring scope is quoted as the ratio of rode length to the vertical distance from the bow roller to the seabed, so the rode is the scope times the water depth plus the bow height.
A straight taut rode of length L dropping a vertical distance H puts the bow √(L² − H²) horizontally from the anchor, which bounds the circle the boat swings through.
A hanging chain forms a catenary rather than a straight line, so the horizontal reach at a given scope is smaller than the taut-ride geometry suggests.

tools.name: Dough Temperature Calculator
tools.description: Find the water temperature that brings a bread dough to a chosen finished temperature, counting the room, the flour, an optional preferment and the friction heat of mixing.
tools.method: The water temperature is the target dough temperature multiplied by the number of temperatures being averaged — 3 for a straight dough of water, flour and room, 4 when a preferment also counts — minus the flour temperature, the room temperature, the preferment temperature when used and the friction rise. The result is the water temperature that makes the mixed dough average out to the target, because the finished dough settles near the average of the temperatures that went into it. Every degree moved on the water moves the dough by one degree divided by the factor count, and cooler flour or a cooler room allows warmer water. The friction rise is the heat mixing itself adds and depends on the mixer type, the dough mass, the speeds and the mixing time, so it has to be measured for the equipment in use rather than assumed; published figures run from roughly 3 °C by hand to 13 °C on a planetary stand mixer. A required water temperature below 0 °C cannot be met with liquid water, so the flour must be chilled or part of the water replaced with ice. Values are refused outside 1 to 45 °C for the target, −20 to 50 °C for the flour, room and preferment temperatures and 0 to 30 °C for the friction rise, and decimal commas are accepted. The page does not estimate fermentation time, judge whether dough is proofed or make any food-safety claim, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: The desired dough temperature formula multiplies the target by 3 for a straight dough or 4 when a preferment is used, then subtracts the flour, room, preferment and friction temperatures to give the required water temperature.

The friction factor is the temperature rise caused by mixing and varies with the mixer, dough mass, speed and mixing time; measured examples run from about 6–8 °F by hand to 22–24 °F on a planetary stand mixer.
The preferment version of the formula multiplies the desired dough temperature by four and subtracts the preferment temperature along with the room, flour and friction temperatures.

tools.name: Uplink Oversubscription Calculator
tools.description: Compare the combined bandwidth of a switch's access ports with the uplinks that carry it: oversubscription ratio, the load those uplinks see at peak, the headroom, and the uplink ports a target ratio needs.
tools.method: The oversubscription ratio is the combined line rate of the access ports divided by the combined line rate of the active uplink ports, both in the same unit and one direction: access capacity is the port count times the access port speed, uplink capacity is the active uplink count times the uplink port speed, and the ratio is the first divided by the second. Forty-eight 1 Gbps ports behind two 10 Gbps uplinks is 48 Gbps against 20 Gbps, or 2.4:1, which means the access ports cannot all send at full line rate through the uplinks at the same time. A ratio at or below 1:1 means the uplinks match or exceed the access capacity, so the boundary is not oversubscribed. The peak demand is the access capacity multiplied by the share of line rate expected at the busiest moment, the uplink load is that demand as a percentage of the uplink capacity, and the headroom is the uplink capacity minus the demand, so a negative headroom means the assumed peak cannot pass in one direction even though the design ratio looks normal. The uplink count a target ratio needs is the access capacity divided by the target ratio times the uplink speed, rounded up to a whole port, and the headroom against the target is the target ratio times the uplink capacity minus the access capacity. Only active, forwarding uplink members are counted: a standby or blocked bundle member adds no usable bandwidth. The ratio describes provisioned capacity, not measured throughput, queueing, latency, per-flow hashing or traffic that stays on the same switch, so it is a planning figure for one boundary rather than a design certification; common guidance allows roughly 20:1 at the access edge and about 4:1 at aggregation and core. Values are refused outside 1 to 4096 access ports, 1 to 256 uplink ports, 1% to 100% peak utilization and a 1:1 to 100:1 target, port speeds come from a fixed list of line rates, and decimal commas are accepted. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Oversubscription is expressed as the ratio of the bandwidth the access ports could demand to the bandwidth the uplink provides, so a 48-port 1 Gbps switch with one 10 Gbps uplink is 4.8:1.

Widely used planning guidance puts the access-to-distribution oversubscription ratio at no more than 20:1 and distribution-to-core at no more than 4:1, and advises monitoring uplink bandwidth before changing the ratio.

tools.name: Mercator Scale Factor Calculator
tools.description: Show how far a Mercator or Web Mercator map stretches at a chosen latitude: the point scale factor sec phi, the scale error, the area inflation, the local scale a nominal 1:N map reaches there and the latitude a target factor is reached.
tools.method: A Mercator map touches the globe along the equator, where its scale is exact, and stretches every other parallel to the same length as the equator. The parallel on the globe has radius R cos phi while the map draws it with radius R, so the point scale factor is k = 1 / cos phi = sec phi for the absolute latitude phi; because the projection is conformal the meridian scale factor is the same value, which is why angles and small shapes are preserved. The scale error is (k - 1) x 100 percent, the area scale factor is the product of the two equal scales, k squared, so a region at 60 degrees covers four times the map area of the same region on the equator. A 1:N map that is true at the equator reaches 1:(N / k) at that latitude, which the page reports rounded to a whole denominator. The Mercator northing is R ln(tan(45 degrees + phi / 2)) with R = 6378137 m, the sphere radius Web Mercator uses, which equals 0 at the equator and 20037.5 km at the Web Mercator latitude limit of 85.0511287798066 degrees; that limit follows from the square world of the XYZ tile scheme and is the range this page accepts, in both hemispheres. The latitude at which a target scale factor k is reached is arccos(1 / k), reported with a note when it falls beyond the Web Mercator limit. Values are refused outside the latitude limit, a nominal scale from 1:100 to 1:1000000000 and a target factor from 1.01 to 100, and decimal commas are accepted. The page reports the properties of the spherical Mercator only: it does not add the small ellipsoidal correction that keeps Web Mercator from being exactly conformal on WGS 84 coordinates, it assumes the tangent case with the equator as standard parallel rather than a secant Mercator, and it is not a replacement for a projection library. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: The Mercator parallel and meridian scale factors are equal and both equal sec phi, so the point scale factor is 1/cos phi: about 1.15 at 30 degrees, 1.41 at 45, 2 at 60, 5.76 at 80 and 11.5 at 85, with an area scale factor of sec squared phi.

Web Mercator is a spherical Mercator that uses the same formulas at every scale, keeps meridians evenly spaced, inflates areas with distance from the equator and is normally cropped near 85 degrees north and south.

tools.name: Partition Alignment Calculator
tools.description: Align a disk partition start and size to the 1 MiB convention, to 512- or 4096-byte sectors and to a RAID stripe: the aligned start LBA, the padding a chosen offset wastes, the aligned end that lets the next partition start cleanly, and whether a 512e drive would have to read-modify-write.
tools.method: The planned start and the partition size are read in MiB with up to six decimals (decimal comma accepted) and converted to whole bytes by rounding to the nearest byte; the start must be 0 to 1,000,000 MiB and the size 0.000001 to 1,000,000 MiB. The logical and physical sector sizes are limited to 512 and 4096 bytes. The alignment unit is 1 MiB on its own; when a RAID stripe is enabled it becomes the least common multiple of 1 MiB and chunk x data disks, so a 256 KiB chunk over 6 data disks (a 1.5 MiB stripe) needs a 3 MiB unit, and a unit above 1 GiB is refused. The aligned start is the first multiple of the unit at or after the planned start, computed as byte arithmetic with no division; the aligned end is the first multiple at or after start plus size, so the next partition also begins on a boundary. All byte offsets are safe integers, and the start and end LBA are the offsets divided by the logical sector size. The verdict reports a start that is not a whole logical sector, a start that is sector-aligned but not aligned to the physical sector (a 512e drive would read-modify-write), a start that needs padding, or a start that is already aligned. The reference table lists the unit required by five common chunk and disk layouts. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: GNU Parted manual: modern partitioning tools default to an optimal MiB alignment for msdos and gpt labels and can warn when a partition start or end is not aligned.
mdadm(8): the chunk size and the number of data disks define the stripe width that RAID0, RAID5, RAID6 and RAID10 write as one unit.
Linux kernel block-layer documentation: a drive reports both a logical and a physical block size, and requests that do not cover whole physical sectors force read-modify-write on 512e media.

tools.name: Swing Ratio Calculator
tools.description: Convert a swing percentage into the long and short note lengths, the long-to-short ratio and the off-beat delay for eighth- or sixteenth-note pairs, with the first four onsets in milliseconds and beats.
tools.method: The swing amount p is read as a percentage of the pair span from 50 to 75 (decimal comma accepted), and the tempo as 20 to 400 BPM (decimal accepted). One beat lasts 60000 / BPM milliseconds; an eighth-note pair spans one beat and a sixteenth-note pair spans half a beat. The first note therefore lasts p% of the pair and the second lasts 100 - p%, the long-to-short ratio is p / (100 - p), and the off-beat shift is the second onset minus the straight midpoint, so 50% is 0 ms and 60% pushes the off-beat late by a tenth of the pair. Feel bands follow the standard swing classification: 1:1 straight at 50%, between 1:1 and 2:1 soft swing, 2:1 triplet swing at 66.67% within 0.05 percentage points (so the rounded 66.7 also reads as triplet), between 2:1 and 3:1 hard swing, and 3:1 dotted hard swing at 75%. The grid lists the first four pairs with onsets in milliseconds and in beats. Values are exact notation timing, not a model of human micro-timing, and everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Pillow Cover Calculator
tools.description: Turn a pillow insert size into an envelope-back cut list: the finished cover, the front panel and the two overlapping back panels with seam, hem and ease allowances, plus the fabric area and the length needed on 44-inch fabric.
tools.method: The finished cover is the insert plus the chosen ease on both sides, and every panel adds the seam allowance to all four cut edges. The back is two rectangles the full width of the front: their combined height covers the front height plus the overlap, and each panel adds the opening hem so the turned-under edge lands on the seam line. Total fabric is the front area plus both back panels, and the length on 44 in (112 cm) fabric stacks the front and the two back panels along one width, so it is the front height plus twice the back panel height. Inputs are inches or centimetres (decimal comma accepted), inserts 2-60 in (5-152 cm), ease 0-3 in, seam 0-2 in, overlap 1-10 in and hem 0-2 in. It warns when the overlap exceeds half the front height and when a panel is wider than the fabric. It does not allow for directional prints, nap, pattern matching, shrinkage or squaring the fabric, and it is a planning estimate rather than a guarantee against a particular insert squishiness.

tools.name: Antenna Downtilt Coverage Calculator
tools.description: Turn an antenna height, downtilt and half-power beamwidths into a ground coverage footprint: the near and far beam edges, the aim distance, the slant range and the path width at the aim point.
tools.method: Ground distance to a depression angle theta is h / tan(theta), with h in metres and theta in degrees. The beam centre uses the downtilt; the near edge uses the downtilt plus half the vertical beamwidth and the far edge uses the downtilt minus half of it, so there is no far ground edge when the upper half-power edge is at or above the horizon. The footprint is the far edge minus the near edge, the slant range is h / sin(theta), and the path width at the aim point is twice the centre distance times tan of half the horizontal beamwidth. The radio horizon is 4.12 x sqrt(h) km and is used only to flag a footprint that curvature would shorten. Inputs are metres or feet (decimal comma accepted), heights 1-300 m (3.3-984 ft), downtilt 1-45 degrees, vertical beamwidth 2-60 degrees and horizontal beamwidth 10-120 degrees. The model assumes flat ground with no terrain, structures or vegetation, a symmetric main beam, and no earth curvature in the footprint distances; it does not account for side lobes, antenna gain beyond the half-power width, or RF exposure limits.

tools.name: Billiards Cut Angle Calculator
tools.description: Measure the cut angle for a pool shot from the cue ball, object ball and pocket positions, with the ghost-ball aim point, contact point, cue and object travel and aim-line offset on 7, 8 or 9 ft tables in inches or centimetres.
tools.method: The cut angle follows from the line of centres. With cue ball C, object ball O and the selected pocket P, the unit vector u points from O to P, and the ghost-ball centre is G = O - 2r u, where r is the ball radius. The cue ball must travel from C to G, so the cut angle is the angle between C to G and u: it is 0 for a straight shot and approaches 90 degrees as the hit gets thinner. An angle above 90 degrees means C lies on the pocket side of O, so a centre-ball hit cannot send the object ball toward that pocket. The contact point on the object ball is O - r u, the cue-ball travel is the distance from C to G, the object-ball travel is the distance from O to P, and the aim-line offset from the object ball's centre is 2r sin(cut). Standard American pool balls are 2.25 in (57.15 mm) in diameter; the playing surfaces are 78 x 39 in (7 ft), 88 x 44 in (8 ft) and 100 x 50 in (9 ft). Coordinates run from the bottom-left corner with x along the long rail, in inches or centimetres, and every ball centre must sit at least one radius inside the cushions. The model assumes a centre-ball hit with no side spin, no throw, no cushion contact and no pocket-jaw effects, so it is a planning aid rather than a prediction that a shot drops.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Billiards: the object ball leaves along the line joining the ball centres at contact, which is the basis of ghost-ball aiming.
Wikipedia, Pool (cue sports): American pool balls are 2.25 in (57.15 mm) in diameter, and 7, 8 and 9 ft tables have 78 x 39, 88 x 44 and 100 x 50 in playing surfaces.
Wikipedia, Cut shot: a cut shot strikes the object ball off-centre and sends it along the line of centres rather than along the cue ball's path.

tools.name: Rice Cooking Ratio Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much water and how big a pot a batch of rice needs and how many servings it makes, from the rice type, the dry cups, grams or cooked servings and an adjustable water-to-rice ratio.
aliases: How Much Water for Rice Calculator
how much water for rice calculator
tools.method: Water is quoted by volume against the dry rice, so the ratio is cups of water per cup of dry rice: the defaults are 1.75 for long-grain and medium-grain white rice, 1.5 for jasmine and basmati, 1.15 for short-grain sushi rice, 2.25 for brown rice, 3 for wild rice and 4.5 for arborio, and the field can be overridden to match a packet or a measured batch. A cup is 236.5882365 ml and the water in millilitres is the rice volume in cups multiplied by the ratio and by that figure. A gram amount is first turned into cups with the type's bulk density (185 g for long-grain, 180 g for jasmine and basmati, 190 g for medium-grain and brown, 200 g for short-grain and arborio, 160 g for wild rice), because the ratio applies to volume rather than mass. A serving is taken as half a cup of cooked rice, and a serving request is converted back into dry rice with the type's cooked expansion (3 cups cooked per cup dry for most white and brown rice, 2.7 for short-grain, 3.5 for wild), so the cooked volume and serving count are estimates of typical absorption rather than a measurement of the pan. The pot figure is simply the dry rice plus the water. Amounts are refused outside 0.05 to 40 cups, 10 to 6400 grams or 1 to 80 half-cup servings, and ratios outside 0.5 to 8; decimal commas are accepted. The page does not model soaking, evaporation, altitude, stirring or absorption differences between crops, and it makes no food-safety claim about cooking, cooling or storing rice. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Cooked rice: rice is generally cooked by absorption with roughly two parts water to one part rice by volume, and one cup of dry white rice yields about three cups cooked, though the exact figures depend on the variety.
Wikipedia, Brown rice: brown rice keeps its bran and germ, so it needs more water and a longer cooking time than white rice.
Wikipedia, Wild rice: wild rice is the grain of a North American water grass rather than a true rice, and the grains split open as they cook.
Wikipedia, Arborio rice: arborio is a short-grain Italian rice used for risotto, cooked by adding hot stock a ladle at a time rather than all at once.

tools.name: Structured Cabling Run Estimator
tools.description: Estimate how much Ethernet cable a set of data drops needs and how many boxes to order, from the drop count, the average run, riser distance, slack allowance and box size.
tools.method: Every drop is charged the average horizontal run plus the riser distance, and that figure is increased by the slack allowance: cable per drop = (average run + riser) x (1 + slack / 100). The job total is that figure multiplied by the number of drops, and the boxes to buy are the total divided by the box size rounded up to the next whole box, with a one-part-in-a-billion tolerance so a total that lands exactly on a full box is not rounded again. Box sizes are the international foot definition (0.3048 m), so the 1000 ft box is 304.8 m and the 500 ft box is 152.4 m, with a 500 m drum as the third choice; feet are reported as metres divided by 0.3048. Patch cords are counted separately as drops x patch cords per drop, because they are bought as assemblies rather than cut from the box. Inputs are refused outside 1 to 1000 drops, 0.5 to 150 m average run, 0 to 100 m riser, 0 to 50 percent slack and 0 to 4 patch cords per drop, drops and patch cords must be whole numbers, and decimal commas are accepted. The page does not survey a building, choose a cable category, check conduit or tray fill or bend radius, allow for waste from failed pulls, or know a manufacturer's actual box length; the average run and the slack allowance are site assumptions the user supplies. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Structured cabling: a structured cabling system runs horizontal cabling from each outlet to a telecommunications room, so a drop needs both a horizontal run and any riser distance to the room.
Wikipedia, Twisted pair: Ethernet cabling is sold on reels and in pull boxes in fixed lengths, which is why a job is ordered in whole boxes with slack for routing and termination.
Wikipedia, Foot (unit): since the 1959 international yard and pound agreement one foot is exactly 0.3048 metres, the conversion used for the 1000 ft and 500 ft box sizes.

tools.name: Map Fit-Bounds Zoom Calculator
tools.description: Find the Web Mercator zoom level that fits a latitude/longitude bounding box into a map viewport, with the box centre, screen span, ground resolution, map scale and tile range.
tools.method: Each edge is projected onto the spherical Web Mercator plane (EPSG:3857): x = (longitude + 180) / 360, and y = (1 - ln(tan(pi/4 + phi/2)) / pi) / 2, with phi the latitude in radians clamped to the +/-85.0511287798066 degree limit where the projection is finite. The box width is the eastward longitude difference divided by 360, taken through 180 degrees when west is larger than east, and the box height is the difference of the two y values. At zoom z the world is tile size x 2^z pixels across, so the box spans box width x tile x 2^z pixels horizontally and box height x tile x 2^z vertically. The exact fit zoom is the smaller of log2(viewport width / (box width x tile size)) and log2(viewport height / (box height x tile size)); that value is rounded down to a whole zoom, with a one-part-in-a-billion tolerance so an exact fit stays at its own zoom, and clamped to the usual 0 to 22 range. At the chosen zoom the page reports the box centre (the wrapped midpoint of the x range and the midpoint of the y range inverted back to latitude), the box size in screen pixels, the ground resolution at the centre 40075016.68557849 m x cos(centre latitude) / world width, the map scale denominator at 96 dpi (metres per pixel divided by 0.0254/96), and the tile columns and rows covering the box, with a one-part-in-a-billion tolerance so an edge that sits exactly on a tile boundary does not add an empty row or column. Inputs are refused outside -90 to 90 degrees latitude, -180 to 180 degrees longitude, a viewport of 1 to 10000 whole pixels and the 256 or 512 pixel tile sizes; north must be greater than south, west and east must differ, and a box that collapses to zero height after clamping is refused. Decimal commas are accepted. The page does not reproject to other datums or projections, report resolution anywhere but the box centre, know about terrain, tilt, padding, tile overlap or retina tile sets beyond the tile-size choice, and it does not fetch or draw any map. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Web Mercator projection: the spherical projection normalises longitude and a stretched latitude, and is only finite up to about 85.0511 degrees, the clamp this page applies.
OpenStreetMap Wiki, Slippy map tilenames: a zoom level z splits the world into 2^z by 2^z tiles of 256 pixels, so the world is 256 x 2^z pixels wide and a viewport fit follows from that ratio.
Wikipedia, Scale (map): map scale is a ratio of map distance to ground distance, computed here from the ground resolution at the box centre with 96 CSS pixels to the inch.

tools.name: Disk I/O Throughput & IOPS Calculator
tools.description: Turn sustained IOPS, block size and average latency into throughput in MB/s, data per hour and per day, time per I/O, the queue depth Little's law needs, and the IOPS a given queue depth can sustain.
tools.method: Every operation is assumed to move exactly the chosen block size, so the throughput is the sustained IOPS multiplied by that block size in bytes: 10,000 IOPS of 4 KiB is 40,960,000 bytes per second. Decimal units divide by 1,000,000 for MB/s and binary units by 1,048,576 for MiB/s; the data per hour is bytes per second x 3600 in decimal GB, the data per day is bytes per second x 86400 in decimal TB, and the time to move 1 TiB is 1,099,511,627,776 bytes divided by the byte rate in hours. The time per I/O is one second divided by the IOPS and is shown in microseconds. Little's law gives the average number of requests in flight as the completion rate times the average latency, so the queue depth needed is IOPS x latency in seconds (2 at 10,000 IOPS and 0.2 ms); when a queue depth is supplied, the IOPS that depth can sustain at the same latency is depth / latency, the headroom is that figure minus the entered rate, the utilization is the entered rate divided by that maximum, and an entered rate equal to the maximum is treated as covered. IOPS accepts 0.001 to 100,000,000, latency 0.001 to 60,000 ms, and the optional queue depth a whole number from 1 to 65,536; the nine block sizes run from 512 bytes to 1 MiB, decimal commas are accepted and exponent notation is refused. All arithmetic is double precision. The figures describe a steady state and do not model bursts, read/write mixes, sequential versus random placement, RAID write penalties, controller caches, filesystem overhead, thin provisioning or network storage, and the page does not benchmark, read or modify any device. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, IOPS: the operation rate a storage device sustains and the block size each operation transfers together determine the byte throughput.
Wikipedia, Little's law: the long-run average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends there, which is the queue depth relation used here.
Linux kernel block-layer documentation: I/O requests are queued against a device queue with a bounded depth, so the queue depth and the per-request latency bound the achievable completion rate.

tools.name: Nashville Number System Converter
tools.description: Convert a chord chart to Nashville numbers in any key and back again: roots become 1 to 7 with b or # degrees, qualities and bar lines are kept, and borrowed chords are listed.
tools.method: The key is read as a letter A to G with up to two sharps or flats, giving the tonic pitch. In the chords to numbers direction each chord token is a root, a quality suffix and an optional slash bass; the root may carry up to two sharps or flats and the suffix is scanned from a fixed vocabulary (m, M, maj, min, dim, aug, sus, add, alt, no, degree and half-diminished signs, digits, altered digits such as b9 or #11, and brackets). The degree number is the semitone distance from the tonic taken on the major scale: 0 semitones is 1, 2 is 2, 4 is 3, 5 is 4, 7 is 5, 9 is 6 and 11 is 7; the five remaining distances are written with a flat as b2, b3, b5, b6 and b7, so F sharp in C becomes b5 rather than #4. The quality suffix and the bar lines are copied through unchanged, so G7 in C is 57 and Am7 is 6m7, and a slash bass note is numbered the same way, so C/E is 1/3 and C/Bb is 1/b7. In the numbers to chords direction a token is an optional b or # (at most two), a degree 1 to 7, the same quality vocabulary and an optional slash degree. The chord root keeps the letter of that degree of the key, so the seventh degree of C sharp is B sharp and the seventh of C flat is B flat, and the accidental is the difference between the degree's pitch and that letter's natural pitch, which is why b3 in C is E flat and #4 in D is G sharp. Bars are the non-empty groups between bar lines. A key is refused when its major scale needs more than two accidentals on any degree, which rules out theoretical spellings such as F double flat. A chart holds at most 200 chords; six-nine chords are refused because a slash always means a bass note, and mixed sharps and flats, unknown qualities, a missing bass and a degree outside 1 to 7 are refused with the offending token named. Numbers are measured from the major scale, so a minor-key song uses its relative major: Am-F-C-G in C is 6m 4 1 5. The page does not model key signatures, roman numerals, superscription, repeat signs, pushes or chord voicings, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Nashville Number System: numbers denote the scale degree a chord is built on, accidentals are written to the left of the number, minor chords use a dash or lowercase m, and a slash gives the bass note's scale degree (1/3 is the 1 chord with the third in the bass).
Hudson Valley Bluegrass Association, The Nashville Number System: in C the numbers run C Dm Em F G7 Am B(m7b5), so chord quality follows the major scale and the number chart works in any key.
Jack W. Cannon, Introduction to the Nashville Numbering System: only b and # may be prepended to a degree number, and chord-type modifiers follow it.

tools.name: Embroidery Stitch & Thread Estimator
tools.description: Estimate a machine embroidery design's stitch count, upper and bobbin thread, smallest hoop and stitch-out time from its size, stitch density and filled coverage.
tools.method: The design is a rectangle measured in inches, and the stitched area is that rectangle multiplied by the filled coverage percentage, so a five by seven design at 40 percent covers 14 square inches. The estimated stitch count is the stitched area multiplied by the stitch density in stitches per square inch, rounded to the nearest whole stitch with an exact half rounded up, and a design that works out to less than one stitch is refused. Upper thread is the stitch count divided by 1,000 multiplied by the thread allowance in yards per 1,000 stitches, which is about 1 yard for 40 weight thread; bobbin thread is taken as one third of the upper thread. Thread is also shown in metres at 0.9144 metres per yard. The hoop or stabilizer minimum is the design plus the margin on every side, reported in inches and millimetres. Stitch-out time is the stitch count divided by machine speed in stitches per minute and is shown in minutes and seconds; it excludes trims, colour changes, rehooping and acceleration. Inputs are limited to a design from 0.1 to 24 inches per side, a density from 200 to 20,000 stitches per square inch, coverage from 1 to 100 percent, a thread allowance from 0.1 to 10 yards per 1,000 stitches, a machine speed from 100 to 2,000 stitches per minute and a hoop margin from 0 to 6 inches; text, negative numbers, scientific notation and out-of-range values are refused with the field named. Warnings appear for hoops larger than a common 200 by 300 millimetre maximum, densities outside 1,000 to 12,000 stitches per square inch, and runs over 500,000 stitches. The estimate assumes the density figure already includes underlay, and it does not model fabric, stabilizer, thread weight, design shape or stitch length. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Machine embroidery planning practice: filled areas are budgeted in stitches per square inch, with solid fills commonly running about 3,000 to 8,000 stitches per square inch.
Machine embroidery thread budgeting: upper thread is planned at roughly 1 yard of 40 weight thread per 1,000 stitches, and bobbin thread at about one third of the upper thread.
Machine embroidery hooping: the hoop and stabilizer must extend beyond the design on every side, and many home machines top out at a 200 by 300 millimetre hoop.

tools.name: Microstrip Trace Impedance Calculator
tools.description: Estimate a microstrip PCB trace's characteristic impedance, effective permittivity, propagation delay, guided wavelength and per-length capacitance and inductance from trace width, substrate height and dielectric constant.
tools.method: The trace width w and substrate height h are entered in millimetres or mils and converted to millimetres with 1 mil = 0.0254 mm; their ratio u = w/h must lie between 0.01 and 100. The characteristic impedance and effective permittivity come from the Hammerstad and Jensen closed-form microstrip equations for a zero-thickness trace over a ground plane. For u at or below 1: ee = (er+1)/2 + (er-1)/2 x [1/sqrt(1+12/u) + 0.04(1-u)^2] and Z0 = 60/sqrt(ee) x ln(8/u + u/4). For u above 1: ee = (er+1)/2 + (er-1)/(2 sqrt(1+12/u)) and Z0 = 120 pi / [sqrt(ee) x (u + 1.393 + 0.667 ln(u + 1.444))]. At exactly u = 1 the first branch is used; the two branches meet within half a percent there. Velocity factor is 1/sqrt(ee). Propagation delay is sqrt(ee)/c, reported in ps/mm and ps/in with c = 299,792,458 m/s, which is 3.33564 ps/mm at ee = 1. Guided wavelength is c/(f sqrt(ee)) for the frequency in GHz, so 299.792458/f millimetres before the square-root factor. Per-length capacitance is sqrt(ee)/(Z0 c), shown in pF/mm with 1 F/m = 1e9 pF/mm, and per-length inductance is Z0 sqrt(ee)/c, shown in nH/mm with 1 H/m = 1e6 nH/mm. Widths run from 0.01 to 50 mm (0.4 to 2000 mils) and heights over the same range; relative permittivity runs from 1 to 100 and frequency from 0.01 to 100 GHz. Text, negative numbers, scientific notation and out-of-range values are refused with the field named, and a width-to-height ratio outside 0.01 to 100 is refused. Results are rounded: the ratio and effective permittivity to four places, impedance to two, velocity factor to four, delay to three, wavelength to two and the per-length values to four. The estimate ignores copper thickness, plating, solder mask and dispersion, and the closed forms lose accuracy outside a width-to-height ratio of roughly 0.1 to 10. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Football Passer Rating Calculator
tools.description: Turn passing attempts, completions, yards, touchdowns and interceptions into an NFL passer rating, with the four capped components and the per-attempt rates behind it.
tools.method: All five inputs are whole numbers: attempts from 1 to 2,000, completions, touchdown passes and interceptions from 0 to 2,000, and passing yards from 0 to 100,000. Completions cannot exceed attempts, touchdown passes cannot exceed completions, and completions plus interceptions cannot exceed attempts, because an intercepted pass is an attempt that was not completed. The four NFL components are computed in double precision: a = 5 x (completions / attempts - 0.30); b = 0.25 x (yards / attempts - 3.0); c = 20 x (touchdowns / attempts); d = 2.375 - 25 x (interceptions / attempts). Each component is then clamped to the closed interval 0 to 2.375, so a completion rate below 30 percent scores zero and one above 77.5 percent hits the cap; the same bounds apply at 3.0 and 12.5 yards per attempt, an 11.875 percent touchdown rate and a 9.5 percent interception rate. The rating is (a + b + c + d) / 6 x 100, which makes 158.3 the maximum and 0 the minimum. The page reports the rating to one decimal place, each component to three decimals, completion and scoring percentages to one decimal and yards per attempt to two, all rounded half away from zero. Passing yards are net yards on the listed passes, and sacks are excluded from attempts. The statistic ignores dropped passes, opponent strength, era, weather, rushing and receiving contributions and two-point conversions; it is not a projection or a cross-league comparison, and NCAA or high-school ratings use different coefficients that this page does not compute. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: NFL passer rating definition: four components each capped at 0 and 2.375, summed, divided by six and multiplied by 100 (Elias Sports Bureau statistic published by the NFL).

A rating of 158.3 is perfect because all four components sit at their 2.375 cap, and the scale's minimum is 0.

tools.name: Roux Thickening Calculator
tools.description: Size a butter-and-flour roux for a soup, sauce or gravy from the liquid volume, or work backwards from a roux on hand to the liquid it will thicken.
tools.method: Amounts follow the classic home roux rule: one level tablespoon of all-purpose flour per US cup of liquid for a thin soup, two for a medium sauce and three for a thick gravy or stew. A US cup is 236.5882365 mL and a level US tablespoon is 14.7868 mL, so one, two and three tablespoons per cup work out to about 3.4, 6.8 and 10.1 percent flour by weight in a water-like liquid. Liquid volume is accepted in US cups from 0.25 to 25, millilitres from 60 to 6000 or litres from 0.06 to 6; it is converted to millilitres and one millilitre is taken as one gram, so milk or stock, which are a few percent denser, shift the percentages by a few tenths. A level tablespoon of all-purpose flour is taken as 8 g and a level tablespoon of butter as 14.2 g. The fat is measured to match the flour's volume, the usual kitchen ratio, which comes to 1.78 times the flour's weight. Flour grams are the liquid in cups times the tablespoons per cup times 8, butter grams are the same tablespoon count times 14.2, the roux weight is their sum, and the flour share is flour grams divided by the liquid mass. The reverse mode takes a roux weight from 5 to 2000 g, splits it 8 to 14.2 into flour and butter, turns the flour back into tablespoons and divides by the selected tablespoons per cup to get the liquid it thickens; a roux that would thicken more than 6000 mL is refused because the documented liquid range ends there. Grams and millilitres are reported to one decimal and whole millilitres, cups and tablespoons to two decimals, and percentages to one decimal, all rounded half away from zero. The estimate ignores evaporation, the flour's continued absorption as a sauce stands, gluten-free blends and cornstarch slurries, and it carries no salt; it is a cooking estimate, not food-safety guidance. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Wake-on-LAN Packet Builder
tools.description: Build the Wake-on-LAN magic packet for a network card: six 0xFF bytes plus the MAC repeated sixteen times, 102 bytes, or 108 with a six-byte SecureOn password, shown as copyable hex with the broadcast destination and as downloadable shell, Python and C senders.
tools.method: The magic packet is built as six 0xFF bytes followed by the target MAC's six bytes repeated 16 times, which is 102 bytes, and an optional six-byte SecureOn password is appended to make 108 bytes. The MAC is read in any common notation - colon, dash, dotted Cisco or bare hex - after whitespace and the colon, dash and dot separators are removed, and must contain exactly 12 hex digits. The null address and the broadcast address are refused because no card can own them, and an address with the multicast bit set in its first byte is refused because a unicast NIC address always has an even first octet; a locally administered address has bit 1 set, is accepted, and is called out because virtual machines and randomised Wi-Fi addresses use one. A SecureOn password must be exactly 12 hex digits; an all-zero password is refused because it disables the feature and cannot be told apart from no password. The packet is emitted as lowercase hex with no separators, and the page also shows the six-byte sync prefix, the 96-byte MAC block and the optional six-byte tail separately. The destination is the limited broadcast address 255.255.255.255 on UDP port 9, which some equipment replaces with port 7; a browser cannot transmit raw UDP, so the hex is meant to be copied into a wake utility, a switch or router wake action, or a script. For the script case the page also generates three runnable senders from the same bytes - a POSIX shell script that pipes a printf-octal packet through socat, a Python 3 script using only the socket module, and a C99 program using POSIX sockets - with the MAC, the optional SecureOn tail and the 255.255.255.255:9 default baked in, each accepting an optional host and port, so the packet the page shows is the packet the file sends. Wake-on-LAN must be enabled in the card's firmware with standby power available, and the packet only reaches cards on the same Layer 2 segment. Everything runs in the browser without storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wake-on-LAN: the magic packet carries six 0xFF bytes, the target MAC repeated sixteen times (102 bytes) and an optional SecureOn password, and is sent to the limited broadcast address on UDP port 7 or 9.
wakeonlan(1): the magic packet consists of 6 times 0xFF followed by 16 times the hardware address, sent as a UDP datagram to 255.255.255.255 on port 9 by default.

tools.name: GPS Track Simplifier
tools.description: Reduce a GPX track or GeoJSON LineString to the points that carry its shape: set a Douglas-Peucker tolerance in metres and see the kept and dropped points, the shortened length and the largest offset lost.
tools.method: The track is read from one of three inputs: a GPX document, whose trkpt, wpt and rtept elements are taken in document order with their lat and lon attributes, a GeoJSON LineString given directly, wrapped in a Feature or in a FeatureCollection that holds exactly one line, or a plain list with one latitude, longitude pair per line separated by commas, spaces, tabs or semicolons, where a third elevation column is ignored. GeoJSON coordinates are read in the standard [longitude, latitude] order and every latitude must be within -90 to 90 and every longitude within -180 to 180. Simplification is Douglas-Peucker: the first and last point are always kept, the point farthest from the line joining them is found, and if that distance exceeds the tolerance the point is kept and the two halves are handled the same way, otherwise every point in that span is dropped. Distances are measured on an equirectangular projection centred on the track's mean latitude with an Earth radius of 6,371,008.8 m, which is accurate within a region and drifts for a track spanning continents, and the projection wraps longitude differences at the antimeridian. The result reports the kept and dropped counts, the reduction, the polyline length before and after simplification with the haversine formula, the largest offset of a dropped point, and the simplified track as six-decimal latitude/longitude pairs and as a GeoJSON feature, with a warning when the tolerance shortens the path by more than five percent. Tolerances must be greater than zero and at most 100 km, and a track above 20,000 points is refused. Everything runs in the browser without uploads or network access.

tools.name: udev Rule Builder
tools.description: Compose a udev rule that matches a device by subsystem, kernel name and parent attributes and gives it a stable /dev symlink with owner, group and mode. Shows the exact rule line, its file name and the reload commands.
tools.method: A rule is composed from six optional decisions in a fixed order: SUBSYSTEM, KERNEL, up to two attribute matches, SYMLINK, OWNER, GROUP and MODE. The subsystem is required and is lowercase letters, digits, underscores or hyphens, written as udev reports it (tty, usb, block, net). The kernel name pattern accepts the usual glob syntax, * ? and character classes such as ttyUSB[0-9] or ttyUSB*|ttyACM*, and is left out when the field is blank. Each attribute match needs both a sysfs attribute name (letters, digits and underscores) and a value; the target selector chooses ATTR, which reads the attribute on the device the event is for, or ATTRS, which searches that device and its parents, where a USB serial adapter's idVendor and idProduct are found. Values are quoted in the rule and may contain spaces, but a double quote or backslash is refused because udev would require it escaped. A link name must be one path component of at most 63 characters from letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens, with no slash, space or % substitution; SYMLINK adds the name beside the kernel-assigned one. Owner and group accept a name or a numeric id up to 4294967294; MODE accepts three or four octal digits and is normalised to four, at most 0777, so setuid, setgid and sticky bits are not offered. The result reports the exact rule line, its length and clause count, the rule file name derived from the link or subsystem (a 99- prefix so it runs after the distribution's own rules) and the reload and trigger commands. Warnings appear when a rule only matches without assigning anything, when nothing narrows it to a device, when MODE is set without OWNER or GROUP, and when permissions change without a SYMLINK. The page composes text only: it reads no device data, installs nothing and uses no network.

sources.title: udev(7), systemd manual: rule files are read in lexical order from /etc/udev/rules.d, and matching keys SUBSYSTEM, KERNEL, ATTR, ATTRS and SYMLINK build one rule per line.
systemd-udevd.service(8): rules are applied when a device is added, and udevadm control --reload-rules plus udevadm trigger apply an edited rule to existing devices.
udevadm(8): control --reload-rules reloads rule files and trigger --subsystem-match replays events for one subsystem.

tools.name: Harmonic Mixing Key Finder
tools.description: Convert a musical key to its Camelot and Open Key codes and list the keys that mix into it: the same key, one number up or down the wheel, and the relative major or minor.
tools.method: The wheel is read from the note rather than from the text that was typed: a note letter A to G with up to two sharps or flats gives a pitch class from 0 to 11, and the mode picks one of two twelve-entry tables that map each pitch class to a wheel position. The minor table puts 1 at A flat, 2 at E flat, 3 at B flat, 4 at F, 5 at C, 6 at G, 7 at D, 8 at A, 9 at E, 10 at B, 11 at F sharp and 12 at C sharp. The major table puts 1 at B, 2 at F sharp, 3 at D flat, 4 at A flat, 5 at E flat, 6 at B flat, 7 at F, 8 at C, 9 at G, 10 at D, 11 at A and 12 at E. Both tables are the circle of fifths: each step from one number to the next is seven semitones, so 8A is A minor and 9A is E minor, and the major key at a number is the relative major of the minor key there, three semitones above its tonic, which is why 8B is C major. A position is written as its number plus A for a minor key or B for a major key, so A minor is 8A and C major is 8B. Open Key labels the same wheel seven positions earlier, so its number is the Camelot number minus seven, wrapped into 1 to 12: 8A becomes 1m, 1A becomes 6m and 12A becomes 5m, with m for minor and d for major. The name shown is the spelling the wheel uses, so a typed G sharp minor is reported as A flat minor on 1A with the typed spelling called out, C flat major is shown as B major and B sharp major as C major, all of which share a pitch class. The listing gives four keys: the same position, the next position (one number on, a perfect fifth up), the previous position (one number back, a fifth down, wrapping from 1 to 12) and the same number with the other letter, which is the relative major or relative minor and shares all seven notes of the scale. Input is one of three forms: a note with an optional mode (A minor, F#m, Bb major, or a bare note that means major), a Camelot code from 1A to 12B, or an Open Key code from 1m to 12d. After the note a lowercase m means minor and the words min, minor, maj and major are accepted; a lone capital M is refused rather than guessed at, because it means major in some charts and is read as minor in others. Mixed sharps and flats, a mode word that is not a mode, a number outside 1 to 12 and text that is neither a note nor a code are refused with the problem named. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access, and the reference table of all 24 positions is built from the same tables as the result so the two cannot disagree.

sources.title: Mixed In Key, Interactive Camelot Wheel: the 24 keys run 1A to 12B, A is minor and B is major, 8A is A minor and 8B is C major, the relative key keeps the number and switches the letter, and one number up or down is the adjacent key.
beaTunes, Open Key Notation: a key harmonizes with itself and with X plus or minus one, d means Dur (major) and m means Moll (minor), and the number can be kept while switching d for m.

ImmerGround, The Camelot wheel explained: the full 1 to 12 table with each minor and major key and its Open Key code, each step clockwise a perfect fifth, and the Open Key number found by adding five to the Camelot number and subtracting twelve when it passes twelve.

tools.name: Gather & Ruffle Calculator
tools.description: Plan a gathered ruffle from a finished edge length and a gather ratio: cut length, take-up, strips to join, fabric per strip and an even section plan.
tools.method: The cut length is the finished edge multiplied by the gather ratio plus the seam allowance at both ends, so a forty inch edge at two to one with a half inch allowance needs eighty one inches of fabric. The take-up is the fabric that disappears into the gathers: the finished edge times the ratio, minus the finished edge itself, which is forty inches at two to one. The gather ratio runs from 1.1 to 4 and the page names the fullness band it falls in: below 1.5 is soft, 1.5 up to 2.5 is medium, 2.5 up to 3 is full and 3 or more is very full. Strips are counted by dividing the cut length by the usable fabric width and rounding up, so the strips can be joined end to end without a short strip at the seam; an exact fit stays one strip. The fabric per strip is the cut length divided by the strip count, which is the average strip rather than a per-strip cutting list when the last strip is short. The section plan divides both the cut length and the finished edge by the section count so the gathers can be pulled evenly between marks. Inches and centimetres are both supported; the arithmetic is unit-free and the page also shows the cut length converted at exactly 2.54 centimetres to the inch. Inputs are limited to a finished edge of 1 to 500 inches (2.5 to 1270 centimetres), a ratio of 1.1 to 4, a usable fabric width of 1 to 120 inches (2.5 to 305 centimetres), a seam allowance of 0 to 12 inches (0 to 30 centimetres) per end and 1 to 8 whole sections; text, negative numbers, exponent notation, empty fields and out of range values are refused with the field named. The page assumes a plain rectangular strip cut to the usable width with no pattern repeat, nap, directional print, selvedge or shrinkage allowance, does not model how the gather is sewn or which stitch length is used, and it stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

sources.title: Sewing and pattern-drafting practice: a gathered strip is cut at the gather ratio times the finished edge, and seam allowances are added at the ends that are joined or turned under.
Ruffle fullness guidance used in dressmaking: roughly 1.5 to 1 reads as a soft gather, 2 to 1 as a standard ruffle, and 3 to 1 or more as a dense, tutu-like gather.
Sewing construction practice: ruffles are gathered in two or more rows of long stitches and divided into equal sections so the fullness is distributed evenly along the seam.

tools.name: RF Attenuator Pad Calculator
tools.description: Design a matched pi or T resistive attenuator: series and shunt resistor values for a chosen loss and system impedance, the nearest 1% E96 parts and the loss they actually produce.
tools.method: A matched resistive pad trades loss for a stable impedance. The voltage ratio is K = 10^(dB/20). A pi pad is one series arm between two shunt arms: the series arm is Z0 times (K squared minus one) divided by twice K, and each shunt arm is Z0 times (K plus one) divided by (K minus one). A T pad is one shunt arm between two series arms: each series arm is Z0 times (K minus one) divided by (K plus one), and the shunt arm is Z0 times twice K divided by (K squared minus one). At six decibels in fifty ohms K is 1.995262, so a pi pad needs 37.352 ohms in series and 150.476 ohms at each end, while a T pad needs 16.619 ohms in each series arm and 66.931 ohms in the shunt arm. The page also picks the nearest 1% E96 value in each decade by relative error, then recomputes the loss of that fitted combination from its chain matrix and reports the input match as a return loss, so the cost of rounding to real parts is visible before the circuit is built; a fitted build that matches poorly is reported with a low return loss rather than hidden. Attenuation is limited to 0.1 to 40 decibels and the system impedance to 5 to 1000 ohms; text, exponent notation, zero, negative values, out of range values and an unknown topology are refused with the field named. The values assume an ideal resistive network terminated in Z0 at both ports: component tolerance drift, lead inductance, stray capacitance, power dissipation and the distributed behaviour of the layout at high frequency are not modelled, and the page stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

sources.title: Attenuator design practice: a matched pi attenuator is a series arm between two shunt arms whose values follow from the voltage ratio K = 10^(dB/20).
Attenuator design practice: a matched T attenuator is a shunt arm between two series arms, derived from the same voltage ratio.
IEC 60063 preferred values: the E96 series is the 1% resistor grid, and the nearest value in each decade is chosen by relative error.

tools.name: Basketball Possessions & Efficiency Calculator
tools.description: Estimate a team's possessions from its box score — field goal attempts, free throw attempts, offensive rebounds and turnovers — then get points per possession, offensive rating, pace per 48 minutes and turnover rate.
tools.method: A box score does not record possessions directly, so they are estimated from the events that end one. Field goal attempts each end a possession, and offensive rebounds are subtracted because a put-back keeps the same possession alive. Turnovers are added. Free throw attempts count as 0.44 of a possession on average: a single free throw ends a possession when missed, but the last of two or three is often made and the resulting rebound is usually a dead-ball team rebound, so a pair of free throws is worth about 0.88 possessions rather than two. The estimate is FGA + 0.44*FTA - OREB + TOV. Points per possession is points divided by that estimate, offensive rating is the same figure per 100 possessions, pace rescales possessions to a 48-minute game, and turnover rate is turnovers divided by field goal attempts plus 0.44 times free throw attempts plus turnovers. A line of 105 points on 85 field goal attempts, 25 free throw attempts, 10 offensive rebounds and 14 turnovers gives 85 + 11 - 10 + 14 = 100 possessions, 1.05 points per possession, an offensive rating of 105.0, a pace of 100 over 48 minutes and a turnover rate of 12.7 percent; the same arithmetic on 78 points, 60 attempts, 20 free throws, 8 offensive rebounds and 12 turnovers over 40 minutes gives 72.8 possessions, 1.071 points per possession, an offensive rating of 107.1, a pace of 87.4 and a turnover rate of 14.9 percent. Counts are whole numbers limited to a plausible box-score range (points 0 to 250, field goal attempts 1 to 150, free throw attempts 0 to 100, offensive rebounds and turnovers 0 to 60, game length 1 to 60 minutes); text, decimals, negatives, exponent notation, out-of-range values and counts that would imply zero or negative possessions are refused with the field named. This is the standard box-score estimator, not an official count: it does not separate team from individual rebounds, ignores possessions that end without a shot, free throw or turnover, and treats the 0.44 factor as constant. The page calculates locally and stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

sources.title: Basketball analytics glossary: possessions are estimated as FGA + 0.44*FTA - OREB + TOV, the standard box-score approximation of Dean Oliver.

tools.name: Video Rendition Ladder Planner
tools.description: Plan an adaptive bitrate ladder from a top resolution, frame rate and bits-per-pixel target, with each rung's resolution, bitrate, storage per hour and peak egress.
tools.method: Each rung is sized from the previous one: the height is multiplied by the chosen step ratio (three quarters, two thirds or one half) and rounded to the nearest even pixel, and the width follows the top frame's aspect ratio, also rounded to even pixels, because encoders and hardware scalers expect even dimensions. The video bitrate is the target bits per pixel per frame multiplied by width x height x frame rate, rounded to a whole kilobit per second, and the rung's audio bitrate is added to give the total muxed bitrate. Storage per minute is total bitrate x 60 / 8 in decimal megabytes, storage per hour is total bitrate x 3600 / 8 in decimal gigabytes, and peak egress is the viewer count times the top rung's total bitrate. The ladder stops before a rung would fall below 64 pixels in either direction or repeat the previous height, so a small top frame can produce fewer rungs than requested; that case is reported rather than invented. The default 1920x1080, 30 fps, 0.08 bits per pixel ladder with 128 kbps audio gives 1920x1080 at 4,977 kbps video and 5,105 kbps total, then 1280x720 at 2,212 and 2,340 kbps, 854x480 at 984 and 1,112 kbps, and 568x320 at 436 and 564 kbps: 9,121 kbps across the ladder, 4.10 GB for an hour of every rung, and 510.50 Mbps of peak egress for 100 viewers on the top rung. Bits per pixel is only a planning heuristic; codec, preset, scene complexity, keyframe density and per-title tuning all change the real figure, and audio is assumed to be the same on every rung. Values are whole numbers of pixels, frames per second, kilobits per second and viewers, with bits per pixel limited to three decimal places between 0.005 and 1, and text, negatives, exponent notation and out-of-range values are refused with the field named. The page calculates locally and stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

tools.name: Multicam Sync Planner
tools.description: Align two to six camera angles on one sync mark: each angle's head and tail trim, the shared window every clip covers, and the angle that limits either end.
tools.method: Each angle is described by three SMPTE timecodes at the chosen rate: the clip in, the sync mark (a clap, flash or beep) and the clip out. Timecodes are compared as whole frame counts, so 24, 25, 30, 50 and 60 fps count straight through while 23.976, 29.97 and 59.94 use their exact 30000/1001-style rates for the seconds column. Drop-frame counting skips two frame numbers (four at 59.94) at every minute boundary except each tenth, which is why 00:01:00:00 has no meaning at 29.97 and is refused rather than shifted, and why a drop minute opens at 00:01:00:02 or 00:01:00:04. Every mark is aligned to sequence zero, so an angle's head trim is its mark minus its clip in and its tail trim is its clip out minus its mark. The shared window opens at the latest of those start offsets and closes at the earliest of the end offsets: the angle that opens latest limits the head and the angle that closes soonest limits the tail, and two angles that both begin or end exactly at their marks leave no shared frames, which is reported instead of a zero-length plan. The default three-angle 29.97 drop-frame example has A from 09:59:40:00 to 10:01:15:00 with its mark at 10:00:00:00, B from 14:22:58:00 to 14:24:05:00 with its mark at 14:23:11:07, and C from 01:04:52:24 to 01:06:10:00 with its mark at 01:05:00:12: head trims of 00:00:20:00, 00:00:13:05 and 00:00:07:16, tail trims of 00:01:15:00, 00:00:53:21 and 00:01:09:18, a shared window of 00:01:01:09 (1,837 frames, 61.29 s) that C limits at the head and B at the tail, and 00:03:59:02 of footage across the three clips. Seconds divide the exact frame count by the true rate, so they run a fraction past the timecode labels at 29.97. Names are limited to 24 characters, two to six angles are accepted, frames must sit inside their rate's range, and the mark must fall inside its clip; each refusal names the field and camera. Timecode labels are arithmetic only: camera clocks, genlock, drift and audio offset are not modelled, so marks are still worth checking on a slate or waveform. The page calculates locally and stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

tools.name: Sourdough Starter Planner
tools.description: Build a levain to an exact weight and hydration from your seed starter: the seed to keep, the flour and water to add, the feed ratio and the starter left in the jar.
tools.method: Every part of seed is split by its own hydration: a seed at hs% is hs/(100+hs) water and 100/(100+hs) flour, so a wetter seed carries water into the levain. With p parts of added flour per part of seed, the added-water parts q that reach a target hydration H must satisfy (q + alpha)/(p + 1 - alpha) = H/100, so q = H/100*(p + 1 - alpha) - alpha; one part of seed plus its flour and water weighs 1 + p + q, and the seed needed is the levain target divided by that. The default example builds 300 g of 100% levain from a 100% seed at 5 flour parts: 27.27 g of seed, 136.36 g of flour and 136.36 g of water, 150 g of total flour and 150 g of total water (the seed brings 13.64 g of each), a 1 : 5 : 5 feed, and 122.73 g left from a 150 g jar. When the seed sits at the same hydration as the target, q equals p*H/100, which is why a 1:5 feed at 100% reads 1 : 5 : 5. A seed wetter than the target can leave no water to add at a low flour ratio; that case is refused rather than shown as a negative weight. Inputs are limited to 1-20,000 g, 50-300% hydration for both the target and the seed, and 0.5-25 flour parts, with starter on hand optional and required to cover the seed. Fermentation mass loss, evaporation and temperature are not modelled, so the weights are the mix as built, and the page stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

sources.title: A sourdough starter is a flour-and-water culture kept by regular feeding; its hydration is the water weight as a percentage of the flour weight.

tools.name: Tonearm Alignment Calculator
tools.description: Check a turntable arm's geometry: the overhang, the two null points where the cartridge is tangent, and the tracking error at the inner groove, between the nulls and at the outer edge.
tools.method: The stylus rides a circle of radius r around the spindle while the arm pivots a distance d away, so with an effective length L the angle at the stylus between the arm and the radius is beta, where cos(beta) = (r^2 + L^2 - d^2) / (2 r L). The cartridge is tangent only when beta = 90 - offset, so the null radii solve r^2 - 2 L sin(offset) r + (L^2 - d^2) = 0 and their product is always L^2 - d^2: nulls = L sin(offset) +/- sqrt(L^2 sin^2(offset) - (L^2 - d^2)). Tracking error is offset - (90 - beta) in degrees: zero at both nulls, positive between them where the fixed offset exceeds what the groove needs, negative outside them, and its positive peak sits at sqrt(L^2 - d^2). The smallest offset that reaches a null anywhere is asin(sqrt(L^2 - d^2) / L), which is refused below rather than reported as zero error; overhang is L - d. The default 230 mm arm mounted 211.5 mm from the spindle at 23.5 degrees has 18.5 mm of overhang, nulls at 76.11 and 107.31 mm, -1.68 degrees at the 60.325 mm inner groove, -2.54 degrees at the 146.05 mm outer edge and a 0.36 degree peak at 90.38 mm, so its worst error is 2.54 degrees at the outer edge. The model is static geometry only: the arm is taken as straight, the stylus exactly at the effective length and the offset angle as stated; stylus shape, wear, anti-skate, VTA and record eccentricity are not modelled and no listening judgement is implied.

sources.title: A pivoted tonearm is tangent to a groove only at two radii; their product is the arm's effective length squared minus its mounting distance squared.
Tracking error is the angle between the cantilever and the groove tangent, signed positive when the cantilever toes toward the record edge.

tools.name: LVM Extent Calculator
tools.description: Plan an LVM volume group: the physical extents each disk contributes after its metadata area, the space a logical volume rounds up to, and what stays free.
tools.method: Each physical volume is one disk minus its metadata area, divided into fixed-size physical extents: extents per disk is floor((disk GiB x 1024 - metadata MiB) / extent MiB), and whatever is left after the last whole extent - the metadata area plus up to one extent of tail slack - is unusable. The volume group is that count multiplied by the number of disks, so its size is extents x extent size; an extent below the metadata area or a disk smaller than one extent is refused rather than reported as zero capacity. A logical volume is allocated a whole number of extents, so its allocation is ceil(requested MiB / extent) x extent, the rounding waste is the difference, the free space left is the group minus that allocation, and a request larger than the group is refused with the largest size it could take. Four 1000 GiB disks with a 1 MiB metadata area and 4 MiB extents give 255,999 extents each and 1,023,996 in the group (4,095,984 MiB, 3,999.984 GiB, 99.9996% of the raw 4000 GiB); a 3000 GiB logical volume takes 768,000 whole extents and leaves 255,996 free (999.984 GiB). Sizes are binary GiB and MiB as LVM reports them, values are rounded to three decimals, and text, negatives, exponent notation, fractional extent sizes or disk counts and out-of-range values are refused with the field named. Thin pools, snapshots, mirrors, stripes, PV labels and any metadata beyond the single field are not modelled, and the page calculates locally without touching a disk or sending anything anywhere.

sources.title: LVM physical volumes are divided into equal-sized extents, and volume groups and logical volumes are composed of those extents.
A logical volume occupies a whole number of extents, so its usable size is the requested size rounded up to the next extent boundary.

tools.name: Pleat Calculator
tools.description: Plan knife, box or inverted pleats from the pleat count, depth and spacing: the fabric needed, the pleated width, the fabric folded away, the fullness ratio and the strips to cut.
tools.method: A knife pleat folds once, so one pleat eats twice its depth and shows one depth of fabric; a box pleat and an inverted pleat fold twice, so one pleat eats four times its depth and shows two. The flat space between pleats is counted once per pleat. The fabric a pleat takes is the spacing plus twice the depth for a knife pleat and the spacing plus four times the depth for a box or inverted pleat, so twelve knife pleats one inch deep with two inches between them take four inches each, forty eight inches in total. The pleated width is the pleat count times what each pleat shows, which is three inches each in the same example, thirty six inches. The folded-away figure is the difference between the two and is the fabric that disappears into the folds. The fullness ratio is the fabric divided by the pleated width, so a ratio of two to one means the panel is cut twice its finished width. Strips are counted by dividing the fabric by the usable fabric width and rounding up, so the forty eight inch pleat run on forty four inch fabric is two strips of twenty four inches; an exact fit stays one strip. Inches and centimetres are both supported; the arithmetic is unit-free and the page also shows the fabric converted at exactly 2.54 centimetres to the inch. Inputs are limited to 1 to 200 whole pleats, a depth of 0.1 to 24 inches (0.25 to 60 centimetres), a spacing of 0 to 24 inches (0 to 60 centimetres) and a usable width of 1 to 120 inches (2.5 to 305 centimetres); text, negative numbers, exponent notation, empty fields and out of range values are refused with the field named. The page assumes the pleats run across one flat panel with even spacing and equal depth, and does not model pattern repeat, nap or directional print, seam allowances, a heading or waistband, pleats that taper or meet at a seam, or the pressing and stitching order; it stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

sources.title: Sewing and pattern-drafting practice: a knife pleat uses twice its depth of fabric and shows one depth, while a box or inverted pleat uses four times its depth because it folds to both sides.
Dressmaking fullness guidance: a pleated panel is cut roughly one and a half to three times its finished width, depending on the pleat depth and the space left between pleats.
Sewing construction practice: pleats are marked and pressed before stitching, and a pleat run wider than the fabric is cut in strips joined at a seam.

tools.name: Tournament Bracket Generator
tools.description: Seed a single-elimination bracket for 2 to 32 teams: standard seeding or entry order, byes for the top seeds, and winners clicked through from the first round to the final.
tools.method: Single elimination in a power-of-two bracket. The bracket is rounded up to the next power of two, so a 12-team field is drawn as a 16-place bracket and the four spare places become byes; a bracket with n teams always plays n-1 matches over log2(size) rounds. Standard seeding builds the slot order recursively: the order starts as 1, 2, and each doubling appends 2m+1 minus each existing seed, which gives 1 v 8, 4 v 5, 2 v 7, 3 v 6 for eight places, so every first-round pair sums to one more than the bracket size and seeds 1 and 2 land in opposite halves and can meet only in the final. Seeds above the team count become byes, so byes go to the best seeds; those matches advance their single entrant automatically and never count as played matches. Entry order instead fills the draw top to bottom in the order the teams are listed and gives the byes to the last first-round matches, one per match, so no first-round match is empty. Clicking a team records the winner of that match and fills the next round from it; clicking the recorded winner again clears the pick, and a later pick that no longer has both of its teams present is dropped rather than carried forward. Inputs are limited to 2 to 32 whole teams, names of 40 characters or fewer that must be unique ignoring case, and the two draw orders; text, fractional, negative, zero, one and out-of-range team counts, an unsupported draw order and a name count that disagrees with the team count are refused with the field named. The page stores nothing, sends nothing and makes no network requests.

sources.title: Tournament practice: a single-elimination bracket is drawn to the next power of two, with byes filling the spare places so the whole field fits.
Standard bracket seeding: each first-round pairing sums to one more than the bracket size, which keeps the top two seeds in opposite halves.
Unseeded draws are filled in entry order and byes are spread across the trailing first-round matches, so no match has two empty places.

tools.name: Yagi-Uda Antenna Element Planner
tools.description: Turn a frequency, a director count and a boom profile into a Yagi-Uda cut list: the length of every element and its position along the boom, in metres or feet.
tools.method: A Yagi-Uda is a driven element with a reflector behind it and any number of directors in front, all cut close to a half wavelength and spaced along a boom. The free-space wavelength is 299.792458 divided by the frequency in MHz. Three conventional starting families are offered, each a set of length and spacing ratios applied to that wavelength: compact (reflector 0.500, driven 0.478, first director 0.445, director taper 0.0012 per element, reflector spacing 0.10, director spacing 0.12), standard (0.495, 0.473, 0.440, 0.0015, 0.15, 0.20) and long (0.500, 0.470, 0.442, 0.0015, 0.20, 0.30). The reflector sits at 0 on the boom, the driven element one reflector spacing behind the first director, and each director a further director spacing along it, so the boom length is the reflector spacing plus the director spacing multiplied by the director count; the boom length is also reported in wavelengths because that is the figure comparable with published gain tables. Every director is shortened by the taper relative to the one before it, which keeps the lengths strictly decreasing down the boom. Frequencies are 10 to 3000 MHz, director counts are whole numbers from 0 to 20, and the three boom profiles are the only choices; blank, non-numeric, negative, out-of-range and fractional values and an unknown profile are refused with the field named rather than defaulted. Element diameter, insulated mountings, the balun, boom and mast interaction, element droop, mutual coupling and ground effects are not modelled, and no gain, front-to-back ratio or SWR is predicted: these are thin-element starting dimensions to cut slightly long and trim with an analyser. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A Yagi-Uda array is a driven dipole with a slightly longer reflector behind it and progressively shorter directors in front, spaced along a boom, and its dimensions scale with the free-space wavelength.
Practical Yagi designs are described by a boom length in wavelengths together with element length and spacing ratios; longer booms with more directors carry the higher gain.

Director lengths taper shorter toward the front of the array, and element diameter, mounting hardware and nearby conductors shift the resonant length, so published dimensions are starting points that need trimming.
The free-space wavelength in metres is 299.792458 divided by the frequency in megahertz.
