tools.name: Fiber Optic Color Code Locator
tools.description: Find a fiber's buffer tube, position and color from its number in a loose-tube cable, using the standard 12-color TIA-598 sequence, with the full color chart and repeat-group warnings.
tools.method: Loose-tube fiber cables name both buffer tubes and the fibers inside them with a repeating 12-color sequence: 1 blue, 2 orange, 3 green, 4 brown, 5 slate, 6 white, 7 red, 8 black, 9 yellow, 10 violet, 11 rose and 12 aqua. Tubes are counted from the start of the cable, so the tube is ceil(fiber / fibersPerTube) and the fiber's position in that tube is ((fiber - 1) mod fibersPerTube) + 1. The tube color is color number ((tube - 1) mod 12) + 1 and the fiber color is color number ((position - 1) mod 12) + 1. A 6-fiber tube uses only the first six colors; a 24-fiber tube repeats the 12 colors in a second pass at positions 13 to 24; tube colors repeat after tube 12. Each repeat group is marked by a tracer, stripe or binder, the exact marking varies by manufacturer, and the tool therefore reports the repeat group without naming the physical marker. Fiber numbers are whole numbers from 1 to 288, fibers per tube is 6, 12 or 24, and blank, fractional, negative and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named rather than defaulted.

sources.title: TIA-598-D, Optical Fiber Cable Color Coding: the twelve-color sequence blue, orange, green, brown, slate, white, red, black, yellow, violet, rose, aqua is applied to both fibers and buffer tubes.

Loose-tube cable construction: fibers are grouped in color-coded buffer tubes, tubes are numbered from the start of the cable, and later groups repeat the colors with a manufacturer-specific tracer or binder.

tools.name: Cross-Track Error Calculator
tools.description: Measure how far a position lies left or right of a great-circle route, with signed cross-track and along-track distance, the nearest point on the route, the distance still to run and the direct distance to the destination.
tools.method: Treat the route start A, route end B and position P as unit vectors on a sphere of mean radius 6,371 km. The route length is the central angle between A and B; identical endpoints and antipodal endpoints are refused because no single course exists. The cross-track angle is minus the arcsine of P's component along the unit normal of the A-B great circle, which is positive when P lies to the right (starboard) of the course. P is projected onto the great circle by removing that normal component, and the signed along-track angle is measured from A toward B with atan2 so that a position behind the start is negative and a position past the destination exceeds the route length. The nearest point on the route is the projection, clamped to the start when the along-track angle is negative and to the destination when it exceeds the route length; distance to the route is the central angle from P to that point. Distance still to run is the remaining route angle clamped at zero. Coordinates are decimal degrees accepted with a decimal point or comma, latitude from -90 to 90 and longitude from -180 to 180; blank, non-numeric, exponent-notation and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named. The model is spherical and ignores ellipsoidal flattening, magnetic variation, currents, leeway, rhumb-line courses and terrain, and results within half a metre of the track are reported as on track.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Great-circle navigation: cross-track distance is the angular distance from a point to a great-circle path, and along-track distance is measured from the start of the path toward the destination.

Ed Williams, Aviation Formulary: the spherical cross-track formula asin(sin(d13) sin(theta13 - theta12)) and the along-track formula acos(cos(d13) / cos(xtd)), with positive cross-track conventionally to starboard.
NOAA Chart No. 1 and nautical navigation practice: cross-track error is the perpendicular offset between a vessel's position and its intended track, reported to port or starboard of the course.

tools.name: Buttercream Quantity Calculator
tools.description: Estimate the buttercream or frosting one cake needs from its shape, size and coat thickness, including a crumb coat, in US cups, millilitres and grams.
tools.method: Model the cake as a prism with a flat top and vertical sides: a round cake as a cylinder with side area pi times diameter times height plus top area pi times diameter squared over four, a square cake as four times the side length times height plus the side length squared, and a rectangular sheet cake as twice the length plus width times height plus length times width. The base, filling layers and board are excluded. Frosted area is multiplied by the finish-coat thickness converted from millimetres to centimetres to give the finish-coat volume in millilitres, because one cubic centimetre is one millilitre. An optional crumb coat adds a second layer of 2 mm over the same area. Total volume is converted to weight at a density of 1.05 grams per millilitre and to US cups at 236.5882365 millilitres per cup. Dimensions are decimal centimetres and thickness decimal millimetres, accepted with a decimal point or comma; blank, non-numeric, exponent-notation and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named. The model assumes sharp edges and one identically frosted tier, and excludes piping, borders, filling, levelling trims and bowl losses.

sources.title: Standard geometry of a cylinder and a rectangular prism: lateral area plus one end area gives the frosted surface of a single-tier cake.
Cake-decorating practice: a crumb coat is a thin sealing layer applied before the finish coat, typically about 2 mm over the same surface.
US customary volume definition: one US cup is 236.5882365 millilitres, and icing density is around 1.05 grams per millilitre for American buttercream.

tools.name: Fretboard Note Finder
tools.description: Map every note on a guitar, bass, ukulele or mandolin fretboard for any tuning, capo position and fret range, and highlight where a chosen note appears.
tools.method: Each open string is read as a note name, optional accidental and octave and converted to a MIDI note number. A capo adds its fret number to every open string, and each displayed fret adds one semitone, so fret numbers are counted from the capo and fret 0 is the capo itself. Pitch classes come from a twelve-name table with sharps or flats selected by the spelling setting, and the octave is the MIDI number divided by twelve, rounded down, minus one. Positions for the selected note are every string and fret whose pitch class matches, reported per string in tuning order. Presets cover standard, drop D, DADGAD, open G and 7-string guitar, 4- and 5-string bass, high-G and low-G ukulele and mandolin; a custom tuning accepts one to eight strings written top row first, each with a note and octave. The fret count is a whole number from 1 to 24 and the capo from 0 to 12, and any tuning, capo and fret combination that would exceed MIDI note 127 is refused.

sources.title: Standard guitar tuning is E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4 from the lowest string to the highest, with twelve equal semitones per octave.
Scientific pitch notation names middle C as C4, which is MIDI note 60; each semitone is one MIDI note number.
A capo clamps across the fingerboard at a chosen fret and raises every open string by that many semitones, so shapes are counted relative to the capo.

tools.name: systemd tmpfiles.d Entry Builder
tools.description: Compose one systemd tmpfiles.d line that creates, adjusts, cleans, removes or symlinks a path, with strict field rules, the exact directive, its file name and the create and clean commands.
tools.method: One tmpfiles.d directive is composed as seven space-separated fields - type, path, mode, user, group, age and argument - with a dash for an unset field and the argument written only for L. Seven types are offered: d creates a directory, e adjusts an existing directory, f creates or truncates a file, q creates a directory with a project quota, r removes a path or glob when cleaning, x excludes matching paths from cleanup and L creates a symlink. Creation types (d, e, f, q, L) produce a systemd-tmpfiles --create command and cleanup types (d, e, q, r, x) produce a --clean command, so d, e and q get both. Field applicability is enforced rather than ignored: MODE is accepted only for d, e, f and q; USER and GROUP for every type except r and x; AGE only for d, e, q, r and x; and the argument only for L, where it is required. The path must be absolute, below /, free of whitespace, quotes, backslashes, //, . and .. segments and a trailing slash, at most 4096 characters, and a glob is accepted only for r and x. MODE takes three or four octal digits, is padded to four, and is capped at 1777 so only the sticky bit can be set above 0777. A user or group is a name that starts with a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens, or a numeric id up to 4294967294; numeric ids are rewritten without leading zeros. AGE is a systemd time span: a bare number of seconds, zero, or one or more number-unit pairs using us, ms, s, min, m, h, d, w, M and y, where M is a 30.4375-day month and y a 365.25-day year. The page reports the span in days, hours, minutes, seconds or milliseconds, so 1M reads as 30.44 days and 1h30min as 1.5 hours. The directive length, field count, file name and /etc/tmpfiles.d path are derived from the entry; the file name comes from the last path segment, drops glob characters, keeps ASCII letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens, is lowercased and capped at 40 characters. Warnings cover a mode left at the created-directory default of 0755 or the file default of 0644, both owner fields left at root, a removal or exclusion with no age, an age-cleaned path outside /tmp, /var/tmp and /run, and a relative symlink target. The page composes text only: it does not read or modify the filesystem and makes no network requests.

sources.title: tmpfiles.d(5): the seven fields are type, path, mode, user, group, age and argument; d, e, f, q, r, x and L are documented types, and files in /etc/tmpfiles.d override same-named files in /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d.
systemd-tmpfiles(8): --create creates and adjusts entries while --clean removes files older than an entry's age.
systemd.time(7): time spans combine number and unit pairs such as 30d, 12h and 1h30min.

tools.name: Basket Weaving Reed Calculator
tools.description: Estimate the round reed a woven basket needs from its base, wall height, rim and reed width: rows of weavers, weft length around a flared wall, stake lengths and a three-rod rim, in metres and feet.
tools.method: Plan a round basket as rows of weavers climbing a wall that interpolates linearly between the base and rim diameters. Rows are the wall height divided by the reed width, rounded to the nearest whole row, because each row of weavers advances the weave by about one reed width; the rounded height is reported so a wall that lands short of the request is visible. Each row takes the diameter at its mid-height, base plus the rim-minus-base difference times the row centre fraction, and its weft length is pi times that diameter times one plus the weave slack percentage, which pays for going over and under the stakes. The sum over all rows equals pi times the slack factor times the rows times the mean of the base and rim diameters, evaluated with an explicit per-row loop. Stake length is the slanted wall length, the square root of the wall height squared plus half the rim-minus-base difference squared, plus four reed widths past the rim for the border. Stake reed is the stake count times that length. The rim figure covers a three-rod wale: three weavers, each once around the rim, at pi times the rim diameter times the slack factor. Totals are converted to metres at 1000 mm and to feet at 304.8 mm per foot. Stakes must be an even whole number from 6 to 64 so pairs cross at the base, and the plan is refused when the stakes would sit closer than twice the reed width at the base, naming the measured spacing. Inputs are decimal millimetres and percent; blank, non-numeric, exponent, negative, multiple-decimal-point and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named. Warnings cover fewer than three rows, a wall leaning more than 40 degrees from vertical, a rounded wall that differs from the requested height by more than 12 percent, rim spacing growing more than 60 percent, and stakes tighter than three reed widths. The page computes text only, stores nothing and makes no network requests.

sources.title: Basket weaving practice: a three-rod wale passes three weavers around the rim, and stakes are turned down past the rim to form the border.
Round reed is sold by diameter, so a #3 reed wove as a weaver advances the wall by about 3 mm per row.
Right-triangle geometry: the slanted wall length is the hypotenuse of the wall height and half the difference between the rim and base diameters.

tools.name: Antenna Factor Calculator
tools.description: Convert an antenna's gain and frequency into its 50-ohm antenna factor in dB/m, then turn a measured received level into field strength in dBµV/m and volts per metre.

sources.title: Antenna factor is the ratio of the incident electric field strength to the voltage induced at the antenna terminals, usually quoted in dB/m for a 50-ohm system.
For a 50-ohm antenna in the far field, AF(dB/m) = 20 log10(9.73 / lambda) - G(dBi), with lambda in metres and the constant derived from 4*pi*sqrt(30/50).
Field strength in dBµV/m is the received level in dBµV plus the antenna factor in dB/m; 0 dBµV is 1 µV and 0 dBµV/m is 1 µV/m.

tools.name: VLAN ID Planner
tools.description: Allocate free 802.1Q VLAN IDs in a range, skipping the IDs the standard reserves and those already in use, and see the tag value for each VLAN.
tools.method: An 802.1Q VLAN identifier is 12 bits, so IDs run from 1 to 4094: 0 and 4095 are reserved for priority-tagged frames, and 1002 to 1005 are reserved for legacy Token Ring and FDDI VLANs. The planner works in the inclusive range you enter, between 1 and 4094. It counts the usable IDs as the range width minus any of 1002 to 1005 that fall inside it, subtracts the distinct in-use IDs that are inside the range and not reserved, and refuses the plan when fewer IDs are free than you asked for. The in-use field accepts space- or comma-separated single IDs and inclusive ranges such as 20 or 30-39; reversed ranges, non-numeric tokens and IDs above 4095 are refused, and IDs outside the range or in the reserved block are counted as ignored. The plan takes the lowest free IDs in ascending order, up to 32 of them, so it is contiguous whenever the free space allows; the number of contiguous blocks the allocation spans and the largest remaining free block are reported so a fragmented result is visible. Each allocated ID is also shown as a 16-bit tag control field, PCP x 8192 + DEI x 4096 + VLAN ID, with the priority code point and drop-eligible bit you choose, which is the value you would match in a packet capture or a switch debug trace. Limits: 1 to 32 VLANs per plan, at most 128 in-use entries or ranges, whole-number IDs only. The planner does not read any switch configuration, does not know which VLANs exist on trunk or access ports, and does not model provider-reserved or private VLAN ranges, so the result is a suggestion to check before applying. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: IEEE 802.1Q carries a 12-bit VLAN identifier: 0 and 4095 are reserved, leaving 1 to 4094 as usable VLAN IDs.
VLAN IDs 1002 to 1005 are reserved for legacy Token Ring and FDDI VLANs and are not available for ordinary Ethernet VLANs.
The tag control information field packs a 3-bit priority code point, a drop-eligible indicator and the 12-bit VLAN ID, so its value is PCP x 8192 + DEI x 4096 + VLAN ID.
VLAN 1 is the default VLAN on most switches and is normally carried untagged on access ports.

tools.name: ECEF Coordinate Converter
tools.description: Convert WGS84 geodetic latitude, longitude and ellipsoid height to Earth-Centered, Earth-Fixed X, Y and Z metres, or convert ECEF coordinates back to a geodetic position.
tools.method: Earth-Centered, Earth-Fixed (ECEF) coordinates are Cartesian metres: X runs through the equator and prime meridian, Y through the equator at 90 degrees east, and Z through the north pole. The WGS84 ellipsoid uses a semi-major axis of 6378137 m and a flattening of 1/298.257223563, giving a semi-minor axis of 6356752.314245 m and a first eccentricity squared of 0.006694379990141316. Geodetic to ECEF uses N = a / sqrt(1 - e2 sin^2(lat)), X = (N + h) cos(lat) cos(lon), Y = (N + h) cos(lat) sin(lon) and Z = (N (1 - e2) + h) sin(lat), with h the ellipsoid height in metres. ECEF to geodetic takes p = sqrt(X^2 + Y^2), longitude = atan2(Y, X), and solves for the geodetic latitude with a fixed-point iteration started at atan2(Z, p (1 - e2)); the height is p / cos(lat) - N, or z / sin(lat) - N (1 - e2) close to the poles. An exact pole has no longitude, so it is reported as 0 degrees with the height |Z| - b, and an all-zero ECEF position is refused because the geodetic position is undefined at the Earth's centre. The geocentric latitude atan2(Z, p) is reported beside the geodetic latitude; the two differ by up to about 0.19 degrees at mid-latitudes. Angles and ECEF metres accept at most six and nine decimals respectively, ellipsoid height at most three, and every field is range-checked. The converter does not transform between datums, apply a geoid model, or convert orthometric height above sea level, and it cannot replace authoritative survey or navigation data. tools.name: .gitignore Pattern Tester
tools.description: Test whether relative paths are ignored by a .gitignore: paste the patterns and paths to see every verdict with the exact rule and line that decides it, following Git's last-match-wins order, slash anchoring, directory-only rules, negation and parent-directory exclusion. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Each nonblank line is a pattern, except lines whose first character is #, which are comments. Trailing spaces are dropped unless escaped with a backslash, and a leading ! negates the pattern. A pattern with a slash anywhere except a trailing one is anchored to the .gitignore directory; a pattern without a slash matches a path component at any depth. A trailing slash restricts the pattern to directories, and a pattern that matches a directory also excludes everything below it. Wildcards never cross a slash: * matches any run of characters except /, ? matches one such character, and [...] is a character class supporting ranges and ! or ^ negation. A leading **/ matches at any depth, a trailing /** matches everything inside the directory, and /**/ matches zero or more directories; consecutive asterisks anywhere else behave like a single *. The last matching pattern decides the outcome, so a later ! rule re-includes a path; however a path is still ignored when any parent directory is excluded, because the parent-exclusion rule prevents re-inclusion below it. Paths are interpreted relative to the .gitignore directory: a leading slash or ./ is removed, repeated slashes collapse, .. segments are refused, and a trailing slash marks the path as a directory. Limits are 500 pattern lines and 500 paths of at most 1,000 characters each within 64 KiB of input per box. The tester reads text only: it does not open a repository, run Git, resolve nested .gitignore files, apply .git/info/exclude or core.excludesFile, or consider tracked files.

tools.name: Ice Cream Mix Calculator
tools.description: Split an ice cream base into cream, milk and sugar for a chosen butterfat and sugar percentage, from the batch weight and the fat content of the cream and milk.
tools.method: Fat and sugar are balanced by weight against the finished mix, which is treated as cream, milk and sugar only. Sugar grams are the batch weight times the sugar target over 100, and the rest of the batch is dairy. The cream weight c is the one that makes the fat add up: c times the cream fat percentage plus the remaining dairy times the milk fat percentage must equal the batch times the butterfat target, so c = (batch x fat - milkFat x dairy) / (creamFat - milkFat) with every percentage taken as a fraction. Milk is the rest of the dairy, and the fat each ingredient carries is reported so the two contributions can be checked against the target. Defaults are a 1,000 g base at 12 percent butterfat and 16 percent sugar from 36 percent cream and 3.5 percent whole milk; in the United States the name ice cream requires at least 10 percent milk fat, and premium recipes commonly sit at 12 to 16. Batch weights are accepted from 100 to 20,000 g, the butterfat target from 1 to 30 percent, sugar from 5 to 30 percent, cream fat from 20 to 50 percent and milk fat from 0 to 15 percent, and decimal commas are accepted. The target must lie strictly between the milk fat and the cream fat, cream fat must exceed milk fat, and a combination whose cream alone would outweigh the dairy - a high fat target with a lot of sugar - is refused rather than returning a negative milk weight. Weights are rounded to 0.1 g and percentages to 0.1, so the rounded parts can miss the batch by a tenth. Milk solids other than fat, egg yolk, stabilisers, flavourings and water lost to cooking are not modelled, and nothing is claimed about freezing point, overrun, texture or food safety. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Pitch-Class Set Analyzer
tools.description: Reduce a group of notes to its set class: normal order, Rahn prime form, Forte number, interval vector, complement and the transpositions or inversions that map the set onto itself.
tools.method: Pitch classes are read from note names with any number of sharps or flats, or from the integers 0 to 11, and duplicates are counted once; each name is reduced modulo 12 so C♯ and D♭ are the same class. Normal order takes each of the rotations of the ascending set, adds 12 to the wrapped notes, keeps the rotations with the smallest span, and among those keeps the one that is smallest when its intervals are compared from the top note downwards (Rahn). Prime form transposes the normal order to begin on 0, does the same for the inversion of the set, and keeps the lower of the two sequences, so C major and C minor both reduce to 0, 3, 7. The Forte number is a lookup of that prime form in the published table of all 223 set classes, with Z marking pairs that share an interval vector without being transpositions or inversions of each other. The interval vector counts, for interval classes 1 to 6, how many pairs of the set are that far apart, taking the shorter way round the octave. Symmetry lists every n for which transposing the set by n, or inverting it about n, leaves it unchanged. The complement is the set of pitch classes not in the input, reported with its own prime form and Forte number. The page was checked against the published prime form and interval vector of all 223 set classes, and a second implementation in Python agrees with it over a hundred inputs. Register, voicing and doubling are ignored, and nothing is claimed about consonance, tonality or suitability.

tools.name: Syslog Priority Decoder
tools.description: Decode a syslog priority such as <34> into its facility, severity and journalctl filter, build a priority from a pair such as auth.crit or local0.info, and see the arithmetic behind every value from 0 to 191.
tools.method: Input is read in the browser and nothing is executed, stored or sent. A leading angle-bracket priority is taken from the start of the text, so both an RFC 5424 line such as <134>1 2026-11-09T05:00:00Z host app - - - started and an older BSD line such as <34>Nov 9 05:00:00 host app: started decode from the same token; the rest of the line is ignored. A bare run of digits is read as a priority, a value with a leading zero is refused because RFC 5424 writes the priority without padding, and anything outside 0 to 191 is refused with the range in the message. A pair is split on a single dot: the facility part is matched case-insensitively against the 24 RFC 5424 facility keywords (kern to local7, with kernel as an alias for kern and a numeric 0 to 23 also accepted), and the severity part against the eight keywords emerg to debug, also accepting panic or emergency for emerg, critical for crit, error for err, warn for warning and informational for info, or a numeric 0 to 7. The priority is facility times 8 plus severity, and the result reports the facility code and description, the severity code, keyword, name and meaning, the equivalent journalctl --priority keyword, and the arithmetic that produced the number. The severity and facility tables below the form are rendered from the same data, and each common-priority shortcut decodes a pair through the same path.

tools.name: Bookbinding Case Calculator
tools.description: Work out the two boards, the spine strip and the covering material for a case-bound hardcover from the text block size, the square, the board caliper, the hinge allowance and the turn-in, in millimetres or inches.
tools.method: Dimensions are worked from the trimmed text block outwards, in the chosen unit. Each board is page width plus the square minus the hinge allowance by page height plus twice the square, so the board overhangs the fore edge by the square but stops short of the joint by the hinge allowance. The spine strip spans the text block thickness plus the hinge allowance on each side, plus one board thickness of lap onto each board. The assembled case is twice the board width plus the spine strip, which reduces to twice the page width plus twice the square plus the text block thickness plus twice the board thickness. The covering material adds the turn-in on all four edges, so its width is the case width plus twice the turn-in and its height is the case height plus twice the turn-in. Area is that rectangle, reported in square metres at one million square millimetres and in square feet at 92,903.04 square millimetres per square foot. Values are parsed from plain decimal text and refused when blank, negative, written with an exponent or more than one decimal point, or outside the bounds for the selected unit: page 40 to 400 mm, block 1 to 120 mm thick, square 0 to 20 mm, board 0.5 to 6 mm, hinge 0 to 20 mm and turn-in 5 to 40 mm, with separate inch bounds. Lengths are reported to two decimals, square metres to six and square feet to four. The page computes in the browser, stores nothing and makes no network requests.

tools.name: Baseball Pitching Stats Calculator
tools.description: Turn a pitching line into ERA, WHIP, strikeouts, walks and home runs per nine innings, plus a strikeout-to-walk ratio.
tools.method: Innings pitched are entered in baseball notation, where .1 is one out and .2 is two outs, so 6.2 means 6 2/3 innings; the page converts the entry to a whole number of outs (whole innings x 3 plus the fraction digit) and calculates from that, so no float fraction is rounded twice. Every rate is rounded half away from zero to two decimals, which is the precision the page displays. The tool models one pitcher's line as entered: it does not separate inherited runners, unearned runs, park or league effects, opponent strength or era, and it makes no projection. tools.name: Polarization Mismatch Loss Calculator
tools.description: Find the mismatch loss between two linearly polarized antennas, or the cross-polar discrimination and linear loss of a circular antenna from its axial ratio.
tools.method: Linear to linear: the polarization loss factor is cos^2(theta), where theta is the tilt between the two linear polarization axes in degrees, accepted from 0 to 90 inclusive (0 aligned, 90 orthogonal). The voltage coupling is cos(theta), the mismatch loss is -10 log10(PLF) dB, and the rejection applied to a signal polarized in the orthogonal plane is -10 log10(sin^2(theta)) dB. At 90 degrees no wanted signal couples, so the mismatch loss is reported as infinite; at 0 degrees the orthogonal rejection is infinite. Linear to circular: the axial ratio AR in dB, accepted from 0 to 40, gives the voltage ratio r = 10^(AR/20); the cross-polar discrimination is 20 log10((r+1)/(r-1)) dB and is infinite for a perfect 0 dB circular antenna; the loss to a linear antenna ranges from 10 log10(1 + 1/r^2) dB, when the linear axis is aligned with the major axis of the ellipse, to 10 log10(1 + r^2) dB, when it is aligned with the minor axis, and an ideal circular wave gives the fixed 3.01 dB at both ends. Coupling fractions below 1e-10 are treated as zero, so anything beyond 100 dB of rejection is reported as infinite. Voltage ratios are rounded half up to four decimals, power ratios to four decimals and decibel values to two. The tool models polarization match alone: it ignores ground reflection, multipath, Faraday rotation along the path, cross-polar pattern lobes, the orientation of the axial-ratio ellipse and antenna efficiency, and it is not a link-budget replacement. Everything is calculated in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.description: Estimate how many Wi-Fi access points a floor needs, then sketch access points, walls, doors and multiple floors on an approximate coverage heatmap. Save the design in the browser or as local JSON.
tools.method: Capacity: the aggregate demand is the peak device count times the target throughput per device in Mbps; the usable throughput of one access point is its throughput after the headroom percentage is held back; the number of access points for capacity is the demand divided by that usable throughput, rounded up. Coverage: the floor area in square metres divided by the coverage area of one access point, rounded up. The plan takes the larger of the two counts, so a capacity-limited plan runs at 100% minus the headroom in airtime when every client asks for its full target, and a coverage-limited plan carries less load per access point. Inputs: floor area 1 to 100000 m2, devices a whole number from 1 to 100000, target throughput 0.1 to 10000 Mbps, usable throughput per AP 1 to 10000 Mbps, coverage area per AP 1 to 20000 m2, and headroom 0 to 50 percent. Throughput values are rounded half up to one decimal, counts are exact integers, and a plan never drops below one access point. The capacity model is a first-pass budget: it assumes uniform device demand and a uniform coverage cell. The optional coverage sketch stores building width and depth (2 to 100 metres), up to 6 floors, 64 access points and 200 partitions. Estimated received signal is transmit power minus the configured loss at 1 metre, 10 times the path-loss exponent times the base-10 logarithm of three-dimensional distance in metres (with a 1-metre minimum), minus 12 dB per wall, 6 dB per door, 3 dB per window and 20 dB per concrete partition crossed on the same floor, and minus the configured 0 to 40 dB for each floor crossed. Cross-floor paths omit partitions. The heatmap selects the strongest access point at each sample and reports the percentage meeting a configurable target from -90 to -40 dBm. Defaults are 20 dBm transmit power, 46 dB reference loss, exponent 3, -67 dBm target, 3-metre floor spacing and 15 dB loss per floor. This comparative model does not include antenna patterns, frequency-specific material response, reflection, interference, roaming, client capability or a site survey; measured results can differ. Capacity calculations and coverage sketches run entirely in the browser with no network access. A sketch remains in memory unless the visitor explicitly saves it in local browser storage or downloads or imports the versioned JSON design file; files are limited to 256 KiB and validated locally.

tools.name: Twilight & Golden Hour Planner
tools.description: Plan a shoot or observing session: from a date, latitude, longitude and UTC offset, get astronomical, nautical and civil twilight, sunrise and sunset, solar noon, day length, and the golden and blue hour windows.
tools.method: The sun's declination and the equation of time are computed from the NOAA solar equations for 00:00 UTC on the entered date, and local solar noon follows from the longitude and the UTC offset: noon = 720 minutes - 4 x longitude - equation of time + 60 x offset. For each event altitude the hour angle comes from cos H = (sin h0 - sin(lat) sin(decl)) / (cos(lat) cos(decl)), and the event times are noon - 4H in the morning and noon + 4H in the evening, rounded to 0.1 minutes. Sunrise and sunset use -0.833 degrees, which carries standard refraction and the solar disc, and civil, nautical and astronomical twilight use -6, -12 and -18 degrees. The blue hour is the band from 6 to 4 degrees below the horizon and the golden hour the band from 4 degrees below to 6 degrees above, so each window is bounded by the crossings at those altitudes. When the cosine falls outside -1 to 1 the sun never reaches the altitude: the tool reports that instead of a time and, for sunrise, a day length of 24 or 0 hours. Times are local clock times for the entered offset, daylight saving is not applied, and the date is the local calendar date. The equations are usually within a minute or two of a full ephemeris but ignore elevation, terrain, pressure and temperature, so treat the times as planning guidance. Everything is calculated in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Merge Conflict Resolver
tools.description: Resolve a file's Git conflict markers in the browser: each block is parsed with its ours, theirs and optional diff3 base sections, and you choose ours, theirs, both or base per conflict to get clean merged text, with malformed markers reported by line.
tools.method: Parses the file line by line and leaves every line outside a conflict block untouched. A line that starts with seven or more < plus an optional label opens a conflict; inside it the parser collects the ours section until an optional ||||||| base line (diff3 or zdiff3) or the ======= separator, collects the base section when present, then collects the theirs section until a line that starts with seven or more >. The chosen section replaces the whole block: ours, theirs, both with ours first, both reversed, the base, or the block left as it is. Marker glyphs must start the line, so a Markdown underline of ==== outside a block stays ordinary text. Malformed input is refused with its line number rather than guessed: a missing separator, an unclosed block, a second separator, a base marker after the separator, a second base marker, a theirs marker inside the ours section and nested conflicts. Line endings are preserved, including CRLF. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Metric Modulation Calculator
tools.description: Carry one pulse into a new tempo: choose the old and new note values to get the new quarter-note BPM, the tempo ratio, the beat equivalence and the shared pulse in milliseconds.
tools.method: A metric modulation keeps one note value's real duration while changing the value it is written as, so the new quarter-note tempo is the old tempo x new note value / old note value. Note values are measured in quarter notes: whole 4, dotted half 3, half 2, dotted quarter 1.5, quarter 1, dotted eighth 0.75, eighth 0.5, dotted sixteenth 0.375, sixteenth 0.25, thirty-second 0.125, half-note triplet 4/3, quarter-note triplet 2/3 and eighth-note triplet 1/3. At 120 BPM the old dotted quarter lasts 750 ms; written as the new quarter it gives 120 x 1 / 1.5 = 80 BPM, and the new quarter also lasts 750 ms. The tempo ratio and the beat equivalence are reduced to whole numbers with the greatest common divisor. Tempo must be a number from 1 to 1,000 BPM and decimal commas are accepted; a missing tempo, a non-numeric tempo, an out-of-range tempo or an unknown note value is refused by name. Results are rounded to three decimals. This is notation timing, not a performance or groove model; everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: systemd Unit Name Escaper
tools.description: Escape an absolute path or any text into a reversible systemd unit name such as var-lib-postgresql.mount, decode an escaped name back to its path or text, and see every UTF-8 escape in the result.
tools.method: Unit names are escaped reversibly. A-Z, a-z, 0-9, ':', '_' and '.' are kept, except a leading dot, which is written \x2e; a slash becomes '-'; every other character becomes one \xHH escape per UTF-8 byte, so 'café' is caf\xc3\xa9 and a literal hyphen is \x2d. Because '-' always stands for '/', the escape can be read back exactly. Path mode requires an absolute path: duplicate and trailing slashes and '.' components are removed, any '..' component is refused rather than simplified, the leading slash is dropped and the remaining components are joined with hyphens, so /var/lib/postgresql becomes var-lib-postgresql and the root path becomes a single '-'. A unit type suffix from the eleven types systemd-escape accepts (service, socket, device, mount, automount, swap, target, path, timer, slice, scope) is appended unescaped, or removed before decoding, and counts toward the limit. Decoding reads '-' as '/', decodes runs of \xHH as UTF-8 and prefixes '/' in path mode; it is stricter than systemd-escape and refuses raw characters that do not belong in an escaped name. Names are limited to 255 characters, NUL is refused, and malformed, non-UTF-8 or \x00 escapes are refused by name. The encoder was compared with systemd-escape from systemd 257 on 1,255 randomised and boundary inputs with no difference. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Microstrip Patch Antenna Designer
tools.description: Design a rectangular microstrip patch antenna from its frequency, substrate permittivity and thickness: get the patch width and resonant length, fringing extension, effective permittivity, guided wavelength and a suggested ground plane.
tools.method: Every result is a closed-form transmission-line estimate worked in millimetres. The frequency is entered in GHz and the substrate thickness in millimetres or mils (1 mil = 0.0254 mm); frequency must lie from 0.1 to 50 GHz, relative permittivity from 1.1 to 20 and thickness from 0.05 to 10 mm or 2 to 400 mil. The free-space wavelength is 299.792458 / f millimetres. Patch width is half that wavelength times sqrt(2/(er+1)), the usual TM10 choice that places the radiating edges about a half wave apart in the dielectric. The width-to-thickness ratio r = W/h feeds the effective permittivity ee = (er+1)/2 + (er-1)/2 / sqrt(1+12/r). Fringing fields extend each radiating edge by delta L = 0.412 h (ee+0.3)(r+0.264) / ((ee-0.258)(r+0.8)), and the physical resonant length is L = lambda0/(2 sqrt(ee)) - 2 delta L. Reported values round half up: millimetre lengths and wavelengths to two places, mils to whole mils, the fringing extension to three places, effective permittivity to four, the width-to-thickness ratio to four and the thickness-to-wavelength ratio to five. The guided wavelength is lambda0/sqrt(ee). A suggested ground plane adds a 6h margin on every side, giving W+12h by L+12h. Inputs that leave no positive resonant length are refused with a message, and the page warns when the width-to-thickness ratio falls below 1, when h/lambda0 exceeds 0.05 (an electrically thick substrate) or above 20 GHz. The model ignores feed inset, copper thickness, substrate loss, surface waves and mutual coupling, so the resonance must be confirmed by simulation and measurement. Everything runs locally in the browser with no storage, uploads or network requests.

tools.name: systemd-networkd .network Builder
tools.description: Write a systemd-networkd .network file for a static IPv4 address or DHCP, with prefix arithmetic, usable ranges and gateway checks shown before you install it.
tools.method: Every field is validated before any text is produced. The interface name is limited to 15 characters chosen from letters, digits, dot, underscore, colon, at sign and hyphen, the Linux limit on interface name length, and the file priority must be a whole number from 1 to 99 written as a two-digit prefix. Static mode accepts 1 to 16 IPv4 addresses written as address/prefix; each octet must be a decimal 0 to 255 without a leading zero, the prefix must be 0 to 32, and a repeated address is refused. For each address the block size is 2^(32-prefix), the network address is the address rounded down to a multiple of that size, and the broadcast address is the last address in the block; the usable count is size minus two for prefixes up to 30, two for a /31 and one for a /32, and the usable first and last addresses follow from those boundaries and are shown in a table. A gateway must be a plain IPv4 address, and it is flagged when it falls outside every configured block, when it lands on a network or broadcast address, or when it sits inside a /31 or /32 range. At most four IPv4 DNS servers and eight search domains are accepted; domains are checked label by label and limited to 253 characters, and they are lowercased. MTU is optional, an integer from 576 to 9000, and a value below the IPv6 minimum of 1280 is reported. DHCP mode writes DHCP=ipv4, ipv6 or yes with matching [DHCPv4] and [DHCPv6] sections carrying UseDNS and UseDomains; static mode writes DHCP=no, one Address line per entry, and optional Gateway, DNS, Domains, IPv6AcceptRA and MTU lines. tools.description: Keep a volleyball set score with rally scoring, win-by-two, six-player rotation, serving position, undo and change-of-ends prompts.
tools.method: FIVB rally-point state machine for one set. Every rally winner gains one point. A serving-team win leaves service and positions unchanged; a receiving-team win transfers service and rotates that team clockwise exactly once, with position 2 moving to position 1 and position 1 moving to position 6. Positions are shown from the team's own side: front row 4, 3, 2 and back row 5, 6, 1. A regular set ends at 25 or more with a two-point lead; a deciding set ends at 15 or more with a two-point lead, with no scoring cap. A change-of-ends event is emitted only when the leading score first reaches 8 in a deciding set. Undo restores the complete prior state and scoring is refused after the set. P1-P6 represent starting-lineup slots. Substitutions, libero replacements, sanctions and multi-set matches are not modelled. Names and scores remain only in page memory.

tools.name: Quilling Coil Calculator
tools.description: Estimate a tight quilling coil from its strip length, or find the strip length, approximate turns, stock strips and joins needed for a target diameter, in millimetres or inches.
tools.method: Model a tight, evenly wound strip as paper filling the annulus between the core and the finished outside diameter. With strip length L, paper caliper t, core diameter c and outside diameter D in one consistent length unit, D = sqrt(c² + 4Lt/π), or L = π(D² − c²)/(4t). Approximate turns are (D − c)/(2t). Strip width does not enter the face-diameter calculation. In target mode D must exceed c. Stock pieces per coil are ceil(L/stock length), with a 12-decimal ratio rounding guard at exact boundaries; joins per coil are one fewer, and offcut is the stock allocated to one coil minus L. Project totals multiply per-coil length and stock pieces by the matching-coil count without sharing offcuts. Decimal inputs are strict: metric caliper 0.05–1 mm, core 0–50 mm, strip 1–10000 mm, target 1–60 mm, stock 10–2000 mm; separate inch bounds are shown in the core. Matching coils are whole numbers 1–100. Results are rounded to four decimals, turns and displayed figures to two (up to three for inch display). The ideal annulus excludes tension, gaps, glue and springback. The page computes in the browser, stores nothing and makes no network requests.

tools.name: SNMP OID Codec
tools.description: Convert dotted SNMP object identifiers to ASN.1 BER value bytes or a complete TLV, and decode hex back to dotted arcs with strict SMIv2 arc, length and minimal-encoding validation.
tools.method: Runs entirely in the browser with BigInt arithmetic. Dotted OIDs are encoded as the combined first value 40×first+second followed by later arcs, each in minimal unsigned big-endian base 128. The result includes universal tag 06 and a definite minimal BER length. Decoding accepts value bytes or one complete TLV, enforces SMIv2 limits of 2–128 arcs and 0..4294967295 per arc, restricts the first arc to 0..2 and the second to 0..39 for first arcs 0 and 1, and rejects non-minimal arcs, truncated values and inconsistent TLV lengths. tools.name: Sauce Reduction Calculator
tools.description: Use a measured simmering trial to find a sauce or stock’s target volume, evaporation rate, estimated time left and concentration multiplier from a chosen reduction percentage.
tools.method: Volumes are converted to millilitres using 1 US cup = 236.5882365 mL and 1 L = 1000 mL. For starting volume Vi, current measured volume Vc, target reduction p percent and elapsed steady-simmer time e minutes, the target volume is Vf = Vi × (1 − p/100), the observed loss is Vi − Vc, and the measured average evaporation rate is r = (Vi − Vc)/e. If Vc is above Vf, liquid left to evaporate is Vc − Vf, estimated remaining time is (Vc − Vf)/r, and total trial-plus-remaining time is e plus that result. At or below Vf, remaining volume and time are zero. Actual reduction is (Vi − Vc)/Vi × 100. The approximate retained-solute concentration multiplier is Vi/Vf. Volumes are rounded to 0.1 mL, rate to 0.01 mL/min, percentages to 0.1 point, times to 0.1 minute and multiplier to 0.01 for catalog comparisons; display rounds to practical kitchen precision. Starting volume accepts 30–10000 mL, 0.03–10 L or 0.125–42 US cups; current volume must be positive and below the start, target is 1–95 percent and elapsed time is 1–1440 minutes. The time estimate deliberately uses the user’s measured trial rather than an assumed burner or pan rate. It assumes a constant rate and retained dissolved ingredients; heat, exposed surface, lid position, solids and viscosity can invalidate that assumption. It does not predict texture, flavour, saltiness or food safety.

tools.name: Crochet Flat Circle Planner
tools.description: Plan evenly increased crochet rounds, copy the stitch pattern and estimate the finished circle's diameter, circumference and edge stitch spacing from your own gauge.
tools.method: Use the traditional evenly increased flat-circle sequence: round 1 contains S stitches in the starting ring, and every later round adds S stitches. Round R therefore contains S×R stitches; the complete project works S×R×(R+1)/2 stitches including round 1. Round 2 places two stitches in every earlier stitch. From round 3 onward, each of S repeats places two stitches in the next stitch followed by one stitch in each of R−2 stitches, consuming S×(R−1) earlier stitches and producing S×R. Gauge is measured on a flat swatch over 10 cm or 4 in. The geometric model gives each round one measured round-height of radius: radius = rounds×gauge span/round gauge, diameter = 2×radius, and circumference = pi×diameter. Circumference divided by final stitches is the edge stitch pitch; gauge span divided by stitch gauge is the swatch stitch width. Their signed percentage difference is 100×(edge pitch/swatch pitch−1). Starting stitches are whole numbers 3–24, total rounds 1–40 and both gauge counts decimals 1–100; blank, negative, exponent and malformed values are refused. Dimensions and pitches are rounded half-up to four decimals and the percentage to two. The estimate assumes even flat rounds and excludes stitch type, yarn, hook, shaping stagger and drape. All computation is local; nothing is stored or requested.

tools.name: Bandpass Sampling Calculator
tools.description: Find alias-free bandpass sampling rates from signal band edges, check a proposed sample rate, and see the sampling zone and spectral inversion.
tools.method: For a real signal confined to fL through fH, bandwidth B=fH-fL and integer zone 1<=n<=floor(fH/B), the non-overlap window is 2fH/n < fs < 2fL/(n-1); zone 1 has no finite upper bound and means fs>2fH. Degenerate zero-width windows and exact boundary rates are excluded so every suggested rate has some ideal margin. The proposed rate is classified directly against all possible integer zones without enumerating a potentially large zone count. Even zones invert the sampled spectrum and odd zones preserve its orientation. Results include 2fH, the theoretical 2B floor (which is not sufficient at every band position), the lowest non-degenerate window and up to twelve lowest-rate windows plus baseband. Frequencies and sample rate use a common Hz/kHz/MHz/GHz unit and are capped at 100 GHz or 100 GS/s. The model assumes no out-of-band energy and does not account for filter transition bands, clock jitter, ADC limitations or other implementation margins.

tools.name: OSPF Path Cost Calculator
tools.description: Calculate Cisco IOS-style OSPFv2 interface metrics from reference bandwidth, add the outgoing-interface costs along a path, and identify truncation and minimum-cost collapses.
tools.method: Uses the Cisco IOS auto-cost convention rather than presenting the formula as an OSPF standard: for each outgoing interface, divide the integer reference bandwidth in Mbps by the interface bandwidth in Mbps, truncate the positive quotient to an integer, and raise results below 1 to 1. Link bandwidth is parsed as a decimal with at most six places and converted to integer micro-Mbps, so truncation at exact integer boundaries does not depend on binary floating-point rounding. A calculated per-interface cost above 65535 is refused rather than clamped because it cannot be represented by the OSPFv2 router-LSA metric field. The path cost is the sum of the individual outgoing-interface costs and may exceed 65535. Results expose raw quotients, truncation, minimum-cost application, and cases where different speeds collapse to cost 1. One to 24 links are accepted; the reference bandwidth is an integer from 1 to 4294967 Mbps and link bandwidths are from 0.000001 to 4294967 Mbps. The RFC defines directional configurable costs, not this bandwidth-derived formula. Manually configured costs, vendor-specific behavior, actual interface bandwidth settings, and the reverse direction must be verified on the target routers. All processing is browser-local.

tools.name: Great-Circle Route Densifier
tools.description: Add evenly spaced points along each leg of a latitude/longitude route, preserve every original waypoint, and copy a GeoJSON LineString with a chosen maximum step spacing.
tools.method: Accepts two through 2,000 signed decimal latitude/longitude waypoints, one pair per line, with latitude in -90 through 90 and longitude in -180 through 180. Each original leg uses its shortest great-circle arc on a sphere of radius 6,371,008.8 m. Haversine central angles determine leg distances; the number of equal steps is ceil(distance / requested spacing), with a relative 1e-12 snap at integer ratios to avoid a floating-point extra step. Intermediate points use spherical linear interpolation of Cartesian unit vectors: A=sin((1-f)delta)/sin(delta), B=sin(f delta)/sin(delta), then atan2 recovers latitude and normalized longitude. Original waypoints and consecutive duplicate points are preserved, shared leg endpoints are emitted once, and antipodal legs are refused because their shortest route is not unique. Spacing must be positive and at most 1,000 km; results above 20,000 points are refused before interpolation. The generated GeoJSON LineString uses longitude/latitude order and six-decimal coordinates. Distances and the longest generated step are computed before that display rounding. This spherical model is for plotting and data preparation, not navigation or surveying. All processing is browser-local.

tools.name: Z85 Encoder / Decoder
tools.description: Encode hexadecimal bytes to ZeroMQ Z85 or decode Z85 back to hexadecimal. Uses the RFC 32 alphabet and exact four-byte/five-character groups, with overflow and invalid-character checks. Runs locally.
tools.method: Implements ZeroMQ RFC 32/Z85. Encoding accepts hexadecimal bytes with optional whitespace, requires complete two-digit bytes and a byte count divisible by four, and treats each four-byte group as an unsigned big-endian 32-bit integer. Repeated exact BigInt division by 85 emits five most-significant-first characters from the fixed 85-character alphabet. Decoding accepts only that alphabet, requires a character count divisible by five, accumulates each group in base 85 with BigInt, refuses any value above 4,294,967,295, and emits four big-endian bytes as uppercase hexadecimal. No padding, whitespace stripping during decode, Adobe framing, zero-group compression, encryption, key generation or network operation is performed. The UI is limited to 100,000 input characters. Empty input and unknown conversion modes are refused.

tools.name: HTTP Accept Header Tester
tools.description: Parse HTTP Accept media ranges and test offered media types against quality values, wildcards, parameters, and specificity locally.
tools.method: Parses one bounded Accept field value into RFC 9110 media ranges, media parameters and q weights. Type and subtype names and parameter names are normalized to lowercase; parameter values retain their case and quoted-string escapes are decoded. q defaults to 1, must be between 0 and 1, and is restricted to at most three decimal places. For each concrete offered media type, every matching range is enumerated. Exact type/subtype takes precedence over type/*, which takes precedence over */*; at the same level, a matching range with more media parameters wins, then declaration order. The selected range alone determines quality, so a more specific q=0 excludes an offer even when a wildcard accepts it. Unmatched offers receive q=0. Positive-quality offers retain input order for highest-quality ties. This does not select language, encoding, or other negotiation dimensions and does not issue a request. Inputs are capped at 20,000 characters, 100 ranges and 100 offers.

tools.name: systemd Path Unit Builder
tools.description: Build paired systemd path and oneshot service units for file or directory activation, with five watch conditions, trigger limits, validation, previews and downloads. Runs locally.
tools.method: Generates a .path unit and a same-base Type=oneshot .service unit, linked explicitly with Unit=. Implements the systemd.path conditions PathExists, PathExistsGlob, PathChanged, PathModified and DirectoryNotEmpty, preserving multiple watched paths as separate directives. Watched and working paths use C-style \x20 and \x22 escapes for spaces and quotes, while executable arguments use double-quoted ExecStart syntax; literal percent signs are doubled, and ExecStart also doubles dollar signs. Accepts 1–32 unique absolute watched paths and 1–256 non-empty argument lines; rejects parent components, backslashes, control characters, relative executables and unsupported account names. Optional MakeDirectory and DirectoryMode support systemd directory creation, except with PathExists where MakeDirectory is ignored by systemd and therefore rejected here. TriggerLimitIntervalSec and TriggerLimitBurst are emitted explicitly (defaults 2s and 200; either may be 0), requiring systemd 250+. The companion service deliberately has no Restart or [Install] section; only the path unit may include WantedBy=multi-user.target. The tool does not inspect the host or execute commands. As documented by systemd, path activation uses inotify and cannot observe changes made by other machines on remote NFS filesystems; existing PathExists/DirectoryNotEmpty conditions trigger immediately, while change conditions do not retroactively trigger.

tools.description: Score a 9 or 18-hole disc golf round for one to four players, with editable par, totals, score to par and CSV export.
tools.method: Supports exactly 9 or 18 holes and 1 through 4 players. Every hole has an editable integer par from 2 through 6, defaulting to 3. tools.method: Validates one literal name per nonblank input line, up to 200 names, 1,024 characters per line and 32,768 input characters. Full refnames require at least one slash. tools.name: Yeast Conversion Calculator
tools.description: Convert fresh or cake yeast, active dry yeast and instant yeast by weight, with approximate teaspoon and standard-packet equivalents for dry yeast. Uses published general baking ratios and runs entirely in your browser.
aliases: Active Dry to Instant Yeast Converter
active dry to instant yeast converter
tools.method: All conversion arithmetic uses ingredient mass. Let F be the fresh-yeast-equivalent mass. For a fresh input F equals the input mass; for active dry input F equals input mass divided by 0.4; for instant input F equals input mass divided by 0.33. The three outputs are F, 0.4F and 0.33F respectively. These are the general conversion multipliers published by King Arthur Baking, not a universal manufacturer specification. Inputs allow 0.1–1000 grams, 0.01–35 avoirdupois ounces, 0.1–300 teaspoons or 0.1–100 standard packets, with at most four decimal places. Fresh yeast accepts grams or ounces only because no standard fresh-yeast teaspoon or packet volume is assumed. One ounce is exactly 28.349523125 grams. Dry-yeast teaspoons and packets are approximate and use Red Star’s convention that one standard 7-gram packet contains about 2.25 teaspoons. Conversion factors and unrounded values are retained throughout the core; the interface rounds gram, teaspoon and packet displays to two decimal places and ounce displays to three. The tool converts ingredient quantity only. It does not prescribe fermentation time, liquid adjustments, bread-machine settings, viability, storage or food-safety handling. Manufacturer instructions and the recipe take precedence where their substitution ratios differ.

tools.name: Steps to Distance Calculator
tools.description: Convert a step count into walking distance, or a distance into an estimated number of steps, from your own step length. Shows metres, kilometres and miles plus steps per kilometre and per mile. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: Distance is the step count multiplied by the length of one step, and the reverse divides the distance by that length, rounding to the nearest whole step because a counter can only report whole footfalls. One step is a single footfall; a stride is two steps, so a stride measurement must be halved before it is entered here. Lengths are converted with exact factors: one centimetre is 0.01 metres, one inch is 0.0254 metres and one mile is 1609.344 metres. The tool accepts 1 to 1,000,000 whole steps, a step length of 20 to 150 centimetres (8 to 59 inches) with at most two decimals, and a distance of 0.001 to 1,000 kilometres or miles (1 to 1,000,000 metres) with at most three decimals for kilometres and miles. Text, negative values, exponent notation, more than one decimal separator and out-of-range values are refused with the field named. Results are exact for the length entered and are not a measurement: real step length changes with pace, slope, surface and footwear, and a GPS watch counts distance and steps independently, so its figure will usually differ. The 76 centimetre default is a placeholder rather than a personal measurement. Nothing is stored, uploaded or transmitted.

tools.name: Shooting Ratio Calculator
tools.description: Work out a shoot's shooting ratio from a finished runtime and the footage recorded, or the footage a target ratio needs. Shows unused footage and the usable share, with durations in seconds, mm:ss or h:mm:ss.
tools.method: Shooting ratio is the total recorded footage divided by the finished runtime, so 10:1 means ten hours were shot for each finished hour. Durations are read as bare seconds, mm:ss or h:mm:ss with the minutes and seconds fields under 60, and are converted to whole seconds. Runtime may be 1 second to 100 hours and footage 1 second to 10,000 hours; footage shorter than the runtime is refused because the cut cannot be longer than the material it came from. The reverse calculation multiplies the runtime by a target ratio from 1 to 1000 with at most two decimals and rounds the required footage to the nearest second. Unused footage is the footage minus the runtime and the usable share is the runtime divided by the footage, expressed as a percentage. The model is an accounting identity, not a measurement: it assumes every second of the cut comes from the footage counted and that all recorded material is available, so it says nothing about camera cards, storage, takes, coverage or what a particular production should shoot. Text, negative values, exponent notation and extra clock fields are refused with the field named. Nothing is stored, uploaded or transmitted.

tools.name: Circle Skirt Calculator
tools.description: Turn a waist measurement and a finished length into circle-skirt pattern radii: waist radius, inner and outer cut radii, hem length and the pattern block needed for a full, three-quarter, half or quarter circle skirt.
tools.method: The waist radius is the waist divided by the arc angle: a full circle wraps 2 pi radians around the waist, a three-quarter circle 1.5 pi, a half circle pi and a quarter circle 0.5 pi, so the same waist needs a larger radius as fullness falls. The inner cut radius subtracts the seam allowance from the waist radius so the seam line sits back from the cut edge. The outer cut radius adds the finished length and the hem allowance. The pattern block is the rectangle one piece fits in: twice the outer radius by twice the outer radius for a full or three-quarter circle, twice by once for a half circle and the outer radius square for a quarter circle. The finished hem length is the arc angle times the waist radius plus the finished length. Waist is limited to 10 to 80 inches (25 to 203 cm), finished length to 2 to 60 inches (5 to 152 cm), seam allowance to 0 to 1 inch (0 to 2.5 cm), hem allowance to 0 to 4 inches (0 to 10 cm) and usable fabric width to 20 to 120 inches (50 to 305 cm); text, exponent notation, empty fields and out of range values are refused with the field named. The page assumes an even hem, a straight waist seam with no waistband, casing or lining, and a single-piece cut; directional prints, nap, bias stretch, pattern matching, squaring the fabric and pieced panels need extra allowance, and a test garment is the check for fit. It stores, uploads and transmits nothing and runs entirely in the browser.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Circle skirt: a circle skirt is cut as a full, three-quarter, half or quarter circle with the waist on the inner arc.
Sewing pattern-drafting practice: the waist radius is the waist divided by the arc angle, and seam and hem allowances are added at the waist and hem edges.

tools.name: Harmonica Key & Position Finder
tools.description: Find the harmonica to play a song in any key: convert a song key and a playing position into the harp key you need, see the mode and scale each position uses, and read every blow and draw note of that harp with the root marked.
tools.method: Each playing position is a mode of the harp's own major scale. A 10-hole Richter diatonic is tuned to one major scale, so the blow notes are the root, third and fifth of that key and the draw notes the second, fifth, seventh, second, fourth and sixth, repeated over ten holes. 1st position plays the harp's key (Ionian), 2nd position (cross harp) plays a fourth below it (Mixolydian), 3rd another fourth below (Dorian), 4th the sixth degree (Aeolian), 5th the third (Phrygian), 6th the seventh (Locrian) and 7th the fourth (Lydian). The harmonica needed for a song key and position is the harp key whose scale degree for that position lands on the song key: the song pitch class minus the degree's semitone offset (0, 4, 2, 6, 8, 10 or 5 for positions 1 to 7). The page lists the seven scale notes of the chosen position, every blow and draw note of the harp key with the root marked, and the key each of the seven positions plays in on that harp. Notes are spelled in the harp's key by letter and accidental, so a D flat song can read as C sharp on an F sharp harp. Only positions 1 to 7 and the standard 10-hole Richter diatonic are modelled: tremolo, chromatic, minor-tuned and alternate tunings, cross-position bending and overblow technique are outside the model. It stores, uploads and transmits nothing and runs entirely in the browser.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Harmonica: a diatonic harmonica is tuned to a single major scale and players reach other keys by playing in different positions, which are modes of that scale.
Richter tuning reference: the blow notes of a 10-hole diatonic are the root, third and fifth of the harp key and the draw notes are its second, fifth, seventh, second, fourth and sixth.
Harmonica position practice: 1st position is straight harp in the harp key and 2nd position is cross harp a perfect fourth below it, with each further position another fourth down the same scale.
Wikipedia, Mode (music): the seven diatonic modes are rotations of the major scale, each starting on a different degree of it.

tools.name: Eb/N0 to BER Calculator
tools.description: Convert Eb/N0 to bit error rate for BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK, 16-QAM and 64-QAM over an AWGN channel, see the Es/N0 and the Eb/N0 each scheme needs for a target BER, and compare every scheme at once.
tools.method: Bit error rate is the probability that a detected bit is wrong on a coherent receiver fed by an additive white Gaussian noise channel with no coding. BPSK and QPSK each carry one coded bit per dimension and give Pb = Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0)); Gray-coded 8-PSK gives Pb = (2/3) Q(sqrt(6 Eb/N0) sin(pi/8)); square M-QAM gives Pb = (4/k)(1 - 1/sqrt(M)) Q(sqrt(3k Eb/N0/(M-1))) with k = log2 M, which is 0.75 Q(sqrt(0.8 Eb/N0)) for 16-QAM and (7/12) Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0/7)) for 64-QAM. The Gaussian tail Q(x) is evaluated as erfc(x/sqrt(2))/2, and erfc is computed as the regularized incomplete gamma function Q(1/2, x^2) through its series and continued-fraction expansions, so small error rates keep their relative accuracy instead of cancelling against 1. The Eb/N0 needed for a target rate is found by 200 bisection steps on the same curve between -10 and 60 dB; an entry that cannot reach the target inside that window is reported as outside the range. Margin is the entered Eb/N0 minus that requirement, and Es/N0 is Eb/N0 + 10 log10(k) for a noise bandwidth equal to the symbol rate. These are the standard Gray-coded approximations, accurate to within a fraction of a decibel at practical error rates but not exact symbol-error expressions; unequal constellations, fading, interference, phase noise, synchronisation loss, equalisation, channel coding and hardware impairments are not modelled, so results are planning and teaching estimates rather than link certification. It stores, uploads and transmits nothing and runs entirely in the browser.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Bit error rate: coherent BPSK and QPSK over an AWGN channel give a bit error probability of Q(sqrt(2 Eb/N0)), with Eb/N0 the energy per bit over the one-sided noise power spectral density.
Wikipedia, Phase-shift keying: the Gray-coded symbol error probability for M-PSK is approximated by 2 Q(sqrt(2 log2 M Eb/N0) sin(pi/M)), which gives the 2/3 factor for bits of 8-PSK.
Wikipedia, Quadrature amplitude modulation: square M-QAM with Gray coding has the bit error approximation (4/log2 M)(1 - 1/sqrt(M)) Q(sqrt(3 log2 M Eb/N0/(M-1))).

Abramowitz and Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions: the complementary error function equals the regularized upper incomplete gamma function Q(1/2, x^2), and the Gaussian tail follows as erfc(x/sqrt2)/2.
Proakis, Digital Communications: these Gaussian-tail expressions are the standard uncoded coherent detection results used to size a link margin for a target bit error rate.

tools.name: tcpdump Capture Filter Builder
tools.description: Build a libpcap BPF capture filter for tcpdump from host, network, port, protocol and TCP-flag conditions, with the exact command line, a plain-English explanation and input validation.
tools.method: The filter is assembled from fixed libpcap BPF primitives rather than free text. Each enabled condition becomes a host, net, port or portrange term with an optional src or dst qualifier, or a bare protocol keyword; several ports are ORed inside one parenthesised group so they bind correctly against the surrounding and/or join; the TCP flag modes expand to the documented tcp[tcpflags] bit tests, where connection attempts are SYN set with ACK clear; conditions are then joined with and or or and optionally wrapped in not (...) for exclusion. Inputs are validated before assembly: hosts must be IPv4 literals, IPv6 literals or RFC 1123 host names, networks must be CIDR blocks and an IPv4 block with host bits set is rewritten to its masked network address because libpcap rejects unmasked values, ports must be numbers from 1 to 65535, low-to-high ranges or service names, at most twelve, and interface names are limited to the 15-character Linux limit. Combinations that cannot match are reported as warnings rather than silently accepted: ICMP or ARP with ports, an IPv4 protocol keyword with an IPv6 address or the reverse, named hosts that resolve only once at capture start, and a named interface that narrows the capture. The page builds text only: it does not open interfaces, capture, resolve names, store or transmit anything, and the expression shown is exactly what tcpdump hands to libpcap, so matching behaviour is libpcap's own. BPF cannot see application payloads, so a filter selects packets by addresses, ports, protocols and TCP header flags only.

sources.title: tcpdump manual page and pcap-filter(7): the host, net, port, portrange, protocol and TCP flag primitives, the src and dst qualifiers, and the not/and/or boolean grammar used here.
The pcap-filter expression grammar in libpcap: qualifiers bind to the following identifier, which is why multiple port terms are parenthesised before being combined with and.
McCanne and Jacobson, The BSD Packet Filter: a register-based filter program compiled from the expression and applied per packet before it is copied to user space.
libpcap pcap_compile and tcpdump -d: the reference implementations that reject a CIDR block whose host bits are set and that compile each generated expression.

tools.name: GNSS Dilution of Precision Calculator
tools.description: Estimate PDOP, HDOP, VDOP, GDOP and TDOP from satellite azimuths and elevations, apply an elevation mask, rate the sky geometry and convert DOP into expected one-sigma horizontal and vertical error.
tools.method: Each satellite is a unit line-of-sight row in the local east, north and up frame: east = -cos(el) sin(az), north = -cos(el) cos(az), up = -sin(el), with a fourth column of 1 for the receiver clock offset. Azimuth is degrees clockwise from true north and elevation is degrees above the horizon, so the geometry needs no site position, Earth model or orbital data. Satellites with an elevation below the mask (inclusive on the mask itself) are discarded before the normal matrix is formed; fewer than four usable satellites cannot give a 3D fix and is reported as an error. The normal matrix is the sum of the outer products of the used rows, a symmetric 4x4 matrix that is inverted by Gauss-Jordan elimination with partial pivoting; a pivot smaller than 1e-10, or any non-finite entry in the inverse, means the directions are geometrically dependent and no unique solution exists. With Q the inverse, GDOP is the square root of the trace of Q, PDOP of Q's position block, HDOP of its east and north terms, VDOP of the height term and TDOP of the clock term, so GDOP squared equals PDOP squared plus TDOP squared and PDOP squared equals HDOP squared plus VDOP squared. Values are rounded to four decimals and compared with the usual PDOP bands: 2 or less ideal, 5 or less excellent, 10 or less good, 20 or less moderate, above 20 poor. The accuracy estimate multiplies HDOP and VDOP by an assumed average range error, which treats range errors as independent and equal on every satellite; real receivers weight satellites by elevation and signal strength, and ionosphere, troposphere, multipath and orbit errors are not modelled, so the figures are a planning estimate rather than a guarantee. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

Standard DOP identities: GDOP^2 = PDOP^2 + TDOP^2 and PDOP^2 = HDOP^2 + VDOP^2, which follow from the trace of the inverse normal matrix.
GNSS receiver practice of screening a solution with an elevation mask and a DOP limit, for example rejecting fixes above a chosen HDOP or PDOP.
Golub and Van Loan, Matrix Computations: Gauss-Jordan elimination with partial pivoting for a small symmetric normal matrix.

tools.name: Picture-in-Picture Layout Planner
tools.description: Place a secondary video inside a main frame: compute the aspect-correct inset size, corner position and pixel rectangle, check it against the 5% title-safe box, and get the FFmpeg overlay expression.
tools.method: Pixel geometry only, with no encoding. The inset's target width is the frame width times the size percentage. Even alignment rounds that width down to the nearest even number (never below 2 px) and rounds the height the same way; nearest-pixel alignment rounds half up. The height is the final width divided by the inset aspect ratio, so the inset keeps the source's shape and only pixel rounding can change the fitted aspect. The margin is the frame width times the margin percentage rounded half up, and the inset is anchored to the chosen corner with that margin on the two edges it touches, which fixes its top-left corner and therefore its overlay coordinates. A layout that cannot fit — a negative corner, or an inset plus its margins wider or taller than the frame — is reported as an error instead of being clipped. The safe check compares the inset rectangle with the legacy 90% title-safe box, whose edges are 5% of the frame width from the sides and 5% of the frame height from the top and bottom; the layout is safe only when all four inset edges stay inside that box, so a 5% margin is safe on a 16:9 frame but not on a tall vertical one. Width share, area share and the fitted aspect ratio expose rounding drift, and the FFmpeg line scales the inset to the computed pixel size and overlays it at the computed corner. The model assumes square pixels, one inset and a static position; it does not scale the main video, animate the inset, model platform interface overlays, avoid faces or subtitles, or render anything. Inputs are limited to frames of 64-16384 px, inset sizes of 5-95%, margins of 0-20% and aspect ratios of 0.1-10. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Audio Latency & Buffer Planner
tools.description: Turn a sample rate, buffer size and buffer count into block time, round-trip samples and milliseconds, add converter and plugin latency, and see which standard buffer sizes still meet a monitoring target.
tools.method: The round trip is the buffer chain plus whatever the converter, driver and plugins add. One buffer holds the buffer size divided by the sample rate, so 128 frames at 48 kHz is 2.667 ms of audio. A round trip crosses the chosen number of buffers, normally one input and one output, so the buffer share is buffer size x buffers / sample rate. Converter, driver and plugin latency are entered in milliseconds with up to three decimals, converted to whole samples at the session rate by rounding half up, and added to the buffer samples; the total is reported in samples and in milliseconds from the same integer, so the two cannot drift apart. The target is converted to whole samples by flooring, and the chain meets it only when its total is at or below that budget. The largest buffer that still fits is the largest power of two from 8 to 8192 frames whose chain stays inside the budget, and the standard-buffer list repeats the same figure for 32 to 2048 frames. Distance is how far sound travels in that time at 20 degrees Celsius (343 m/s). This is the nominal delay of the buffer chain, not a measurement: an interface's own converter and driver latency has to be supplied by the user, and the tool does not model CPU load, dropouts, plugin delay compensation or direct-monitoring paths. Inputs are limited to 8000-192000 Hz, 8-8192 frames, 1-4 buffers, 0-200 ms of converter and driver latency, 0-1000 ms of plugin latency and a 1-200 ms target. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Legacy Code Page Converter
tools.description: Convert text to and from CP437, CP850, Windows-1252, ISO-8859-1 and EBCDIC CP037 or CP500 bytes, listing the code point for every byte and reporting unmappable characters instead of dropping them. Runs locally.
tools.method: Implements single-byte code page conversion as a direct 256-entry table lookup. Each page maps byte values 0x00–0xFF to one Unicode code point taken from the published mappings for IBM CP437 and CP850 (printable range 0x20–0xFF), Microsoft Windows-1252, ISO-8859-1, and EBCDIC CP037 and CP500; the six tables were generated from those reference mappings and every defined byte was verified to round-trip back to its own value before release. Encoding walks the input by Unicode code point and writes one byte per character, substituting 0x3F (question mark) for any character the selected page cannot represent and reporting both the count and the first five positions, so a substitution is never silent. Bytes 0x00–0x1F and 0x7F keep their C0 and delete code points rather than the graphic glyphs a DOS screen or 3270 terminal may draw for those positions. Decoding accepts two-digit hexadecimal bytes with optional whitespace, rejects non-hexadecimal characters, incomplete pairs and more than 4,096 bytes, and renders the five undefined Windows-1252 bytes 0x81, 0x8D, 0x8F, 0x90 and 0x9D as U+FFFD instead of guessing a character. Input is limited to 4,096 characters or bytes. There is no charset auto-detection, transliteration, multi-byte or DBCS code page support, encryption, or network access, and the tool does not claim a page is correct for an unknown source system.
