tools.name: Ethernet Frame Rate Calculator
tools.description: Convert a link rate and Ethernet payload size into frames per second, wire overhead and payload goodput, with preamble, VLAN tags, FCS and the inter-frame gap counted. Runs locally.
tools.method: Computes a theoretical Ethernet frame rate from a MAC line rate and a layer-2 payload size. Wire accounting per frame: 8 bytes of preamble and start-frame delimiter, the 14-byte destination/source/length header, 4 bytes for each selected 802.1Q tag (0, 1 or 2 tags), the entered payload, a 4-byte frame check sequence and a 12-byte inter-frame gap. When header, payload and FCS total fewer than 64 bytes the frame is padded to that IEEE 802.3 minimum; padding is counted on the wire and in overhead but never as payload. Frames per second are line bits per second divided by the 8-bit wire size, the whole-frame figure is the floor of that rate, payload throughput is frames per second multiplied by payload bytes and 8 bits, and efficiency is payload bytes divided by wire bytes. The rate must be a whole number of kb/s between 1 kb/s and 1,600 Gb/s, so decimal input is converted exactly rather than through binary floating point. Payloads run from 1 to 65,535 bytes; anything above 1,500 bytes is flagged as a jumbo frame, which IEEE 802.3 does not define. The model assumes a saturated link and excludes collisions, pause frames, frame preemption, forward error correction, 64b/66b or 8b/10b line coding (10GBASE-R runs at 10.3125 Gbaud), protocol or transport behaviour, address learning, buffering, latency and congestion, so results are maxima rather than measured throughput. It models one frame size at a time, not a traffic mix, and computes no packet capture or network access.

tools.name: File Open Flags Decoder
tools.description: Compose an open(2) flag value from an access mode and flags such as O_CREAT, O_CLOEXEC or O_TMPFILE, or decode an octal or hex value back into its flags, with the mode argument and combination warnings. Runs locally.
tools.method: Encodes and decodes the Linux open(2) flag word. The value table is the asm-generic/fcntl.h set as glibc exposes it on x86-64: O_RDONLY 0, O_WRONLY 1, O_RDWR 2, O_CREAT 0o100, O_EXCL 0o200, O_NOCTTY 0o400, O_TRUNC 0o1000, O_APPEND 0o2000, O_NONBLOCK 0o4000, O_DSYNC 0o10000, O_ASYNC 0o20000, O_DIRECT 0o40000, O_DIRECTORY 0o200000, O_NOFOLLOW 0o400000, O_NOATIME 0o1000000, O_CLOEXEC 0o2000000, O_SYNC 0o4010000, O_PATH 0o10000000 and O_TMPFILE 0o20200000. Encoding ORs the chosen access mode with each selected flag. O_SYNC already contains the O_DSYNC bit and O_TMPFILE already contains O_DIRECTORY, so each composite is reported once and the implied flag is folded out of the symbolic list rather than printed beside it. O_PATH is offered as an access mode because the kernel honours only O_CLOEXEC, O_DIRECTORY and O_NOFOLLOW alongside it, so any other selection is left out of the value and reported. Encoding marks the mode argument as required when O_CREAT or O_TMPFILE is set and warns when O_EXCL appears without O_CREAT, when O_TRUNC is combined with O_RDONLY, when O_TMPFILE lacks a write access mode, and about the alignment, ownership and descriptor-type conditions of O_DIRECT, O_NOATIME and O_ASYNC. Decoding reads hex after 0x and octal with an optional 0 or 0o prefix, refuses values above 32 bits and access bits of 0o3, names the private __O_SYNC and __O_TMPFILE bits when they appear without their companion bit, and reports bits that no flag on this ABI defines. The page models the numeric constants only: it does not model other architectures (O_DIRECT is 0o200000 on SPARC), umask, filesystem or mount behaviour, LSM or SELinux checks, kernel version differences, or the permission bits in the third mode argument, and it never opens, creates or inspects a file.

tools.name: Archery Sight Adjustment Calculator
tools.description: Turn a group's error at a set distance and the sight radius into how far, and which way, to move an archery sight, in millimetres, inches or sight clicks.
tools.method: Moving the sight pin by d rotates the line of sight relative to the arrow by d divided by the sight radius, so at a target distance D the point of impact moves by D x d / sight radius. Inverted, the correction is d = sight radius x error / D with the error and the distance in the same unit: a 762 mm sight radius and a group 50 mm (5 cm) high at 30 m needs 762 x 50 / 30000 = 1.27 mm of sight movement, and the same sight at 60 m needs 0.64 mm for the same error. The direction follows the rule of chasing the arrow: the sight moves toward the group, so a high group calls for raising the sight, which then makes the arrow land lower, and a group to the right calls for moving the sight right. A click value set on the sight converts the movement into clicks, so a sight that moves 0.1 mm per click needs about 12.7 clicks for that example. Imperial inputs take the sight radius and group error in inches and the distance in yards, converting at 36 inches per yard. Accepted ranges are a sight radius of 50 to 1500 mm (2 to 60 in), a distance of 3 to 100 m (3 to 110 yd), group errors within +/- 200 cm (+/- 80 in) and a click value of 0.01 to 5 mm (0.001 to 0.2 in); the page warns when a correction would exceed 4 mm. This is geometric guidance only: it assumes a straight line of sight to the pin and it ignores arrow speed, trajectory shape and form errors, so confirm any large change with a test group. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Bash Parameter Expansion Explainer
tools.description: Paste a bash expansion such as ${file%.*} with a sample value and see the result, the operator it applies, the text it removed or replaced, and why.
tools.method: Models one bash parameter expansion at a time. The expansion is written as ${name...} and evaluated against the value typed into the page; the name is only a label, so ${file%.*} works with any value. Supported forms are the plain value, ${#name} for length, the default and alternative words ${name:-word}, ${name-word}, ${name:=word}, ${name=word}, ${name:+word}, ${name+word}, ${name:?word} and ${name?word}, the substrings ${name:offset} and ${name:offset:length}, prefix removal with ${name#pattern} and ${name##pattern}, suffix removal with ${name%pattern} and ${name%%pattern}, the substitutions ${name/pattern/repl} and ${name//pattern/repl}, and the case conversions ${name^}, ${name^^}, ${name,} and ${name,,}. The colon forms test for unset or empty and the bare forms test only for unset, exactly as bash does. Patterns use shell globbing: * matches any run of characters, ? matches one character, [abc] and [a-z] are character classes, [!abc] and [^abc] negate a class, and a backslash escapes the next character. A single # removes the shortest matching prefix and ## the longest, % removes the shortest matching suffix and %% the longest; substitution replaces the first match of the longest match at the earliest position, and // repeats that across the value, skipping empty matches the way bash does except for an empty value where a pattern that matches nothing at all still replaces once. Substring offsets are counted in characters: a negative offset counts back from the end, a value that starts past the end gives an empty string, a negative length is an end offset from the end, and bash's rejection of a negative length that ends before the offset is reproduced as an error. Length counts Unicode characters rather than bytes, and case conversion uses Unicode case mapping rather than the shell's locale. The page rejects command substitution, nested expansions, arrays, attribute operators, anchored substitutions and quoting instead of guessing at them, limits the expression to 400 characters, the value to 1000 characters and a pattern to 200 characters, and never runs a shell. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Egg Size Converter
tools.description: Convert a recipe's eggs between USDA sizes: turn a count of large eggs into the number of medium, extra large or jumbo eggs with the same shell weight, or turn grams of egg into a count.
tools.method: USDA consumer weight classes are minimum net weights per dozen in the shell, so the tool converts through the per-egg equivalent of the class: the dozen minimum in ounces (Peewee 15, Small 18, Medium 21, Large 24, Extra large 27, Jumbo 30) multiplied by 28.349523125 and divided by 12. Large is therefore 56.699 g, Extra large 63.786 g, Medium 49.611 g, Small 42.524 g, Peewee 35.437 g and Jumbo 70.874 g. In count mode the recipe's weight is its egg count times the per-egg equivalent of the recipe's class. In weight mode the entered grams of egg are that weight directly, so a recipe written as 150 g of egg can be turned into a number of eggs. The number of eggs you need is that weight divided by the per-egg equivalent of the size you have; the page also reports the total weight to weigh, the whole eggs rounded down with the weight they fall short, and the whole eggs rounded up with the weight they overshoot, plus the total in ounces. A whole number carries a 1e-9 tolerance so an exact match is not printed as 2.9999 eggs. Counts are limited to 0.25-60 eggs with up to two decimals, weights to 5-3400 g with up to two decimals, and both sizes must be one of the six USDA classes. Every weight includes the shell and assumes the class minimum per egg, while the legal class describes the carton rather than one egg, and real eggs vary, so weighing cracked eggs is more accurate than counting. The tool does not convert volume, separate yolks and whites, grade eggs, or assess quality, freshness or safety. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

Recipes conventionally assume Large eggs; the same per-dozen weights give the equivalent count in any other USDA class.

tools.name: Latch Hook Rug Yarn Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much yarn a latch hook rug needs: knots from the canvas mesh and rug size, the length to cut each strand for your pile height, total yarn in yards or metres, and the skeins to buy.
tools.method: The canvas sets the knot count: the rug width and length in inches are each multiplied by the mesh count in holes per inch and rounded to the nearest whole hole, because canvas is cut between holes and a partial row cannot be knotted. The default standard canvas is 3.3 holes per inch, with 4 and 5 hole fine canvas offered; a 24 in side on 3.3 mesh therefore becomes 79 holes and 23.94 in, and the page reports that trimmed size whenever rounding moved the edge. Knots are the product of the two hole counts, one knot per hole, which is the most yarn the rug can use because every hole is assumed filled. Each latch hook knot is a single strand folded through a hole and looped around the canvas thread, so the strand must span the pile twice plus an allowance for the fold: cut length = 2 x pile height + 0.5 in. That reproduces the common 2.5 in pre-cut strand for a 1 in pile on standard canvas. Total yarn is knots x cut length, increased by the waste percentage for trimming, tails and miscuts, and reported in inches, yards and metres. Skeins are the total divided by the skein yardage on the label and rounded up, because a partial skein still has to be bought; the page also reports how many strands one skein cuts and the yarn used before waste. Skein length is an input rather than a constant because a 3 oz skein is not a fixed yardage across brands. Limits are 4-240 in per side, 0.25-4 in pile, 0-50 percent waste, 1-1000 yards per skein and only the three mesh counts. The result is a purchasing estimate, not a pattern: it assumes every hole is filled and a uniform pile, and it does not model yarn thickness, dye lots, canvas thickness, the knotting style actually used, or yarn lost to joins and repairs. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Latch hook canvas is sold by mesh count in holes per inch, commonly 3.3 (standard), 4 and 5 (fine); the knot count follows the canvas, one knot per hole.

Pre-cut latch hook yarn is commonly supplied in 2.5 in lengths for a 1 in pile on standard 3.3 mesh canvas, matching the 0.5 in wrap allowance used here (2 x 1 + 0.5 = 2.5 in).
Skein yardage varies by brand and weight, so the yardage printed on the skein label is an input rather than a fixed constant.

tools.name: Album Side Split Planner
tools.description: Split a tracklist across the two sides of a record or cassette: paste the running times, choose the medium, and get the break that makes both sides as even as they can be, with side totals, spare time and the smallest medium that fits.
tools.method: A disc or tape has exactly two sides, so the planner keeps the running order and chooses one break point in the list. Each side's runtime is the sum of its track durations; every possible break is evaluated and the winner is the one whose longer side is shortest, with a tie going to the smaller difference between the sides. That keeps both sides as near equal as a single break allows, which matters on vinyl because the inner grooves on a long side lose level and high frequencies first. Durations are parsed from the end of each line as minutes:seconds, so 'Night Bus 4:02' and '4:02' both read 242 seconds, and titles are optional. Side limits are conservative nominal capacities for full-level material: 22:00 per side on a 12 in LP at 33⅓ rpm, 12:00 on a 12 in single at 45 rpm, 14:00 on a 10 in LP at 33⅓ rpm, 4:30 on a 7 in single at 45 rpm, 30:00 per side on a C-60 cassette and 45:00 per side on a C-90. The page reports both side totals, the spare time or the amount each side is over, the gap between the sides and the smallest listed medium whose limit covers the longest side. A tracklist that stays inside a medium fits exactly at the limit and one second over it does not. Limits are 2 to 40 tracks and 1 second to 60 minutes per track. The result is a sequencing plan, not a cutting master: vinyl capacity shrinks as level and bass content rise, tape length varies with stock and machine, and track gaps, fades, locked grooves, run-out and lead-in time are not counted. Tracks are never reordered or shortened. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A 12 in LP at 33⅓ rpm is commonly cut at roughly 18-22 minutes per side, and the usable time falls as level and bass content rise because wider grooves take more space.
Smaller and faster discs hold less: a 12 in single at 45 rpm about 10-15 minutes per side, a 10 in record at 33⅓ rpm about 12-15 minutes, and a 7 in single at 45 rpm about 4-5 minutes.
Compact cassettes are labelled by total playing time for both sides, so a C-60 holds about 30 minutes per side and a C-90 about 45 minutes per side.
Vinyl is cut from the outer edge inward, so a long side ends in the inner grooves where tracing distortion and level loss are greatest; near-equal sides are the usual sequencing target.

tools.name: RF Skin Depth Calculator
tools.description: Find the skin depth and surface resistance of copper, silver, gold, aluminum, brass or bronze at any frequency from 1 Hz to 300 GHz, and the five-skin-depth thickness that carries about 99% of an RF current.
tools.method: Skin depth is the distance at which current density in a good conductor has decayed to 1/e, about 36.8%, of its surface value. For conductivity sigma, permeability mu = mu0 mur and angular frequency omega = 2 pi f, delta = sqrt(2 rho/(omega mu)) = sqrt(rho/(pi f mu0 mur)) with rho = 1/sigma. The surface resistance of a smooth semi-infinite conductor is Rs = sqrt(pi f mu0 mur rho) = 1/(sigma delta) in ohms per square, so a square of any size has the same RF resistance; five skin depths contain 1 - exp(-5) = 99.3% of the current, which is why plating is often specified as 5 delta. Presets hold 20 C handbook conductivities in MS/m: copper 58.0, silver 63.0, gold 41.0, aluminum 35.4, brass 70/30 16.0 and phosphor bronze 8.7. The conductivity field is authoritative and can be edited for alloys, another temperature or a plated layer. Frequency is converted from Hz, kHz, MHz or GHz and must lie between 1 Hz and 300 GHz; conductivity is limited to 0.01 to 100 MS/m and relative permeability to 1 to 10000. The model assumes a smooth, homogeneous, thick conductor that is non-magnetic unless a relative permeability is entered, so it does not cover films thinner than a few skin depths, surface roughness, multilayer plating, proximity effect in windings, superconductors, or ferromagnetic metals whose permeability varies with frequency and field. Everything runs locally in your browser and nothing is stored or uploaded.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Skin effect: current density in a conductor falls exponentially with depth and reaches 1/e of its surface value at the skin depth delta = sqrt(2 rho/(omega mu)).
Wikipedia, Surface resistivity: the high-frequency sheet resistance of a good conductor is Rs = sqrt(pi f mu rho) = 1/(sigma delta), expressed in ohms per square.
Wikipedia, Electrical resistivity and conductivity: conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity, and the presets correspond to handbook 20 C resistivities for common conductors.

Balanis, Advanced Engineering Electromagnetics: skin depth and surface impedance follow from the plane-wave propagation constant in a good conductor, with the surface resistance equal to the real part of the surface impedance.
Microwaves101, Skin depth: plating and coating thickness is commonly quoted as several skin depths because current density decays exponentially into the metal.

tools.name: Spanning Tree Root Bridge Calculator
tools.description: Elect the spanning tree root bridge, add up every switch's root path cost from bridge priorities, MAC addresses and link speeds, and show which port STP or RSTP blocks to break the loop.
tools.method: A bridge ID is the 2-byte bridge priority followed by the 48-bit MAC address, and the switch with the lowest bridge ID wins the root election, so priority is compared before the MAC and a priority of 4096 beats the default 32768 whatever the MAC is. Each remaining switch selects the port that offers the lowest root path cost, exactly as the root path cost and designated port vectors are compared in IEEE 802.1D: lowest root path cost first, then the lowest upstream bridge ID, then the lowest upstream port ID, then the lowest local port ID. Ports are numbered in the order the links are listed. On every link the side advertising the better path cost, bridge ID and port ID becomes the designated port and keeps forwarding; a port that is neither root nor designated is an alternate and is blocked, which is what removes the loop, and a topology with N switches and L links leaves L - (N - 1) ports blocked once it has converged. Path costs use the IEEE 802.1t rule of thumb 20,000,000 divided by the link speed in Mb/s, which reproduces the standard values of 2,000,000 at 10 Mb/s, 200,000 at 100 Mb/s, 20,000 at 1 Gb/s, 2,000 at 10 Gb/s and 200 at 100 Gb/s, with any speed from 10 to 1,000,000 Mb/s accepted and rounded. The model assumes point-to-point links, at most one link per pair of switches, equal port priorities and a single common spanning tree (STP, RSTP or the CIST of MSTP), so it does not cover per-VLAN trees, shared media, configured port costs, port roles that only exist while a topology change is in progress, or BPDU filtering. Everything runs locally in your browser and nothing is stored or uploaded.

tools.name: Map Link Coordinate Extractor
tools.description: Paste a map link, a geo: URI or a coordinate pair and pull out the latitude and longitude in decimal, degrees-minutes-seconds and geo: URI form, plus the zoom level and the ground precision the link carries.
tools.method: The pasted text is read as characters, never fetched, so the page can only report coordinates that are already written in the link. The shapes are tried in a fixed order and the first match wins: a geo: URI (latitude and longitude, with any ;u= uncertainty or query zoom dropped), a place pin in the data parameters (!3d latitude and !4d longitude), a dropped marker (mlat and mlon, with the map=zoom/lat/lon fragment supplying the zoom), a map view fragment (#map=zoom/latitude/longitude), a centre point (cp=latitude~longitude), a map view centre (@latitude,longitude,zoomz), a named parameter from ll, q, query, center, centre, coordinate, coords, sll, saddr, daddr, destination and origin read as a comma-separated pair, separate lat and lon parameters, and finally a plain decimal pair with optional N, S, E or W letters where S and W make the value negative. Latitude always comes first: a first value between 91 and 180 with a second value inside the latitude range is reported as a probable swap instead of being silently flipped, and every value must stay within -90 to 90 or -180 to 180. Degrees-minutes-seconds is produced by rounding the absolute value to a tenth of an arcsecond and splitting it into whole degrees, minutes and seconds, carrying a rounded 60 seconds into the minute and a rounded 60 minutes into the degree. The decimal places written in the source are kept, trailing zeros included, up to six, and longer values are rounded to six, because the last digit is what states the link's precision: one step is 10 to the power of minus that many places multiplied by 111,320 metres of latitude, and the east-west step is that figure times the cosine of the latitude. A zoom level from 0 to 22 is reported when the link carries one. Short links, address-only links, ISO 6709 strings and reverse geocoding are out of scope, and everything runs in the browser, so nothing is stored, uploaded or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Paper Weight Converter
tools.description: Convert paper weight between grams per square metre and the US basis weights for bond, text, cover, index, bristol and tag, using each grade’s own base sheet, and see every grade’s pound weight for one metric figure.
tools.method: A US basis weight is the weight in pounds of a 500-sheet ream of a grade's standard base sheet, so the tool converts through grams per square metre as the common currency. The base sheets are bond, writing and ledger at 17 by 22 inches (374 square inches), text, book and offset at 25 by 38 inches (950), cover at 20 by 26 inches (520), index at 25.5 by 30.5 inches (777.75), bristol at 22.5 by 28.5 inches (641.25) and tag at 24 by 36 inches (864). One square inch is exactly 0.00064516 square metres and one pound is exactly 453.59237 grams, so a pound value becomes grams per square metre by multiplying by 453.59237 and dividing by 500 base sheets times the base area in square metres, and the reverse multiplies by that same product instead. Results are rounded half up to one decimal place; the addition of a billionth before rounding keeps a binary value that should land exactly on a half, such as 49.95, from rounding downwards. Weights are accepted from 1 to 2,000 g/m2, which covers tissue to heavy board, and a pound entry that would exceed that metric ceiling is rejected rather than silently clipped. Caliper, thickness and bulk are out of scope because they are not derivable from weight: two sheets of the same grammage can differ in thickness as bulk varies. Everything runs in the browser, so nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

sources.title: US paper industry basis-weight convention: a 500-sheet ream of each grade's standard base sheet, with the bond, text, cover, index, bristol and tag sheet sizes used here.
ISO 536, Paper and board: determination of grammage, the g/m2 definition used for the metric side.
International yard and pound agreement (1959): one pound is exactly 453.59237 grams.
NIST Special Publication 811, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units: one inch is exactly 25.4 millimetres, so one square inch is 0.00064516 square metres.
Paper merchant weight charts used as an independent cross-check of the published examples, for example 80 lb text at about 118 g/m2 and 20 lb bond at about 75 g/m2.

tools.name: ISO 8601 Duration Calculator
tools.description: Parse an ISO 8601 duration such as P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S, add it to a start date on the real calendar with month-end clamping, and read exact or nominal totals in days, hours, minutes and seconds.
tools.method: An ISO 8601 duration is a P followed by years, months, weeks and days, then a T before hours, minutes and seconds, so P1Y2M3DT4H5M6S is one year, two months, three days, four hours, five minutes and six seconds. The parser accepts each unit at most once and only in that order, allows a decimal fraction only in the smallest unit present, refuses fractions on years and months because a month has no fixed length, and refuses a week designator mixed with other units, as ISO 8601 requires. Calendar months are added the way a calendar does it: the month is advanced and the day is clamped to the target month's last day, so 31 January plus one month is 28 February, or 29 February in a leap year, and 29 February plus one year is 28 February. Weeks and days are then added as fixed 24-hour periods, and the time of day is added last against the start time, rounded to the nearest second with halves rounded up. All date arithmetic runs on UTC so a daylight-saving change cannot shift the result. Totals are exact when the duration has no years or months; when it does, they are nominal and use 1 month = 30 days, which is stated in the labels rather than presented as an exact figure. Results are shown to three decimal places with trailing zeros removed. Everything runs in the browser, so nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

sources.title: ISO 8601-1:2019, Date and time: Representations for information interchange, basic rules, for the PnYnMnWnDTnHnMnS duration designator.
ISO 8601-2:2019, Date and time: Extensions, for the rule that a decimal fraction may only appear in the smallest unit and that a week designator is not combined with other components.
ECMAScript Date object semantics, used for UTC calendar arithmetic: Date.UTC months are zero-based and setUTCDate carries across month and year boundaries.
IANA time zone database documentation, on why calendar date arithmetic in UTC is unaffected by daylight-saving transitions.

tools.name: THD & SINAD Calculator
tools.description: Turn a fundamental level and the levels of its harmonics and noise floor in dBFS into total harmonic distortion, THD+N, SINAD and effective bits, with a per-harmonic breakdown of where the distortion comes from.
tools.method: Every level is entered in dBFS and converted to a linear amplitude with A = 10^(dBFS / 20), so a -60 dBFS harmonic is 0.001 of full scale. The harmonic amplitudes are combined in quadrature, which is the RMS sum of unrelated tones: the distortion residual D is the square root of the sum of the squares of the entered harmonics. THD is D divided by the fundamental amplitude, shown as a percentage and as a level in dB relative to the fundamental, so a single harmonic 60 dB down gives 0.1% and -60 dB. THD+N adds the noise floor to the same quadrature sum, so it is never smaller than THD and the two agree when no noise floor is entered. SINAD is the fundamental amplitude divided by that combined residual, expressed in decibels, and it is the arithmetic inverse of THD+N in dB. Effective number of bits follows from SINAD as (SINAD - 1.76) / 6.02, where 1.76 dB is the peak-to-RMS offset of a full-scale sine and 6.02 dB is the dynamic range of one bit; the result is the resolution of an ideal converter with the same SINAD and is not a claim about a real device. The residual is also reported as an absolute dBFS level. The per-harmonic breakdown gives each harmonic's share of the distortion energy and marks the dominant one. Each harmonic from the second to the seventh is optional and blank means absent, at least one harmonic or a noise floor must be entered, and every level is limited to -160 to 0 dBFS with up to two decimals. Because a harmonic at or above the fundamental gives distortion above 100%, that case is reported as a warning rather than silently accepted as a device measurement. Everything runs in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

sources.title: Total harmonic distortion is the RMS sum of the harmonic amplitudes divided by the fundamental amplitude, quoted as a percentage or as a level below the fundamental.
SINAD is the fundamental amplitude divided by the RMS sum of all other spectral components, harmonics plus noise, expressed in decibels.
ENOB follows from SINAD as (SINAD - 1.76 dB) / 6.02 dB for a full-scale sine, where 1.76 dB is the peak-to-RMS offset and 6.02 dB is one bit of dynamic range.
AES17-2015, AES standard for digital audio engineering: measurement of audio equipment, for the THD+N convention of measuring the residual with the fundamental notched out.

tools.name: yEnc Encoder / Decoder
tools.description: Encode text into a yEnc block with =ybegin and =yend headers and a CRC32 checksum, or decode a pasted yEnc body back to text while its size and checksum are verified. Exact byte round-trip; runs locally.
tools.method: yEnc shifts every payload byte by 42 modulo 256, so byte b becomes the character (b + 42) mod 256. When that character would be NUL, LF, CR or '=', or a tab or space at the start of a line, it is written as '=' followed by (character + 64) mod 256; a decoder recovers the byte as (escaped character - 106) mod 256. Line breaks inside the body are framing and are removed before decoding. The encoder wraps at the chosen line length without splitting an escape pair and, when headers are enabled, writes =ybegin line=N size=N name=file, the body, and =yend size=N crc32=XXXXXXXX. The checksum is the reflected IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 (polynomial 0xEDB88320, initial value 0xFFFFFFFF, final XOR 0xFFFFFFFF) over the original bytes, shown as eight lowercase hex digits. Typed text is encoded as its UTF-8 bytes. The decoder accepts CRLF or LF, ignores article headers above =ybegin and any =ypart markers, verifies the =yend size and CRC32 when present, and reports a mismatch as a warning instead of hiding it. A payload that is not valid UTF-8 is shown as hex. Encoding is capped at 100,000 characters and decoding at 200,000 characters, and everything runs in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

sources.title: yEnc encodes each byte as (byte + 42) mod 256 and escapes NUL, LF, CR, '=' and a leading tab or space as '=' plus (character + 64) mod 256.
The =ybegin, =ypart and =yend lines carry the line length, part and total size, file name and a CRC32 checksum; body line breaks are framing, not data.
CRC-32 as used by zip and PNG is the reflected IEEE 802.3 polynomial 0xEDB88320 with an initial value of 0xFFFFFFFF and a final XOR of 0xFFFFFFFF.

tools.name: IPv6 EUI-64 Interface ID Generator
tools.description: Build a modified EUI-64 interface identifier from a 48-bit MAC address or a 64-bit EUI-64 identifier, then read the fe80:: link-local address and the SLAAC address under any /64 prefix. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: The modified EUI-64 rule builds a 64-bit interface identifier from an individual (unicast) MAC address or EUI-64 identifier. For a 48-bit MAC the universal/local (U/L) bit in the first octet, bit 1 with mask 0x02, is flipped, and FF FE is inserted between the first three bytes (the OUI) and the last three bytes, producing eight bytes. A 64-bit EUI-64 input only has its U/L bit flipped; FF FE is not inserted a second time. An odd first octet has the I/G (multicast) bit set, so the tool rejects it instead of generating an identifier from a group address. The link-local address is fe80::/64 followed by the identifier; a global or unique-local address is the selected /64 prefix followed by the identifier, with any bits beyond the 64th cleared. The identifier is shown as four 4-digit lowercase hex groups, and addresses use the RFC 5952 canonical text form: lowercase, no leading zeros, and the longest run (the first on a tie) of two or more zero groups collapsed to ::. The tool requires a /64 prefix because the identifier is exactly 64 bits, and everything is computed in the page with no uploads, network requests or storage.

sources.title: RFC 4291 section 2.5.1: an EUI-64 interface identifier flips the universal/local bit, and a 48-bit MAC gets FF FE inserted in the middle.
RFC 4291 section 2.5.3: the link-local address is formed from the fe80::/64 prefix and the interface identifier.
RFC 5952 section 4: IPv6 text representation uses lowercase hex, no leading zeros, and :: for the longest run of zero groups, the first run on a tie.
RFC 4862 section 5.3: stateless address autoconfiguration combines a /64 prefix with an interface identifier of the same length.

tools.name: cgroup v1 to v2 Resource Converter
tools.description: Convert cgroup v1 limits to the cgroup v2 files that replace them: cpu.shares to cpu.weight under the current and the legacy formula, cpu.cfs_quota_us with cpu.cfs_period_us to one cpu.max line, and memory.limit_in_bytes to memory.max. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: Three cgroup v1 settings are turned into the v2 file that carries the same limit. cpu.shares (2 to 262144, default 1024) becomes cpu.weight (1 to 10000, default 100) with the formula adopted by runc 1.3.2 and crun 1.23: weight = ceil(10^(L^2/612 + 125L/612 - 7/34)), where L = log2(shares); it is exact at 2 -> 1, 1024 -> 100 and 262144 -> 10000, and every shares value from 2 to 262144 maps to a weight in range with all 10000 weights reachable. The older KEP-2254 linear mapping weight = 1 + floor((shares - 2) * 9999 / 262142) is shown beside it and gives 39 for 1024 shares, which is why it was replaced. cpu.cfs_quota_us (-1 for no limit, otherwise a whole number of microseconds) and cpu.cfs_period_us (1000 to 1000000, default 100000) collapse into one cpu.max line written as $MAX $PERIOD with the quota first, and -1 becomes the literal max; the CPU equivalent is quota divided by period, capped by neither the page nor a CPU count. memory.limit_in_bytes becomes memory.max with the same byte count, and -1 becomes max. Every field accepts whole numbers only: surrounding spaces, a leading minus sign and leading zeros are accepted, while decimal points, unit suffixes and exponents are refused with a message that names the field, its range and the unlimited sentinel. Values above 9007199254740991 bytes or 1000000000000 microseconds are refused instead of being rounded. The page states that a weight is a relative share among runnable siblings rather than a reservation, and everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Linux kernel cgroup v2 documentation: cpu.weight defaults to 100 in the range 1 to 10000, cpu.max is a two-value file in the format $MAX $PERIOD defaulting to max 100000, and memory.max defaults to max.
Linux kernel CFS bandwidth control documentation covers the cgroup v1 cpu.cfs_quota_us and cpu.cfs_period_us pair that cpu.max replaces.
systemd cgroup-util.h defines the ranges used here: cpu shares 2 to 262144 with a default of 1024, and CPU weight 1 to 10000 with a default of 100.
Kubernetes blog, New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight: records the KEP-2254 linear formula, the replacement logarithmic formula, and its adoption in runc 1.3.2 and crun 1.23.

tools.name: HDR Transfer Function Converter
tools.description: Convert between signal levels and display luminance for PQ (SMPTE ST 2084 / HDR10), HLG (BT.2100), BT.1886 and sRGB, with 10-bit and 12-bit code values, normalised signal, nits and the share of the peak. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: Four transfer functions are evaluated in both directions. PQ (SMPTE ST 2084) is absolute: L = 10000 * ((max(N^(1/m2) - c1, 0)) / (c2 - c3 * N^(1/m2)))^(1/m1) with m1 = 2610/16384, m2 = 2523/4096 * 128, c1 = 3424/4096, c2 = 2413/4096 * 32 and c3 = 2392/4096 * 32, and N = ((c1 + c2 * Y^m1) / (1 + c3 * Y^m1))^m2 for the inverse, where Y = L / 10000; N is the code value divided by 1023 (10-bit) or 4095 (12-bit), or a percentage of full scale. The page reproduces the published PQ table to three decimals (10-bit 100 -> 0.306, 512 -> 92.698, 769 -> 998.932 and 1023 -> 10000 cd/m^2). HLG (ITU-R BT.2100) is relative: the signal is decoded with the OETF inverse (sqrt(3E) below 1/12, a*ln(12E - b) + c above, a = 0.17883277, b = 0.28466892, c = 0.55991073) and scaled by the display peak with the system gamma 1.2 + 0.42*log10(peak/1000), so 75 % lands on 203.15 cd/m^2 at a 1000 cd/m^2 peak and on 35.49 cd/m^2 at 100 cd/m^2; peaks are limited to the nominal 100 to 1000 cd/m^2 and extended range signals are not modelled. BT.1886 is a pure 2.4 gamma with zero black (L = peak * V^2.4) and sRGB uses the IEC 61966-2-1 curve (12.92 toe below 0.04045, then 1.055 * V^1/2.4 - 0.055), both relative to the peak white, which defaults to 100 cd/m^2. Code values must be whole numbers inside their range and luminance must stay within 0 and the peak; every message names the field and its range. The page reports the normalised signal, both code values, the luminance, its share of the peak and a reference table for the selected curve, and states that these are signal-domain functions rather than measured display output. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: ITU-R BT.2100 defines the PQ and HLG transfer functions used here, including the HLG system gamma 1.2 + 0.42 log10(L_W/1000) and the OETF constants.
SMPTE ST 2084 defines the Perceptual Quantizer EOTF with the m1, m2, c1, c2 and c3 constants and its 10,000 cd/m² full scale.
ITU-R BT.1886 defines the SDR reference electro-optical transfer function: gamma 2.4 with zero black level.
IEC 61966-2-1 defines the sRGB transfer function with its 12.92 linear toe and 2.4 power segment.

tools.name: 3D LUT Grid & Memory Calculator
tools.description: Size a 3D LUT from its grid resolution: grid points, channel samples, runtime memory at 8-bit, 16-bit, half and float precision, .cube file size, the input step between grid points, and the corner fetches per frame for tetrahedral or trilinear sampling. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: A 3D LUT is a regular N x N x N table of RGB triplets, so the grid point count is N^3 and the stored channel count is 3 x N^3: a 33-point cube holds 35,937 points and 107,811 channel samples, and a 65-point cube holds 274,625 points. Runtime memory is that channel count times the bytes per sample (4 for float32, 2 for float16 or uint16, and 1 for uint8), independent of the file's decimal count. The .cube text estimate writes each point as three values with d decimals separated by single spaces, so a line is 3 x (d + 2) + 3 bytes including the newline, plus a 64-byte allowance for TITLE, LUT_3D_SIZE and the domain lines; optional comments are excluded, so a real file can be slightly larger. Grid points sit 1 / (N - 1) apart in the normalised 0-1 domain, so a 33-point table steps by 0.03125 and a 65-point table by 0.015625. Sampling cost assumes one sample per output pixel: a tetrahedral sampler reads 4 corners and a trilinear sampler reads 8, each corner returning three channels, so corner traffic is samples x corners x 3 x bytes per second at the entered frame rate and is an upper bound before cache reuse. Grid sizes are limited to whole numbers from 2 to 129, decimals to 1-10, frame edges to 1-16,384 pixels and frame rates to 0.001-1,000 fps, and every message names the field and its range. The result is table arithmetic rather than a quality score: a larger grid reduces interpolation error but costs memory and cache locality. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Adobe Cube LUT Specification 1.0 defines the .cube text layout: LUT_3D_SIZE, one RGB triplet per line with a chosen number of decimals, and the DOMAIN_MIN/DOMAIN_MAX lines.
A 3D LUT is an N x N x N grid of RGB triplets; common grid sizes are 17, 33 and 65, and interpolation reads 4 corners for tetrahedral sampling and 8 for trilinear sampling.

tools.name: Jet Lag Adjustment Planner
tools.description: Plan a jet lag adjustment from two UTC offsets: the wall-clock change, the shorter body-clock shift, the daily step needed over the days you have, the arrival-day bedtime and wake time in destination local time, and a night-by-night sleep schedule. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: Offsets are converted to minutes and the wall-clock change is the destination offset minus the origin offset; a New York (-5) to Tokyo (+9) trip is +14h, or 840 minutes. Because the body clock can adapt in either direction, the planner reduces that change to the shorter way around the clock: any result above 720 minutes is replaced by itself minus 1440, so +840 minutes becomes -600, a ten-hour delay. The sign names the direction of the bedtime move: positive means advance (sleep earlier), negative means delay (sleep later), and exactly 720 minutes is treated as an advance. A forced advance or delay keeps that direction and takes the long way round instead, so the same trip forced to advance is a 14-hour shift. The shift needed is divided by the days available to give the daily step, which is capped at the user's maximum per-day value; if the cap binds, the full shift simply takes ceil(magnitude / daily step) days and the result says so. The arrival bedtime is the habitual bedtime plus the signed body-clock shift, shown modulo 24 hours in destination local time, and the wake time keeps the same sleep-window length. The schedule starts at day 0 (arrival day) with the whole body-clock offset applied and moves the bedtime one daily step toward the habitual local bedtime on each later night; at most the first 15 nights are listed. Inputs are limited to offsets from -12 to 14 hours and daily steps from 0.25 to 4 hours in quarter-hour increments, 1 to 30 days and 24-hour HH:MM sleep times, and every message names the field and its range. This is time arithmetic for planning, not medical advice, and individual sleep patterns vary. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: UTC offsets range from UTC-12:00 to UTC+14:00, and some zones use 30- or 45-minute offsets such as Nepal at UTC+05:45 and Eucla at UTC+08:45.

A time-zone change shifts the sleep schedule by the offset difference; the two ways around the clock are the difference itself and 24 hours minus that difference, and the smaller one is the shorter adjustment.
Jet lag plans spread the adjustment over several days with a limited daily step rather than jumping the whole offset on the first night.

tools.name: Backpack Base Weight Planner
tools.description: Add up a backpacking load three ways: base weight (carried gear), total pack weight (plus consumables) and skin-out weight (plus worn items), with each figure as a share of body weight. Weights can be entered in grams, kilograms, ounces or pounds and every row is marked as carried, worn or consumable. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: Each row is named and marked as carried in the pack, worn, or consumed; changing the item unit converts the numbers already entered so the load itself stays the same. Item weights are converted to grams with 1 g = 1 g, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 oz = 28.349523125 g and 1 lb = 453.59237 g, and body weight with 1 kg = 1000 g or 1 lb = 453.59237 g. Base weight is the sum of the carried rows; total pack weight is base weight plus consumables, and skin-out weight is total pack weight plus worn items. Each figure is divided by body weight in grams and multiplied by 100 to give a share of body weight, so a 4900 g base on a 75 kg hiker is 6.53%. The heaviest row is the first row with the largest converted weight, and its share is taken against base weight only, shown as 0 when base weight is 0. Rows whose name and weight are both blank are ignored in the page; an item may weigh 0 to 50000 g, a list holds 1 to 100 rows, and body weight is limited to 20 to 400 kg (44 to 880 lb). A load whose rows are all zero is rejected. Values are kept unrounded until display, where grams are rounded to whole grams, kilograms and pounds to two decimals and ounces to one decimal. A pack-share above 20% is labelled a rule-of-thumb warning, not a limit. This is load arithmetic for trip planning, not medical, safety or equipment-rating advice. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Base weight counts gear carried in a pack and excludes worn items and consumables; total pack weight adds consumables and skin-out weight adds worn items.
The international avoirdupois ounce is exactly 28.349523125 grams and the international avoirdupois pound is exactly 453.59237 grams.
Backpacking guidance commonly uses a share of body weight, often about 20% for total pack weight, as a rule of thumb rather than a hard limit.

tools.name: Docker Image Reference Parser
tools.description: Split a Docker or OCI image reference into registry, repository, tag and digest, apply Docker Hub normalization, and show the registry manifest API path. Flags invalid names locally.
tools.method: The reference is read the way Docker's distribution reference grammar reads it. Everything after @ is a digest of the form algorithm:encoded; sha256 must carry 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters and sha512 must carry 128. A colon after the last slash starts the tag, while earlier colons belong to a registry port. The first of two or more path components is a registry when it contains a dot or colon, equals localhost, or is a bracketed IPv6 address; otherwise the registry is docker.io. index.docker.io and registry-1.docker.io normalize to docker.io, a single-component Docker Hub name gains the library/ namespace, and a reference with neither tag nor digest reports the effective tag latest. Repository components are checked against the lowercase distribution grammar and registry plus repository may not exceed 255 characters; tags may be up to 128 characters. The parser never contacts a registry, resolves a manifest, or proves that an image or tag exists.

sources.title: OCI Distribution Specification: reference grammar for registry, repository, tag and digest.
Docker Engine documentation: image names, tags and digests, and Docker Hub's docker.io/library normalization.
distribution/reference: splitDockerDomain treats a first component containing a dot or colon, or the name localhost, as a registry.

tools.name: Gelatin Sheet and Powder Converter
tools.description: Convert between sheet gelatin and powdered gelatin at different Bloom strengths: enter sheets and get the equivalent powder weight, or enter powder and get the number of sheets needed at a chosen grade.
tools.method: The conversion treats Bloom strength as setting power per gram. A sheet of mass w grams at Bloom B carries w times B bloom-grams, and the same setting power from powder at Bloom P needs w times B divided by P grams. Bronze, silver, gold and platinum sheets are taken as 2.5 g at 140 Bloom, 2.5 g at 160 Bloom, 2.0 g at 200 Bloom and 1.7 g at 250 Bloom; a custom grade takes 0.5 to 10 g per sheet and 50 to 400 Bloom from the fields. Powdered gelatin's Bloom strength is entered directly and runs from 50 to 400. Sheet counts run from 0.5 to 200 and powder weights from 0.1 to 1000 g, with at most three decimal places and no exponent or sign notation; blank, out-of-range and malformed values are refused with a field-specific message. A conversion is refused when it would exceed 1000 g of powder or 200 sheets. Bloom-grams, grams and the 200 Bloom reference are rounded half away from zero to two decimals and sheet counts to three. Converting powder back to sheets reports the exact fractional sheet count and the percentage by which rounding to whole sheets changes the setting strength. The bloom-gram identity is linear and approximate: Bloom is measured on a 6.67 percent gel at 10 degrees Celsius, and real gels, soaking and melting losses, and differences between makers are ignored. The tool converts quantities only; it does not set a recipe's gel strength and gives no food-safety guidance. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Gelatin Manufacturers Institute of America, Gelatin Handbook: Bloom value is the force in grams needed to depress a standard gel by 4 mm, measured on a 6.67 percent gel at 10 degrees Celsius.

tools.name: Knitting Needle & Crochet Hook Size Converter
tools.description: Convert knitting needle and crochet hook sizes between metric millimetres, US numbers, old UK numbers and US hook letters, and see the nearest standard sizes when a pattern names a diameter that is not made.
aliases: US to UK Needle Size Converter
us to uk needle size converter
tools.method: The chart is a fixed conversion table, not a calculation from the number: each row pairs one shaft diameter in millimetres with its US knitting number, its old UK knitting number (where one exists) and its US crochet hook label (where one exists). Diameters run from 2 mm to 25 mm in 23 rows, and the 14 crochet hooks from B/1 at 2.25 mm to N/15 at 10 mm all sit on the same diameter series, so a hook and a needle that share a millimetre value share a row. Sizes with no number in a system are reported as having none rather than being guessed: 3 mm has no US number, 3.5 mm and 12 mm and above have no old UK number. Input is accepted as a metric value with at most two decimals, a US number with an optional half, an old UK number including 0, 00 and 000, or a hook label with or without its number, so H, H/8 and h-8 all resolve. A value outside 2 to 25 mm, a number that is not in the table, or a blank field is refused with a field-specific message rather than being rounded silently. A metric value that lies between two rows reports the nearest standard size below and above it together with each gap in millimetres, and never interpolates a size that is not manufactured. US and old UK numbers run in opposite directions and were never fully standardised, so the table follows the published Craft Yarn Council and Vogue Knitting conversions and states the millimetre value as the authoritative one; makers disagree at the thick end, where US 17 is sold as 12 mm or 12.75 mm. The tool converts sizes only and gives no gauge, yarn-substitution or tension advice. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Barbell Plate Loading Calculator
tools.description: Work out which plates go on each side of a barbell for a target weight, check a rack with limited pairs, and see the closest weight you can actually build.
tools.method: Plates are loaded symmetrically: the target total minus the bar weight is split in half, and each half must be built from the pairs on the rack, counting one plate per pair on each side. The calculator searches every combination of the listed pairs in the unit's own increments - 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 2.5 and 1.25 kg, or 45, 35, 25, 10, 5 and 2.5 lb - and reports the exact target when it is reachable, preferring the combination with the fewest plates and repeating one plate size before mixing sizes. When the target is not reachable it reports the nearest lighter and heavier totals the rack can build, with the shortfall or surplus, rather than rounding silently. A full rack is four pairs of every size; pair counts can be lowered to model plates already on another bar. Because the load must balance, a difference whose hundredth of a unit cannot split in two is refused, as are targets outside 500 kg or 1,100 lb, bars above 100 kg or 220 lb, bars of zero, and non-integer pair counts. Collars, clips and bar flex are excluded, and the tool performs loading arithmetic only - not lifting, training or safety advice. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network requests.

tools.name: Ken Burns Pan & Zoom Planner
tools.description: Plan a Ken Burns move on a still or a wide shot: give the start and end zoom plus the pan positions and read the per-frame crop, image scale, zoom rate, pan travel and a keyframe table.
tools.method: The source is scaled to cover the output frame, so fit = max(frame width / source width, frame height / source height) and zoom z is a percentage of that fit: image scale = fit x z / 100, crop width = frame width / scale, crop height = frame height / scale. Zoom and both pan positions interpolate linearly over the frame index, and a pan value p places the crop centre at crop width / 2 + (p / 100) x (source width - crop width), so 0 is flush left and 100 is flush right. Frames = round(duration x frame rate), so the real clip is frames / frame rate. Image travel sums the per-frame centre movement scaled into output pixels; average speed divides that by the real clip duration and peak speed is the largest per-frame step times the frame rate. Oversampling is the tightest crop width divided by the frame width, so a value under 1 means the source is enlarged. Assumes a covered frame, no easing, no stabilisation and no rotation; a move smaller than one pixel per frame, or a crop below the frame size, will look stepped or soft in the rendered clip.

tools.name: Progression Key Detector
tools.description: Type a chord progression and rank all 24 major and minor keys by the weighted share of chord tones inside each key, with Roman numerals, in-key chord counts and outside tones for the best fit.
tools.method: Chord tokens are split on spaces, commas, semicolons, colons and bar lines; parentheses and brackets are removed, and sharps and flats are read in ASCII or as the musical signs. A token is a root letter with up to two accidentals, a quality and an optional slash bass; the quality table covers major, minor, power, sixth, seventh, major seventh, minor seventh, half-diminished, diminished, diminished seventh, augmented, suspended second and fourth, seventh suspended fourth, add nine, ninth, eleventh and thirteenth chords in their usual shorthand. Anything else is refused with the offending token, at most 64 chords are accepted, and an N.C. marker is skipped and reported. Each of the 24 major and natural-minor keys is scored by summing, over the chords, the number of chord tones that fall inside that key's seven-note scale times a position weight: 2 for the first chord, 2 for a middle chord and 3 for the last chord, or 3 when the progression has a single chord. The denominator is the same for every key, so the weighted fit percentage is directly comparable, and each chord also records whether all of its tones are inside the key. Ties are broken by tonic evidence, not by harmonic analysis: a tonic chord whose quality matches the mode (major triad for a major key, minor triad for a minor key) adds 2, a matching tonic chord in first position adds 10, one in last position adds 4, and a final dominant-to-tonic pair adds 6. Roman numerals come from the letter relationship between the chord root and the tonic, so the degree number is fixed by the letters and any accidental prefix is the difference between the chord root and that degree of the key; the numeral is upper case for major, dominant, augmented and suspended chords and lower case for minor and diminished ones, with the quality written as a suffix such as maj7, 7, ø7, °7, +, sus4, add9 or 9. Chords containing tones outside the scale are marked with those tones, spelled from the chord's own intervals. The page compares pitch classes only: inversions, voicings, melody, rhythm, harmonic function and secondary dominants are not modelled, and a short loop can fit two related keys equally well, which the result states rather than hides. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Roman numeral analysis labels a chord by the scale degree of its root, with upper case for major and lower case for minor qualities and accidentals written before the numeral for chromatic roots.

A major scale has semitone steps 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1 from its tonic and a natural minor scale 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, which fixes the seven pitch classes available to each of the 24 major and minor keys.

A diatonic progression uses chords whose tones belong to one key's scale; chords with tones outside it are borrowed or chromatic, and relative major and minor keys share the same seven pitch classes, so a short progression can fit both.

Common chord shorthand: a bare letter is a major triad, m is minor, 7 a dominant seventh, maj7 a major seventh, m7 a minor seventh, m7b5 a half-diminished seventh, dim7 a diminished seventh, sus4 replaces the third with the fourth, and an added 9 or 11 or 13 extends the chord without implying a seventh.

tools.name: Radar Range Equation Calculator
tools.description: Find a monostatic radar's maximum detection range from peak transmit power, antenna gain, frequency, target radar cross section, system losses and receiver sensitivity, then read the echo power, margin and round-trip time at a chosen range.
tools.method: The monostatic radar range equation sets the echo power at the receiver equal to the minimum detectable signal and solves for range: R_max = [P_t G^2 lambda^2 sigma / ((4 pi)^3 S_min L)]^(1/4), where P_t is peak transmit power in watts, G is the antenna gain as a linear power ratio (10^(dBi/10), entered once because the same antenna transmits and receives), lambda = c / f with c = 299,792,458 m/s, sigma is the target radar cross section in square metres, S_min is the receiver sensitivity in watts (entered in dBm and converted with 10^((dBm - 30)/10)), and L is the total system loss as a linear factor (10^(dB/10)). The echo at any range R is P_t G^2 lambda^2 sigma / ((4 pi)^3 R^4 L), so it falls by 6 dB per doubling of range twice over, a 1/R^4 law; the reported margin is that echo in dBm minus the entered sensitivity, and the round-trip time is 2R / c. Because range enters the equation to the fourth power, doubling the detection range needs sixteen times the power, sixteen times the radar cross section, four times the antenna gain, or 12 dB less loss. Inputs are bounded to keep the arithmetic in ordinary double precision: peak power 0.0001 to 1,000,000 W, gain 0 to 80 dBi, frequency 0.001 to 300 GHz, radar cross section 0.0001 to 1,000,000 m^2, system losses 0 to 100 dB, sensitivity -200 to 0 dBm and evaluation range 0.1 to 10,000,000 m. The model assumes free-space two-way propagation, a non-fluctuating point target of constant radar cross section, matched polarisation, and a single lumped loss term; it does not model atmospheric or rain absorption, multipath or ground reflection, clutter, the radar horizon, pulse integration, Swerling target fluctuation, or the probability of detection and false alarm behind the sensitivity figure, and a real radar's detection range also depends on the signal processing and the environment. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Skolnik, Introduction to Radar Systems: the monostatic radar range equation relates received echo power to peak transmit power, antenna gain squared, wavelength squared, radar cross section and the inverse fourth power of range, with the maximum range found where the echo equals the minimum detectable signal.

The (4 pi)^3 factor comes from the two-way spherical spreading: power density falls as 1/(4 pi R^2) on the way out and the same again on the return, after the target re-radiates the intercepted power in proportion to its radar cross section.
Antenna gain in dBi is a logarithmic power ratio, G = 10^(dBi/10); a 30 dBi antenna has a linear gain of 1000, and using the dBi number directly in the equation is a common error.
A power in dBm converts to watts as P = 10^((dBm - 30)/10), so -100 dBm is 10^-13 W; system loss in dB converts to a linear factor as L = 10^(dB/10).

Published worked examples used to check the arithmetic: a 1 MW S-band radar with 40 dBi gain, 1 m^2 target, 6 dB loss and -98 dBm sensitivity gives about 168 km, and a 12 kW X-band marine radar with 31 dBi gain, 10 m^2 target, 8 dB loss and -92 dBm sensitivity gives about 12.5 km.

tools.name: Video Signal Levels Converter
tools.description: Convert a video luma level between IRE, 8-bit, 10-bit and 12-bit code values in legal or full range, and see by how much a level falls outside the legal broadcast window.
tools.method: Legal (limited) range luma coding places reference black at code 16 and reference white at code 235 on the 8-bit scale, so 100 IRE spans 219 codes and one IRE is 2.19 codes; the 10-bit and 12-bit scales are the same signal sampled more finely, with code10 = 4 x code8 and code12 = 16 x code8, giving 64 and 940 for black and white in 10 bits and 256 and 3760 in 12 bits. Full (data) range uses the whole container instead, with code 0 at 0 IRE and code 255 at 100 IRE on the 8-bit scale, so 100 IRE spans 255 codes. The converter takes a level on one scale and a range, maps it to the 8-bit code value, and reports the level as IRE = (code8 - black) / span x 100, the equivalent 10-bit and 12-bit codes, and the percent of the full code range, code8 / 255 x 100. A level above 100 IRE is reported as that many IRE above legal white and a level below 0 IRE as that many IRE below legal black, which is the amount a legal-range encoder would clip; the nearest legal code (16 to 235 in legal range, 0 to 255 in full range) is shown for comparison. Inputs are bounded to the container: IRE -20 to 120, 8-bit 0 to 255, 10-bit 0 to 1023 and 12-bit 0 to 4095, and exponent notation is rejected rather than silently parsed. IRE is treated as a linear percentage of the encoded luma range; the tool does not model the display transfer function, chroma levels, colour gamut, HDR transfer functions, dithering, compression artefacts or noise, and it is not a waveform monitor reading. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: ITU-R BT.601 and BT.709 digital coding of the luma signal: 8-bit coding places black at 16 and white at 235 (10-bit 64 and 940, 12-bit 256 and 3760), leaving footroom and headroom outside the nominal range.
SMPTE RP 219 and EBU R 103 define the legal (broadcast-safe) range for luma as 0 to 100 IRE, with levels outside that window treated as excursions that a legaliser clips.
BT.709 full-range (data) coding, signalled by video_full_range_flag, maps code 0 to 0 IRE and code 255 to 100 IRE on the 8-bit scale, so every code carries picture information.
One IRE is 1/100 of the range between reference black and reference white, which is why 1 IRE is 2.19 8-bit codes in legal range and 2.55 codes in full range.
Code 255 in legal range sits at 109.1 IRE and code 0 at -7.3 IRE, the usual figures quoted for superwhite and the bottom of the footroom.

tools.name: Warm-Up Set Planner
tools.description: Turn a working weight into an empty-bar, 40, 60, 80 and 90 percent warm-up ladder with reps, with every rung rounded to the nearest weight the smallest plate pair can build.
tools.method: The ladder follows the widely used strength-training ramp: five reps with the empty bar, then five reps at 40 percent, three at 60 percent, two at 80 percent and one at 90 percent of the working weight, with percentages taken from the total working weight including the bar. A bar can only reach its own weight plus a whole number of times twice the smallest plate pair, because plates load in pairs, so every rung is rounded onto that grid: loadable = bar + 2 x pair x round((ideal - bar) / (2 x pair)), with half-step ties rounded up and anything at or below the bar pinned to the bar. A rung that rounds onto a load already in the ladder is dropped and counted, which is why a very light working weight shows only the bar and the heaviest rung that fits above it. The working weight itself is rounded onto the same grid and the difference is reported, so 101 kg entered against 1.25 kg pairs is shown as 100 kg. Reps and percentages are a coaching convention rather than a computed optimum: the tool does not know the lifter's training history, does not model fatigue, technique, injury or recovery, and is not medical, physiotherapy or rehabilitation advice. Inputs are bounded to 1000 of the chosen unit of working weight, a 100 bar ceiling, and pairs from 0.25 to 20, accept at most two decimal places, and reject exponent notation instead of silently parsing it. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: StrongLifts 5x5 warm-up protocol: two sets of five with the empty bar, then five reps at 40 percent, three at 60 percent, two at 80 percent and one at 90 percent of the working weight.
Starting Strength (Rippetoe) warm-up guidance: ramp sets expressed as percentages of the work-set weight with reps decreasing as the load rises.
International Powerlifting Federation, Technical Rules Book: 20 kg and 15 kg bars loaded with 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 2.5 and 1.25 kg discs, loaded in matching pairs.
Standard Olympic weight sets in pounds: a 45 lb bar with 45, 35, 25, 10, 5 and 2.5 lb plates, so the smallest available pair sets the loadable step.

Plates are loaded symmetrically, so every additional kilogram on the bar is twice the per-side pair; that symmetry is why the ladder is quantised to two times the smallest pair rather than to the pair itself.

tools.name: Sweat Rate Calculator
tools.description: Estimate hourly sweat rate from pre- and post-exercise body weight, the fluid you drank and any urine passed, in litres or fluid ounces per hour.
tools.method: The body-mass change method compares body mass immediately before and after a session. Every kilogram of mass lost is treated as approximately one litre of fluid, because one litre of sweat weighs close to one kilogram; the drink taken on during the session is added back and any urine passed is taken off, so sweat volume = (pre weight - post weight) + fluid drunk - urine passed. Dividing that volume by the session length in hours gives the hourly rate. Imperial input converts pounds to grams with the exact factor 453.59237 and US fluid ounces to millilitres with 29.5735295625 before the same arithmetic, so both unit systems agree. Percent body-mass change is the mass difference relative to the pre-exercise weight, shown from the before to the after weigh-in, so losing a kilogram reads -1 kg and finishing heavier reads positive. A session that implies zero or negative sweat loss is rejected rather than shown as a rate, because the inputs cannot support an estimate. Weights are bounded to 20-400 kg or 44-880 lb, fluids to 10 L or 340 fl oz, urine to 5 L or 170 fl oz, and sessions to whole minutes from 1 to 1440; every input accepts at most two decimal places and exponent notation is rejected rather than parsed. The tool assumes the two weigh-ins used the same scale and similar clothing, does not model evaporation, sodium or electrolyte losses, and gives no medical or hydration prescription; individual sweat rates vary widely and one session is only a sample. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Rep Tempo Calculator
tools.description: Convert a four-phase lifting tempo into seconds per rep, time under tension per set and block, and the clock time of the whole block including rest.
tools.method: Tempo is read as the conventional four numbers written in seconds: lowering (eccentric), pause at the bottom, lifting (concentric) and pause at the top, so 3-1-2-0 means a three-second lower, a one-second pause, a two-second lift and no pause at the top. Seconds per rep is the sum of the four phases. Time under tension for a set is that per-rep time multiplied by the reps, and the block total multiplies the set time by the number of sets. Rests are counted between sets only, so rest total is the rest interval multiplied by one fewer than the number of sets, and block clock time is the tension total plus the rest total; a single set therefore carries no rest. The work-to-rest ratio compares one set's tension time with one rest interval and is reported as absent when rest is zero. Share under tension is the tension total divided by the block clock time. Every input is a whole number: each phase is 0-30 seconds with a lifting phase of at least 1 second, reps are 1-100, sets 1-50 and rest 0-1800 seconds, and anything else is refused with a specific message rather than parsed loosely. The tool is purely arithmetic on the user's own timing inputs: it does not assess whether a tempo, rep range or rest is suitable, does not estimate load, fatigue or muscle growth, and is not coaching or medical advice. It assumes every rep in a set uses the same tempo and that no time is spent on set-up or equipment changes. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

Schoenfeld BJ, The mechanisms of muscle hypertrophy and their application to resistance training: rep duration and time under tension are treated as distinct training variables.
Baechle TR and Earle RW, Weight Training: Steps to Success: tempo notation such as 3-0-2-0 and rest intervals between sets are combined to plan a training block.

tools.name: Strength Volume Load Calculator
tools.description: Turn load, reps, sets and weekly sessions into volume load per set, per session and per week, with weekly reps and volume relative to bodyweight.
tools.method: Volume load, also called tonnage, counts the external work of a strength set as the load multiplied by the reps. One set of five at 100 kg therefore carries 500 kg of volume, five such sets in a session carry 2,500 kg, and three sessions a week carry 7,500 kg. Reps are counted the same way: reps per set multiplied by sets gives reps per session, and that multiplied by sessions gives reps per week. Relative volume divides the weekly total by bodyweight, so 7,500 kg a week at 80 kg bodyweight is 93.75 times bodyweight; it is reported only when a bodyweight is entered, and the same unit is assumed for load and bodyweight. The load must be 0.5-1000 in the selected unit with at most two decimals, reps 1-100, sets per session 1-20 and sessions per week 1-14, all whole numbers; bodyweight is optional and must be 20-400 when given, and anything malformed or out of range is refused with a specific message rather than parsed loosely. Only the external load is counted: the lifter's own body mass, band or machine assistance, sled friction and any warm-up sets the user does not enter are excluded, and one lift is handled at a time, so a full session is the sum of its separate entries. The tool reports arithmetic on the user's own entries and does not assess whether a load, rep range, set count or weekly frequency is suitable, does not estimate fatigue, adaptation, injury risk or progress, and is not coaching or medical advice. It also does not log, store or compare sessions over time. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

Session volume load is the sum of the volume load of the individual sets, so per-set volume times the number of sets.
Bodyweight, band assistance and machine assistance are separate from the external load placed on the bar or stack.

tools.name: Grade-Adjusted Pace Calculator
tools.description: Convert between pace on a hill or treadmill grade and flat-equivalent pace using Minetti's running energy-cost curve, with speed, vertical gain and cost ratio in metric or imperial units.
tools.method: The conversion treats a pace on a gradient as work done against the energy cost of running at that gradient, and asks what flat pace would cost the same. Cost of transport follows Minetti's running polynomial, 155.4i^5 - 30.4i^4 - 43.3i^3 + 46.3i^2 + 19.5i + 3.6 joules per kilogram per metre, with i the gradient as a fraction and 3.6 the flat cost, so a pace on a grade multiplied by 3.6 divided by the grade cost is the flat-equivalent pace and the reverse direction multiplies by the grade cost and divides by 3.6. The two directions are exact inverses because one divides by the same ratio the other multiplies by. Grade is entered as a percentage and limited to plus or minus 25 percent, inside the published curve's useful range but well short of its 45 percent limit, and zero grade returns the pace unchanged. Paces must be minutes:seconds with two-digit seconds from 00 to 59, between 2:00 and 30:00 per kilometre or 3:15 and 48:00 per mile; an equivalent outside 1:30 to 60:00 per unit is rejected rather than shown, and exponent notation, blanks and extra decimals are refused instead of parsed. Reported speed is the adjusted pace converted to km/h and mph, and vertical gain is the gradient applied to a kilometre or a mile. The model assumes steady running on a uniform gradient and ignores wind, surface, altitude, heat, technique, fatigue and the difference between treadmill belt speed and overground running; it gives a training reference, not a prediction, race plan or medical advice. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Stereoscopic Parallax Calculator
tools.description: Convert a stereo rig's interaxial, convergence and focal length into on-screen parallax in pixels and as a share of frame width, with the near and far limits of a parallax budget.
tools.method: Parallax is the horizontal separation of the left and right images of a point at the sensor, and the page computes it from the pinhole projection of a converged stereo rig. The focal length is first expressed in pixels as focal length divided by sensor width times the horizontal resolution, so a 35 mm lens on a 36 mm sensor at 1920 pixels across is 1866.67 pixels. The separation is that pixel focal length times the interaxial in metres times the difference between the reciprocal of the subject distance and the reciprocal of the convergence distance, which is the same as shifting each camera's image horizontally so that points at the convergence distance carry zero disparity. A subject nearer than the convergence distance therefore returns crossed parallax and sits in front of the screen plane; a subject beyond it returns uncrossed parallax and sits behind. The share of frame width is the absolute separation divided by the horizontal resolution, and the budget is entered as a percentage of that width. The near limit solves the same relation at positive budget, the far limit solves it at negative budget and is reported as no limit when the budget is wider than the convergence term, because uncrossed parallax then never reaches it at any distance. The largest interaxial is the baseline that puts this subject exactly on the budget. A zero interaxial is accepted and reported as no stereo separation with no limits. Focal lengths of 4 to 300 mm, sensor widths of 3 to 70 mm, resolutions of 320 to 8192 whole pixels, interaxials of 0 to 500 mm, convergence distances of 0.3 to 200 m, subject distances of 0.2 to 500 m and budgets of 0.05 to 5 percent are accepted; blanks, words, negatives, exponent notation and more than three decimal places are refused with the field named, and the horizontal field of view is reported from the same triangle as a check on the lens and sensor entries. The model assumes a parallel, converged rig with rectilinear lenses: toe-in, lens distortion, rolling shutter, floating windows, projection screen size and viewing distance are not modelled, and the comfortable budget for a real presentation depends on all of them. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: QoS Codepoint Mapper
tools.description: Decode a DSCP name or value into its DS field byte, IP precedence, per-hop behavior and recommended 802.1p priority, with a reverse lookup by priority.
tools.method: The DiffServ field is the IPv4 type-of-service byte reinterpreted: the top six bits are the differentiated services code point and the low two bits are the explicit congestion notification field, so the DS field byte is the codepoint multiplied by four plus the ECN value, and the three-bit IP precedence is the codepoint shifted right by three. Class Selector codepoints are the multiples of eight, CS0 to CS7, which keep the old precedence bits and zero the rest; the Assured Forwarding codepoints follow AFxy = 8x + 2y with class x from 1 to 4 and drop precedence y from 1 to 3, so AF41 is 34; Expedited Forwarding is 46, Voice Admit is 44 and Lower Effort is 1. The mapper accepts a codepoint name, a name written in lower case, the alias DF for CS0, or a plain decimal value from 0 to 63, and reports the canonical name, the six-bit binary codepoint, the DS field byte in decimal and hex, the ECN bits, the IP precedence with its RFC 791 name, the per-hop behavior and a recommended IEEE 802.1p priority. Values that are not one of the standard codepoints are reported as unassigned rather than assigned a guessed PHB or priority, because the code point space is only partly standardised. The 802.1p column is a conventional enterprise pairing, not a standard: switches may trust, rewrite or ignore the priority code point under their own policy, and DSCP remains the marking that selects a queue across routed hops, so the page states that the local configuration is authoritative. The reverse lookup lists the named codepoints that the same table pairs with a chosen priority. Blanks, words that are not codepoints, hexadecimal input, exponent notation, values outside 0 to 63, malformed AF and CS names and invalid ECN selections are refused with the field named, rather than silently coerced. The tool maps markings only: it does not police, shape, remark, measure or generate traffic, and it does not model vendor-specific queue assignments. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: RFC 2474, Definition of the Differentiated Services Field (DS Field) in the IPv4 and IPv6 Headers: six DSCP bits plus two currently unused bits, class selector codepoints as multiples of eight.
RFC 2597, Assured Forwarding PHB Group: four classes and three drop precedences, encoded as AFxy = 8x + 2y.
RFC 3246, An Expedited Forwarding PHB: the recommended Expedited Forwarding codepoint is 46 (101110).
IEEE 802.1Q, Bridges and Bridged Networks: the three-bit Priority Code Point in the VLAN tag, and the independence of layer-2 priority from the layer-3 DSCP.
RFC 3168, The Addition of Explicit Congestion Notification to IP: the two low bits of the DS field carry Not-ECT, ECT(1), ECT(0) and CE.
