tools.name: Grid Convergence Calculator
tools.description: Find the angle between true north and UTM grid north at a latitude and longitude, and convert a bearing between true and grid azimuths.
tools.method: Work on the WGS84 ellipsoid with a = 6,378,137 m and f = 1/298.257223563. A UTM zone's central meridian is 6z - 183 degrees, and the longitude difference from it is wrapped to -180..180 degrees. Grid convergence is evaluated with the transverse Mercator series through the third power of the longitude difference, gamma = delta sin(phi) + (delta^3 / 3) sin(phi) cos^2(phi) (1 + 3 eta^2), where phi is the geodetic latitude and eta^2 = e'^2 cos^2(phi) uses the second eccentricity squared; delta is in radians and the result is converted to degrees. A positive value means grid north lies east of true north, so true azimuth = grid azimuth + gamma and grid azimuth = true azimuth - gamma, each normalised to 0..360 with 360 treated as due north. Convergence is zero on the central meridian and at the equator and grows with latitude and with the distance from the central meridian. A longitude more than 6 degrees from the chosen zone's central meridian is refused and the refusal names the zone that contains it, because the series is only accurate to about 0.01 arc seconds within 3 degrees and 0.1 arc seconds out to 6 degrees. Latitude is accepted from -80 to 84 degrees (the UTM band), longitude from -180 to 180, the zone from 1 to 60 with a blank zone derived from the longitude, and the bearing from 0 to 360 degrees. Decimal commas are accepted; blank, non-numeric, exponent-notation and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named. Magnetic declination, local attraction, projection scale factor, geoid height and grid-to-ground distance reduction are not modelled.

sources.title: J. P. Snyder, Map Projections - A Working Manual (USGS Professional Paper 1395): transverse Mercator equations and the series for grid convergence.
EPSG Guidance Note 7-2, Coordinate Conversions and Transformations including Formulas: transverse Mercator convergence and the true/grid azimuth relationship.
C. F. F. Karney, Transverse Mercator with an accuracy of a few nanometers (2011): the Krueger n-series used as the independent reference for this page's values.
Ordnance Survey, A guide to coordinate systems in Great Britain: grid convergence, grid north and the sign convention for converting bearings.

tools.name: Cycling Power Zone Calculator
tools.description: Turn an FTP into Coggan cycling power zones with wattage and watts-per-kilogram bands, or estimate FTP from a 20-minute, 8-minute or ramp test.
tools.method: Functional threshold power is taken as the power a rider can hold for about an hour. It is either entered directly or derived from one test effort: a 20-minute average multiplied by 0.95, an 8-minute average multiplied by 0.90, or the final minute of a ramp test (maximal aerobic power, MAP) multiplied by 0.75. The product is rounded to the nearest whole watt with halves rounded up, and that integer is used for every zone so the displayed FTP and the bands always agree. The seven Coggan levels are active recovery up to 55% of FTP, endurance 56-75%, tempo 76-90%, lactate threshold 91-105%, VO2 max 106-120%, anaerobic capacity 121-150% and neuromuscular above 150%. Each upper edge is that percentage of FTP rounded to the nearest whole watt; each band then starts one watt above the previous edge, so the zones are contiguous integers and no watt belongs to two zones. Watts per kilogram divides the same watt bounds by the entered body mass and is reported to two decimals; it describes the same power, not a different zone set. The target intensity is a percentage of FTP between 1 and 200, converted to whole watts and labelled with the zone whose watt band contains that power, so the label always matches the number a rider would set on a head unit. FTP and test power are accepted from 40 to 2000 and 2500 watts respectively, body mass from 20 to 300 kilograms, and decimal commas are accepted; blank, non-numeric, exponent-notation and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named. The test conversion factors are population approximations, not measurements of an individual rider, and watts per kilogram says nothing about aerodynamics, terrain or fatigue. Heart rate, cadence, torque, glycogen use, training-load targets and any medical or performance-diagnostic claim are not modelled.

sources.title: A. Coggan and H. Allen, Training and Racing with a Power Meter: the seven power training levels defined as percentages of functional threshold power.

A. Coggan, training-level guidance for shorter tests: the 0.90 conversion from an 8-minute effort and the ramp-test MAP approximation used at about 0.75.
USA Cycling coaching levels and Coggan power-profile charts: watts per kilogram as threshold power relative to body mass.

tools.name: Subtitle Line Reflow
tools.description: Rewrap SRT or WebVTT cue text to a character and line limit, with even breaks, visible-character counting, and flags for cues that cannot fit or read too fast.
tools.method: Subtitle reflow rewrites only the cue text lines: the sequence number or identifier, the timestamp line, any cue settings and the order of the blocks are copied through as they are, and the file's line endings are normalised to LF. A cue's text is split into words; a line whose first non-space character is a hyphen, en dash or em dash starts a new run, so two-speaker dialogue keeps its break, and clearing the option merges every line of the cue. Each run is wrapped in two steps: greedy packing counts the fewest lines that hold its words inside the character limit, then the break points are chosen among those lines to minimise the sum of squared slack, the square of the limit minus each line width, so the words are spread as evenly as the line count allows. A word wider than the limit keeps its own line and is reported. Widths count visible characters: angle-bracket markup and an entity such as &amp; are kept in the output but use no character, so a styled line is measured as it renders, and the reading speed is the cue's visible characters divided by its duration in seconds. A cue is flagged when the reflowed text needs more lines than the maximum, when one word is longer than the line length, or when its reading speed exceeds the budget; flagged cues are still emitted, because shortening the wording is an editorial decision. Accepted limits are 5 MB of text and 5,000 cues, 10 to 100 characters per line, 1 to 5 lines and 5 to 60 characters per second, and blank, non-numeric, fractional or out-of-range settings are refused with the failing field named. Blocks without a valid timestamp line, and WebVTT NOTE, STYLE and REGION blocks, are passed through unchanged. The result is layout arithmetic on text the user supplies: it does not judge translation quality, caption sync or a platform's style guide, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: W3C, WebVTT: The Web Video Text Tracks Format - cue timings, cue settings, cue identifiers and NOTE, STYLE and REGION blocks.
SubRip (.srt) caption format - sequence number, a timestamp line with a comma before the milliseconds and one or more text lines per cue.

tools.name: Vertical Jump Power Calculator
tools.description: Convert a vertical jump height, or a flight time from a jump mat, into takeoff velocity and estimated peak power from the Sayers and Harman jump-power equations.
tools.method: Jump height is either entered directly as a jump-and-reach score or derived from a measured flight time on the kinematic relation for a vertical projectile, using g = 9.80665 m/s2: a jump that leaves the ground at v rises to h = v^2/(2g) and returns after t = 2v/g, so a flight time t corresponds to h = g*t^2/8 and the takeoff velocity is sqrt(2gh). Height, flight time and takeoff velocity are therefore three views of one jump and cannot disagree, and the same numbers are used for the power estimates. Peak power comes from two published regressions on squat-jump height in centimetres and body mass in kilograms: Sayers et al. (1999), 60.7 x height + 45.3 x mass - 2055, and Harman et al. (1991), 61.9 x height + 36.0 x mass - 1822. The Sayers equation is the headline figure because it was cross-validated on a larger and more varied sample, and the Harman result is shown beside it so the two estimates and their spread are visible; no averaging or ranking is invented. Both regressions were fitted to jump-and-reach scores against force-plate measurements, so they estimate mechanical power at takeoff within a few hundred watts and do not measure force, rate of force development, jump strategy or asymmetry. Metric input is centimetres and kilograms, imperial input is inches and pounds with 2.54 cm per inch and 0.45359237 kg per pound, flight time is always in seconds, and the units are converted before any arithmetic. Jump height is accepted from 5 to 150 cm (2 to 59 in), flight time from 0.10 to 1.20 s, and body mass from 20 to 300 kg (44 to 661 lb); decimal commas are accepted and blank, non-numeric, exponent-notation and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named. A height-and-mass pair at which either regression returns a non-positive power is refused rather than shown as a negative or zero figure. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: S. P. Sayers, D. V. Harackiewicz, E. A. Harman, P. N. Frykman and M. T. Rosenstein, Cross-validation of three jump power equations, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 31(4):572-577, 1999: squat-jump peak power = 60.7 x jump height (cm) + 45.3 x body mass (kg) - 2055.

E. A. Harman, M. T. Rosenstein, P. N. Frykman, R. M. Rosenstein and W. J. Kraemer, Estimation of human power output from vertical jump, Journal of Applied Sport Science Research 5(3):116-120, 1991: peak power = 61.9 x jump height (cm) + 36.0 x body mass (kg) - 1822.

Evaluation of power prediction equations: peak vertical jumping power in women, Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research: the same Harman and Sayers coefficients with the Harman constant subtracted, which is the form the published regressions use.
Standard projectiles kinematics: flight time t = 2 sqrt(2h/g) and takeoff velocity sqrt(2gh) for a jump with equal rise and fall times, with g = 9.80665 m/s2.

tools.name: H.264 Level Checker
tools.description: Find the lowest H.264 level that carries a frame size, frame rate and optional bitrate, with the frame-size, macroblock-rate, bitrate and DPB limits at that level.
tools.method: A frame is measured in 16x16 macroblocks: the width and height are each divided by 16 and rounded up, their product is the picture size in macroblocks, and that product times the frame rate is the macroblock rate. ITU-T H.264 Annex A states a level's limits as MaxFS (picture size in macroblocks), MaxMBPS (macroblocks per second), MaxDpbMbs (decoded picture buffer) and MaxBR (bitrate), and a stream conforms to a level when the picture fits MaxFS, neither side exceeds sqrt(8 x MaxFS), and the macroblock rate does not exceed MaxMBPS; the bitrate is limited to MaxBR multiplied by the profile's cpbBrNalFactor from Table A-2, which is 1.2 for Baseline, Main and Extended, 1.5 for High, 3.6 for High 10 and 4.8 for High 4:2:2 and High 4:4:4 Predictive. The tool walks Table A-1 from level 1 to 6.2 in order and returns the first level that satisfies all applicable constraints, so 1920x1080 at 30 fps is level 4 and at 60 fps is level 4.2. The reported DPB figure is MaxDpbMbs divided by the picture size, capped at 16 frames, which is how many reference frames a decoder at that level must hold; the reported maximum frame rate is MaxMBPS divided by the picture size, floored to two decimals so the figure is never above the limit. The binding line names the constraints that the level below fails, which is why the level was raised. Blank, non-numeric, exponent-notation, fractional-pixel and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named, and an input combination that no level carries is refused with level 6.2's limits for the chosen profile rather than reported as a level. Level 1b is excluded because it only applies to constrained-baseline streams; VBV buffer size, the MinCR bitrate floor, interlaced field coding, slice and reference-frame signalling and the level-signalling syntax itself are not checked, and a level is a decoder capability label rather than a picture-quality setting. The tables assume frame-coded progressive pictures. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Yarn Count Converter
tools.description: Convert a yarn count between tex, decitex, denier, metric count (Nm), cotton count (Ne), worsted, woolen run and linen counts, including plied yarns.
tools.method: Yarn count systems are either direct - mass per length, so a larger number is thicker - or indirect - length per mass, so a larger number is finer. Tex is grams per 1,000 m, so decitex is ten times the tex value and denier is nine times it, and every entry is converted through tex. An indirect count C is the number of hanks of its own length that weigh one pound, so its tex equivalent is 1,000 x 453.59237 / (hanks x yardsPerHank x 0.9144) / C: 1,000 for the metric count (1 km per kg), and 590.541, 885.812, 310.034 and 1,653.515 per unit of count for the cotton (840 yd), worsted (560 yd), woolen run (1,600 yd) and linen (300 yd) hanks. Both 0.9144 m per yard and 453.59237 g per pound are exact definitions, so those factors are computed from them rather than transcribed, and they agree with the six-figure factors in ASTM D2260 (0.590541, 0.885812, 0.310034 and 1.65352). The ply field multiplies the mass per length by the number of plies, which is the same as dividing an indirect count, so 2/28 Nm is two plies of 28 Nm and behaves as 14 Nm or 71.4 tex. Results are rounded half up to three significant figures, with a billionth of slack added before rounding so a value that should land exactly on a half rounds up rather than down. Counts are accepted for yarns from 0.01 to 10,000 tex (0.09 to 90,000 denier), and that range test allows a billionth of relative slack so a boundary written in another unit, such as 0.09 denier, is not refused because of binary representation error. Twists, retraction and shrinkage are out of scope: twisting takes up length, so a real plied yarn can be slightly finer than the arithmetic resultant, and a count is a nominal linear density rather than a measured diameter, so the tool does not estimate yarn thickness, gauge or fabric sett. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Time Scale Converter
tools.description: Convert a UTC instant into TAI, GPS time, GPS week and seconds of week, and TT, using the IERS leap-second table.
tools.method: UTC is a compromise between atomic time and the Earth's rotation. TAI counts SI seconds continuously on atomic clocks, while UTC inserts a leap second at 23:59:60 whenever the two drift towards 0.9 s, so TAI minus UTC is always a whole number of seconds. The converter reads a UTC date and time, looks the offset up in the IERS leap-second table (27 leap seconds since the system began in 1972, the last effective 2017-01-01, where the offset became 37 s), adds it, and prints TAI on the proleptic Gregorian calendar. GPS time is TAI minus 19 s, because the GPS epoch 1980-01-06T00:00:00Z is defined as the instant TAI minus UTC was 19 s; GPS seconds are counted from that epoch, so the GPS week is the whole number of 604,800-second weeks elapsed and the seconds of week are the remainder, with day 0 as Sunday. The week counter rolls over every 1,024 weeks (the last rollover began 2019-04-06T23:59:42Z, week 2048), and the full count since 1980 is reported here. TT, terrestrial time, is TAI plus 32.184 s exactly. A leap-second label 23:59:60 is accepted only on the 27 leap days in the table and is converted with the offset in force before the step, so 2016-12-31T23:59:60Z is 2017-01-01T00:00:36 TAI while the following midnight is 00:00:37 TAI. Dates are covered from 1972-01-01, before which UTC used fractional offsets, through 2100-12-31; GPS fields stay blank before 1980-01-06, and after the last table entry the offset is assumed to remain 37 s, which is a projection rather than an announcement. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Projector Brightness Calculator
tools.description: Convert projector lumens into screen luminance in foot-lamberts and nits for any screen size and gain, or find the lumens a brightness target needs.
tools.method: Screen luminance is the light a screen sends back to the audience. The calculator splits the image diagonal into width and height for the chosen aspect ratio, because h = d / sqrt(a^2 + 1) for a = width / height, multiplies the two to get the screen area, and spreads the projector's light output over it. Illuminance on the screen is lumens divided by the area in square metres; screen luminance in foot-lamberts is lumens x screen gain / area in square feet, and in cd/m2 it is that figure x 3.4263, which is the same as lumens x gain / (pi x area in m2). Gain 1.0 is a plain matte white surface that reflects light evenly in every direction; a gain 2.4 screen returns 2.4 times the luminance at its centre but narrows the viewing cone. One foot-lambert is 1/pi candela per square foot and one foot is exactly 0.3048 m. Three targets are offered: the DCI cinema 2D value of 48 cd/m2 (14 fL) from SMPTE ST 431-1, the 16 fL (55 cd/m2) that 35 mm film prints were graded for under SMPTE 196M, and the 7 fL (24 cd/m2) of legacy lamp-based 3D projection. Working back, the lumens a target needs are target fL x area in ft2 / gain, and the largest screen that still reaches the target at the available light follows from the same equation. The result is a centre-of-screen figure: real screens fall off towards the edges, and lens transmission, port glass and lamp ageing all remove light, so treat the number as a best case. Inputs are limited to 10-1,000 in, 10-100,000 lm and gain 0.1-10. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Aerobic Decoupling Calculator
tools.description: Compare the two halves of a steady endurance session: efficiency factor, aerobic decoupling and heart-rate drift from each half's time, distance and average heart rate.
tools.method: Aerobic decoupling compares how much speed a steady session produced per heartbeat in its first and second halves. The efficiency factor is speed divided by average heart rate: speed is the half's distance in metres divided by its duration in minutes, so the factor is in metres per minute per beat, and heart rate is the half's average in bpm. Decoupling is (first-half factor - second-half factor) / first-half factor x 100, so a positive value means the second half produced less speed per beat than the first, and a negative value means heart rate fell relative to the output. Pace is the half's duration per unit of distance, rounded to the nearest second. The 5% and 10% band edges are inclusive on the lower side: 5.0% or less is reported as coupled, just over 5% up to 10% as moderate drift, and above 10% as high drift, with the same sizes labelled negative drift when the sign is negative. Distances are converted with 1 km = 1,000 m and 1 mi = 1,609.344 m. Durations are accepted as MM:SS or H:MM:SS between 1:00 and 10:00:00, distances between 0.1 and 1,000 in the chosen unit, and average heart rates between 40 and 250 bpm. The figure is only meaningful when the halves are comparable: same route or trainer, similar terrain and cadence, steady effort, no stops, and consistent fuelling. Heat, dehydration, caffeine, illness and poor sleep raise heart rate without any loss of fitness, and a harder first half lowers the second-half efficiency factor for the same reason, so a single session is a signal and a repeated pattern is the trend. This is a training-analysis figure, not a medical measurement or a prediction of performance. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

Coyle, E. F. and Gonzalez-Alonso, J. (2001), Cardiovascular drift during prolonged exercise: new perspectives, Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews 29(2):88-92: heart rate rises and stroke volume falls during prolonged steady exercise, so pace per beat declines without a change in fitness.

Sawka, M. N. et al. (2007), ACSM position stand: Exercise and fluid replacement, Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise 39(2):377-390: dehydration and heat increase cardiovascular strain and heart rate at a fixed workload.

tools.name: CBOR Encoder & Decoder
tools.description: Decode CBOR bytes from hex or base64 into a value tree with byte offsets and a JSON view, or encode JSON into deterministic CBOR.
tools.method: CBOR is the Concise Binary Object Representation of RFC 8949. Decoding reads items from the first byte to the last: the first byte of each item carries a major type in its top three bits and additional information in the low five, so major types 0 and 1 are unsigned and negative integers (a negative integer n encodes the value -1 - n), 2 and 3 are byte strings and UTF-8 text strings, 4 and 5 are arrays and maps, 6 wraps a tag around one nested item, and 7 holds false, true, null, undefined, simple values and IEEE 754 binary16, binary32 and binary64 floats. Lengths and integer values below 24 sit in the header byte itself, and larger ones follow in 1, 2, 4 or 8 big-endian bytes; additional information 31 marks an indefinite-length string, array or map, which runs until a 0xff break byte. The page reports each item's byte offset and encoded length, validates UTF-8 strictly (rejecting overlong forms, surrogate code points, code points above U+10FFFF and cut-off sequences), and rejects truncation, reserved additional information 28 to 30, a break outside an indefinite item, indefinite strings whose chunks are not of the same major type, and simple values below 32 encoded as a following byte. Integers above 2^53 are shown as exact decimal strings because JavaScript numbers cannot hold them, and tags 2 and 3 whose payload is a byte string also show the decimal bignum value. Maps with text keys become JSON objects; maps with any other key type, or with a repeated key, are shown as an ordered $map list of pairs. Items that use more bytes than the shortest form are counted as non-minimal rather than rejected, and duplicate map keys, indefinite lengths, tags and the bignum note are listed per item, so the page inspects CBOR as it is rather than re-serialising it. Encoding parses a JSON value and writes canonical CBOR: the shortest integer form, definite lengths, UTF-8 text, 64-bit floats for non-integral numbers, and map keys ordered by encoded key length and then bytewise, the deterministic encoding of RFC 8949 section 4.2.1. Byte strings, tags, wide integers, undefined, simple values and special floats are written from the markers $bytes, $tag, $bigint, $undefined, $simple and $float, and $map writes an ordered map whose keys are not limited to text. Inputs are limited to 4,096 bytes, 2,000 items and 32 levels of nesting, and every value is computed in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: RIAA Equalization Calculator
tools.description: Read the RIAA disc equalization curve at any frequency: playback and record gain in decibels relative to 1 kHz, the amplitude ratio, the standard curve table and chart, and the phono-stage gain a cartridge needs.
tools.method: RIAA equalization is the disc recording characteristic adopted in the 1950s and still used for vinyl: the cutter reduces low frequencies and boosts high frequencies, and the phono stage applies the inverse on playback. The curve is fixed by three time constants, 3180, 318 and 75 microseconds, which put its corners at 50.05 Hz, 500.5 Hz and 2122 Hz. The playback magnitude is sqrt(1 + (2 pi f T2)^2) divided by sqrt(1 + (2 pi f T1)^2) times sqrt(1 + (2 pi f T3)^2), with T1 = 3180 us, T2 = 318 us and T3 = 75 us, normalised so that 1 kHz is 0 dB. That gives the familiar shape: a flat bass shelf at about +19.3 dB below 50 Hz, a 6 dB per octave bass slope between 50 Hz and 500 Hz, a flat mid band from 500 Hz to 2122 Hz, and a 6 dB per octave treble roll-off above 2122 Hz that reaches about -19.6 dB at 20 kHz. The record curve is the exact inverse, so the same numbers are shown with the opposite sign as the cut applied to the master. The standard defines no upper limit above the 75 microsecond corner, so the treble slope continues; the 3.18 microsecond correction sometimes called the Neumann pole is not part of the standard and is not added here, and the withdrawn 1976 IEC amendment that added a 7950 microsecond pole near 20 Hz is not applied either. Amplitude ratio is the linear form of the same gain, 10^(dB / 20). The stage gain follows from the cartridge output at 1 kHz and the target line level as 20 log10(target / cartridge), and the output at any other frequency is that target multiplied by the ratio there, which is why a stage sized for 1 V at 1 kHz must swing about 9.2 V at 20 Hz. Inputs are limited to 1 to 100000 Hz, 0.05 to 20 mV of cartridge output and 50 to 20000 mV of target output; results outside 20 Hz to 20 kHz are labelled as an extrapolation. Everything is computed in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

tools.name: HRV Baseline Calculator
tools.description: Compare the latest morning rMSSD heart-rate-variability reading with a 7, 14 or 28-night baseline: mean, sample standard deviation, coefficient of variation, z-score, trend, a band chart and a reading-by-reading table, all computed locally.
tools.method: rMSSD is the root mean square of successive differences between R-R intervals, a time-domain heart-rate-variability measure that consumer wearables commonly report for an overnight or morning reading; this page works in milliseconds. The baseline is the arithmetic mean of the most recent 7, 14 or 28 readings you paste, and the spread is the sample standard deviation with n minus 1 in the denominator, sqrt(sum of squared deviations / (n - 1)). The coefficient of variation is the standard deviation divided by the mean, times 100, so variability can be compared between windows whose absolute rMSSD differs. The z-score is (latest reading - baseline mean) / standard deviation: it is labelled inside one standard deviation when |z| < 1, outside one standard deviation when 1 <= |z| < 2, and two or more standard deviations otherwise, always with the direction shown, and it is not computed at all when every reading in the window is identical. The trend is an ordinary least-squares slope of reading against position in the window, reported in milliseconds per reading; it describes the past window and is not a forecast. The chart plots at most the last 28 readings with the baseline mean and the mean plus or minus one standard deviation band. Readings are limited to 3 to 180 values of 5 to 300 ms, and the window is limited to 7, 14 or 28 readings; when fewer readings are available than the window asks for, every available reading is used and the page says so. The page reports descriptive statistics for the user's own numbers only: it makes no diagnosis, produces no readiness score, gives no training or medical advice, and does not account for device, sensor, posture or measurement-time differences. Everything is computed in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

tools.name: Flicker-Free Shutter Planner
tools.description: Find the shutter angle that covers a whole number of mains-light pulses so 50 Hz and 60 Hz lighting stops banding: pulse period, pulses per frame, brightness swing, safe angles and the nearest safe shutter at any frame rate.
tools.method: Mains-powered tungsten, fluorescent and HMI lamps follow the supply voltage, so their light output ripples at twice the mains frequency: 100 Hz on a 50 Hz supply and 120 Hz on a 60 Hz supply, one pulse every 1 / ripple seconds. A camera frame integrates the light while the shutter is open, so an exposure that spans a whole number of pulses collects the same light in every frame, while the fractional remainder leaves a frame-to-frame brightness swing of roughly that fraction of the lamp's modulation. The page computes the exposure as shutter angle / (360 x frame rate), divides it by the ripple period to get the pulses covered, and calls the setting flicker-safe when the result is within 0.5% of a whole pulse; the leftover fraction is also reported as a percentage brightness swing. The whole-pulse shutter speeds are k / ripple for integer k, which at frame rate p correspond to the angles 360 x k x p / ripple; the page lists up to twelve of them that fit inside one frame and recommends the one whose exposure is closest to the entered target in stops, breaking a tie towards the shorter exposure. When the ripple is faster than a frame, no shutter angle can cover a whole pulse and the page names frame rates that divide the ripple instead. A custom ripple frequency covers dimmed LED fixtures whose driver rate differs from the mains ripple. Frame rates are limited to 1-240 fps, shutter angles to 1-360 degrees and custom frequencies to 10-2000 Hz. Rolling-shutter readout skew, aperture, ND filtration and camera-specific flicker filters are outside the model, and the result is a planning aid rather than a guarantee for a particular camera and lamp. Everything is computed in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

sources.title: Mains-powered tungsten, fluorescent and HMI lamps follow the supply voltage and ripple at twice the mains frequency, 100 Hz on a 50 Hz supply and 120 Hz on a 60 Hz supply.

A frame integrates light over its exposure, so an exposure spanning a whole number of ripple periods collects the same light every frame, and the fractional remainder sets the brightness swing between frames.
Exposure time is shutter angle / (360 x frames per second), the relation used in camera manuals such as the American Cinematographer Manual, ARRI and RED documentation.
The conventional workarounds are 172.8 degrees at 24 fps on a 50 Hz supply (1/50 s) and 144 degrees at 24 fps on a 60 Hz supply (1/60 s).

tools.name: Critical Swim Speed Calculator
tools.description: Turn a 400 and a 200 time trial into critical swim speed: CSS in metres or yards per second, threshold pace per 100, distance reserve and repetition times from 70% to 110% of CSS.
tools.method: Critical swim speed is the slope of the distance-time line through two maximal trials: CSS = (400 - 200) / (T400 - T200) in metres or yards per second, with both times in seconds. The page reports that speed, the equivalent pace per 100 as 100 / CSS, which is also exactly (T400 - T200) / 2 seconds, the average pace of each trial, the distance reserve D' = 400 - CSS x T400 (the part of the 400 that stored work covered rather than the sustainable rate), and a table of pace and repetition time at 70, 75, 80, 85, 90, 95, 100, 105 and 110 percent of CSS speed, where pace = CSS pace / (percent / 100) and repetition time = distance / speed. Times are entered as minutes:seconds or whole seconds, must fall between 1:00 and 1:00:00, the 400 must be the longer swim, and the resulting speed must fall between 0.3 and 2.5 units per second; a 200 faster than half the 400 time (a negative distance reserve) or a 400 more than 2.5 times the 200 time is reported as a caution. The protocol is fixed at 400 and 200, in metres or yards. Critical swim speed is a model of the sustainable rate: swimmers usually hold it for tens of minutes rather than indefinitely, pacing errors in either trial shift it, and 25 m and 50 m pools give different values. It is a training aid, not a lab measurement or medical advice, and everything is computed in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

tools.name: Beat Cut Planner
tools.description: Turn a tempo into a frame-accurate cut list: beat and bar lengths, frames per beat, SMPTE timecode and frame numbers for every cut, and the drift of a fixed whole-frame spacing.
tools.method: A tempo fixes the length of a musical beat: one beat lasts 60 / BPM seconds and one bar lasts that beat times the beats per bar, so 120 BPM in 4/4 gives a 500 ms beat and a 2 s bar. At a project frame rate the same beat is beat seconds x frames per second long; the page lists that value exactly, then places each requested cut on the nearest whole frame and reports the frame number, the SMPTE timecode built from that frame index, and the distance in milliseconds between the cut and the exact beat. Cuts can be listed every beat, every bar, every 2 bars or every 4 bars, with an optional first-beat offset in seconds or minutes:seconds, and the plan covers 1 to 64 bars. Placing every cut independently on the nearest frame keeps the error bounded by half a frame (about 20.8 ms at 24 fps) rather than accumulating, while holding one whole number of frames per gap accumulates: the page reports that fixed-spacing drift at the last cut. Timecode uses the nominal rate, with drop-frame labels at 29.97 and 59.94 that skip frame numbers at the top of each minute except every tenth, and standard non-drop labels at 23.976, which run about 0.1% behind wall-clock time. Tempo is limited to 20-300 BPM, bars to 1-64, the offset to 0-600 s and the list to 240 cut points. The page does not detect beats, and live performance drifts away from a click, so the plan is a starting point to check against the waveform. Everything is computed in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.

sources.title: A beat at a given tempo lasts 60 / BPM seconds, and a bar is that beat multiplied by the beats per bar; this is the standard relation between tempo, note value and duration used by DAWs and notation software.

Frame rate converts a duration into frames: a time in seconds multiplied by frames per second gives the frame position, and rounding to the nearest whole frame bounds the quantisation error by half a frame.

SMPTE timecode labels a frame index as hours:minutes:seconds:frames, and drop-frame counting at 29.97 and 59.94 skips frame numbers at the top of each minute except every tenth so the label follows the clock.

tools.name: Altitude Oxygen Calculator
tools.description: Estimate the oxygen available to breathe at an elevation: standard-atmosphere station pressure, inspired oxygen partial pressure, the share of the sea-level value and the pressure altitude, with an optional measured-pressure override.
tools.method: Altitude oxygen turns an elevation into the pressure of the air, then into the oxygen pressure a breath delivers. Standard station pressure follows the International Standard Atmosphere: p = 1013.25 hPa x (1 - 2.25577e-5 x h)^5.25588, with h in metres, a sea-level temperature of 15 C and a 6.5 C/km lapse rate, the tropospheric model valid to 11 km. The page accepts elevations from -500 to 9,000 m and converts feet with 1 ft = 0.3048 m. Inspired oxygen pressure is FiO2 x (p - 6.266 kPa), with FiO2 = 0.20946 and 6.266 kPa the saturated water-vapour pressure of air at 37 C; it is reported in kPa and mmHg (1 kPa = 7.50062 mmHg). Oxygen availability divides that value by its sea-level result of 19.91 kPa, so sea level is exactly 100% and elevations below sea level are above it. An optional measured station pressure from 300 to 1100 hPa replaces the standard value, and the pressure altitude is the standard-atmosphere altitude that would produce the pressure in use, obtained by inverting the same formula. A caution is raised when the elevation is 2,500 m or more, when a measured pressure differs from the standard atmosphere by more than 3%, and when the elevation is below sea level. Display is rounded: pressure to 0.1 hPa, inspired oxygen to 0.01 kPa and 0.1 mmHg, availability and pressure ratio to 0.1%, altitudes to the nearest metre and foot, with calculations in double precision. The reference table lists the standard atmosphere every 500 m from 0 to 5,000 m. The standard atmosphere is a reference model rather than a weather report, so real station pressure varies by a few percent with weather and temperature and humidity shift density further. The result is physics, not a medical measurement: it does not predict altitude illness, acclimatisation, oxygen saturation or performance. Everything runs in the browser with no network access, uploads or storage.

sources.title: International Civil Aviation Organization, Manual of the ICAO Standard Atmosphere, Doc 7488/3 (1993): sea-level pressure 1013.25 hPa, 15 C, a 6.5 C/km tropospheric lapse rate and the barometric formula used here.

West, J. B., Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials, 9th edition: inspired oxygen pressure is FiO2 x (PB - PH2O), with PH2O about 47 mmHg (6.27 kPa) at 37 C and FiO2 about 0.2095 in dry air.

tools.name: Multicast MAC Address Mapper
tools.description: Map an IPv4 or IPv6 multicast group to the Ethernet MAC address it is sent to, and work backwards from a multicast MAC to every group that can share it. Pure bit arithmetic, in your browser.
tools.method: An IPv4 multicast group (224.0.0.0/4) maps to the Ethernet MAC 01:00:5e followed by the low 23 bits of the group address (RFC 1112), so bits 27 to 23 are dropped and 32 groups share one MAC; the fourth MAC octet can only reach 7f, so a 01:00:5e address whose fourth octet is 80 to ff has no IPv4 group. An IPv6 multicast group (ff00::/8) maps to 33:33 followed by the low 32 bits (RFC 2464), so 96 bits are dropped and 2^96 groups share one MAC. The page accepts an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address (any valid group syntax, an optional %zone id, a dotted IPv4 tail) or a MAC in colon, dash, Cisco dotted or bare form, checks the multicast (I/G) bit in the first octet, and refuses unicast MACs and multicast MACs outside the 01:00:5e and 33:33 prefixes. IPv4 results list all 32 groups with the same low 23 bits; IPv6 results give the low 32 bits and the link-local example group. Address blocks are labelled (224.0.0.0/24 link-local, 224.0.1.0/24 internetwork control, 232.0.0.0/8 source-specific, 233.0.0.0/8 GLOP, 239.0.0.0/8 administratively scoped) and the IPv6 scope comes from the low nibble of the second octet. The page states that a switch forwarding table cannot distinguish groups that share a MAC. Everything runs in the browser with no network access, uploads or storage.

sources.title: RFC 1112, Host Extensions for IP Multicasting (1989): IPv4 multicast groups in 224.0.0.0/4 and the Ethernet mapping to 01:00:5e plus the low 23 bits.
RFC 2464, Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Ethernet Networks (1998): the multicast MAC 33:33 followed by the low 32 bits of the IPv6 group.
RFC 4291, IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture (2006): the ff00::/8 format, its flags and scope fields, and the scope values reported here.
IEEE 802-2014, IEEE Standard for Local and Metropolitan Area Networks: the I/G bit in the first octet separates group (multicast) from individual (unicast) MAC addresses.

tools.name: Linux Device Number Decoder
tools.description: Decode a Linux device number between major:minor and dev_t, with the glibc bit packing, the kernel value, the node name, a mknod line and the driver registered for the major. Runs in your browser.
tools.method: A Linux device number is a 12-bit major and a 20-bit minor, so the page refuses a major above 4095 or a minor above 1048575 instead of silently truncating it. The input is auto-detected: a pair with one colon (the /proc/partitions and lsblk form), a pair with one comma (the ls -l device column), a run of digits (a decimal dev_t), or a 0x-prefixed value (a hex dev_t); anything else is refused with the accepted forms in the message. Userspace packs the pair with glibc makedev, which keeps the major in bits 8 to 19, the low minor byte in bits 0 to 7 and minor bits 8 to 19 in bits 20 to 31; the page also reports the kernel MKDEV value, major times 1048576 plus minor, because the two layouts differ and only the first is what stat, ls and mknod use. Device numbers whose minor needs the high field (above 255) exercise the split directly, for example 8:300 becoming 0x10082c. The major table follows the kernel devices.txt registry: memory devices, TTY and alternate TTY devices, misc devices, input core, Unix98 PTY masters and slaves, USB devices and USB serial, DRI, RAM disks, loop devices, SCSI disks, metadisks, SCSI CD-ROM and MMC, plus the dynamic and local ranges 234-254 and 240-254. Node names are derived only where the registry documents the mapping: sd letters use 16 minors per disk (8:17 is sdb1), MMC cards use the default 8-minor stride, UART ports start 64 minors after the virtual consoles, and the input core splits joystick, mouse and event minors on 32-minor boundaries. Majors that appear in both tables, such as 1, are reported as ambiguous rather than given one node, and an unregistered major says so instead of guessing a driver. Everything is computed locally with integer arithmetic: no network access, uploads or storage.

sources.title: Linux kernel Documentation/admin-guide/devices.txt: the registry of major numbers, the names and node numbers used by the table, and the note that 259 block is a dynamic extended major.
makedev(3) from the Linux man-pages: makedev combines a major and minor into a dev_t, and major() and minor() split the st_rdev or st_dev value returned by stat(2).
glibc misc/sys/sysmacros.h: the exact gnu_dev_makedev and gnu_dev_major bit layout reproduced on this page, with the major in bits 8 to 19 and the minor split across bits 0 to 7 and 20 to 31.
Linux kernel include/linux/kdev_t.h: MINORBITS is 20, so MKDEV packs the major above the minor and the two encodings differ for the same pair.

tools.name: Triathlon Split Planner
tools.description: Plan a triathlon split: set a target finish time, both transitions and two leg paces, and get the swim, bike and run splits with the speed or pace the open leg has to hold. Runs in your browser.
tools.method: The plan is fixed by the target and the two legs you do not leave open. Each known leg is its distance times its pace: the swim in metres divided by 100 times the swim pace, the run in kilometres times the run pace, and the bike in kilometres divided by its speed times 3600 to get seconds. Both transitions are subtracted from the target first, so the open leg takes whatever remains and must still be a positive time: the target minus T1, T2 and the two known legs. When the bike is open its average speed is the bike distance divided by that remaining time, and the page reports it in km/h; when the run is open its pace is the remaining time divided by the run distance in km; when the swim is open its pace is the remaining time divided by the swim distance in hundreds of metres. The four course presets fill the standard distances - sprint 750 m, 20 km and 5 km; Olympic 1.5 km, 40 km and 10 km; 70.3 1.9 km, 90 km and 21.0975 km; Ironman 3.8 km, 180 km and 42.195 km - and leave the paces alone, so the same target can be re-costed on a longer course. Times accept h:mm:ss, mm:ss or plain seconds with at most one decimal place, and are range-checked rather than clamped: the target must fall between 5 minutes and 36 hours, each transition between 0 and 2 hours, swim distance between 50 and 10000 m, bike distance between 1 and 500 km, run distance between 1 and 100 km, swim pace between 0:30 and 20:00 per 100 m, run pace between 2:00 and 30:00 per km, and a typed bike speed between 5 and 100 km/h. A solved leg outside those same ranges is refused instead of printed, so a target that would demand 100.8 km/h on the bike or a 0:15 swim pace says so. The splits are averages for the whole leg: no wind, gradient, drafting, wetsuit, sighting or pacing strategy is modelled, and the transitions are the fixed times entered rather than estimates. Times are displayed rounded to the nearest second and the solved speed to one decimal, so a shown split can differ from the underlying value by up to half a second. Everything is computed locally with arithmetic on the numbers typed: no network access, uploads, accounts or storage.

sources.title: World Triathlon competition distances: sprint 750 m swim, 20 km bike, 5 km run; standard distance 1.5 km, 40 km, 10 km; middle distance 1.9 km, 90 km, 21.0975 km; long distance 3.8 km, 180 km, 42.195 km.
Pace convention used by race results: swim pace is quoted per 100 m and run pace per kilometre, each as time per unit distance.
Arithmetic: leg time is distance times pace, the open leg is the target minus both transitions and the two known legs, and average speed is distance divided by time.

tools.name: JUnit XML Report Summarizer
tools.description: Paste a JUnit XML report and get the pass, fail, error and skip counts, each suite's totals, the slowest test cases and the failing tests with their messages. Runs in your browser.
tools.method: The report is read by a strict XML reader built into the page. Each <testcase> element counts once. Its status comes from its child elements: a <failure> child makes it a failure, an <error> child makes it an error, a <skipped> child makes it skipped, and a test case with none of those children passes. When a test case carries more than one of those children the precedence is failure, then error, then skipped, so a test case that was both skipped and failed is reported as a failure. The pass count is the total number of test cases minus the failures, errors and skips. A test case is attributed to the nearest enclosing <testsuite>, so a suite row counts only the test cases directly inside it and the rows of a report with nested suites do not add up to the file total. Each suite row also shows the suite time attribute when it has one, and otherwise the sum of its own test case times. The report duration is the sum of the suite time attributes when every suite carries a numeric time, otherwise the sum of every test case time, otherwise it is reported as having no timing attributes. Declared attributes are not trusted: the tests attributes are summed and compared with the counted <testcase> elements, and a difference is shown as a warning instead of replacing the counted total. Numeric attributes must be a non-negative decimal; a time that does not match is ignored rather than guessed at. The slowest list holds the five test cases with the largest time values, ties kept in document order, and only the first 50 failing test cases are listed with their type, message and the first line of the failure text. The reader rejects what it cannot read exactly: a DOCTYPE declaration, an unknown entity, a repeated attribute, a malformed or unclosed tag, more than one root element, text outside the root, more than 200000 elements or more than 4000000 characters. The root element must be <testsuites> or <testsuite>, element names may carry a namespace prefix, and element and attribute names are matched by their local name. Names and messages are whitespace-collapsed and truncated at 140, 240, 240 and 80 characters respectively for display. No validation harness is run, no test is re-executed and nothing is uploaded: the file is parsed as text in the browser tab with no network access, accounts or storage.

sources.title: JUnit XML report format as emitted by pytest, Maven Surefire, Gradle, Jest and gotestsum: testsuites and testsuite elements carrying tests, failures, errors and time attributes, with testcase children.
XML 1.0 specification: element and attribute syntax, quoted attribute values, the five predefined entities and numeric character references.
XSD schema for the common JUnit report format: testcase elements carry name, classname and time, and failure, error and skipped are child elements.

tools.name: Coffee Cupping Score Calculator
tools.description: Add up a specialty-coffee cupping form from the six attribute scores, the overall score, the uniformity, clean-cup and sweetness cup counts and any defect deductions, and read the total out of 100 with its grade band.
tools.method: The page adds up a specialty-coffee cupping form exactly as the scores are entered. Six descriptive attributes - fragrance / aroma, flavor, aftertaste, acidity, body and balance - and the overall score each accept 6.00 to 10.00 in steps of 0.25. The three cup-consistency rows, uniformity, clean cup and sweetness, are entered as a count of cups from 0 to 5 and are worth 2 points per counted cup, so five clean cups score 10 in each row. Defects deduct 2 points for each tainted cup and 4 for each faulty cup, and the two counts may not add up to more than the five cups because a cup carries one defect level. All arithmetic is done in quarter-point units, so no rounding error can move a total across a grade boundary; the total is the six attribute scores plus the overall score plus the cup points minus the defect deduction, out of 100. Grade bands are 90 and above outstanding specialty, 85 to 89.75 excellent specialty, 80 to 84.75 very good specialty, and below 80 not specialty. Decimal commas are accepted, exponent notation is not, and scores not on a 0.25 step, outside 6 to 10, or cup counts that are not whole numbers from 0 to 5 are refused with the exact reason. The page does not taste anything, does not calibrate a cupper and makes no commercial claim: it is ordinary arithmetic on the scores supplied. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads, accounts or network access.

sources.title: Specialty Coffee Association cupping protocol and cupping form: ten attributes, six descriptive and overall scores marked 6 to 10 in 0.25 steps, uniformity, clean cup and sweetness scored 2 points per cup across five cups, defects deducted 2 points per tainted cup and 4 per faulty cup.
SCA cupping score interpretation: totals are out of 100 and 80 points is the specialty-coffee threshold, with 85 to 89.75 and 90 and above as the excellent and outstanding bands.
Specialty Coffee Association cupping form instructions: a tainted cup carries a defect at the 2-point level and a faulty cup at the 4-point level.

tools.name: Dovetail Layout Calculator
tools.description: Divide a board's width into equal tails and pins at your chosen pin-to-tail ratio, with the tail and pin widths and every marking position from the left edge.
tools.method: The joint is laid out across the board's width with a half pin at each end, then alternating tails and pins, so n tails sit between n-1 full pins and two half pins. The pin-to-tail ratio is the pin width divided by the tail width. With board width w, n tails and ratio k, the tail width is w divided by n times (1 + k), the pin width is k times the tail width, and each edge half pin is half a pin width, so n tails plus n pin widths fill the board width exactly. The marks are the cumulative positions of every tail and pin boundary measured from the left edge, excluding the board's own edges; there are twice as many marks as tails. Widths, half pins and marks are rounded to 0.001 mm and displayed to two decimals, so a long run of marks can drift by a few hundredths of a millimetre. A board width from 10 to 1000 mm, a whole tail count from 1 to 10 and a pin-to-tail ratio from 0.2 to 3 are accepted. A layout that would leave tails or pins under 3 mm wide is refused because the joint cannot be marked or cut at that size, and text, exponent notation, a blank field, a board outside the range, a tail count that is not a whole number, and a ratio outside the range are refused with the exact reason. Decimal commas are accepted. The layout does not model saw kerf, board thickness, the dovetail slope, deliberately uneven spacing or the mirrored cut on the mating board, and it is a marking aid, not a structural claim. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Hand-cut dovetail layout: the joint is divided into equal tails with a half pin at each end and pins between them, so the tail and pin widths fill the board's width.
Dovetail pins are commonly cut narrower than the tails, and the sides are sawn at about 1:6 in softwood and 1:8 in hardwood.
Dovetail marks are measured from one edge along the end grain so the tails and pins stay centred and the joint closes without a gap.

tools.name: TDR Fault Distance Calculator
tools.description: Turn a time-domain reflectometer's round-trip delay and the cable's velocity factor into the distance to a fault, with the one-way delay, signal speed, dielectric constant and the position along the run.
tools.method: The reflectometer launches a pulse down the cable and times the echo, which travels out to the fault and back, so the distance to the fault is half the round-trip delay multiplied by the signal speed. The signal speed is the velocity factor times the speed of light in vacuum, 299792458 m/s, and the dielectric constant of a homogeneous insulator is one over the velocity factor squared. With velocity factor vf and round-trip delay t in nanoseconds the distance is vf * c * t * 1e-9 / 2, the one-way delay is t / 2, the round-trip delay for a cable of length L is 2L / (vf * c), and when a cable length is supplied the position along the run is the distance divided by that length as a percentage. Feet are metres divided by 0.3048. Distances in metres and feet are rounded to 0.001, the one-way delay to 0.001 ns, the signal speed to the nearest m/s, the dielectric constant to 0.001 and the position to 0.1 percent. Velocity factors from 0.1 to 0.99, round-trip delays greater than 0 and at most 1000000 ns, and an optional cable length greater than 0 and at most 100000 m are accepted. Text, exponent notation, a blank velocity factor or delay, a value outside those ranges, zero or negative values and a malformed decimal are refused with the exact reason, and decimal commas are accepted. A distance beyond the supplied cable length is reported with a warning rather than refused. This is arithmetic on the numbers you measured: it does not measure the cable, does not model dispersion, a splice, a splitter or a bridged tap, and cannot tell a fault from the far end of an unmatched cable. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A time-domain reflectometer times the echo of a pulse that travels to the discontinuity and back, so the cable distance is half the round-trip time times the signal speed in the cable.
The velocity factor of a cable is the signal speed divided by the speed of light in vacuum, about 0.66 for solid polyethylene and 0.80 to 0.88 for foam dielectric.
For a homogeneous dielectric the velocity factor is one over the square root of the relative permittivity, so the dielectric constant is the reciprocal square of the velocity factor.

tools.name: SLA Uptime Budget Calculator
tools.description: Turn an availability target such as 99.9 percent into the downtime it allows in a day, week, month, quarter or year, and see the achieved availability and budget left after a downtime you enter.
tools.method: Availability is the share of a period a service is usable, so a target of p percent leaves (100 - p)/100 of the period for outages. With a fixed period of P hours the allowed downtime is (1 - p/100) * P * 3600 seconds, the achieved availability after an observed downtime d is (1 - d / (P * 3600)) * 100 percent, the share of the budget used is d divided by the allowed downtime times 100, and the budget left is the allowed downtime minus d. The periods are the fixed lengths the page lists: a day is 24 h, a week 168 h, a month 730 h, a quarter 2190 h and a year 8760 h, so months and years divide evenly and a quarter is three months. The nines shorthand counts the 9s in the target, which is the nearest whole number to minus the base-10 logarithm of the shortfall (100 - p)/100, reported only when that logarithm is a whole number from one to six, so 99.9 percent is three nines and 99.9999 percent is six. Allowed and remaining seconds are rounded to 0.01, the achieved availability to 0.0001 percent and the share of the budget to 0.1 percent. Targets greater than 0 and at most 99.9999 percent are accepted, downtime greater than or equal to 0 and at most the length of the period in minutes is accepted and may be left blank, and the period must be one of the listed keys. Text, exponent notation, a blank or out-of-range target, an unknown period, negative downtime and downtime longer than the period are refused with the exact reason, and decimal commas are accepted. Downtime above the budget is reported as an overrun with a warning rather than refused. This is arithmetic on the target and the downtime you supply: it does not measure availability, does not decide how partial failures are counted, and treats planned maintenance as downtime. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Availability is the fraction of a period a service is usable, so an n percent target leaves (100 - n)/100 of the period available for outages.
The nines shorthand counts the 9s in the target: 99.9 percent is three nines and 99.99 percent is four, and each extra nine divides the allowed downtime by ten.
Availability budgets are usually quoted over fixed period lengths, with a month taken as 730 hours and a year as 8760 hours so the figures are reproducible.

tools.name: Map Tile Download Estimator
tools.description: Estimate how many Web Mercator tiles a latitude and longitude box needs at each zoom level and how much an offline cache of them would download at an average tile size.
tools.method: The count uses the Web Mercator XYZ tile scheme. At zoom z the world is 2^z tiles wide and high, so n = 2^z. A longitude l lies at fractional column (l + 180) / 360 * n and a latitude p at fractional row (1 - asinh(tan p) / pi) / 2 * n, with p in radians. A box takes the columns from the floor of the west edge to one less than the ceiling of the east edge, and the rows from the floor of the north edge to one less than the ceiling of the south edge, so a box that ends exactly on a tile boundary does not claim the next tile and edges are clamped to the first and last tile. When the east edge lies west of the west edge the box crosses the antimeridian and is counted as two longitude ranges, from the west edge to 180 degrees and from -180 degrees to the east edge, and a range with no width adds nothing. Tiles at a level are the column count times the row count, the estimated size at that level is the tile count times the average tile size in kilobytes with a kilobyte taken as 1024 bytes and rounded to the nearest byte, and the total is the sum over the levels from the lowest zoom to the highest. The share of the world at the highest zoom is the tile count at that level divided by 4^z times 100, rounded to 0.000001 percent. Longitudes must lie between -180 and 180 degrees, latitudes between -85.05112878 and 85.05112878 degrees because that is where Web Mercator runs out, the south edge must be below the north edge, the west and east edges must differ, zoom levels must be whole numbers from 0 to 22 with the lowest not above the highest, and the average tile size must be greater than 0 and at most 1024 kilobytes. Text, units, exponent notation, blanks and out-of-range values are refused with the exact reason, and decimal commas are accepted. This is an estimate: every tile the box touches is counted including the partial tiles along each edge, real tile sizes vary with imagery detail and compression, 512 px retina tiles are about four times heavier, and only Web Mercator is handled. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: The Web Mercator XYZ scheme numbers tiles from 0 to 2^z - 1 in each direction, with longitude mapped linearly to columns and latitude through asinh(tan(latitude)).
A bounding box selects every tile it overlaps, so the count is the inclusive column span times the inclusive row span, and a box ending exactly on a tile boundary does not include the next tile.
Web Mercator is undefined beyond about 85.05112878 degrees of latitude, where the projected world becomes a square and the tile grid stops.

tools.name: Call Sheet Builder
tools.description: Build a shoot-day call sheet from a first-shot time, scene durations and a meal break: crew call, timed scene blocks, the meal and wrap, plus a copyable sheet.
tools.method: Production and location are trimmed, control characters are replaced with spaces and whitespace is collapsed; production is required and both are limited to 80 characters. The shoot date is optional and must be a real Gregorian date in YYYY-MM-DD form, including 29 February in leap years. First shot is a 24-hour HH:MM time. Setup is 0-240 minutes and must not push the crew call before midnight. Scenes run back to back from the first shot, each 1-600 whole minutes, with at most 40 scenes. The meal time is the crew call plus 3-8 hours and may not fall before the first shot. When the schedule reaches the meal time a 15-90 minute meal is inserted: a scene in progress is split, the meal takes its place and the scene resumes afterwards; a meal is not scheduled when the day wraps before the meal time. Wrap is the end of the last scene plus a 0-120 minute wrap-down, and a schedule that would end more than a day past midnight is refused. All arithmetic is in whole minutes, and times display in 24-hour form with a +1 marker past midnight. The tool plans a schedule from durations the user supplies: it does not know travel, lighting changes, overtime rules or meal-penalty rules, and it stores and transmits nothing.

tools.name: Sheet Metal Bend Allowance Calculator
tools.description: Turn thickness, inside radius, bend angle and K-factor into the bend allowance, outside setback, bend deduction and the flat length of a two-leg sheet metal part.
tools.method: The bend is described by the material thickness t, the inside radius R, the bend angle A in degrees and the K-factor k, which is the share of the thickness from the inside face to the neutral axis. The angle is converted to radians, theta = A * pi / 180. The neutral-axis radius is Rn = R + k * t, the bend allowance is the arc length of the neutral axis, BA = theta * Rn, the outside setback is OSSB = (R + t) * tan(theta / 2), and the bend deduction is BD = 2 * OSSB - BA, the amount by which the flat blank is shorter than the sum of the two outside leg dimensions. For a part with two outside legs L1 and L2 the flat length is L1 + L2 - BD. Values are computed unrounded and then rounded to three decimals for display, so the deduction uses the unrounded allowance and setback. The units label applies to every length and no conversion is performed, so millimetres and inches give the same numbers for the same figures. Thickness must be 0.001 to 100, inside radius 0 to 500, bend angle 0.1 to 179.9 degrees, K-factor 0 to 0.5, and each leg 0 to 100000 in the chosen units; each leg must also be at least R + t to clear the bend, and the flat length must be greater than zero. Blank fields, text, exponent notation, negatives and out-of-range values are refused with the exact reason, and a decimal comma is accepted. An inside radius smaller than the thickness, and a bend of 165 degrees or more, produce warnings rather than refusals. The tool computes developed length from the K-factor you supply: it does not choose tooling, a minimum bend radius, springback compensation or a material-specific K-factor, and it does not check whether the finished part is strong enough for its job. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: The neutral axis of a bent sheet sits part-way through the thickness, at the inside radius plus the K-factor times the thickness.
The bend allowance is the arc length of the neutral axis over the bend angle, and the outside setback is (R + t) times the tangent of half the bend angle.
The bend deduction is twice the outside setback minus the bend allowance, so a part with two outside legs has a flat length of both legs minus one bend deduction.

tools.name: Four-Part Writing Checker
tools.description: Check a four-part SATB progression for voices outside their usual ranges, crossing, wide spacing, voice overlap and parallel perfect fifths or octaves, with every parsed note shown.
tools.method: Each line is one chord: four notes in soprano, alto, tenor, bass order. A note token is a letter A-G, an optional single sharp or flat, and an octave digit, so C4 is middle C and Bb3 is the B flat below it. Tokens are converted to MIDI note numbers with C4 = 60 and no double accidentals are accepted. Bar lines split chords within a line, blank lines are skipped, and one to eight chords are checked. The checker applies mechanical part-writing rules only. Ranges: soprano C4-C6 (60-84), alto G3-E5 (55-76), tenor C3-G4 (48-67), bass E2-C4 (40-60); a note outside its voice's range is reported. Crossing: in every chord the soprano must not sit below the alto, the alto not below the tenor, and the tenor not below the bass. Spacing: soprano to alto and alto to tenor must stay within twelve semitones; the tenor-bass gap is not limited. Overlap: across consecutive chords a voice must not move past the previous note of its neighbour, so an alto above the previous soprano note, or a soprano below the previous alto note, is reported. Parallels: for each of the six voice pairs an interval of a unison/octave or a perfect fifth that stays the same between consecutive chords is reported when both voices move and move in the same direction; a voice that repeats a note, or two voices moving in opposite directions, are not parallel. Intervals compare pitch classes, so a fifth displaced by an octave still counts as a fifth. The first chord has no previous chord, so no parallel or overlap check runs on it. There is no key, chord identification, doubling, dissonance or harmonic analysis, no voice-exchange or hidden-octave check, and no style judgement. Everything is computed in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Climbing Grade Converter
tools.description: Convert a rock-climbing grade between YDS (5.10a), French (6a+), UIAA (VI+) and, for boulders, the V-scale (V5) and Fontainebleau grades, highlighting the matching rows of the comparison chart.
tools.method: The chart follows the common middle of published YDS, French and UIAA comparison tables, which agree in the lower grades and drift by up to one step at the top. Each row carries one French grade, the YDS grade or grades that share it, and the UIAA grade or grades that share it: 3/III/5.3 up to 9c/XII+/5.15d, with 30 rows. Two rows therefore hold two YDS values (French 6c covers 5.11a and 5.11b) and some UIAA values appear twice (VIII- in 6c and 6c+; VIII+ in 7a+ and 7b; IX- in 7b and 7b+), which is why a UIAA input can resolve to two rows. Boulder problems are kept on a separate 19-row table, VB/3 up to V17/9A, where one V grade covers one or two Font grades (V5 is 6C or 6C+). The input is matched case-insensitively after trimming, an en dash or minus sign is read as a hyphen, a YDS grade must look like 5.10a, a French route grade like 6a+, a UIAA grade like VI+, a V grade like V5 or VB, and a Font grade like 6C+; anything outside the chart is refused with the reason rather than snapped to the nearest row. The page highlights every matching row and prints the equivalents for that row. Route grades and boulder grades are never converted into each other, because the two styles measure different things. Results are approximate by nature: grades are local consensus, gyms often grade softer than rock, and tables disagree, so the chart is a guide rather than a measurement. Everything is a local lookup in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Thermal Conductivity Converter
tools.description: Convert thermal conductivity between W/(m·K), mW/(m·K), kW/(m·K), W/(cm·°C), Btu/(h·ft·°F), Btu·in/(h·ft²·°F), cal/(s·cm·°C) and kcal/(h·m·°C), with typical values for common materials.
tools.method: Thermal conductivity is a material property measured in watts per metre-kelvin. Every listed unit is reduced to that SI base by one exact factor: watt per metre-kelvin is 1, milliwatt is 0.001, kilowatt is 1000, watt per centimetre-degree Celsius is 100, and the calorie-based units use the thermochemical calorie of exactly 4.184 J, so cal/(s·cm·°C) is 418.4 W/(m·K) and kcal/(h·m·°C) is 4184/3600 W/(m·K). The Btu units use the International Table Btu of exactly 1055.05585262 J, 3600 s per hour, 0.3048 m per foot, 0.0254 m per inch and a temperature interval of 5/9 K per °F: Btu/(h·ft·°F) is 1.73073466637 W/(m·K) and Btu·in/(h·ft²·°F) is 0.144227888864 W/(m·K). A conversion multiplies by the source factor and divides by the target factor, so every pair round trips. Input is trimmed and must be a plain decimal, optionally with grouped thousands; a leading decimal point is accepted, an exponent form is refused, and values below zero or above 1,000,000 W/(m·K) are rejected with the reason. Results carry six significant digits with trailing zeros trimmed and thousands grouped. The reference table lists typical handbook conductivities near room temperature for pure metals, common alloys and dry insulants; it is a material property, not a U-value or R-value. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Mid/Side Stereo Width Calculator
tools.description: Work out the left and right output peaks when a stereo pair is narrowed or widened around its mid signal, with mid and side levels, mono fold-down, polarity and peak headroom, plus a sweep across common width settings.
tools.method: A stereo pair splits into a mid signal M = (L + R) / 2, the part that survives a mono fold-down, and a side signal S = (L - R) / 2, the part that cancels. The channels are rebuilt as L' = M + wS and R' = M - wS for a width w of 0 to 2, so 0 % collapses both channels to the mid signal, 100 % returns the inputs unchanged and 200 % doubles the side gain. Levels are peak amplitudes converted from dBFS as 10^(dB/20), and both channels are assumed to peak at the same instant, which is the worst case for a width change; decorrelated program material peaks lower. The mid level is 20 log10 of M, the side level the same of |S|, and the side-to-mid ratio is their difference in decibels. Because L' + R' = 2M, the mono fold-down is exactly the mid signal and does not change with width. A negative output is reported as a polarity inversion rather than a level, and a peak above 0 dBFS is reported with the trim needed to bring it back. Inputs are trimmed and must be plain decimals, optionally with a leading decimal point and a minus sign; channel levels outside -120 to 0 dBFS and widths outside 0 to 200 % are refused with the reason. Results carry two decimals. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Easter Date Calculator
tools.description: Find the date of Western and Orthodox Easter for any year from 1583 to 4099, with the Julian calendar date behind the Orthodox result, the gap between the two calendars and the moveable feasts that count from Easter Sunday.
tools.method: Easter is the Sunday after the ecclesiastical full moon that falls on or after 21 March, so it is fixed by arithmetic on the year alone. The Western churches use the Gregorian calendar and the anonymous Gregorian computus, which reduces the month and day through the epact and the Sunday letter to month = floor(n / 31) and day = (n mod 31) + 1 with n = h + l - 7m + 114. The Orthodox churches keep the Julian calendar for the paschal full moon, so the Meeus Julian computus gives a Julian calendar date which is then converted to the civil calendar by adding the offset floor(year / 100) - floor(year / 400) - 2 days, the number of days the Julian calendar trails the Gregorian one in that year. The result is the Gregorian date of Orthodox Easter, and the difference between the two Easters is always a whole number of weeks because both fall on a Sunday. The nine moveable feasts are fixed offsets from Western Easter: Ash Wednesday -46 days, Palm Sunday -7, Maundy Thursday -3, Good Friday -2, Easter Monday +1, Ascension Day +39, Pentecost +49, Trinity Sunday +56 and Corpus Christi +60. The supported range is 1583, the first year after the Gregorian reform of 1582, to 4099, which keeps the offset formula and the four-digit input inside their valid span. All date arithmetic uses UTC midnight so a local timezone cannot shift a date, and the weekday is read from that UTC date. Input must be a plain four-digit year; empty fields, decimals, signs, five-digit years and years outside 1583 to 4099 are refused with the reason. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Bencode Encoder / Decoder
tools.description: Decode BitTorrent bencode — the format inside .torrent metainfo files — to JSON, or encode JSON back to canonical bencode with bytewise-sorted dictionary keys. Strict offsets, no network use.
tools.method: Implements the bencode grammar from BitTorrent BEP 3. Decoding reads the whole input as UTF-8 bytes and accepts exactly one value: i<digits>e integers, <length>:<bytes> byte strings, l…e lists and d…e dictionaries. Integers may be negative but must not use leading zeros or negative zero, and must stay within the safe integer range of ±9,007,199,254,740,991. Byte-string lengths are decimal byte counts with no leading zeros and must fit inside the input. Dictionary keys must be byte strings in strictly increasing bytewise order, so unsorted and duplicate keys are refused. Truncation, trailing data, nesting deeper than 64 levels and inputs longer than 200,000 characters are refused, and every structural error reports the byte offset. Encoding parses the supplied JSON with JSON.parse, sorts object keys by their UTF-8 bytes, writes strings as UTF-8 byte strings, arrays as lists and whole numbers as integers, and refuses decimals, booleans, null and unsafe integers because bencode has no such types. Decoded byte strings are shown as UTF-8 text with JSON escaping, or as uppercase 0x-prefixed hex when the bytes are not valid UTF-8; a dictionary key is shown the same way and keys that would collide after display are refused. No encryption, hashing of piece data, file writing, account access or network request is performed.

tools.name: Ephemeral Port Exhaustion Planner
tools.description: Estimate the ephemeral source ports an outbound connection rate keeps in TIME_WAIT per IP, and the safe sustained rate before NAT, proxy or client ports run out.
tools.method: Models Linux's ephemeral source-port pool as a Little's-law queue. Each completed outbound connection holds one source port for the TIME_WAIT duration (2 x MSL, 60 s by default), so a steady rate of r new connections per second pins about r x TIME_WAIT ports at once; the port count is rounded up because ports are indivisible. Ports needed per source IP = ceil(r x TIME_WAIT) + concurrent sockets. The pool size is end - start + 1 from the configured range (Linux defaults to net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999; Windows uses 49152-65535). Utilisation = needed / pool, shown to one decimal place. The safe sustained rate per IP = (pool - concurrent sockets) / TIME_WAIT, floored at zero, which is the rate at which the pool is exactly full; the churn ceiling = pool / TIME_WAIT is the same figure with no long-lived sockets. Status is evaluated on the unrounded ratio: exhausted when needed >= pool (the next connection fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL), tight at 85 % or more, watch at 70 % or more, otherwise healthy. Aggregate figures multiply the per-IP pool, demand and connection rate by the source IP count, because NAT gateways and proxies draw from one pool per source address. Inputs are validated as whole numbers (ports 1-65,535, TIME_WAIT 1-3,600 s, sockets 0-1,000,000, source IPs 1-10,000) or numbers with up to three decimals for the connection rate, with the end port required to be at least the start port. Pure arithmetic over the entered values: no storage, no network access, no host inspection.

tools.name: Memory Overcommit Planner
tools.description: Plan Linux commit-limit headroom: model vm.overcommit_memory modes 0, 1 and 2, derive CommitLimit from RAM, swap and vm.overcommit_ratio, and see whether a new allocation is admitted, refused with ENOMEM, or accepted into overcommit where the OOM killer decides.
tools.method: Linux accounts for committed virtual memory rather than resident pages, so admission of a new mapping depends on the overcommit mode and on CommitLimit, both visible in /proc/meminfo. The RAM share available for commit is RAM multiplied by vm.overcommit_ratio and divided by 100, rounded half up to whole MiB, because the kernel works in pages and the tool reports whole MiB. In mode 2 (never overcommit) CommitLimit is that RAM share plus swap, and the kernel refuses a request that would push Committed_AS past it: the allocation fails with ENOMEM and nothing is killed. In mode 0 (heuristic) no arithmetic limit is enforced; the kernel only rejects obviously excessive requests, so the tool reports RAM plus swap as the reference ceiling at which the workload stops being supportable and labels anything above it as oversubscribed. In mode 1 (always overcommit) no limit exists, so the ceiling is reported for context only, required swap is not applicable, and any allocation is admitted while the OOM killer arbitrates once pages are touched. Committed after this request is current Committed_AS plus the new commit; headroom is the mode ceiling minus Committed_AS before and after; utilisation is committed after divided by the ceiling as a percentage to one decimal, reported as 100 % when the ceiling is zero and anything is committed; the largest request that still fits is the headroom before the request, floored at zero. The swap top-up needed to admit the request is the excess of committed memory over the RAM share (mode 2) or over RAM (mode 0) minus existing swap, floored at zero, because extra swap raises CommitLimit byte for byte. Verdict bands use the unrounded utilisation: refused in mode 2 when committed after exceeds the limit, oversubscribed in modes 0 and 1, tight from 85 %, watch from 70 %, otherwise healthy headroom. Inputs are whole MiB: RAM and swap 1-16,777,216 and 0-16,777,216, the overcommit ratio 1-100, Committed_AS 0-33,554,432 and the new commit 1-33,554,432; only mode 2 uses the ratio. This is a planning model of kernel accounting for a host you describe, not a reading of any host; it does not change sysctl values, and it ignores per-cgroup memory limits, memlock rlimits and hugetlb reservations. Everything runs in the browser.
