tools.name: JSON Patch Applier (RFC 6902)
tools.description: Apply an RFC 6902 JSON Patch to a JSON document — add, remove, replace, move, copy and test operations over RFC 6901 pointers — with a per-operation log or the exact operation and pointer that rejected the patch.
tools.method: A JSON Patch is an ordered JSON array of operations, and the tool applies them in order to a deep copy of the parsed document, so a rejected patch leaves the input untouched and no partial result is shown. Every operation needs a string op and a string path; add, replace and test also need a value member, and move and copy need from. Unknown ops, non-string fields and non-object entries are refused before any value changes. A path or from is an RFC 6901 JSON Pointer: the empty string addresses the whole document, otherwise it must start with / and each reference token is the text between slashes with ~1 decoded to / and ~0 decoded to ~, in that order; other tildes are left literal. Objects are addressed by own property names only, so inherited names never resolve. Arrays are addressed by a base-10 index without a leading zero, and an index must be below the current length for resolution, removal, replacement and test; add also accepts the length itself to insert at the end, and the token - to append. A - token anywhere except the last token of an add path is refused. add sets an object member whether or not it exists, inserts into an array, or replaces the document when the path is empty; remove deletes an existing member or element and refuses an empty path because the result would be no document; replace rewrites an existing value or the document itself; copy deep-copies the value at from and adds it at path; move reads from, removes it, then adds it at path, refuses a from that is a proper prefix of path, and treats identical pointers as a no-op. test resolves the value at path and compares it with value: numbers compare by numeric value, arrays element by element, objects by identical own key sets with equal values, and any mismatch reports the found and expected JSON. Operation log notes are added, inserted, appended, replaced, removed, copied, moved, unchanged, passed or document replaced. The first failure stops the run and names the 1-based operation index, the operation and the pointer; the original values and all earlier steps are discarded. Limits: 200,000 characters per input and 200 operations. Pure local JSON processing; no storage, uploads or network use.

tools.name: Priming Sugar Calculator
tools.description: Work out the priming sugar for bottle conditioning: subtract the CO2 already dissolved at the warmest temperature the beer reached from the target volumes, then weigh the difference as table sugar, corn sugar or anhydrous dextrose, for the batch and per bottle.
tools.method: Priming sugar is the difference between the carbonation you want and the CO2 the beer already holds. Residual CO2 follows the published fit 3.0378 - 0.050062*T + 0.00026555*T^2 volumes, with T the warmest temperature the beer reached at or after fermentation in degrees Fahrenheit, so 68 F holds 0.86 volumes. The CO2 still to add is the target minus that residual, rounded to two decimals and floored at zero: when the beer already holds the target the answer is no sugar at all. One volume of CO2 is taken as 1.96 g per litre, and a gram of sugar yields a fixed share of its mass as CO2 from the balanced fermentation equation with IUPAC 2021 atomic weights: 0.5143 g for sucrose, 0.4442 g for dextrose monohydrate (retail corn sugar, 9.09 percent water of hydration) and 0.4886 g for anhydrous dextrose. Sugar per litre is therefore 3.811 g for sucrose, 4.413 g for corn sugar and 4.012 g for anhydrous dextrose per volume added, and the batch weight is that rate times the volume in litres. One US gallon is 3.785411784 litres. Batch volume runs from 0.5 to 500 litres or 0.13 to 132 gallons, the target from 0.5 to 4 volumes and the warmest temperature from 0 to 30 degrees Celsius or 32 to 86 degrees Fahrenheit, each with at most three decimals and no exponent or sign notation; blank, malformed and out-of-range values are refused with a field-specific message. The per-bottle dose is the rate times the chosen bottle size, and the bottle count is the batch volume divided by that size, rounded down. Amounts are rounded half away from zero: grams to one decimal and volumes and grams per litre to two. Published priming charts disagree by several per cent because they assume different sugar yields and CO2 constants, so figures from other calculators will differ slightly; above 3 volumes the page warns that the bottles must be rated for the pressure, and above 80 F it marks the residual fit as an extrapolation. The tool gives amounts only; it does not judge yeast health, fermentation completeness or bottle safety. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Hall, M., Brew By Numbers: residual CO2 in beer follows 3.0378 - 0.050062*T + 0.00026555*T^2 volumes with T in degrees Fahrenheit, giving 0.86 volumes at 68 F.
Brew Your Own, Carbonation Priming Chart: 0.85 volumes of residual CO2 after fermentation at 68 F, and 4.5 oz (128 g) of corn sugar in 5 US gallons adding about 1.53 volumes.
Palmer, J., How to Brew: priming sugar weights and bottle-conditioning practice.
IUPAC 2021 standard atomic weights and the balanced fermentation equations for sucrose, dextrose monohydrate and anhydrous dextrose.

tools.name: Bead Stringing Calculator
tools.description: Count the beads that fill a strand: take the finished length, subtract the clasp allowance, and fit beads and their spacers into what is left, with the beaded length, the room remaining, the beads to buy with a spare and the cord to cut.
tools.method: A strung strand is a fixed finished length shared out between a clasp and whole beads. The clasp allowance (the clasp itself plus the end knots at both ends) comes off the finished length first, leaving the usable length; each bead then takes its own diameter plus the spacer between beads. The bead count is the largest whole number that fits, remembering that the final bead needs no spacer after it: beads = floor((usable + spacer) / (bead + spacer)), evaluated in millimetres so that inch inputs behave identically. The beaded length is beads * bead + (beads - 1) * spacer, and the room left before the clasp is the usable length minus that, floored at zero. Working the other way, a known bead count gives the beaded length from the same formula and the finished length adds the clasp allowance back. The cord to cut is the finished length plus a tail at each end for holding while knotting and for the clasp loops. One inch is exactly 25.4 millimetres, and every length can be entered in either unit: the finished length runs from 50 to 2000 millimetres, the bead diameter from 2 to 40, the spacer from 0 to 20, the clasp allowance from 0 to 100 and the cord tail from 0 to 500, while the bead count runs from 1 to 1000 as a whole number. Inputs accept at most four decimals and no sign or exponent notation; blank, malformed and out-of-range values are refused with a field-specific message. Results are rounded half away from zero to two decimals in millimetres or three in inches. A clasp allowance that leaves less room than one bead returns no beads and a warning rather than an error, a bead count that runs past 2000 millimetres is flagged, and spacers wider than the beads themselves are flagged too. The tool gives lengths and counts only: it does not judge bead hole size, cord thickness, stringing tension or clasp strength, and everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Fire Mountain Gems and Beads, stringing and finishing guides: standard necklace strands run about 16 to 18 inches and bracelets about 7 to 8 inches, with roughly an inch allowed for the clasp and end knots.
Jewelry-making practice for knotted and strung strands: beads are fitted bead by bead with a fixed spacer, and the cord is cut at the finished length plus a working tail at each end.
ISO 31-1 / NIST unit definitions: one inch is exactly 25.4 millimetres.

tools.name: Two-Ray Path Loss Calculator
tools.description: Over flat ground the direct ray and the ray bounced off the ground arrive out of phase, so path loss climbs 40 dB per decade of distance once the link is past the breakpoint set by the two antenna heights: enter frequency, span and heights to get the breakpoint, the path loss and the power that reaches the receiver.
tools.method: A link over flat ground sees two rays: the direct path between the antennas and the path that reflects off the ground. Their length difference grows with the span, so beyond a breakpoint the two rays arrive almost out of phase and their sum falls away faster than in free space. The wavelength is lambda = c / f with c = 299792458 metres per second. The breakpoint distance, where both models cross, is d_bp = 4 * pi * h_t * h_r / lambda with both antenna heights and the result in the same unit. Inside the breakpoint the tool uses the free-space law L = 20 * log10(4 * pi * d / lambda); past it, the plane-earth law L = 40 * log10(d) - 20 * log10(h_t) - 20 * log10(h_r), with the span and heights in metres. Both branches give exactly the same loss at the breakpoint, and ten times the distance adds 40 dB past it instead of 20 dB inside it. The received power is P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r - L, because the quoted path loss is between isotropic antennas and each antenna gain is counted once. The extra loss from the ground is the path loss minus the free-space loss, floored at zero. One foot is exactly 0.3048 metres, and every length can be entered in metres or feet; the frequency runs from 1 to 10000 MHz, the span from 1 to 50000 metres, each antenna height from 0.1 to 500 metres, the transmit power from 0 to 100 dBm and each antenna gain from 0 to 60 dBi. Inputs accept at most four decimals and no sign or exponent notation; blank, malformed and out-of-range values are refused with a field-specific message. Results are rounded half away from zero to two decimals for losses, powers and lengths, and four for the wavelength. A span shorter than the two heights added together, an antenna below one wavelength, or more than 40 dB of extra ground loss each raise a note rather than an error. The model assumes smooth flat ground, no obstruction, both antennas well above the ground in the far field and a total reflection; terrain, buildings, vegetation and the curved earth all change the answer, so treat it as a planning estimate. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Standard treatments of the two-ray ground reflection (plane-earth) model, such as Rappaport, Wireless Communications: Principles and Practice, which gives the breakpoint distance 4*pi*h_t*h_r/lambda and the 40 dB per decade loss law beyond it.
Radio planning practice for VHF and UHF links: the flat-ground two-ray result is a best-case estimate used where the ground is smooth and no obstruction, curvature or vegetation intervenes.
NIST / ISO 31-1 constants: the speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299792458 m/s and one foot is exactly 0.3048 m.

tools.name: PoE Voltage Drop Calculator
tools.description: PoE loses volts along the cable before the powered device sees them: enter the 802.3 standard, supply voltage, load, cable gauge and run length to get the device voltage, the drop, the cable loss and the longest run that still clears the class minimum.
tools.method: Power over Ethernet sends direct current down the twisted pairs, and the cable resistance turns part of the supply voltage into heat before the powered device sees it. A conductor of the given gauge has resistance R' = rho / A per metre, with annealed copper rho = 1.724e-8 ohm-metres at 20 C and the cross-section taken from the AWG diameter d = 0.127 mm * 92^((36 - n)/39); that gives about 0.0842 ohm/m for 24 AWG and 0.0668 ohm/m for 23 AWG. Current leaves the switch on one pair and returns on another, and each pair is two conductors in parallel, so a 2-pair standard has loop resistance R_loop = R' * L. When all four pairs carry the load (802.3bt Type 3 and Type 4) the two paths sit in parallel and R_loop = R' * L / 2. A powered device behaves as a constant-power load, because its input drives a DC-DC converter, so the current rises as the voltage sags: solving V_pd = V_s - I * R_loop together with P = V_pd * I gives I = (V_s - sqrt(V_s^2 - 4 * R_loop * P)) / (2 * R_loop), the smaller of the two roots, and V_pd = P / I. A negative discriminant means no operating point exists and the run is refused as unable to deliver the load. The voltage drop is V_s - V_pd and its share of the supply is quoted in per cent; the cable loss is I^2 * R_loop; delivery efficiency is the device power divided by the power sent. Each class guarantees a minimum device voltage: 37.0 V for 802.3af (12.95 W, 350 mA over two pairs), 42.5 V for 802.3at (25.5 W, 600 mA over two pairs) and for 802.3bt Type 3 (51 W over four pairs, 600 mA), and 41.1 V for 802.3bt Type 4 (71.3 W, 960 mA over four pairs). The margin is the device voltage minus that floor, and the longest run is where the device sits exactly on it: (V_s - V_floor) / ((P / V_floor) * R' / 2) for a four-pair run. Supply voltage runs from 44 to 57 V, load power from 0.1 to 100 W, each conductor gauge from the four listed AWG sizes, and the run from 1 to 200 metres or 3.2808 to 656.168 feet, with one foot exactly 0.3048 metres. Inputs accept at most four decimals and no sign or exponent notation; blank, malformed and out-of-range values are refused with a field-specific message. Notes rather than errors cover a device below the class floor, less than 1 V of headroom, a run past the 100 m TIA-568 channel limit, a supply below the class minimum, a load above the class guarantee and a current above the class limit. The model assumes steady state, 20 C copper, a uniform cable and no connector, patch-lead or bundling losses, so treat the result as a planning estimate. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: IEEE 802.3af, 802.3at and 802.3bt Power over Ethernet: source output voltage ranges and the minimum voltage guaranteed at the powered device (37.0 V, 42.5 V and 41.1 V), with the class power and pair-current limits for Type 1 to Type 4.

tools.name: Choropleth Class Breaks Calculator
tools.description: Choropleth class breaks: paste a column of values, choose quantile or equal-interval breaks and a class count, and get the break values, each class range with its count and share, and a legend you can copy into a GIS.
tools.method: Class breaks turn a column of values into the handful of shades a choropleth map can carry. Equal interval divides the full span into k classes of the same width, w = (max - min) / k, with breaks at min + i*w, so every class covers the same number of units and the map reads directly in the data's own unit; a single large value, however, stretches the first class until nearly every area falls inside it. Quantile sorts the values and reads the breaks at i/k of the way through the order statistics, with linear interpolation between neighbouring values - the type 7 definition of Hyndman and Fan, which is the default in R's quantile() and NumPy's percentile - so each class holds roughly the same count; the cost is that the value width of each class varies with the data and the map hides the true spacing. Both methods return k+1 breaks including the minimum and the maximum. Breaks are rounded to six significant figures of the data range before the values are counted: the decimal places are 6 - floor(log10(max - min)), clamped to 0 through 12, so a range in the hundreds keeps four decimals, a range in the billions keeps none and a range in millionths keeps twelve. A value joins the class whose lower bound it meets or exceeds and whose upper bound it falls below, so a value sitting exactly on an interior break joins the class above it; the top class also includes the maximum. Counts and shares follow from the rounded breaks, which keeps the table self-consistent. Duplicate values that straddle a break leave the class between them empty, and that is reported rather than hidden; a class holding more than half of the values (with at least three classes and eight values) raises a note, and fewer than two values per class warns that quantile breaks sit on individual values. Inputs accept 2 to 5000 values separated by commas, semicolons, spaces or new lines, each with up to six decimals and no exponent notation, within -1,000,000,000 to 1,000,000,000; the class count is a whole number from 2 to 9. Blank, malformed, out-of-range and single-value lists are refused with a field-specific message, and a list whose values are all identical is refused because no classification exists. Natural breaks (Jenks), geometric intervals, standard-deviation breaks, areal weighting, projection and geometry are out of scope. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Cynthia A. Brewer, Designing Better Maps: A Guide for GIS Users - quantile and equal-interval class intervals for choropleth maps, their trade-offs, and the practical limit of five to seven shades.

Hyndman and Fan (1996), Sample Quantiles in Statistical Packages, The American Statistician 50(4) - the type 7 quantile definition, linear interpolation between order statistics, used for the quantile breaks.
QGIS and ArcGIS documentation for graduated classification - equal interval and quantile break methods, lower-inclusive class bounds, and the legend ranges they produce.

tools.name: Animation Exposure Calculator
tools.description: Animation exposure calculator: turn a scene length and frame rate into the drawings an exposure sheet needs, or a drawing count into running time, with the hold of every drawing and the frames it covers.
tools.method: An exposure sheet times animation by how long each drawing stays on screen. The hold is the exposure, written in frames per drawing: on ones every frame carries a new drawing, on twos the drawing changes every second frame, and so on up to twelves. Given a scene length in seconds and a whole frame rate, the frame count is the length times the rate rounded to the nearest whole frame, because a shot can only be an integer number of frames long; the drawing count is that frame count divided by the hold and rounded up, so the sheet can end with a drawing that covers fewer frames than the rest. The last hold is what remains after the earlier drawings, the drawings per second are the frame rate divided by the hold, one drawing's on-screen time is the hold divided by the rate, and the runtime is the frame count divided by the rate. The timing table lists the first twelve drawings with their frame ranges, then the final drawing whenever the sheet is longer, because the hold then simply repeats. In the other direction a drawing count times the hold gives the frames and the frames divided by the rate give the runtime exactly, with no rounding of their own. Frame rates are whole frames per second from 1 to 120 and holds run from 1 to 12 frames, so fractional and drop-frame rates such as 23.976 and 29.97 are out of scope, as are camera-move timing, audio breakdowns and shooting schedules. A scene length accepts up to three decimals from 0.001 to 3600 seconds and a drawing count runs from 1 to 100000. A length that is not a whole number of frames is reported with the exact frame count it rounds from, a short final drawing is named rather than hidden, a sheet longer than the table is said to repeat, and a hold of a whole second or more is flagged as stop-motion pacing rather than smooth animation. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Richard Williams, The Animator's Survival Kit - exposure sheets, timing charts, and the holds used for ones, twos and threes.
Harold Whitaker and John Halas, Timing for Animation - frame-by-frame timing, holds, and how a drawing count follows from running time and frame rate.
Toon Boom Harmony and Adobe Animate documentation on exposure sheets and frame-by-frame drawing timing at integer frame rates.

tools.name: Guitar Action & Saddle Adjustment Calculator
tools.description: Guitar action calculator: turn a measured string height and a target action at any fret into the saddle height or nut slot movement needed, using equal-tempered fret positions.
tools.method: Action is the gap between the top of a fret and the underside of the string. A string that runs straight from the nut slot to the saddle sits on a slope, so its height at fret f is the nut height plus the saddle-to-nut height difference multiplied by the fraction of the scale length at which the fret sits. In 12-tone equal temperament that fraction is x = 1 - 2^(-f/12): exactly one half at the 12th fret, three quarters at the 24th and about 0.056 at the first. A saddle height change therefore moves the action at the fret by x times that change and a nut slot change moves it by (1 - x) times, so reaching a target action means moving the saddle by the action change divided by x and the nut by the change divided by (1 - x). At the 12th fret both multipliers are two, which is the familiar rule that the saddle travels twice the wanted action change. Because the multipliers are fractions of the scale, they are independent of scale length: a 24.75 in and a 25.5 in instrument need the same saddle travel for the same action change, and only the fret number matters. The measurement is taken open, from the top of the fret to the underside of the string. Relief is excluded: a truss-rod adjustment bends the middle of the neck and shifts the action at the fret without moving the saddle, so relief must be set first and the neck allowed to settle. Measuring frets run from 1 to 24, the current and target actions accept up to three decimals and must stay between 0.30 and 8.00 mm or 0.012 and 0.315 in, and results are shown in the chosen unit to 0.01 mm or 0.001 in, with the saddle movement repeated in 64ths of an inch. A table gives the height factor and both multipliers for every fret, with the measured fret marked. Adjustments beyond 3 mm of saddle travel or 0.8 mm of nut slot are reported as cautions, and a measuring fret below 5 is described as a nut-height measurement because the nut then sets almost all of the height. Out of scope: saddle position and intonation along the string, string gauge and tension, fret wear and levelling, nut slot angle and back-cut, and instruments where the string leaves a zero fret or a capo rather than the nut. Everything is computed in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Golf Club Distance Gapping Calculator
tools.description: Enter the carry distance of each club and see the gap to the club below it, the widest hole in the bag, an evenly spaced ideal carry and a wide, tight or twin flag.
tools.method: Carry distances are entered in yards or metres, 3 to 400 yd (3 to 366 m), with at most two decimals, for 2 to 14 clubs drawn from a fixed list of 19 so a name cannot be invented and each club can appear once. Distances are converted to yards with 1 yd = 0.9144 m, sorted longest first with ties keeping the typed order, and each gap is the difference between a club and the next shorter one, so the gaps always add up to the span between the longest and shortest club. A gap above 15 yd (13.716 m) is flagged wide, meaning no club covers that distance; a gap below 8 yd (7.3152 m) is tight, and below 3 yd (2.7432 m) the two clubs are twins. The average gap is the span divided by the number of intervals, which is one fewer than the number of clubs. The ideal carry of the k-th club below the longest is longest minus k times the average, so a set spaced exactly on the average puts every club on its own step; the off-ideal column is the actual carry minus that ideal. Reported values are rounded half away from zero to one decimal in the chosen unit, while the flags are decided on the unrounded yard gaps, so a gap of exactly 15 yd is not wide and one of exactly 8 yd is not tight. Total distance (which adds roll), launch data, dispersion, wind, altitude, club fitting and the loft gaps inside a single wedge are out of scope. Pure local arithmetic with no storage, uploads or network use.

tools.name: Headphone Amp Power Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much power, voltage and current your headphones need: enter impedance and sensitivity in dB/mW or dB/V, pick a listening level and headroom, and get the amplifier swing required plus a phone, dongle, desktop or high-voltage verdict.
aliases: How Much Power Do My Headphones Need
how much power do my headphones need
tools.method: Headphone drive requirement from the published sensitivity spec and the load. Sensitivity is quoted either as dB SPL for 1 mW into the rated impedance or as dB SPL for 1 V rms across it, and the two are tied together by S(dB/V) = S(dB/mW) + 10 log10(1000 / R) for an impedance R, so both readings are shown. Power needed at a level L with H dB of headroom is 10^((L - S(dB/mW) + H) / 10) milliwatts. When the spec is per volt, the voltage is 10^((L - S(dB/V) + H) / 20) volts rms and the power follows from P = V^2 / R; either way the rms voltage is sqrt(P R), the current is V / R, and the peak swing is sqrt(2) times the rms value. Headroom multiplies voltage by 10^(H/20) and power by 10^(H/10), and every reported figure includes it. Accepted inputs: impedance 1 to 2000 ohms, sensitivity 70 to 140 dB SPL per mW or 90 to 145 dB SPL per V rms, listening level 60 to 130 dB SPL, headroom 0 to 24 dB; numbers outside those bounds, blank fields or text are refused with the reason. Results carry three significant figures and are scaled to W, mW, µW or nW, and to V or mV; current switches to µA below one milliamp. A voltage-based verdict calls a load phone-friendly at 0.5 V rms or less, dongle territory up to 2 V, desktop up to 7 V, and very hard to drive above that, and the table repeats the power and voltage for 90, 100, 110 and 120 dB plus the chosen level. Output impedance, damping factor, distortion, noise, amplifier matching and listening-duration guidance are not modelled. Everything is arithmetic in the browser: no storage, uploads or network.

tools.name: VoIP Bandwidth Calculator
tools.description: Work out what one VoIP call really costs on the wire: codec, packet time, IP version and Ethernet framing in, per-call bandwidth in both directions, header overhead and calls per link out. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Models a single constant-rate voice stream. Payload per packet is the codec rate in kb/s multiplied by the packet time in milliseconds and divided by eight, which is exact for the codecs offered: G.711 and G.722 at 64 kb/s, G.726-32 at 32 kb/s and G.729 at 8 kb/s. Packet time must be a whole number of milliseconds from 5 to 120; G.729 carries a 10 ms frame, so its packet time must be a multiple of 10 and at least 10. Header bytes are 12 for RTP (no contributing source list and no header extension), 8 for UDP and 20 for IPv4 or 40 for IPv6; layer 2 adds 18 bytes for the Ethernet header and frame check sequence, or 38 when the 8-byte preamble and 12-byte inter-frame gap are counted as well, and the layer-3 view adds none. Packets per second is 1000 divided by the packet time; the layer-3 rate is the payload plus headers times 8 times that packet rate, the wire rate adds the layer-2 bytes, and the bidirectional figure is twice the wire rate. Overhead share is the header and layer-2 bytes divided by the whole frame, and it classifies the result as below 50 percent, from 50 to 70 percent, and above 70 percent. The call count is the link capacity in Mb/s times one million divided by the bidirectional per-call rate, rounded down, so a call that does not fit returns zero; the same capacity is also evaluated for G.711 at the same packet time and framing so the codec difference is visible. Inputs: packet time 5 to 120 ms, capacity 0.1 to 100000 Mb/s, four codecs, two IP versions and three framing choices; anything else is refused with the field named rather than coerced. The model excludes silence suppression, RTP header compression, SRTP authentication and encryption bytes, retransmission, signalling, jitter-buffer delay, codec lookahead, traffic mix, queueing and variable-rate codecs such as Opus, whose payload size depends on the encoder setting. It reports a link budget, not a measurement of a live network. Pure local arithmetic: no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: ext4 Stride & Stripe Width Calculator
tools.description: Turn a RAID level, disk count, chunk size and filesystem block size into the mkfs.ext4 -E stride and stripe-width values, the matching XFS su/sw, and the full-stripe size. Runs locally in your browser.
aliases: RAID Stride and Stripe Width Calculator
raid stride and stripe width calculator
XFS Stripe Unit and Width Calculator
xfs stripe unit and width calculator
tools.method: Converts RAID geometry into the ext4 stride and stripe-width values. The chunk size in KiB is multiplied by 1024 to bytes, and the stride is that figure divided by the filesystem block size, which must leave no remainder: chunk sizes are whole KiB values from 4 to 4096 and multiples of 4, so the 1, 2 and 4 KiB block sizes always divide exactly and every result is a whole number of blocks. The data-disk count follows the RAID level: all members for RAID 0, one for a single disk or a mirror, members minus one for RAID 5, members minus two for RAID 6, and half the members for RAID 10, which is the near-2 layout mdadm creates by default and therefore requires an even member count. The stripe width is the stride multiplied by the data disks, and one full stripe is the chunk multiplied by the data disks. Arrays are limited to 1 to 64 members with the minimum member count of each level enforced: 2 for RAID 0, RAID 1 and RAID 10, 3 for RAID 5 and 4 for RAID 6. The commands shown are mkfs.ext4 with -b and -E stride,stripe-width, and the equivalent mkfs.xfs -d su,sw with the parity disks excluded from sw; when the array has no striping the stride options are omitted and said to be unnecessary. A stride below four blocks is reported as too narrow to matter. Anything outside those bounds, a non-numeric or out-of-range disk count, a chunk that is not a multiple of 4 KiB, an unsupported block size, or a RAID level the member count cannot satisfy is refused with the field named rather than coerced. Not modelled: partition and 1 MiB alignment, 4Kn and 512e sector sizes, SSD erase blocks and zoned storage, thin provisioning and snapshots, far or offset RAID 10 layouts, XFS stripe width handling on parity arrays beyond excluding parity from sw, and measured throughput. Pure local arithmetic: no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Nginx Location Matcher
tools.description: Work out which nginx location block answers a request URI: exact match, longest prefix, ^~ and regex precedence, plus what every other block did. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Resolves a request path against nginx location blocks in the documented search order. The pasted text is scanned for location headers of the form location [modifier] pattern {, accepting no modifier, =, ^~, ~ and ~*, with the opening brace on the same line or the next one, and each block records its one-based line number. Blocks are rejected rather than guessed when the list is empty, when a pattern is longer than 200 characters, when a modifier is put on a named location, when a prefix does not start with /, when a regex does not compile, or when two blocks repeat the same modifier and pattern, which nginx itself refuses as a duplicate. The match is made on the path with the query string and fragment removed. An exact = block whose pattern equals the path wins immediately. Otherwise every block without a modifier and every ^~ block whose pattern prefixes the path is collected, the longest wins, and if that longest prefix carries ^~ the search ends there. Only when it does not does the regex pass run, in file order, with ~ case-sensitive and ~* case-insensitive; the first regex that matches wins even over a longer prefix. If no regex matches the longest prefix answers, and if nothing matches the result is a 404. Every block is then labelled with its outcome: the winner, an exact block on another path, the longest prefix that was outranked, a shorter matching prefix, a prefix that does not cover the path, a regex that would have matched but lost to a ^~ prefix or an exact match, a regex that would have matched after an earlier regex, a regex that does not match, or a named @location which no URI can reach. The page also reports the match kind, the longest prefix, the block count and the reason in plain words, and warns when several regexes would match the same path so the later ones are dead for that URI. Not modelled: percent-decoding, dot-segment and repeated-slash normalisation of the URI, rewrites that change $uri before location matching, try_files and error_page fallbacks, nested locations, include and map expansion, and PCRE-only regex syntax, since patterns are compiled as JavaScript regular expressions. Pure local text processing: no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Okumura-Hata Path Loss Calculator
tools.description: Median path loss from the Okumura-Hata equations, with the COST-231 2 GHz extension, the term-by-term breakdown, the free-space comparison and the fitted input ranges.
tools.method: Computes median path loss with the Okumura-Hata equations, or the COST-231 Hata extension for 1500–2000 MHz. Inputs are the model, the environment, the frequency in MHz, the base and mobile antenna heights in metres and the distance in kilometres. Okumura-Hata evaluates 69.55 + 26.16 log10(f) − 13.82 log10(h_b) − a(h_m) + (44.9 − 6.55 log10(h_b)) log10(d). The mobile correction a(h_m) is (1.1 log10 f − 0.7) h_m − (1.56 log10 f − 0.8) for a medium–small city, 8.29 (log10 1.54 h_m)² − 1.1 for a large city at 200 MHz and below, and 3.2 (log10 11.75 h_m)² − 4.97 for a large city at 400 MHz and above, with the 400 MHz form applied in the 200–400 MHz gap that Hata leaves undefined. In the Okumura-Hata model, suburban paths then take the medium-city loss less 2 (log10(f/28))² + 5.4 dB, and open or rural paths take it less 4.78 (log10 f)² − 18.33 log10 f + 40.94 dB, both using the medium-city mobile correction. COST-231 Hata replaces the constant with 46.3 and the frequency term with 33.9 log10 f, keeps the same base-height and distance terms and the medium-city a(h_m), and adds C_m = 3 dB for a dense urban centre and 0 dB for a medium city or a suburb; it defines no open-area form, so that combination is refused rather than extrapolated. Inputs are refused outside the fitted ranges: 150–1500 MHz for Okumura-Hata, 1500–2000 MHz for COST-231, base height 30–200 m, mobile height 1–10 m and distance 1–20 km. The result reports the median loss, the mobile correction, the distance slope in dB per decade, the free-space loss over the same path and the excess above it, and lists the additive terms so the arithmetic can be checked by hand. Predictions are medians: terrain profiles, buildings, foliage, building penetration, antenna patterns, feeder loss and site height above the clutter are not modelled, and microcells, indoor paths and street canyons fall outside the models' assumptions. Pure local arithmetic: no storage, uploads or network access.

ITU-R P.1546, Method for point-to-area predictions for terrestrial services in the frequency range 30 MHz to 4000 MHz — the wider prediction framework these models sit in.

tools.description: Worst-case and root-sum-square tolerance stack-ups for an assembly chain: signed dimensions in, the nominal total, both bands, per-dimension shares and a fit check against your limits out.
tools.method: Adds the dimensions of an assembly chain as a tolerance stack. Each dimension is a nominal value with a symmetric plus-or-minus tolerance and a direction: an adding dimension enters the total with a plus sign, a subtracting dimension (a bore, a spacer that closes a gap, a cover thickness) with a minus sign. The nominal total is the signed sum of the nominals. The worst-case total is that nominal less and plus the arithmetic sum of the tolerance magnitudes, T_wc = sum of t_i, which is the extreme reached when every dimension sits at a limit in the least favourable direction. The statistical total uses the root-sum-square of the same magnitudes, T_rss = sqrt(sum of t_i squared), which assumes the individual errors are independent, centred on nominal and approximately normal; it needs a real process behind it (inspected samples, a capable supplier or a control plan) and should not be used to excuse a stack that fails at worst case on a safety-relevant fit. Each dimension also reports its share of the worst-case range, t_i / T_wc, and of the total variance, t_i squared over the sum of squares, so the dominant contributor is visible. Optional lower and upper limits for the total are checked against both bands, and the result is reported dimension by dimension and as a total. Units are labels only: the arithmetic never converts between millimetres and inches, so every input must be in the same unit.

tools.name: Luminance Unit Converter
tools.description: Convert luminance between cd/m² (nits), kilonits, millinits, the stilb, candela per square foot, foot-lambert, lambert and apostilb, with typical surface values.
tools.method: Luminance is luminous intensity per unit of projected area, measured in candela per square metre, the unit the display industry calls the nit. Every listed unit is reduced to candela per square metre by one exact or definitional factor: the nit is 1, the kilonit 1,000 and the millinit 0.001; the stilb is one candela per square centimetre, 10,000 cd/m²; one candela per square foot is 1/0.09290304 = 10.76391041670972 cd/m² because a square foot is 0.3048 m squared; the foot-lambert is one candela per square foot divided by pi, 3.426259099635391 cd/m²; the lambert is one candela per square centimetre divided by pi, 3183.098861837907 cd/m²; and the apostilb is one candela per square metre divided by pi, 0.318309886183791 cd/m². A conversion multiplies by the source factor and divides by the target factor, so every ordered pair round trips. Input is trimmed and must be a plain decimal, optionally with grouped thousands; a leading decimal point is accepted, exponent form is refused, and a negative value or a base value above 10,000,000,000 cd/m² is rejected with the reason. Results carry six significant digits with trailing zeros trimmed and thousands grouped, and magnitudes outside 1e-6 to 1e12 switch to exponential form. The reference table lists rounded order-of-magnitude surface luminances, not specifications; the page states separately that luminance is not illuminance in lux and that a display's quoted nits are a small-area peak figure. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Daylight Saving Transition Finder
tools.description: List every daylight-saving clock change in a time zone for a chosen year: the local date, the hour that jumps, the UTC offset on both sides, and the next change from now. Uses the IANA time-zone database built into the browser, so nothing is uploaded.
tools.method: A daylight-saving transition is the instant a zone swaps between its standard and summer offsets. The offset of a zone at an instant is read from the browser's Intl.DateTimeFormat: the zone's wall clock is formatted at that instant, that wall clock is reinterpreted as UTC, and the difference gives the offset. A change is located by sampling the offset every six hours across the requested year plus three days of margin on each side, then bisecting between the last instant on the old offset and the first on the new one down to the millisecond; only changes whose local date falls inside the year are kept. The skipped or repeated hour is the wall clock at the change instant measured with the old offset, and the other side is the wall clock at the same instant under the new offset, so a spring change reads 02:00 to 03:00 and an autumn change 02:00 to 01:00. A zone that shifts at local midnight names the earlier date on the new side. Offsets, dates and shift sizes are exactly what the IANA database copy inside the browser reports: historical years come from its back-zone data and future years from its projection of legislation as of that copy, so a later statutory change cannot appear here until the browser's copy is updated. Everything runs locally; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent.

tools.name: Crockford Base32 Encoder / Decoder
tools.description: Encode a whole number in Douglas Crockford's Base32 alphabet and decode it back, with an optional modulo-37 check symbol and hyphen grouping. Decoding accepts lower case, reads I and L as 1 and O as 0, and ignores hyphens. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: A code is the number written in base 32, five bits per symbol, using the 32 characters 0-9 and A-Z without I, L, O and U; the digit loop divides by 32 with BigInt arithmetic so any length is exact, letters are emitted in upper case, and zero encodes as a single 0. Leading zeros carry no value and are dropped, so the code is the shortest form of the number and has no fixed width. Decoding is case-insensitive, maps I, i, L and l to 1 and O and o to 0 before lookup, and ignores hyphens and whitespace; any other character is refused with its position. The optional check symbol is the value modulo 37, written with the 32 symbols plus * ~ $ = U (values 32 to 36); when enabled, the last symbol of the code is read as the check symbol, a mismatch is reported with the expected symbol, and the decoded value is withheld. Input is limited to 4,096 characters. Nothing is uploaded, stored or sent.

tools.name: Cream to Butter Yield Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much butter and buttermilk a batch of cream churns into, from the cream weight and its fat content, for the butter and buttermilk fat percentages you expect. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: Butter and buttermilk are the two halves of the cream, so both the weight and the milkfat have to add up: butter plus buttermilk equals the cream weight, and butter times its fat percentage plus buttermilk times its fat percentage equals the cream weight times the cream's fat percentage. Solving those two equations for the butter weight gives cream times (cream fat minus buttermilk fat) over (butter fat minus buttermilk fat), with every percentage taken as a fraction; the buttermilk is the rest of the cream and the fat each half carries is reported so the balance can be checked. Cream weight is accepted in grams, ounces (28.349523125 g) or pounds (453.59237 g) and converted to grams first. Defaults are 1,000 g of 36 percent heavy cream churning into butter at 82 percent milkfat and buttermilk at 0.5 percent, which gives about 436 g of butter - the familiar pound of butter from a little over a quart of cream. Salt is a share of the churned butter weight and is added after the churn, so it does not change the yield, and commercial salted butter carries about 1.5 to 2 percent. Cream weight is accepted from 50 to 20,000 g, cream fat from 10 to 50 percent, butter fat from 70 to 90 percent, buttermilk fat from 0 to 5 percent and salt from 0 to 3 percent; those ranges already keep the butter fat above the cream fat and the cream fat above the buttermilk fat, so the butter weight is always positive and smaller than the cream. Cream under 30 percent fat, butter under 80 percent milkfat, buttermilk above 2 percent and salt above 2.5 percent each raise a warning rather than a refusal. Churn technique, washing, working and the water left in the butter all shift the real yield, homogenised cream may not churn at all, and nothing is claimed about food safety, shelf life or the standard of identity of the butter made. Weights are rounded to 0.1 g and percentages to one decimal. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: TCP Retransmission Timer Calculator
tools.description: Turn measured round trips into the smoothed RTT, the round-trip variation and the retransmission timeout a TCP sender keeps, following the RFC 6298 algorithm. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: The RFC 6298 algorithm keeps two running values from each round-trip sample. The first sample R sets SRTT to R and RTTVAR to R/2; each later sample R' moves RTTVAR to three quarters of its old value plus one quarter of the gap between the old SRTT and R', and only then moves SRTT to seven eighths of its old value plus one eighth of R' - in that order, because the variation update uses the old smoothed value. The timeout is SRTT plus max(G, 4 x RTTVAR), where G is the clock granularity and K = 4, and RFC 6298 rounds any result below one second up to one second. This page starts the timer at the RFC 6298 initial value of 1000 ms, applies the one-second floor after every sample, and optionally caps the result at 60000 ms, the minimum maximum the RFC allows. One to 24 samples are accepted, each from 0 to 60000 ms, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons or line breaks; the granularity is accepted from 0 to 1000 ms and defaults to 1 ms. The page reports the plain average, SRTT, RTTVAR, the timeout before the floor, the applied floor and cap flags, the initial 1000 ms timer and the timeout after each sample, so the smoothing can be followed step by step. A single sample, a floored result, a capped result, a variation above half the smoothed value and a zero-millisecond sample each raise a warning rather than a refusal. The timer modelled is the measurement-driven one: a real sender doubles it on each retransmission until a good sample arrives, and implementations differ in the maximum they keep. Times are shown to 0.001 ms. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Segmented Ring Calculator
tools.description: Work out the miter angle and cut length for a segmented woodturning ring: finished and inner edge, kerf-included cut length, strip length and segment count.
tools.method: The ring is treated as a regular n-gon: the finished outer diameter D fixes the circumradius D/2, and each segment's outer edge is the chord between two neighbouring vertices, D times sin(180 degrees divided by n). The inner edge is the same chord taken on the inner diameter, which is D minus twice the wall, so the segment is a trapezoid with parallel short and long edges. Both ends are mitered at 180 degrees divided by n from square, which makes the two cut faces of one segment meet at 180 minus 360/n degrees and lets n segments close the ring at n glue joints. Because the saw removes its kerf at every cut, the cut length is the finished outer edge plus one kerf; the strip to prepare is as wide as the ring wall and as long as the n cut lengths summed, and the kerf allowance is reported separately so offcuts can be planned. The page accepts 3 to 96 segments per ring, an outer diameter from 50 to 2000 mm, a wall from 5 to 250 mm, a kerf from 0 to 6 mm and 1 to 50 rings. A wall that leaves an inner diameter under 20 mm is refused, and so is a segment count that would leave outer edges under 8 mm, because such a piece cannot be cut or clamped. Segments under 20 mm across the outer edge, an inner edge under 5 mm, and a kerf that removes more than a tenth of the cut length each raise a warning rather than a refusal. Lengths are reported to 0.001 mm and angles to 0.0001 degrees, and decimal commas are accepted. The model assumes straight parallel miter cuts and a constant kerf; blade runout, glue-line thickness, snipe, ring stacking, the hollowing allowance and wood movement are not modelled, and the result is a cut list rather than a structural claim. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Course to Steer Calculator
tools.description: Work out the heading that holds a track in a current: enter the course to make good, the boat speed through the water and the current's set and drift to get the course to steer, the offset to port or starboard and the speed over the ground.
tools.method: Ground velocity is the vector sum of the boat's velocity through the water and the current. The boat is steered on an unknown heading at a known speed through the water b, the current sets towards a known bearing with drift d, and the ground track must run along the requested bearing. In a frame rotated onto the track the current splits into an along-track component d cos(track - set) and a cross-track component d sin(set - track), positive to starboard. The water velocity that cancels the cross-track part is (-crossTrack, speed made good - alongTrack) and its length must equal b, so the speed made good solves s = alongTrack + sqrt(b^2 - crossTrack^2). The larger root is taken because the smaller one puts the boat stern-first down the track. The heading is then track + atan2(-crossTrack, s - alongTrack), normalised to 0 to 360, and the offset is that angle to port or starboard. Two insoluble cases are refused: a cross-track component wider than b, where the current is stronger across the track than the boat can claw back and no heading holds it, and s of zero or less, where the current runs dead against the track faster than the boat makes way. Bearings are accepted from 0 to 360 degrees true and normalised, so 360 reads as north; the boat speed is accepted from 0.1 to 60 knots and the drift from 0 to 10 knots. Bearings are reported to 0.1 degrees and speeds to 0.01 knots. Warnings fire when the offset reaches 30 degrees, when the speed made good falls below half the boat speed, and when the cross-track current reaches 80 percent of the boat speed. Leeway, a stream that varies with time or position, gusts and any tidal prediction are outside the model, so the heading assumes a set and drift measured from recent fixes.

tools.name: Pickup & Cable Resonance Calculator
tools.description: Find the resonant peak a passive guitar or bass pickup makes with its cable: enter the pickup inductance, winding resistance, cable capacitance and load to get the peak frequency, how tall the peak is, Q, the -3 dB corner and the level at 2, 5 and 10 kHz.
tools.guidance: Electrical model only: it shows how cable capacitance, winding resistance and load move the resonant peak, not how an instrument sounds. The winding's own self-capacitance and any tone control are not counted, so a real guitar usually peaks somewhat lower and lower in level than shown, and cable capacitance varies with construction, so use the cable's measured or published figure.
tools.method: A passive magnetic pickup is modelled as an ideal voltage source in series with its winding inductance L and winding resistance Rdc, driving the cable capacitance C and the load resistance R in parallel. The divider gives the second-order low-pass H(s) = R / (s^2 L C R + s (L + R C Rdc) + R + Rdc), whose undamped resonance is f0 = sqrt((R + Rdc) / (L C R)) / 2 pi and whose quality factor is Q = sqrt(L C R (R + Rdc)) / (L + R C Rdc). The total capacitance is the cable capacitance per metre times the length. When Q exceeds 1/sqrt(2) the magnitude peaks at f0 sqrt(1 - 1/(2 Q^2)) and the peak stands Q / sqrt(1 - 1/(4 Q^2)) above the flat (DC) level, reported in decibels as 20 log10 of that ratio; at or below that threshold the response falls monotonically and no peak is reported. The -3 dB corner is the frequency where the magnitude is 3 dB below the DC level, and the levels at 2, 5 and 10 kHz are reported against the same DC level, so 0 dB means no change at that frequency. Inputs are accepted from 0.5 to 12 H of pickup inductance, 0.5 to 15 kilo-ohms of winding resistance, 30 to 300 pF/m of cable capacitance, 0.3 to 30 m of cable and a 50 to 2000 kilo-ohm load; decimal commas are accepted. Frequencies are reported to the nearest hertz, Q to two decimals, capacitance to 0.1 pF and levels to 0.1 dB. Warnings fire when Q falls below 0.71 and there is no peak, when the peak sits above 10 kHz or below 2 kHz, and when the peak boost exceeds 6 dB. The model counts only cable capacitance: coil self-capacitance, tone controls, pickup position, string and body resonances and amplifier input non-linearity are outside it.

tools.name: Secondary Dominant & Borrowed Chord Finder
tools.description: Pick a key to see every secondary dominant it offers, spelled for that key signature with the chord each one resolves to, plus the chords borrowed from the parallel mode and the seven diatonic chords.
tools.guidance: The natural minor scale is assumed, so melodic and harmonic minor chords appear as borrowings. Applied dominants target diatonic chords only: leading-tone chords, tritone substitutions and chromatic mediants are not listed.
tools.method: The key is a tonic letter with at most one accidental from fourteen supported spellings, and the mode is major or natural minor. Scale degrees are the tonic pitch class plus the major [0,2,4,5,7,9,11] or natural minor [0,2,3,5,7,8,10] step pattern, and each degree's letter advances one step through the note alphabet, so its accidental is whatever makes that letter match the pitch class. The diatonic triads use the mode's qualities (major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished; and minor, diminished, major, minor, minor, major, major). An applied dominant V7/x sits seven semitones above its target's root on the letter four steps higher, stacked as a dominant seventh (root, major third, perfect fifth, minor seventh), so its third is always one semitone above the target and it resolves a fifth down. Applied dominants are listed for every diatonic target except the tonic and a diminished degree (major vii, minor ii). Borrowed chords sit on the parallel mode: minor iv, flat VI, flat VII, flat III and the Neapolitan flat II in a major key; major IV, major V and the Picardy major I in a minor key, rooted on the parallel degree with the numeral's flat lowering the root a semitone. Every chord tone is spelled as a stacked third, so double sharps and double flats appear in the far keys; a spelling that would need more than two accidentals on one note is refused rather than respelled enharmonically.

tools.name: Emergency Water Supply Planner
tools.description: Plan household emergency water: gallons and liters for a chosen headcount and duration, the drinking and sanitation split, how long stored water lasts, and the jugs or bottles that close the gap.
tools.guidance: Quantities only. The one gallon per person per day rate covers drinking and sanitation for a normally active household; hot weather, hard physical work, pregnancy, illness, nursing and pets raise the real need and are not modelled. No treatment, container or medical advice is given.
tools.method: The requirement is headcount x days x one US gallon per person per day, the Ready.gov baseline for drinking and sanitation. The same volume is converted to liters at 3.785411784 L per gallon, three quarters of a gallon per person per day is reported as the drinking share and the remainder as sanitation and cooking, stored gallons divided by the daily rate give the days covered, and the difference from the requirement is reported as a shortfall or a surplus. Each container plan divides the requirement by the container volume (5 gal jug, 1 gal bottle, 0.5 L bottle, 12 L case of 24) and rounds up to whole containers, so the capacity column exceeds the requirement except where it divides exactly. The replacement date is today plus six calendar months, clamped to the last day of the month, for water that is not commercially bottled. Inputs are a whole headcount from 1 to 12, a whole day count from 1 to 30 and a stored volume from 0 to 2000 gallons; everything runs in the browser with no uploads, storage or network calls.

tools.name: Magic Number & Games Behind Calculator
tools.description: Work out a league race from two win-loss records and the games left: games behind, winning percentages, most wins still possible, and the magic or elimination number.
tools.method: Games behind compares won-loss difference, not raw wins: games behind = ((first wins - second wins) + (second losses - first losses)) / 2, so a leading team is zero games behind itself and is shown as a dash. Winning percentage is wins / (wins + losses) and is reported to three decimals, or as a dash when no games have been played. The most wins a team can still reach is its wins plus its remaining games. The magic number is second wins + second games left - first wins + 1: it counts combined first-team wins and second-team losses after which the second team, even winning every remaining game, cannot finish with more wins than the first team already has. The one is dropped when the first team would win a tiebreaker, because finishing level is then enough, and kept when the second team would win one. The elimination number is the same count read from the chasing side. A magic number of zero or less means the first team has clinched, a total of zero games left means the season is complete, and a negative games behind means the second team leads, in which case no magic number is reported for the first team. Wins, losses and games left are whole numbers from 0 to 199, team names are trimmed and limited to 24 characters, and a tiebreaker must be one of the three listed values. The model reads win-loss records only: ties, overtime losses, points systems and goal-difference tables are not converted, it assumes these two teams are the only contenders, and it treats an unplayed game as half a win and half a loss, so unequal games played can mislead. It keeps no schedule and stores nothing. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no uploads, accounts or network access.
tools.guidance: A two-team race on win-loss records only. It does not convert ties, overtime losses or points tables, and it does not know about head-to-head results beyond the tiebreaker you choose.

tools.name: Recording Card Capacity & Offload Planner
tools.description: Plan recording media for a shoot: how long one card records at a camera's bitrate, which cards the footage fills, the drive space every copy needs and how long an offload takes.
tools.method: Recording time per card = card size in GB x 8000 / bitrate in Mbps: a GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes and a megabit is 1,000,000 bits, so the constant folds the eight bits in a byte and the two decimal prefixes together. Space per hour = bitrate x 0.45 GB of decimal gigabytes, and per minute that value divided by 60. The cards a shoot needs is the planned minutes divided by the minutes one card holds, rounded up to a whole card. Storage for every copy = planned minutes x space per minute x the number of copies chosen. Offload read time = card size in GB x 1000 / the reader's rated MB/s, one read pass per card whatever the number of copies. The same capacity is also reported in GiB (2^30 bytes) because operating systems often show a card as smaller than its label. Card size runs from 1 to 8192 GB with up to one decimal, bitrate from 1 to 20000 Mbps, cards from 1 to 99, footage from 1 to 60000 minutes and reader speed from 1 to 20000 MB/s; every field is validated and each error names the field and its range. No container, file-system, clip or proxy overhead is counted, the bitrate is held constant for the whole shoot, audio is assumed to sit inside the bitrate entered, and the reader's rated speed is taken at face value, so real recording times are a few percent shorter and real offloads slower. It plans media only: it reads no card, lists no camera's approved media, computes no encoder target size and no recorder retention, keeps no record, and runs entirely in the browser with no uploads, accounts or network access.
tools.guidance: Media card planning only: it turns a card size and a camera bitrate into recording time, card fill, copy storage and offload time. It is not an encoder bitrate or target-size planner, and not a recorder retention calculator.

tools.name: IPv4 Route Summarizer
tools.description: Summarize a list of IPv4 prefixes into the smallest set of CIDR routes that covers exactly the same addresses, with the covering supernet, the entries that added nothing and any gaps.
tools.method: Every IPv4 prefix is held as an inclusive integer range: its first address is its value rounded down to a multiple of its block size 2^(32-length), and its last is that plus the size minus one, so a prefix with host bits set is refused instead of being guessed at. Duplicates are dropped, then any prefix already inside a broader one, and the survivors are merged by repeatedly folding two prefixes of the same length that are aligned siblings into their parent, until no pair can merge. The result is the minimal set of CIDR blocks covering exactly the input addresses, so nothing extra is announced. Addresses covered is the sum of the aggregate block sizes; the smallest covering supernet is the longest common prefix of the lowest and highest address, its size is 2^(32-length) and the addresses it adds are its size minus the covered count. Contiguity is tested by merging the aggregate blocks into runs: one run means the set is a single contiguous range, and otherwise the run boundaries give the number of gaps and the first gap. Input is up to 64 prefixes as CIDR text, separated by newlines, spaces, commas or semicolons; prefix lengths run from 0 to 32, octets must be decimal 0 to 255 without leading zeros, IPv6 is refused, and every error names the line and the prefix. The model covers IPv4 only and takes no view of routing policy: it counts no AS paths, metrics, longest-prefix behaviour or prefix origin, and announcing the covering supernet would also announce the gaps between the blocks. It reads no routing table, keeps no record, and runs entirely in the browser with no uploads, accounts or network access.
tools.guidance: CIDR aggregation only: it turns a list of IPv4 prefixes into the minimal set of routes covering the same addresses. It is not a subnet calculator, an address-planning tool, a VLSM allocation planner or a routing policy simulator.

tools.name: POSIX ACL Effective Rights
tools.description: Paste POSIX ACL entries and see what the mask really allows: the effective rights behind g:: and every named user and group, the mode ls -l prints, and each entry the mask is quietly cutting down.
tools.method: Entries follow the acl(5) text form: an optional default: prefix, then a tag (user/u, group/g, mask/m, other/o), an optional qualifier and a permissions field. Permissions may be written as r, w and x in any order with dashes ignored, or as a single octal digit, and they become the three-bit value r=4, w=2, x=1. Comments from a hash to the end of the line are stripped, which makes getfacl output paste directly, including its #effective: notes. Validity follows acl(5) and setfacl(1): exactly one u::, one g:: and one o::, at most one m::, no duplicate qualifier for a named user or group, and a default ACL that, when any default entry is present, repeats those three base entries and carries its own mask when it names a user or group. Default entries are refused unless the object is marked as a directory. When a mask entry exists it is the ceiling: the effective rights of g::, every named user and every named group are the granted bits AND the mask, while u:: and o:: are never masked. When named entries exist and no mask was written, the mask is what setfacl would add - the union of g:: and every named user and group - and it is reported as added rather than given. The mode ls -l prints comes from u::, the mask (or g:: when there is no mask) and o::, because acl(5) maps the group permission bits onto the mask; a + follows the mode when the ACL goes beyond the three base entries or a default ACL exists. The canonical short form always writes the mask explicitly, which keeps setfacl from recalculating it. Input is up to 32 entries and every refusal names the line and the entry. It reads no file, runs no command, and keeps no record.
tools.guidance: ACL reading only: it explains the entries you paste and the mask that governs them. It is not a chmod or umask converter, it does not read or change any file, and it takes no view on whether the rights it shows are the ones you should grant.

tools.name: EditorConfig Settings Resolver
tools.description: Resolve the effective EditorConfig settings for each file path: paste a .editorconfig and the paths to see every property, the section and line that decided it, the properties left to editor defaults, and how one indent level is built from tabs and spaces. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Each line is read in order: a line starting with # or ; is a comment, a line wrapped in [ ] opens a section, and any other line holding = is a pair whose key and value are trimmed and lowercased. Pairs before the first section form the preamble, where only root takes effect. Section names are globs: * matches any run of characters except /, ** matches any run including /, ? matches one character other than /, [seq] and [!seq] match one listed or one unlisted character, {a,b} matches any alternative with nesting allowed, and {1..4} matches the integers of an increasing range. The slashes written around ** stay literal, so a/**/b requires at least one directory between a and b. A brace without a comma, an unclosed bracket and a decreasing range are matched literally, a backslash escapes the next character, a - inside a class is a literal dash rather than a range, and a section name ending with / matches nothing. A name containing a / is anchored to the directory that holds this file, a name without one matches at that level and below, and a leading / changes nothing. Every matching section is applied in file order, so the last value for a property wins, unset clears a property, and an unsupported value for a recognised key is ignored so that an earlier value stands. tab_width defaults to indent_size, indent_size = tab takes the tab_width, and one indent level is built from as many whole tabs as fit with the remainder as spaces. Recognised keys are indent_style, indent_size, tab_width, end_of_line, charset, spelling_language, trim_trailing_whitespace and insert_final_newline; other keys are still reported. Limits are 400 lines and 64 KiB of configuration, 60 paths of at most 1,024 characters, and 1,024-character lines. Only the pasted file is read: parent .editorconfig files, the root search, editor integration and any file or network access are out of scope.

tools.name: Spectrum Analyzer Sweep Time Calculator
tools.description: Turn a frequency span and a resolution bandwidth into the sweep time of a swept spectrum analyzer, with the sweep rate, the resolution elements across the span, whether that rate sits inside the k = 2 to 3 relation for near-Gaussian filters, and the widest RBW that fits a time budget.
tools.method: For a near-Gaussian analog resolution filter the sweep time is the constant k times the span divided by the resolution bandwidth squared, so narrowing the RBW by ten multiplies the sweep time by a hundred. The span is the stop frequency minus the start frequency, both taken in the chosen unit; the sweep rate is the span divided by the sweep time, which equals the RBW squared divided by k; the resolution elements across the span are the span divided by the RBW. A k of 2 to 3 covers the Gaussian filters swept analyzers were built around, so a rate above RBW squared over 2 (k below 2) is reported as faster than the filter can settle, a rate from RBW squared over 3 to RBW squared over 2 as typical, and a slower rate as waiting longer than needed. With an optional time budget the widest usable RBW is the square root of k times the span divided by the budget, the resolution elements at that RBW are the span divided by it, and the rate at that RBW is the span divided by the budget; an RBW wider than the 1 GHz cap is reported with a note. Span, RBW, rates and resolution elements are rounded to 12 significant digits and the sweep time and its ten-times neighbours likewise. Start and stop frequencies from 0 to 1 THz with the stop above the start, an RBW above 0 and at most 1 GHz, k from 1 to 10 and an optional budget above 0 and at most 1000000 s are accepted. Text, exponent notation, a blank required field, an unknown unit and a value outside those ranges are refused with the exact reason, and decimal commas are accepted. This is the formula for a swept analog analyzer: it does not model a particular instrument's sweep-time limit, its FFT, oversweep or error-correction modes, or its errors at a given rate. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Keysight, Optimizing Spectrum Analyzer Measurement Speed (application note 5968-3411): for near-Gaussian analog resolution filters the sweep time is k times the span divided by the RBW squared, and a ten times narrower RBW multiplies the sweep time by a hundred.

UC Santa Barbara ECE 145A, Spectrum Analyzer notes: the filter rise time is K over the RBW with K = 2 to 3 for a Gaussian filter, so the sweep time is K times the span over the RBW squared, and sweeping faster than that leaves the response uncalibrated.

tools.name: Four-Bar Linkage Calculator
tools.description: Solve a planar four-bar linkage from its four link lengths and a crank angle: the Grashof type, the rocker and coupler angles in both assembly modes, the transmission angle against the usual 40 degree limit, and the rocker swing range when the input link is a crank.
tools.method: A planar four-bar linkage is classified from its four link lengths by the Grashof condition, the shortest link plus the longest against the two others: when that sum is the smaller the shortest link turns through a full circle and the link that is shortest decides the type - the ground link gives a double crank, one of the grounded links a crank-rocker and the coupler a Grashof double rocker - while a larger sum leaves no link able to turn fully (a triple rocker) and an exact equality is a change point where the linkage folds through a dead position; ties are broken in the order ground, input, coupler, output. For a given input angle the end of the crank is placed at the input length from the first pivot, and the coupler joint at the intersection of a circle of radius equal to the coupler about that end and a circle of radius equal to the output link about the second pivot, which is the closed-loop position solution; the two intersections are the two assembly modes, and when the circles miss each other the linkage cannot be assembled at that angle. The rocker angle is measured at the second pivot from the ground line, the coupler angle at the crank end, and the transmission angle is the acute angle between the coupler and the rocker, which reflection leaves the same in both assembly modes. A transmission angle below 40 degrees is the usual practical limit, because the coupler then pushes the rocker mostly along its own length. When the input link is a crank the rocker turns between the two positions where the crank and the coupler lie in line, and that range and its swing are reported. Lengths above 0 and at most 100000 in any single unit, and input angles from 0 to 360 degrees, are accepted; text, exponent notation, a blank field, a zero or negative length and a value outside those ranges are refused with the exact reason, and decimal commas are accepted. Angles are rounded to 12 significant digits. This is the position geometry of an ideal planar linkage with four pin joints: it does not model joint clearance, link deflection, out-of-plane offsets, friction, inertia or the loads the mechanism carries, and it assumes the ground line is horizontal with the input angle measured counter-clockwise from it. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Four-bar linkage (Wikipedia): the Grashof condition S + L <= P + Q decides whether the shortest link can turn fully, its classification names the crank-rocker, double crank and double rocker cases, and the ground, input, coupler and output links are defined.

Middle East Technical University, Machine and Mechanism Theory, chapter 7, Four-bar mechanism: the transmission angle is the acute angle between the coupler and the output link, 90 degrees is optimal, and a deviation beyond 40 or 50 degrees makes the mechanism lock.

Union College ESC104, Graphical linkage synthesis: the extreme (toggle) positions occur when the input crank and the coupler lie in line, and the transmission angle should stay between 40 and 120 degrees.

tools.name: Heat Transfer Coefficient Converter
tools.description: Convert a heat transfer coefficient (U-value) between W/(m²·K), kW/(m²·K), Btu/(h·ft²·°F), Btu/(h·ft²·°C), CHU/(h·ft²·°F), kcal/(h·m²·°C) and cal/(s·cm²·°C), with the imperial R-value of each result.
tools.method: A heat transfer coefficient, or U-value, is the heat flow through a unit area per kelvin of temperature difference: watts per square metre-kelvin, the base unit here. Every listed unit is reduced to that base by one definitional factor. Watt per square metre-degree Celsius equals watt per square metre-kelvin because a temperature difference of one degree Celsius is one kelvin, and the kilowatt unit is 1000 times the watt unit. The imperial units use the International Table Btu of exactly 1055.05585262 J, 3600 s per hour, 0.3048 m per foot (a square foot is 0.09290304 m²) and a temperature interval of 5/9 K per degree Fahrenheit: Btu/(h·ft²·°F) is 5.67826334111349 W/(m²·K), and the same Btu per hour-square foot over a Celsius interval is 3.15459074506305 W/(m²·K). The Celsius heat unit is exactly 1.8 Btu, the heat that raises one pound of water by one degree Celsius, so CHU/(h·ft²·°F) is 10.2208740140043 W/(m²·K). The calorie-based units use the thermochemical calorie of exactly 4.184 J: kcal/(h·m²·°C) is 4184/3600 = 1.16222222222222 W/(m²·K) and cal/(s·cm²·°C) is 4.184/0.0001 = 41840 W/(m²·K). A conversion multiplies by the source factor and divides by the target factor, so every ordered pair round trips. The reciprocal of the imperial result is reported as an R-value in h·ft²·°F/Btu, the US convention; layers of a wall add their imperial R-values in series before the sum is inverted again. Input is trimmed and must be a plain decimal, optionally with grouped thousands; a leading decimal point is accepted, exponent form is refused, and values below zero or above 1,000,000 W/(m²·K) are rejected with the reason. Results carry six significant digits with ties away from zero, trailing zeros trimmed, thousands grouped, and magnitudes outside 1e-6 to 1e12 in exponential form. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Sidereal Time Calculator
tools.description: Convert a UTC date, time and longitude into Greenwich mean and apparent sidereal time, local sidereal time and the equation of the equinoxes, and get the hour angle and transit time of a target right ascension.
tools.method: Sidereal time is the hour angle of the vernal equinox: the right ascension standing on a meridian, so whatever shares that right ascension is at its highest. The page follows the U.S. Naval Observatory's approximate algorithm. The UTC date and time become Julian dates through integer day-number arithmetic, so the day's 0 h Julian date JD0 (ending in .5) and the hours H elapsed since midnight are exact. With D = JD0 - 2451545.0 and T the centuries from J2000.0, Greenwich mean sidereal time is 6.697375 + 0.065709824279 D + 1.0027379 H + 0.0000258 T squared hours, reduced modulo 24. The equation of the equinoxes is the nutation in longitude times the cosine of the obliquity, with dpsi = -0.000319 sin(Omega) - 0.000024 sin(2L) hours and Omega = 125.04 - 0.052954 D, L = 280.47 + 0.98565 D, epsilon = 23.4393 - 0.0000004 D degrees; adding it turns mean into apparent sidereal time. East longitude divided by 15 shifts either figure to the local meridian, so western longitudes are negative and the value wraps through zero. An optional right ascension is subtracted from local apparent sidereal time to give the hour angle, folded into -12 to +12 hours: negative when the target is still east of the meridian, which is also the sidereal interval until it transits, positive once it has crossed. Times print as hh:mm:ss.ss, rounded to the nearest hundredth of a second and carried into minutes, hours and around midnight; right ascension on the meridian prints to four decimal degrees. The input is UTC: UT1 and UTC differ by at most 0.9 s and the Observatory quotes 0.432 s maximum error for 2000-2100 with UT1, so the seconds are good to about one second. Dates are accepted from 1800 to 2100, real calendar days only, with times from 00:00 to 23:59:59, longitudes from -180 to 180 degrees and right ascensions from 0 up to but not including 24 hours. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Universal Integer Codes
tools.description: Encode a whole number as an Elias gamma, Elias delta, Fibonacci, Golomb-Rice or Golomb code word, and decode any of those self-delimiting bit codes back to its value, with bit counts and any left-over bits shown.
tools.method: Universal codes map the whole numbers to bit strings that carry their own length, so a stream of values needs no separators. Elias gamma writes the bit length of the value as that many zeros and then the value itself, which takes 2 floor(log2 n) + 1 bits. Elias delta prefixes a gamma code for the bit length instead, which is shorter for large values. Fibonacci coding writes the Zeckendorf representation - the unique sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers, using 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and so on - least significant digit first and appends a 1, so every code word ends in 11 and no earlier 11 appears; decoding strips that final 1, reads 1, 2, 3, 5 and so on against the remaining digits and sums the ones. Golomb and Golomb-Rice codes split the value into a quotient and a remainder: the quotient as that many ones and a closing zero, the remainder in truncated binary, which uses b bits when r < 2^(b+1) - m and b + 1 bits by adding the cutoff when it does not, with b = floor(log2 m); Rice is the case m = 2^k, so its remainder is simply the low k bits. The first three codes are defined for values of 1 or more, while Golomb and Rice also take 0: the page feeds every scheme the same value, so a zero shows the three positive-only codes as unavailable and encodes it in the other two. Decoding reports how many bits the first code word consumed, lists anything left over and flags a code word that is not the shortest form of its value. Code words longer than 4,096 bits are refused and values are held to 1,000,000 so the page stays responsive. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.
