tools.name: Hop Bitterness (IBU) Calculator
tools.description: Estimate a beer's bitterness in IBUs from the weight, alpha acid percentage and boil time of each hop addition in your kettle volume and boil gravity. Shows the modelled utilisation and alpha acid concentration for every charge and adds them up with the Tinseth equation.
tools.method: The page estimates bitterness with the Tinseth utilisation model, the standard home-brewing equation. Utilisation is the product of a gravity factor, 1.65 x 0.000125^(SG - 1), which falls as the wort thickens, and a boil-time factor, (1 - e^(-0.04 t)) / 4.15, which rises with minutes and levels off. The two factors are multiplied and applied to the alpha acid mass, (alpha% / 100) x grams x 1000 x utilisation / litres of kettle volume, so one IBU is one milligram of isomerised alpha acid per litre. The page asks for the kettle volume and the average boil gravity rather than the topped-up fermenter figures, evaluates each addition independently, and shows the utilisation and alpha acid concentration behind every contribution. The model covers the boil only: a 0-minute addition contributes nothing, and whirlpool, hop-stand and dry-hop additions are not counted, so the result is a floor for heavily late-hopped beers. It assumes whole-cone hops, since pellets isomerise somewhat better, and kettle geometry, boil vigour, pH and altitude are not modelled; the figure is an estimate of measured IBU, not a measurement, and does not predict how bitter the beer tastes.

tools.name: Lampshade Fabric Calculator
tools.description: Work out the fabric a drum or empire lampshade needs from the ring diameters, the shade height, the seam and edge allowances and the usable fabric width, with the panel count, the size to cut and the trim for both rims.
tools.method: The page sizes a lampshade cover from the frame. Each panel is treated as a trapezoid whose bottom edge is the bottom ring circumference (pi times the bottom diameter) and whose top edge is the top ring circumference, with a panel height equal to the slant height plus an edge allowance at the top and bottom. The slant height is the straight shade height for a drum shade, or the square root of the height squared plus half the difference between the bottom and top diameters squared for an empire shade, which is the true distance between the rings along the fabric. Because fabric comes in fixed usable widths, the page takes the smallest whole number of equal panels, from one to eight, whose width including a seam allowance at both sides fits the usable width, then lays those panels across the fabric and reports how many lengths down the bolt the cover needs. Seam and edge allowances are entered by the user: one seam allowance is added at each side of every panel and one edge allowance at the top and at the bottom. Lining is assumed to take the same length as the cover. A pattern repeat, nap or directional print, print matching across the seams, fabric shrinkage, bias stretch and any trimming or straightening of the cut edges are not modelled, so the figure is a minimum to buy rather than a guaranteed cut.

tools.name: RJ45 Pinout Checker
tools.description: Read the T568A and T568B wire colours for all eight pins of an RJ45 plug and check whether a lead is straight-through or a crossover, with every pair's pins and continuity at both ends.
tools.method: The page holds the ANSI/TIA-568 pin-to-pair table for an eight-conductor 100-ohm lead terminated on 8P8C plugs. Each standard lists eight pins in order: T568A is white/green, green, white/orange, blue, white/blue, orange, white/brown, brown from pin 1 to pin 8, and T568B is white/orange, orange, white/green, blue, white/blue, green, white/brown, brown. Pair 1 is blue and sits on pins 4-5 in both standards, pair 4 is brown on pins 7-8 in both, and pair 2 (orange) and pair 3 (green) take pins 1-2 and 3-6 in the opposite order in the two standards, so the pair grouping pins 1-2, 3-6, 4-5 and 7-8 is the same everywhere and no pair ever straddles another pair's pins. The page joins pin n at the left plug to pin n at the right plug, the way a lead is actually wired, then reports every pin's colour, its pair number and pair name at both ends and regroups the pins by pair at each end. A pair is continuous when it reaches the same two pins at the far end; the lead is straight-through when all four pairs are continuous, and a crossover when pairs 2 and 3 are the only pairs that move, which is exactly what pairing a T568A plug with a T568B plug does. Any other pattern is reported as mixed wiring, with each pair listed against the pins it actually occupies. Both ends accept T568A or T568B in either case, and anything else - a blank end, an unknown code such as T568C, or a cable category such as Cat6 - is refused by name rather than defaulted. The page reports the eight plug pins only: it does not model shielded or screened plugs, the colour code printed on a keystone jack's rear block, the polarity a PoE injector applies, or cable performance such as category or length. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: OS National Grid Reference Converter
tools.description: Convert a WGS84 latitude and longitude to an Ordnance Survey National Grid reference such as TG 51409 13177 at one-metre to 100 km precision, and read a grid reference back to latitude and longitude.
tools.method: The page converts between WGS84 latitude and longitude and an Ordnance Survey National Grid reference in two steps. The position is first treated as an ellipsoid height of zero and turned into Earth-centred cartesian coordinates on the WGS84 ellipsoid (a = 6378137 m, b = 6356752.314245 m), then shifted to OSGB36 with the seven-parameter Helmert transformation Ordnance Survey publishes for this purpose (translation -446.448, +125.157, -542.060 m; rotation -0.1502, -0.2470, -0.8421 arc-seconds; scale +20.4894 ppm), and finally projected by Transverse Mercator on the Airy 1830 ellipsoid (a = 6377563.396 m, b = 6356256.909 m) with the true origin at 49 N 2 W, false origin easting 400 000 m and northing -100 000 m, and a central-meridian scale factor of 0.9996012717. The eastings and northings are then named the National Grid way: the 100 km square is found from two letter indices that skip the letter I, and the figures inside the square are truncated, never rounded, at the chosen precision, so a reference always names the south-west corner of its cell. Five figures per ordinate is a 1 m cell, four is 10 m, three is 100 m, two is 1 km, and letters alone name the whole 100 km square. Reading a reference runs the same chain backwards: the letters are decoded to a square origin, the figures to an easting and northing, the inverse Transverse Mercator series with its iterative footpoint latitude recovers OSGB36 latitude and longitude, and the inverse Helmert shift returns WGS84. Both directions reproduce the two worked examples printed in the Ordnance Survey guide: the annexe C.1 projection of 52 39 27.2531 N 1 43 04.5177 E to 651409.903 m east and 313177.270 m north, and the annexe D Helmert transformation of 3790644.900, -110149.210, 5111482.970 m to 3790269.549, -110038.064, 5111050.261 m, which projects to 422297.792 m east and 412878.741 m north in square SE. The Helmert shift is an approximation: Ordnance Survey rates it at about 3.5 m (95%) in Great Britain, so the page says so rather than implying survey accuracy, and OSTN15 remains the precise transformation. A latitude or longitude whose projection falls outside the National Grid, a pair of letters the grid does not define as a square, and a reference without two letters or with unequal or oversized groups of figures are all refused by name instead of being answered. Heights, Ordnance Datum Newlyn, offshore areas and the OSGM15 geoid model are not modelled. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Song Key Fit Planner
tools.description: Find the key to sing a song in: enter the lowest and highest notes of its melody and the notes a singer can comfortably reach, and get every transposition that keeps the whole melody inside that voice, ranked by how evenly it then sits.
aliases: Transpose a Song to Fit a Voice
tools.method: Notes are read as scientific pitch notation, with middle C at C4 and A4 at the 440 Hz reference, so a note's MIDI number is (octave + 1) x 12 plus its pitch class and accidental, and inputs are limited to C0 to B8. A transposition shifts every note of the melody by the same number of semitones, so the melody keeps its shape and the interval between its lowest and highest note never changes; the page tests shifts of -12 to +12 semitones. A shift counts as a fit only when the transposed lowest note is at or above the voice's lowest comfortable note and the transposed highest note is at or below the voice's highest comfortable note, which is equivalent to the closed window from voice low minus melody low to voice high minus melody high. When the melody already fits at a shift of zero that is the recommendation, because a song that fits is normally left in its key; otherwise the recommended shift is the fitting one whose smaller end margin, min(melody low minus voice low, voice high minus melody high), is largest, which puts the melody as near the middle of the voice as the search allows, with the smaller absolute shift breaking a tie. When no shift fits, because the melody is wider than the voice, the page says so and lists the three shifts that leave the fewest semitones outside the voice, counting an overflowing note once per semitone it misses by. The key you would sing in is the starting key moved by the same number of semitones, named from the conventional twelve spellings of the major mode (C, Db, D, Eb, E, F, F#, G, Ab, A, Bb, B) and of the natural minor mode (C, C#, D, Eb, E, F, F#, G, G#, A, Bb, B), and transposed melody notes are spelled with flats when the new key's name carries a flat and with sharps otherwise. Tessitura, stamina, passaggio, breath, ornamentation, voice leading and any Fach classification are not modelled, so the result is a range comparison rather than a decision. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Film Footage Running Time Calculator
tools.description: Turn a length of film into frames and running time: choose the gauge and perforation layout, set the camera frame rate, and read the frame count, clock time, linear film speed and the reels your load needs.
tools.method: Frames per foot is fixed by the gauge. 35 mm advances four perforations per frame at a 3/16 inch perforation pitch, so 64 perforations, or 16 frames, fill one foot; 3-perf and 2-perf layouts use the same 64-perforation foot and therefore 21 1/3 and 32 frames per foot. 16 mm advances 7.62 mm per frame, which gives 40 frames per foot, Super 8 gives 72 and regular 8 mm 80. The frame count is the footage multiplied by the frames per foot, rounded to the nearest whole frame with ties rounded up; a length that holds less than one whole frame of the chosen gauge is refused rather than reported as zero. Running time is the frame count divided by the camera frame rate, printed as hours, minutes, seconds and tenths, with hours omitted below an hour. Linear film speed is the frame rate divided by the frames per foot and multiplied by sixty, so 4-perf 35 mm at 24 frames per second moves 90 feet of film past the gate each minute. Reels are the footage divided by the reel or magazine load, rounded up, and the final reel is reported with the footage it actually carries. The frame rates offered are 18, 23.976, 24, 25, 29.97, 30, 48 and 60 frames per second, and the constants are nominal: short and long perforation pitch, lab splices, leaders, edge numbers and the frames a camera loses when it starts and stops are not modelled, so a real camera report may run a frame or two either side. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Phon to Sone Loudness Converter
tools.description: Convert between loudness level in phons and perceived loudness in sones: read the matching figure, the level at 1 kHz, how much louder or quieter the sound is than a reference, and the phon step that doubles it.
tools.method: Loudness level in phons and loudness in sones describe the same percept on two scales. By definition the phon figure of a sound is the sound pressure level of a 1 kHz pure tone that listeners judge equally loud, so at 1 kHz the phon number and the dB SPL number are the same. One sone is the loudness of a 1 kHz tone at 40 dB SPL, and loudness doubles for every 10 phon, which is Stevens' power law with an exponent near 0.3 written in its doubling form: sone = 2^((phon - 40) / 10) and phon = 40 + 10 x log2(sone). The page accepts either quantity with a reference level in phons, and reports the matching figure, the level at 1 kHz in dB SPL, the ratio to the reference as a multiple of its sone value with the doublings behind it, the level difference in phon and dB, and the levels that would double or halve the loudness. Values are limited to 0 to 140 phon, the 0.0625 to 1024 sone the scale covers; a value outside that range, a reference outside it, an unknown unit, a word instead of a number, a loudness of zero or less, or a length reading with no digits is refused with the reason. Below 40 phon the straight power law overstates quietness because the equal-loudness contours flatten near the threshold of hearing, so results under 40 phon are marked indicative; the law describes single tones and narrowband signals, and a broadband signal needs a critical-band loudness model such as the one in ISO 532 rather than a single sone value. Everything is computed in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Sandbag Flood Barrier Calculator
tools.description: Estimate the sandbags a flood barrier needs: bags along one course, courses for the height, the wall total, a spare allowance, the sand volume and weight to buy, and the count for the other common filled bag sizes.
tools.guidance: A materials count, not a design. Nothing here says whether a barrier will hold back water at a site, and a temporary sandbag wall can fail or be overtopped, so follow local flood-fighting guidance and emergency instructions. Filled bag sizes and weights are typical trade figures, not a product specification, and the wall is counted as one bag thick.
tools.method: Bags along one course is the barrier length divided by the filled bag length and rounded up: ceil(length / 20 in) for a standard bag, 16 in for a small bag and 24 in for a heavy bag, with the bags laid end to end. Courses is the height divided by the filled bag thickness, 6, 5 or 8 in, rounded up. The wall total is bags per course times courses for a wall one bag thick. The spare is the chosen whole percentage of the wall total, rounded up, and covers split bags and the half-bag offsets at the ends. Sand weight is the total bags times the trade weight of a filled bag, 35 lb standard, 25 lb small, 50 lb heavy, converted to kilograms at 0.45359237 kg per lb and to volume at 100 lb of dry sand per cubic foot and 27 cubic feet per cubic yard. Wall face is length times height in square feet, converted at 0.09290304 m2 per ft2, and bags per square foot of face is the wall total divided by that area, shown to one decimal because it is a rough rate. Lengths convert at 12 in per foot and 39.37007874015748 in per metre; heights at 1 in per inch and 0.3937007874015748 in per centimetre. Inputs are a length from 1 to 500 ft or 0.5 to 150 m with at most two decimals, a height from 6 to 120 in or 15 to 300 cm with at most two decimals, one of three bag sizes and a spare allowance from 0 to 50 whole percent. Bag counts round up; sand and area figures round half up at the displayed decimals. Everything runs in the browser with no uploads, storage or network calls.

tools.name: HTTP Range Request Planner
tools.description: Plan an HTTP Range request locally: enter a representation size and a bytes range header to see the status, Content-Range, Content-Type, body size, bytes saved and every part of a multipart response.
tools.guidance: A description of what a conforming server should answer, not a probe of a particular one. Servers may ignore or reject a Range header, caches and proxies may recombine parts, and a body is counted on the bytes as sent, after any content coding.
tools.method: The header is read per RFC 9110 section 14: a range unit, an equals sign and a comma-separated list of byte ranges, where first-last gives inclusive offsets counted from zero, first- runs to the end of the representation, and -N asks for the last N bytes. An int-range with a last byte below its first byte, a missing unit, a non-numeric field or an empty range specifier makes the ranges-specifier invalid and the header is treated as ignored. A last byte at or past the representation length is replaced by the last byte of the representation, and a suffix longer than the representation selects all of it. A range is satisfiable when its first byte is below the representation length, or when it is a suffix range with a non-zero length. If at least one range is satisfiable the response is 206 with only those ranges: one part carries Content-Range bytes first-last/length, and several parts use multipart/byteranges with one Content-Range per part. If none is satisfiable the response is 416 with Content-Range bytes */length and no body. The body size is the sum of the served part lengths, and the saving is that sum against the full length, reported as a percentage with enough decimals to stay honest at the extremes. An If-Range validator that does not match discards the header before it is applied, so the whole representation is sent with 200. Sizes are whole bytes from 1 to 1,099,511,627,776 and a header may list at most 32 ranges. Everything runs in the browser with no uploads, storage or network calls.

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics, Section 14 (Range Requests)

tools.name: Core Dump Pattern Builder
tools.description: Expand a Linux core_pattern template for a sample crash and see the core file name or pipe command line it produces, with every % specifier resolved, unknown ones dropped, the legacy .PID suffix applied and the 128-byte limit checked.
tools.method: One core_pattern template is expanded for the sample crash. A leading | makes the value a pipe command line instead of a file name, and the rest is split on white space into a program and its arguments after expansion. Each % is read together with the character that follows it: %% is a literal %, %p and %P are the PID in its own and in the initial PID namespace, %i and %I the triggering thread IDs in those same namespaces, %u and %g the numeric real UID and GID, %h the hostname, %s the signal number, %t the dump time in seconds since the epoch, %d the PR_GET_DUMPABLE mode, %c the soft RLIMIT_CORE in bytes, %C the CPU the task ran on, %e the comm cut to its first 15 bytes, %E the executable path with every slash replaced by !, %f the last segment of that path and %F the pidfd. A % followed by a character core(5) does not list is dropped together with that character, and a single trailing % is dropped, with a row in the table for each. When the template has no %p and the core_uses_pid switch is set, .PID is appended to the name; setting the switch while %p is present is reported as ineffective. Lengths count UTF-8 bytes against the 128-byte maximum core(5) gives a resulting name or a pipe command line. The page warns about a pipe whose program is not absolute, a pipe with no program, a relative file name that fs.suid_dumpable=2 would reject, a zero core size limit with a file template, a comm holding a space in a pipe template, and a space before the leading | that makes it literal. Numeric fields are bounded: PID and thread IDs 1 to 2147483647, UID and GID 0 to 4294967294, signals 1 to 64, CPUs 0 to 8191 and the dump time 0 to 253402300799, while the core limit takes up to 18446744073709551615 as digits without floating point. The pipe marker is shown as not part of the command line, the handler arguments are listed one per line, and the page only expands text: it reads no files, writes no sysctl and makes no network request.

sources.title: core(5): a leading | pipes the dump to a program, %c %C %d %e %E %f %F %g %h %i %I %p %P %s %t %u are the template parameters, a % before any other character is dropped with it, .PID is appended when core_uses_pid is set and %p is absent, and the resulting name is limited to 128 bytes.

Documentation for /proc/sys/kernel/: core_pattern is the core dump file name template, its default value is core, the file holds at most 127 characters, and .PID is appended for backward compatibility when the template omits %p and core_uses_pid is set.
coredumpctl(1): the tool retrieves and processes core dumps and metadata saved by systemd-coredump(8), which is why a systemd host usually never uses the kernel's own file naming.

tools.name: Shell Quote Builder
tools.description: Quote any text as one shell word and see the POSIX single-quoted form with the bare, double-quoted and bash ANSI-C forms where the shell would read them literally, each read back by the page's own quote-removal parser; decode mode turns a quoted word back into the value a program receives.
tools.method: One text is quoted for the shell. The single-quoted form wraps it in single quotes and writes each embedded single quote as a close quote, a backslash-escaped quote and a reopened quote, because a single quote cannot appear between single quotes; an empty text becomes two single quotes and still does not count as a bare word. The bare form is offered only when every character is in the set A-Z a-z 0-9 _ @ % + = : , . / -, which the shell reads literally. The double-quoted form is offered for one-line text without control characters and escapes the dollar sign, the backquote, the double quote and the backslash, which POSIX keeps special between double quotes, while a backslash before any other character is left as it is. The ANSI-C form is offered when the text holds control characters and writes them as \a \b \t \n \v \f \r \E or \xHH, escaping the backslash and the single quote, a form bash, ksh93 and zsh understand and POSIX sh does not. Every form is read back with the page's own quote-removal rules - single quotes keep every character, double quotes drop a backslash only before $ ` " \ or a newline, an unquoted backslash protects the next character, and $'...' decodes named, octal, \xHH, \uHHHH and \UHHHHHHHH escapes - and each must reproduce the text exactly. Each extra nesting layer quotes the previous line again for an outer sh -c, su or ssh. Decode mode runs the same rules on one word, reports the quote styles it used and the canonical single-quoted form of the result, refuses an unquoted space, tab or newline, an unterminated quote and a trailing unquoted backslash, and warns when an unquoted dollar sign, backquote, glob character, tilde, exclamation mark, brace or control operator means a real shell would expand the word or read it as more than one command. Lengths are counted in code points and UTF-8 bytes. Text holding a NUL byte is refused because a shell word cannot carry one, and the text is limited to 8192 characters on the page.

sources.title: POSIX.1-2017 Shell Command Language, 2.2 Quoting: single quotes preserve the literal value of each character and a single quote cannot appear between them, while double quotes preserve every character except the dollar sign, the backquote and the backslash, which keeps its escape meaning only before $, `, ", \ or a newline.

bash(1) QUOTING: four quoting mechanisms - the escape character, single quotes, double quotes and $'...' dollar-single quotes - where ANSI-C escapes such as \a, \n, \xHH and \uHHHH are decoded, ! stays special between double quotes while history expansion is enabled, and a backslash before any other character inside double quotes is left unmodified.

tools.name: Playing Time Rotation Planner
tools.description: Share playing time fairly: set the squad, how many players are on the field, the periods and their length, then read a period-by-period rotation where nobody finishes more than one period behind anyone else, with minutes and bench spells for every player.
tools.method: A rotation is built one period at a time. For each period the players are ordered by periods played so far, then by the period in which they last played (a player who has not played yet sorts first), then by player number; the first players on the field are taken and the rest are listed as resting. Because every period adds one period to the players with the lowest counts, the counts stay inside a band of at most one: if a players sit at the lower count and k are needed, taking k <= a moves k of them up and the band is unchanged, while taking k > a lifts all a and k - a of the upper count, leaving the others at the upper count, so the spread is still one. The totals are therefore floor(times k / n) and that value plus one, which is the best any rotation can do when the slots do not divide evenly; the page reports the gap in periods and minutes. Bench spells are the runs of consecutive periods a player is off the field, reported per player with the longest run. Minutes are whole periods multiplied by the period length, so a player pulled in the middle of a period is not modelled. The tie-break keeps the rotation deterministic and gives the longest rest to whoever has waited longest. The page handles 2 to 30 players, 1 to 20 periods and 1 to 120 minutes per period, does not know positions, match-ups, injuries, extra time or opponent strength, and is a planning aid, not a rulebook: competition rules on minimum playing time and re-entry override it.

tools.name: Third-Order Intercept (IP3) Calculator
tools.description: Turn a two-tone measurement into an output and input third-order intercept point: enter both tone levels, the measured IM3 product and the stage gain, and read IIP3, OIP3, how far the product sits below each carrier and, with a noise floor, the two-tone spurious-free dynamic range.
tools.method: The intercept is the extrapolated crossing of two straight lines: the fundamental, which rises 1 dB for every dB of drive, and the third-order product 2f1 - f2, which rises 3 dB. The product therefore stays twice as far below tone 1 as the intercept sits above it. With tone levels P1 and P2 and product PIM, all measured at the device output in dBm, the output intercept is OIP3 = P1 + (P2 - PIM)/2, which is the same as (2P1 + P2 - PIM)/2; the input intercept is IIP3 = OIP3 - G, where G is the small-signal gain in dB, so a loss stage refers the input intercept upward. P1 is the carrier that appears twice in the product: enter the lower tone as tone 1 for 2f1 - f2, or swap the tones if 2f2 - f1 was measured. The page also reports the suppression of the product below each tone, P1 - PIM and P2 - PIM in dBc, and when a noise floor N at the output is given, the two-tone spurious-free dynamic range (2/3)(OIP3 - N), the range of input levels over which the third-order product stays under the noise. Levels are accepted from -200 to 100 dBm for the tones and -300 to 100 dBm for the product and noise floor, the gain from -100 to 100 dB, and the product must sit below both tones while the noise floor must sit below the product, otherwise no sensible intercept exists and the page refuses. Results are rounded to six decimal places. The model assumes a pure third-order slope and a product above the noise: it does not cover gain compression, memory effects, swept-frequency or modulated tests, measurement uncertainty, or cascaded stages, and an intercept point is an extrapolation rather than a level that can be measured directly. It is an engineering estimate, not a compliance or spectrum-authorisation determination. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Bearing L10 Rating Life Calculator
tools.description: Estimate a rolling bearing's basic rating life from its catalogue dynamic load rating, the equivalent dynamic load and the running speed: enter C, P, rpm and the bearing type to read L10 in millions of revolutions and L10h in operating hours, with a caution when the load leaves the range where the basic life equation is validated.
tools.method: The basic rating life is the life that 90 % of a large group of apparently identical bearings reach or exceed before the first signs of fatigue, at constant load and speed on good-quality steel with conventional lubrication. ISO 281 expresses it in millions of revolutions as L10 = (C/P)^p, where C is the basic dynamic load rating from the bearing catalogue, P is the equivalent dynamic bearing load — the single constant load that produces the same fatigue as the actual combined radial and axial loading — and p is the life exponent, 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings. To read the same life in operating hours at a constant speed n in rpm, multiply by the 10^6 revolutions in a million and divide by the 60 n revolutions each hour makes: L10h = (10^6 / (60 n)) · (C/P)^p, the form in which catalogues usually tabulate the result. Because the exponent exceeds one, life grows faster than the rating: doubling C multiplies L10 by 2^p, eight times for a ball bearing, while doubling P divides it by the same factor. C is accepted from 0.001 to 1000000 kN, P from 0.001 to 1000000 kN, the speed from 0.001 to 1000000 rpm, and the type must be a ball or a roller bearing; results are rounded to six decimal places. When the equivalent load reaches half of the basic dynamic rating or more the page raises a caution, because ISO 281 warns that the life equation is not validated in that region and that the static load rating C0 and the bearing's minimum load then govern the selection. The basic life ignores the modified rating life, which adjusts for lubrication, contamination, the fatigue load limit and reliabilities other than 90 %, and it assumes the load and speed are steady. It is a preliminary engineering estimate, not a design review or a guarantee of service life. Everything runs locally in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Specific Heat Capacity Converter
tools.description: Convert a specific heat capacity between J/(kg·K), J/(kg·°C), kJ/(kg·K), cal/(g·°C), Btu/(lb·°F) and kWh/(kg·K), with International Table and thermochemical calorie values listed separately and a reference table of round values.
tools.method: A specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of a unit mass by one kelvin, an intensive material property measured in joules per kilogram-kelvin. Every listed unit is reduced to that SI base by one exact factor. The joule per kilogram-kelvin and the joule per kilogram-degree Celsius carry the same factor, because a temperature interval of one kelvin is one degree Celsius, and the kilojoule is 1000 joules. The calorie units follow NIST Special Publication 811 Table B.8: the International Table calorie is exactly 4.1868 J and the thermochemical calorie exactly 4.184 J, so cal_IT/(g·°C) is 4186.8 J/(kg·K) and cal_th/(g·°C) is 4184 J/(kg·K). The Btu units use the International Table Btu of exactly 1055.05585262 J, a pound of 0.45359237 kg and a temperature interval of 5/9 K per degree Fahrenheit, which makes Btu_IT/(lb·°F) exactly 4186.8 J/(kg·K) — the well-known equality with the International Table calorie per gram — while Btu_th/(lb·°F) is 4184 J/(kg·K). A kilowatt-hour is exactly 3.6 MJ. A conversion multiplies by the source factor and divides by the target factor, so every pair round trips. Input is trimmed and must be a plain decimal, optionally with grouped thousands; a leading decimal point is accepted, an exponent form is refused, and values that are zero, negative or above 100,000,000 J/(kg·K) are rejected with the reason. Results carry six significant digits with trailing zeros trimmed and thousands grouped. The reference table holds round capacities in four systems for checking a conversion, and the output also states the joules one kilogram takes for one kelvin, which equals the base value. Temperature-dependent capacities are not tabulated and no material is recommended. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Nth Weekday of Month Calculator
tools.description: Find the date of the first Monday, third Thursday, fifth Sunday or last Friday of any month, or name which occurrence of its weekday a given date is, with every matching weekday in the month listed.
aliases: Last Friday of the Month Calculator
tools.method: Finding the nth weekday of a month is pure Gregorian calendar arithmetic, so the page never consults the system clock, a time zone or the network. Every date is first reduced to an integer count of days since 1970-01-01 with the era-based civil-date conversion: a year is split into 400-year eras of 146,097 days, the day of the year comes from a 153-day cycle that starts in March, and the leap rule is the Gregorian one — divisible by four, except centuries, except multiples of 400. The ISO weekday is that day count taken modulo seven with Monday as 1, so 1970-01-01 is a Thursday, and the same count inverts back to a calendar date when the Thursday of a week is needed. The first requested weekday in a month is day 1 plus the distance from that month's first weekday to the target, wrapped into 0-6; each later occurrence adds seven days, so the nth occurrence is the first plus 7(n-1). The last occurrence is counted back from the month's final day the same way, which is why it is not always the fifth. A requested fifth occurrence beyond the month's length is refused with the actual count, because only a 29-, 30- or 31-day month in the right alignment holds one. The reverse direction divides (day - 1) by seven and adds one to name the occurrence, and marks a date whose weekday does not return within seven days as the last of the month. The ISO 8601 week comes from the Thursday of the date's own week: the week number counts weeks from 1 January of that Thursday's year, so 1 January 2027 reports 2026-W53. Year input is trimmed and must be one to four digits between 1583 and 9999, the page refusing earlier years rather than pretending to convert them from the Julian calendar; month and weekday accept either their number or their English name. Output is English, with an ordinal suffix, the long date, the ISO week and the day of the year, plus a table of every matching weekday in that month. Nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Base91 Encoder / Decoder
tools.description: Encode text or hexadecimal bytes to basE91, Joachim Henke's 91-character binary-to-text encoding, and decode basE91 back to UTF-8 text or hex. No padding, data-dependent 14-23% overhead.
tools.method: basE91 is Joachim Henke's binary-to-text encoding: 91 printable characters (A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and 29 punctuation marks, including the double quote and excluding the space, the single quote and the backslash) carry 13 or 14 bits at a time. The encoder keeps a bit queue in an integer. Each input byte is appended at the queue's current bit offset in little-endian bit order, and once 14 or more bits are queued it reads the low 13 bits; when that value is 88 or less the 13-bit reading is unambiguous, so 13 bits are consumed, otherwise the low 14 bits are read and 14 are consumed. The value is written as two characters, least-significant digit first: value modulo 91 and value divided by 91. When the input ends, the leftover 1 to 16 bits are written as one character, plus a second character when more than 7 bits remain or the leftover value exceeds 90, so no padding characters exist. Decoding mirrors the process: each pair of alphabet characters forms value = first + 91 * second, its width is 13 bits when value AND 8191 is 88 or less and 14 bits otherwise, and the queue is drained one byte at a time while more than 7 bits remain; a final unpaired character contributes one last byte. Because the scheme is a continuous bit queue rather than fixed frames, the overhead is data dependent: at most 23% and as little as 14%, against 33% for Base64. Characters outside the alphabet are ignored by the decoder, which is how a line-wrapped payload still decodes; the page counts and reports them. Input text is encoded as UTF-8 with lone surrogates replaced by U+FFFD, and hex mode reads pairs of hexadecimal digits as bytes so binary data can be encoded. Decoded bytes are shown as UTF-8 text when they form valid sequences and as uppercase hexadecimal otherwise, and the decoder rejects truncated, overlong, surrogate and out-of-range sequences instead of substituting replacement characters. Input is limited to 100,000 characters, the arithmetic is plain integer work with no clock, storage, network or third-party library, and the encoding is not encryption.

sources.title: basE91 — an advanced method for encoding binary data as ASCII characters (Joachim Henke): its overhead is at most 23% and can range down to 14%, against 33% for base64
Henke's basE91 reference implementation (base91.c): the 91-character encode table, the 13/14-bit queue shared by encoder and decoder, the trailing-bit rules and the decoder's 91-value ignore table

tools.name: Beer Color (SRM & EBC) Calculator
tools.description: Estimate a beer's color in SRM and EBC from its grain bill: enter each malt's weight and Lovibond or EBC color rating with the batch volume, and Morey's equation turns the summed malt color units into a predicted color, with each malt's share of it.
tools.method: The page implements Dan Morey's color estimate. Each malt contributes malt color units, MCU = (pounds of grain x degrees Lovibond) / gallons of batch volume, and the bill's units are summed before the curve is applied: MCU = sum(lb x degL) / gal. Morey's power fit turns that sum into the predicted color, SRM = 1.4922 x MCU^0.6859, which tracks measured beers well below 50 SRM and flattens above it, where 50 SRM is effectively black. EBC is the same 430 nm absorbance scaled by 25 instead of 12.7, so EBC = SRM x 25 / 12.7 (about 1.97 x SRM); a rating entered in EBC is converted back with 12.7 / 25 before it enters the sum, so a bill can be entered in either scale. Weights are kilograms or pounds (1 lb = 0.45359237 kg) and volume is litres or US gallons (3.785411784 L), all converted to pounds and gallons for the formula; entered values are echoed back in the unit that was used. Limits are 0.5-2,000 L, 0.001-500 kg per grain, 0.5-2,000 degL (1-4,000 EBC) per grain and 12 malts; rows that are left blank are ignored and the page reports MCU, SRM, EBC, total grain weight, and each malt's MCU and share of the color. It predicts measured color, not perceived darkness: wort pH, boil time and vigor, kettle caramelization, fermentation and the beer's own haze all move the real figure, and the fit is an approximation of a spectrophotometric measurement.

sources.title: Goldman, J., Craft Beer & Brewing: Seeing the Color in your Future (MCU = (pounds of grain x degrees Lovibond) / gallons, and Morey's SRM = 1.4922 x MCU^0.6859, which holds below 50 SRM where 50 SRM is effectively black)
Wikipedia: Standard Reference Method (SRM = 12.7 x the 430 nm absorbance through 1 cm of beer, and EBC = 25 x the same absorbance, so EBC = SRM x 25 / 12.7)

tools.name: Wood Movement Calculator
tools.description: Estimate how much a solid-wood board or panel shrinks or swells across its width when its moisture content changes: pick the species and grain, enter the width and the two moisture readings, and the Wood Handbook shrinkage values give the movement, the new width and the room to leave in a groove or frame.
tools.method: The page implements the Wood Handbook's linear shrinkage relation for wood below the fiber saturation point. Shrinkage at moisture content x is Sx = S0 x (1 - x / 30), a percentage of the green dimension, where S0 is the species' total shrinkage from green to oven-dry from Table 4-3 and 30% MC is the fiber saturation point the handbook says to assume when it is not measured. Because the width the user measures is the width at the current moisture content, that width is first scaled back to the green dimension, green = width / (1 - S(mcNow) / 100), and then forward to the later reading, later = green x (1 - S(mcLater) / 100); the movement is later - width. Tangential shrinkage is used for flat-sawn widths and radial shrinkage for quarter-sawn ones, as the handbook specifies, and the page also reports what quarter-sawn stock would move for the same board. The 27 species presets are Table 4-3 values transcribed as printed (for example northern red oak 4.0% radial and 8.6% tangential, white oak 5.6% and 10.5%, eastern white pine 2.1% and 6.1%); they are species averages, and the handbook puts the coefficient of variation at about 15% for a single piece, with reaction wood, juvenile wood and mixed ring angles moving more than the average suggests. Widths are entered in inches or millimetres (1 in = 25.4 mm) and the result is reported in the unit used, with the movement per 1% of moisture change. Moisture readings are limited to 0-30%, because above fiber saturation the free water in the cell cavities changes weight but not size: a reading above 30% is rejected with an explanation rather than silently clamped. Widths are limited to 1-12,700 mm (0.04-500 in). Only the cross-grain width moves; longitudinal shrinkage is 0.1-0.2% and is ignored. The result is an allowance for grooves, slots, breadboard ends and frame and panel clearances, not a substitute for measuring the board in the shop.

sources.title: Glass, S.V. and Zelinka, S.L., USDA Forest Service Forest Products Laboratory: Wood Handbook, Chapter 4 'Moisture Relations and Physical Properties of Wood' (FPL-GTR-282, 2021) — shrinkage at moisture content x is Sx = S0 (1 - x/MCfs) (Eq. 4-9) with 30% MC assumed for the fiber saturation point, tangential S0 for flat-sawn widths and radial S0 for quarter-sawn, and Table 4-3 green-to-ovendry shrinkage percentages by species

tools.name: Data Center PUE Calculator
tools.description: Work out a data center's power usage effectiveness (PUE) and DCiE from its IT load and total facility energy, see the overhead, and compare the facility with a target PUE.
tools.method: The page divides total facility energy by IT equipment energy, the definition The Green Grid gives for power usage effectiveness (PUE); the quotient is reported to two decimals and its inverse, data center infrastructure efficiency (DCiE), as the IT share in percent. Total facility energy covers everything the data center draws: the IT equipment itself plus power delivery (UPS, switchgear, generators, PDUs, batteries and distribution losses), cooling (chillers, cooling towers, pumps, CRAHs, CRACs, DX units) and miscellaneous loads such as lighting, so the ratio can never fall below 1.0 and a facility with no overhead at all would score exactly 1.0. The overhead is the facility total less the IT load, also expressed as a share of the facility total and as overhead per unit of IT load (PUE minus one). The target field compares the facility with a chosen PUE: the facility figure the same IT load would need at that target is IT load multiplied by the target, and the difference is reported as an absolute amount and as a share of the facility total, so a facility below the target is shown as a saving. Figures may be entered as energy over a period (kWh) or as average power (kW); because the same window cancels in the ratio, PUE is identical either way, but the period matters for PUE itself, which the Green Grid defines as an energy metric and recommends reporting over a period rather than as an instantaneous reading, since the ratio moves with the weather, the load and the way the plant is run. Thousands separators and spaces are accepted in either figure. Both inputs must be greater than zero and no more than 1,000,000,000,000, and the facility total may not be smaller than the IT load: that combination is physically impossible rather than worth reporting, so it is refused with an explanation instead of being clamped. The target is limited to 1.0-20.0. Comparing figures measured at different levels (the paper's L1 to L3 meter placements) or over different windows is not valid, and PUE says nothing about how much useful work the IT equipment does.

sources.title: The Green Grid Association: PUE: A Comprehensive Examination of the Metric, White Paper #49 (2012) - PUE is total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy (Equation 1), total facility energy includes the IT load plus UPS, PDUs, batteries and distribution losses, chillers, CRAHs and CRACs and lighting, DCiE is its inverse, PUE is defined as an energy metric reported over a period, values run from 1.0 upward with 1.6 or better achievable by design, and measurements differ by the L1-L3 meter placements

tools.name: Azimuthal Equidistant Projection Calculator
tools.description: Project a latitude and longitude onto an azimuthal equidistant map centred on a place you choose: the easting and northing from the centre, the great-circle distance and azimuth, and how much the map stretches at that point.
tools.method: The azimuthal equidistant projection puts one chosen point at the centre of a circular map and keeps two properties there: every other point is drawn at its true great-circle distance and on its true initial bearing, so the radial scale is exactly 1 and a straight line out of the centre is a great-circle track. The page places the point at x = rho sin(theta) east and y = rho cos(theta) north of the centre, where rho = R c is the great-circle distance for an angular distance c and theta is the initial azimuth. The angular distance comes from the haversine form, c = 2 atan2(sqrt(a), sqrt(1 - a)) with a = sin^2(dphi/2) + cos(phi1) cos(phi) sin^2(dlambda/2), which stays accurate for the metre-scale separations where the usual arccos(sin phi1 sin phi + cos phi1 cos phi cos dlambda) form loses precision; the change of longitude is wrapped into -180 to 180 degrees first, so a pair that straddles the antimeridian needs no special sign. The bearing is theta = atan2(sin dlambda cos phi, cos phi1 sin phi - sin phi1 cos phi cos dlambda) in degrees clockwise from true north. The sphere radius is R = 6371.0088 km, the IUGG mean radius, so distances are spherical great-circle distances and not geodesics on the WGS 84 ellipsoid, which differ by up to about 0.3 percent. Distortion away from the centre is purely tangential: the scale around the centre is k = c / sin c, about 1.0066 at 1,000 km, 1.0689 at 4,000 km, 1.2747 at 7,500 km, 1.5696 at 10,007 km (a quarter of the circumference), 1.9795 at 12,000 km and 3.3237 at 15,000 km, and the page reports that factor, the stretch it implies and the band it falls in: under 10,000 km close to a globe, 10,000 to 15,000 km visibly distorted, beyond 15,000 km severe. The antipode cannot be drawn: every azimuth is valid there and its image is the whole circle of radius pi R = 20,015.1 km, so the page reports that distance with no easting, northing, azimuth or scale instead of inventing an angle, and a point within a few metres of the antipode is treated the same way because the haversine no longer resolves the direction. A point that coincides with the centre returns zero distance, no bearing and a scale of 1. Latitudes are limited to plus or minus 90 degrees and longitudes to plus or minus 180 degrees, decimal commas and a leading plus are accepted, and the projection is spherical with no ellipsoid, datum shift or false easting; the page computes one point rather than drawing the map or a graticule.

sources.title: Azimuthal equidistant projection - all points are at proportionally correct distances from the centre point and at the correct azimuth from it, the projected radius is the great-circle arc length, cos(rho/R) = sin(phi0) sin(phi) + cos(phi0) cos(phi) cos(lambda - lambda0) with tan(theta) = cos(phi) sin(lambda - lambda0) / (cos(phi0) sin(phi) - sin(phi0) cos(phi) cos(lambda - lambda0)), the maximum plotted distance is half the circumference at about 20,000 km, distortion is minimal under 10,000 km, moderate between 10,000 and 15,000 km and severe beyond, the antipode smears into a whole circle, and a polar centre reduces to rho = R (pi/2 - phi) and theta = lambda

tools.name: Drumhead Tuning Calculator
tools.description: Relate a drumhead's tension to the pitch it sounds: give the head size, the film weight and the membrane tension to get the fundamental and the first overtones, or give a target pitch to get the tension it needs.
tools.method: A drumhead is modelled as an ideal circular membrane of radius a clamped at the hoop, carrying a uniform tension T in newtons per metre and an areal density sigma in kilograms per square metre. The transverse wave speed is c = sqrt(T / sigma) and the natural frequencies are f(m,n) = alpha(m,n) c / (2 pi a), where alpha(m,n) is the n-th positive zero of the Bessel function J(m): alpha(0,1) = 2.404826 for the fundamental, alpha(1,1) = 3.831706, alpha(2,1) = 5.135622 and alpha(0,2) = 5.520078 for the next three modes, so the overtones sit at about 1.59, 2.14 and 2.30 times the fundamental rather than at whole-number ratios. The page solves that relation both ways: from a tension it reports the fundamental and the three overtones, and from a target frequency f it reports the tension T = sigma (2 pi a f / alpha(0,1))^2 that produces it. The wave speed, the fundamental, the nearest equal-tempered note with its offset in cents (A4 = 440 Hz) and the total radial force around the rim, T times the circumference, are reported with them. The diameter is the playing diameter inside the hoop and may be entered in inches, centimetres or millimetres; the film weight is the areal density in grams per square metre, about 249 for 7 mil, 356 for 10 mil and 498 for 14 mil clear PET film, and it is converted to kilograms per square metre internally. Diameters are limited to 2 to 40 inches (50.8 to 1,016 mm), areal density to 50 to 2,000 g/m2, tension to 1 to 50,000 N/m and target pitch to 20 to 20,000 Hz; a target pitch whose tension would fall outside that band is refused with the reason instead of being reported, which is why 20 kHz is unreachable even on a 2 inch head of the lightest film. The model is the ideal membrane and not a real drum: the trapped air under the head adds mass, the film's bending stiffness, the collar and the glue ring stiffen the edge, and the tension is never perfectly uniform, so a real head sounds a few percent higher than the figure here. The tension is the membrane tension per unit length, not a lug torque, a DrumDial reading or a tuning recipe, and the page computes one head at a time with no shell, air cavity or two-head coupling.

sources.title: Vibration of a circular membrane - an ideal drumhead is a circular membrane of uniform thickness under tension attached to a rigid frame, the wave speed is c = sqrt(N_rr* / (rho h)) for the membrane tension and density, and the normal modes have angular frequencies omega_mn = alpha_mn c / a with alpha_mn the n-th positive zero of the Bessel function J_m

Bessel function - Bessel functions describe the radial part of the vibrations of a circular membrane and give the modes of a thin circular membrane such as a drumhead, and the zeros of J_0 occur at approximately 2.40483, 5.52008 and 8.65373

tools.name: DCP Delivery Planner
tools.description: Size a digital cinema package: give the runtime, DCI container, picture format, frame rate and image bit rate to get the frame count, the per-frame budget, the picture and sound data, and how many packages fit on a delivery drive.
tools.method: A DCP is a delivery container rather than a video file: the picture is a JPEG 2000 track of whole frames in CIE XYZ at 12 bits per component, the sound is uncompressed 24-bit PCM, and both are wrapped in MXF beside a composition playlist and a packing list. The page budgets that package from its runtime, container, active picture, frame rate, image bit rate, audio channels, sample rate and delivery drive. The container is 2048 x 1080 (2K) or 4096 x 2160 (4K); the active picture is flat at 1998 x 1080 or 3996 x 2160, scope at 2048 x 858 or 4096 x 1716, HDTV at 1920 x 1080 or 3840 x 2160, or the full container, and the page reports the pillarbox or letterbox bars around it. The frame count is the runtime times the frame rate, the frame budget is the image bit rate divided by 8 and by the frame rate, and the picture track is the frame count times that budget. The sound track is channels x sample rate x 3 bytes for the presentation time, so 5.1 at 48 kHz costs 6.912 Mbit/s. A 1% allowance covers the MXF wrapping, the playlist, the packing list and their hashes; subtitles, encryption, closed captions and the reel splits of a long feature are not modelled, and every size is a decimal gigabyte because drives are sold that way. The DCI limits drive the refusals: the image essence is capped at 250 Mbit/s, a 4K container carries 24, 25 or 30 fps while a 2K container carries 24, 25, 30, 48, 50 or 60, and a stereoscopic package is 2K at 24 or 48 fps with both eyes sharing the 250 Mbit/s, so each eye is budgeted at half the entered rate. Frame rates are whole numbers, because a DCP counts frames rather than following a 23.976 timeline, and the runtime is limited to 8 hours. The result is the encoder's target, not a measurement: JPEG 2000 is variable rate, so the finished picture track lands near the budget, and an encrypted or subtitled package is slightly larger.

sources.title: Digital Cinema Package - a DCP carries JPEG 2000 picture essence and 24-bit linear PCM sound, allows 24, 25, 30, 48, 50 and 60 fps at 2K and 24, 25 and 30 fps at 4K, places flat 1998 x 1080 or 3996 x 2160 and scope 2048 x 858 or 4096 x 1716 pictures in 2048 x 1080 or 4096 x 2160 containers, and caps the picture at 250 Mbit/s shared by both eyes of a stereoscopic package

Digital cinema - the DCI specification encodes picture as JPEG 2000 in CIE XYZ at 12 bits per component, supports 2K at 24 or 48 fps and 4K at 24 fps, and carries up to 16 channels of 24-bit uncompressed audio at 48 kHz or 96 kHz

tools.name: Bass Reflex Port Calculator
tools.description: Tune a ported speaker box: give the net volume, the port diameter and the port count to turn a cut length into the tuning frequency, or a target tuning into the tube length you have to cut.
tools.guidance: Geometric model only: it computes the Helmholtz tuning of a tube in a box, not the response of a loudspeaker. Use the net volume the driver sees (after the driver, port and bracing are removed), and subtract the tube's own volume, because a port that takes up air volume changes the tuning it was sized for. The 0.3 D end correction assumes both ends are free; a flared port, a slot port or a port flush with a wall tunes somewhat differently. A design that works on this page can still chuff, bottom out or sound wrong, because the driver's Thiele/Small parameters and excursion are not part of the calculation.
tools.method: A bass reflex port is a Helmholtz resonator: the air in the tube is the moving mass and the air in the cabinet is the spring, so the port resonates at f = (c / 2 pi) x sqrt(A / (V x L_eff)), with A the total cross-sectional area of the ports, V the net internal volume of the box and L_eff the tube's effective length. Both ends of the tube open into free air, so the effective length is longer than the cut length by an end correction of 0.3 D, where D is the inside diameter; the page applies that correction itself and reports the effective length beside the cut length. The speed of sound is fixed at 343 m/s, the value in dry air at 20 C, so a colder room tunes the box slightly flat and a warmer one slightly sharp. With several identical ports the areas add and every tube keeps the same length, which is why two ports need a longer tube than one for the same tuning. The page works in both directions: given a cut length it returns the tuning, and given a target tuning it solves the same resonance condition for the effective length and subtracts the end correction to give the tube to cut. Inputs are 2 to 500 litres of net volume, a 2 to 40 cm inside diameter, 1 to 8 ports, a 2 to 120 cm port length and a 10 to 150 Hz target; decimal commas are accepted and the areas are reported per port, in total and per litre of box volume. A target that would need no real tube, because the end correction alone is already longer than the effective length, is refused rather than reported as a negative length, as is a target that needs a tube shorter than 2 cm. The page also compares the cut length with the cube root of the box volume, a rough stand-in for the internal depth, and warns when the tube will not fit straight. It models the port alone: it does not know the driver's Thiele/Small parameters, so it cannot choose the box volume, predict the -3 dB point or the excursion, or say how the port sums with the driver, and it does not model flared ends, slot ports, passive radiators, the air speed in the port or the volume the tube and driver displace. The port area per litre is shown as information, not as a pass or fail: the area a design needs depends on the driver and the playback level.

sources.title: Helmholtz resonance - the resonant frequency of a cavity with a neck is f = v/(2 pi) x sqrt(A / (V0 x Leq)) and the equivalent neck length adds an end correction of 0.3 D to the physical length

Loudspeaker enclosure - ported or bass reflex cabinets vent the rear radiation through a port tube, deliberately exploit Helmholtz resonance, and take their tuning frequency from the port's cross-sectional area and its length

tools.name: Ladder Setup Calculator
tools.description: Set a leaning ladder from the height it has to reach: the base set-back, the working length along the rails, the rail length with its extension above the landing, the lean angle, and whether a ladder you own is long enough.
aliases: Four to One Ladder Rule Calculator
tools.method: A non-self-supporting (leaning) ladder stands at the angle OSHA's construction rule describes: the foot is set back one quarter of the working length, the distance along the ladder from the foot to the top support (29 CFR 1926.1053(b)(5)(i)). With the set-back s and the working length L related by s = L/4, the support height is h = sqrt(L^2 - s^2) = L*sqrt(15)/4, so the page turns a height into L = h*4/sqrt(15) and s = h/sqrt(15). That pair always gives a lean of acos(0.25) = 75.5 degrees from horizontal, the same 75.5 degrees the standard names when it load-tests a portable ladder, and the page reports the angle as a check rather than as an input. Because a ladder used to reach an upper landing must stand at least 3 ft (0.9 m) above it (1926.1053(b)(1)), the rail length the page asks for is the working length plus that extension; a ladder between the working length and that rail length is reported as low rather than as wrong, with the standard's alternative of securing the top to a rigid support and providing a grasping device such as a grab rail. A ladder shorter than the working length is reported as short, because its rails never reach the support. Limits: a support height of 1 to 15 m and a rail length of 1 to 20 m, both convertible to feet at 0.3048 m per foot. The page warns above an 8 m climb, where a portable ladder is rarely the right access, and when more than 3 m of rail would stand above the landing. It is geometry only: it does not check the ladder's duty rating or condition, the ground, the tie-off, overhead lines or the footing, it does not apply to self-supporting stepladders (used fully open, top step never used as a step), and it does not decide whether a ladder is the right access for the job.

tools.name: IPv6 Prefix Delegation Planner
tools.description: Split a delegated IPv6 prefix into per-site prefixes: how many sites fit, the /64 subnets each site receives, and the exact address range of every one.
tools.method: An IPv6 delegation is split on power-of-two boundaries. A delegated prefix of length D carved into site prefixes of length S, with D <= S <= 64, gives 2^(S-D) site prefixes; each one holds 2^(64-S) subnets of length /64, so the whole delegation holds 2^(64-D) of those /64 subnets. The page does the split with 128-bit integer arithmetic: the delegation is aligned to its length (a prefix whose host bits are set is refused, and the aligned block is named in the error), site i starts at base + i * 2^(128-S), and the /64 range inside a site runs from that address to base + i * 2^(128-S) + (2^(64-S) - 1) * 2^64. IPv6 expects a subnet to be a /64 because interface identifiers are 64 bits long (RFC 4291, Section 2.5.1), which is why a site prefix longer than /64 is refused and every site is reported as an exact /64 range. The /56 default follows RFC 6177, the best-current-practice guidance on assignments to end sites, which recommends giving a site significantly more than a single /64 and names /56 as a reasonable default for home sites; /48 remains common for larger sites, and /64 is offered for a delegation that is itself a single subnet. Addresses are shown in the canonical RFC 5952 form (lower case, no leading zeros, the longest run of zero groups collapsed and a single zero group left alone); IPv4-embedded input such as 2001:db8::192.0.2.1 is accepted and rewritten in hex. Limits: a delegation length from 0 to 64, a site length from the delegation length to 64, and 1 to 64 sites listed (the first 16 are shown, with the count of the rest stated). Warnings appear when every site is a single /64, when the site prefix equals the delegation length so there is nothing to split, and when a site prefix shorter than /48 would hand out an unusually large block. The page plans a block it is given: it does not talk to a router or DHCPv6 server, does not verify that the prefix is delegated to the user, and does not configure router advertisements, SLAAC, routing or firewalls.

tools.name: systemd Mount Unit Builder
tools.description: Build a systemd .mount unit and an optional matching .automount unit from a mount point, source and options, with unit-name escaping, validation, previews and downloads. Runs locally.
tools.method: Builds a .mount unit from a mount point, a What= source, an optional file system type and a comma-separated option list, and can add the matching .automount unit for on-demand mounting. The unit file name is escaped from the mount point exactly as systemd escapes it: A-Z, a-z, 0-9, ':', '_' and '.' are kept (a leading dot is written \x2e), every slash becomes '-', and every other character becomes one \xHH escape per UTF-8 byte, so /mnt/My Backup becomes mnt-My\x20Backup.mount. Duplicate and trailing slashes and '.' components are normalized away, '..' is refused instead of simplified, the root path is refused because the root filesystem is mounted before systemd starts, and a name longer than the 255 characters systemd allows is refused. What= accepts an absolute device or image path, UUID=/LABEL=/PARTUUID=/PARTLABEL=/ID= identifiers, a host:/export specification for network file systems, or tmpfs, and refuses spaces, backslashes and percent signs. Options= tokens accept letters, digits and _ . : = + @ / - only; empty tokens, embedded spaces, duplicates and x-systemd. options are refused, the last because systemd-fstab-generator reads those only from /etc/fstab and silently ignores them in a unit file. Type= may be left empty to rely on detection. The builder emits [Unit], [Mount] and - unless an automount unit is requested - [Install] WantedBy= on the chosen target; the automount unit carries [Automount] Where=, an optional TimeoutIdleSec= and the [Install] section, while the .mount it activates deliberately has none, and the install command enables whichever unit was generated. Warnings name the automatic ordering of network mounts (after network-online.target, before remote-fs.target), of tmpfs mounts (after swap.target) and the effect of nofail, which stops the mount from being ordered before local-fs.target. The tool does not verify that the source device exists, that the mount point is empty, or that the file system type is right, and it never runs mount, umount or systemctl.

tools.name: URI Template Expander
tools.description: Expand an RFC 6570 URI template against a JSON object of variables and see each expression's operator, expansion and skipped names, with prefix, explode and percent-encoding applied locally.
tools.method: The template is read with the RFC 6570 level 4 grammar: literals outside braces, and expressions of an optional operator, + # . / ; ? &, followed by a comma-separated variable list. An operator sets the prefix and separator, whether values are written as name=value, and whether reserved characters and existing pct-encoded triplets pass through (+ and #) or are percent-encoded (every other operator). A varspec may carry a prefix modifier :N, which keeps the first N characters of a string value and is refused on lists and objects, or an explode * . Values come from a JSON object: strings, numbers and booleans expand as text, arrays expand as lists, objects as name/value pairs, and null or a missing key is undefined. Undefined values are skipped, an empty list or object is undefined, and an expression whose variables are all undefined expands to nothing, prefix included. Every other code point is percent-encoded as UTF-8, and a pct-encoded triplet such as %2F is not encoded a second time under + or #. Literal characters outside the template grammar are percent-encoded and reported. Templates are limited to 2048 characters and the variables document to 20000. Nothing is fetched: the page does not resolve the resulting URI, contact the host, or prove that the API accepts the query or the escaping.

tools.name: Soccer Pitch Marking Calculator
tools.description: Check a soccer pitch against IFAB Law 1, then list every marking, the total length of line to paint and the paint it takes from the line width and coverage.
tools.method: Law 1 fixes the goal at 7.32 m between the inside of the posts and 2.44 m high, the goal-area lines 5.5 m from the inside of each post and 5.5 m into the field, and the penalty-area lines 16.5 m from the inside of each post and 16.5 m into the field, so the goal area is 18.32 m wide and the penalty area 40.32 m wide. The penalty mark is 11 m from the goal line and the arc of radius 9.15 m about it is drawn outside the penalty area: the front line lies 5.5 m from the mark, so the arc spans 2 x acos(5.5 / 9.15) = 1.8524 rad and is 16.9445 m long. The centre circle is the full 9.15 m circle (57.4911 m), the halfway line joins the midpoints of the touchlines, and each corner arc is a 1 m quarter circle (1.5708 m). The painted length is therefore 2L + 3W + 2 x (2 x 16.5 + 40.32) + 2 x (2 x 5.5 + 18.32) + 2 x 16.9445 + 4 x 1.5708 + 57.4911, which is 716.94 m for a 105 x 68 m pitch. Paint area is that length times the line width, and paint per coat is the area divided by the coverage per litre entered from the tin. Two penalty marks and the centre mark are listed but not counted as line, and the goals are not painted. Lengths are accepted from 90 to 120 m and widths from 45 to 90 m, with the touchline longer than the goal line as Law 1 requires, lines no wider than 12 cm, and the international range (100-110 m by 64-75 m) reported separately. This is marking arithmetic only: it does not survey a site, set competition markings, cover small-sided formats or replace a competition's field regulations.

tools.name: Radar PRF & Ambiguity Calculator
tools.description: Turn a carrier frequency, PRF and pulse width into the pulse repetition interval, unambiguous range, range resolution, near blind range, unambiguous velocity and duty cycle, and see why range and velocity cannot both be maximised.
tools.method: The pulse repetition interval is the reciprocal of the PRF, T = 1 / f_prf, and range follows the round-trip time with c = 299,792,458 m/s. Because a pulse can only listen for echoes that arrive before the next pulse leaves, the maximum unambiguous range is R_u = c T / 2, which is 149.896 km at 1 kHz and 1499 km at 100 Hz. If the whole echo has to be received rather than only its leading edge, the usable range shortens to c (T - tau) / 2, listed separately as the full-echo range. Range resolution for a simple unmodulated pulse is delta R = c tau / 2 (1.499 m per 0.01 microsecond, 149.9 m per microsecond), and the near blind range is the same c tau / 2 because a target inside half a pulse length is hidden by the transmit pulse itself. Doppler gives the velocity: a target's radial velocity shifts the carrier by f_d = 2 v / lambda, and with the direction of travel unknown the measurement folds at half the PRF, so the unambiguous velocity is v_max = lambda f_prf / 4, which equals c f_prf / (4 f_c) and is about 25 m/s at 3 GHz and 1 kHz. A moving-target canceller is blind where f_d is a whole multiple of the PRF, so the first blind speed is lambda f_prf / 2, twice the unambiguous velocity. Duty cycle is tau / T = tau f_prf, average power is peak power times duty cycle, and the number of range bins in one interval is T / tau. Because R_u = c / (2 f_prf) and v_max = lambda f_prf / 4, their product is R_u v_max = c^2 / (8 f_c), a constant fixed by the carrier alone: raising PRF buys unambiguous velocity and gives up unambiguous range in exact proportion, and changing the carrier moves both together. Inputs are bounded to keep the arithmetic in ordinary double precision: carrier 0.001 to 300 GHz, PRF 10 Hz to 1 MHz, pulse width 0.005 to 1000 microseconds, peak power 0.001 to 100,000 kW, and the pulse must be shorter than the interval. This is simple-pulse timing arithmetic: it does not model pulse compression or coded, chirped or stepped-frequency waveforms, staggered or multiple PRFs, antenna beam shape, atmospheric or rain attenuation, clutter, eclipsing beyond the blind range, or detection probability, and velocity means radial velocity only.

sources.title: Radartutorial, PRF and PRT: pulse repetition frequency is the number of pulses per second, the pulse repetition time is its reciprocal, and the receiving time is shorter than the interval less the pulse length.
Radartutorial, Maximum Unambiguous Range: R_max = c (PRT - PW) / 2 for a fully received echo and c PRT / 2 when the pulse length is negligible, with the worked 1 kHz example giving about 150 km.
Radartutorial, Minimal Measuring Range: the blind range where the transmit pulse still covers the echo, with a 1 microsecond pulse corresponding to a minimum range of about 150 m.

Radartutorial, Doppler Dilemma: unambiguous radial velocity v_r < c f_PRF / (4 f_tx) when the direction of travel is unknown, and the product R_max v_r < c^2 / (8 f_tx) fixed by the carrier frequency.

Radartutorial, Blind Speeds and the Doppler Dilemma: a moving-target indicator is blind where the inter-pulse phase shift is a whole multiple of 360 degrees, and the first blind speed is v_blind = lambda / (2 T_s).

tools.name: Interference Fit Calculator
tools.description: Turn the fit diameter, hub outside diameter, shaft bore, diametral interference and friction into the contact pressure, holding torque, axial force, hub and shaft stresses, safety factor and the temperature rise needed to assemble a press fit or shrink fit.
tools.method: The contact pressure of a press or shrink fit follows from Lamé's thick-walled cylinder solution: the hub is a cylinder pressed on its inside, the shaft one pressed on its outside, and the two elastic deflections together must absorb the diametral interference. With d the fit diameter, D the hub outside diameter, di the shaft bore (zero for a solid shaft), E and ν the moduli and Poisson's ratios, and the subscripts o and i for hub and shaft, the pressure is p = δ / { d [ ((D²+d²)/(D²−d²) + νo)/Eo + ((d²+di²)/(d²−di²) − νi)/Ei ] }, which for a 50 mm solid steel shaft in a 90 mm steel hub with 40 µm of interference gives 58.07 MPa. The hub carries a tensile hoop stress p(D²+d²)/(D²−d²) at its bore and 2pd²/(D²−d²) at its outside, and with the radial stress −p its bore von Mises stress is p√(k²+k+1) for that bore ratio k; the safety factor divides the hub yield strength by it. The shaft is in compression: a solid shaft sits under uniform hydrostatic pressure −p, so its von Mises stress equals p, while a hollow shaft is most stressed at its bore. Friction over the contact area πdL carries an axial slip force F = μpπdL and a torque T = Fd/2 = μpπd²L/2. That same friction force is what a press must supply while the parts slide, because once they are seated the pressure comes from the interference and not from the press. Heating only the hub opens the bore by αdΔT, so the interference alone needs ΔT = δ/(αd) and a 20 µm slip clearance needs (δ + 0.02 mm)/(αd). Because the pressure is linear in the interference, doubling the interference doubles the holding capacity and the bore stress together. Inputs are bounded: fit diameter 1 to 5000 mm, hub outside diameter above the fit diameter up to 10000 mm, shaft bore from 0 to just under the fit diameter, diametral interference 0.1 to 5000 µm, engagement 1 to 5000 mm, friction 0.01 to 1.5, moduli 1 to 1000 GPa, Poisson's ratios 0 to 0.49, hub expansion 0.1 to 50 × 10⁻⁶/°C and hub yield 10 to 3000 MPa. This is a linear-elastic, plane-stress estimate of a single cylindrical fit: it ignores surface roughness and taper, centrifugal growth and service temperature differences, edge stress concentration, fretting and fatigue, and the plastic redistribution that begins once the bore yields, so it is preliminary sizing rather than a design review. Everything runs locally in the browser.

tools.name: Heat Flux Density Converter
tools.description: Convert a heat flux density between W/m², kW/m², mW/cm², W/cm², W/in², Btu/(h·ft²), Btu/(s·ft²), cal/(s·cm²) and kcal/(h·m²), with the exact NIST factors behind every one of them.
aliases: Density of Heat Flow Rate Converter
Btu per hour square foot Converter
tools.method: A heat flux density is a power divided by an area, so every unit reduces to the SI unit watt per square metre by one exact factor and nothing here depends on a measurement. The watt per square metre is the base; the kilowatt is 1000 and the milliwatt 0.001; a square centimetre is 1e-4 m² and a square inch 0.00064516 m², so W/cm² is 10 000 W/m², mW/cm² is 10 W/m² and W/in² is 1550.0031 W/m². The Btu is the International Table Btu of exactly 1055.05585262 J, the calorie the thermochemical calorie of exactly 4.184 J, the hour 3600 s and the foot 0.3048 m, which gives Btu/(h·ft²) = 1055.05585262 / (3600 × 0.09290304) = 3.154590745 W/m², Btu/(s·ft²) = 11 356.52668 W/m², cal/(s·cm²) = 41 840 W/m² and kcal/(h·m²) = 1.1622222 W/m². Results keep six significant digits, trailing zeros are trimmed and thousands are grouped; a magnitude below 1e-6 or from 1e12 up is written in exponential form. Zero is accepted because a surface can carry no heat flow; negative values are refused because a heat flux density has a direction, and anything above 1e9 W/m² is outside the supported range. Typed input may carry grouping commas but not a unit. All arithmetic runs in the browser and the page makes no network request.

tools.name: Hebrew Calendar Converter
tools.description: Convert a Gregorian date to its Hebrew date and back, with the Hebrew year type, month length, weekday and day of the Hebrew year, using the fixed arithmetic Hebrew calendar.
tools.method: The Hebrew calendar is a fixed arithmetic calendar, so a Hebrew date is a pure function of the year and needs no observation. Each 19-year cycle holds twelve common years and seven leap years: year y is leap when (7y + 1) mod 19 is less than 7, and a leap year carries thirteen months by inserting Adar I (30 days) before Adar II (29 days). Days are counted from a fixed epoch. The months elapsed since year 1 are 235 per completed cycle, plus 12 per regular year of the current cycle, plus the leap months of that cycle; the molad of Tishrei then follows from 29 days, 12 hours and 793 parts per month, and the four dehiyyot postpone Rosh Hashanah by at most two days. The first defers a molad at or after midday (18 hours from the start of the Hebrew day at 6 pm). The second defers a Tuesday molad at or after 9 hours and 204 parts in a common year, the third a Monday molad at or after 15 hours and 589 parts at the end of a leap year, and the fourth a Sunday, Wednesday or Friday that would otherwise be 1 Tishrei. The resulting year is 353, 354 or 355 days when common and 383, 384 or 385 when leap, which is what fixes Cheshvan at 29 or 30 days (30 only in a complete year) and Kislev at 29 or 30 (30 except in a deficient year); Tishrei, Shevat, Nisan, Sivan and Av always keep 30 days and Tevet, Iyar, Tammuz, Elul and Adar II 29. Both directions go through one continuous day count shared with the Gregorian calendar, so the weekday is that count modulo 7 and the two calendars cannot drift apart. Adar I exists only in leap years and Adar II only in leap years too, so a month that the chosen year does not have is refused, and a day beyond the month's length is refused with the length that month has in that year. Civil dates from 1600-01-01 to 2200-12-31 are supported, Hebrew years 5360 to 5961, and a Hebrew date whose civil day falls outside that window is refused. The result is the Hebrew date in force during the daylight hours of the civil date entered, because a Hebrew day begins at sunset, so the evening before already belongs to the next Hebrew date; no time of day or location is taken. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
