tools.name: Intel HEX Inspector
tools.description: Check an Intel HEX file record by record: verify every checksum, resolve linear and segment addresses, and report the byte count, address range, gaps, overlaps and entry point.
tools.method: Intel HEX is a text encoding of a memory image: one record per line, each a colon followed by the byte count, a 16-bit load offset, a record type, the data bytes and a checksum, with every field written as pairs of hexadecimal digits. The checksum is the two's complement of the bytes from the byte count to the last data byte, so a correct record sums to zero over its whole binary form. This page splits the text on line breaks, ignores blank lines, and checks each line in turn: the colon, hexadecimal digits only, an even digit count, at least a 10-digit header and checksum, a record length that matches the byte count, and a checksum that makes the record sum to zero. A record that fails a structural check is reported with its line number and left out of the image rather than guessed at. Type 00 records carry data, 01 ends the file and must be the empty :00000001FF, 02 sets the upper bits of a segment base by shifting its two big-endian bytes left four places, 03 sets a start address as a CS:IP pair, 04 sets the upper 16 bits of a 32-bit base and 05 a 32-bit start address; a type 2, 3, 4 or 5 record must carry exactly 2, 4, 2 or 4 data bytes, and any other type is reported as undefined. Each data byte lands at the current base plus the load offset plus its index, wrapped modulo 4 GiB in linear addressing and modulo 64 KiB inside the segment from a type 02 base, which is the difference the specification draws between the two modes. The page counts distinct addresses, so a byte written twice is reported as an overlapping byte rather than counted twice, sorts the addresses to count contiguous blocks, the bytes in the gaps between them and the largest gap, and reports the lowest and highest address, the record and data-byte counts, the end-of-file records and the entry point with the record type that supplied it. A missing end-of-file record, more than one, data after it, an empty data record and a file with no data records are reported too. Input beyond 1,000,000 characters or 50,000 records is refused with the limit named. Everything is parsed in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Brewing Water Salt Additions
tools.description: Enter the batch volume, your starting water profile and the grams of gypsum, calcium chloride, Epsom salt, table salt or baking soda you weighed, and read the final calcium, magnesium, sodium, chloride, sulfate and bicarbonate in ppm, total hardness and alkalinity as CaCO3, and the sulfate to chloride ratio.
tools.method: Brewing salts add ions by mass, so the arithmetic is stoichiometric. The mole fraction of each ion in a salt's formula mass turns a weighed dose into milligrams per litre: ppm = 1000 x grams x (ion mass / salt molar mass) / litres, with ion masses Ca 40.078, Mg 24.305, Na 22.9898, Cl 35.45, SO4 96.056 and HCO3 61.0168 built from IUPAC standard atomic weights. The salts are the hydrates brewing suppliers sell: gypsum CaSO4.2H2O (172.164 g/mol) gives 61.5 ppm calcium and 147.4 ppm sulfate per gram per US gallon, calcium chloride dihydrate CaCl2.2H2O (147.008) gives 72.0 ppm calcium and 127.4 ppm chloride, Epsom salt MgSO4.7H2O (246.466) gives 26.1 ppm magnesium and 103.0 ppm sulfate, table salt NaCl (58.440) gives 103.9 ppm sodium and 160.3 ppm chloride, and baking soda NaHCO3 (84.006) gives 72.3 ppm sodium and 191.9 ppm bicarbonate. The first three sit inside the ranges Brew Your Own publishes; table salt and baking soda follow the same formula. Anhydrous calcium chloride would give 95 ppm calcium from the same weight, so the page names the hydrate form. Starting-water concentrations are added to the contributions before any rounding. Total hardness and alkalinity are reported as calcium carbonate equivalents through the 50.043 g/eq half-mole of CaCO3: hardness = calcium x 50.043 / 20.039 + magnesium x 50.043 / 12.153, alkalinity = bicarbonate x 50.043 / 61.017. The sulfate to chloride ratio comes from the exact concentrations, is shown to two decimals, and is suppressed as no chloride when none is present. ppm is milligrams per litre, so a US gallon is 3.785411784 L. Volume runs from 0.1 to 10,000 litres or 0.1 to 2,600 US gallons, each salt from 0 to 1,000 grams and each starting concentration from 0 to 2,000 ppm, all with at most three decimals and no sign or exponent notation; a malformed or out-of-range value is refused with a field-specific message. The page reports ion concentrations only: it does not model mash pH or acid additions, and chalk is not offered because it dissolves poorly. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Brewhouse Water Planner
tools.description: Plan a brew day's water backwards from the fermenter: enter the batch size, grain bill, mash thickness, boil-off and kettle loss to get the strike water, sparge water, pre-boil and post-boil volumes. The sparge is the remainder after the grain has absorbed its share.
tools.method: The plan runs backwards from the fermenter, because the batch volume in the fermenter is the number the brewer is trying to hit. The wort needed at flameout, chilled, is the batch plus the kettle loss; hot, it is that volume divided by 0.96, because wort contracts about 4 percent as it cools from boiling to pitching temperature (water is 0.9584 kg/L at 100 C against 0.9982 kg/L at 20 C). Adding the boil-off, the rate in litres per hour times the boil length in hours, gives the pre-boil volume. The grain holds its absorption rate times the grain bill, and adding that gives the total water to heat. Strike water is the grain bill times the mash thickness, and sparge water is the remainder of the total: cold = batch + kettle loss; hot = cold / 0.96; pre-boil = hot + boil-off x hours; absorbed = grain x absorption; total = pre-boil + absorbed; strike = grain x thickness; sparge = total - strike. Units are metric (litres, kilograms) or US customary (US gallons, pounds); 1 US gallon is 3.785411784 L, 1 pound is 0.45359237 kg, and 1 qt/lb is 2.086351 L/kg through 1 qt = 0.946352946 L. The absorption default of 1 L/kg sits near the middle of the 0.8-1.1 L/kg that homebrewing guides quote for a drained mash (0.1-0.125 gal/lb); it is equipment data, so the page takes it as an input rather than asserting a constant. Accepted ranges are 1-2,000 L batch, 0.1-500 kg grain, 1-10 L/kg mash thickness, 1-300 minutes boil, 0.1-50 L/h boil-off, 0-100 L kettle loss and 0.3-2 L/kg absorption, each with field-specific messages for blanks, malformed or out-of-range values. If the chosen mash thickness needs more water than the whole batch contains, the page refuses rather than printing a negative sparge: it names the thickness and the batch volume as the two numbers to change. The page plans volumes only. It does not estimate gravity, brewhouse efficiency, mash pH, hop absorption or fermentation, it leaves mash-tun dead space to be folded into the kettle loss, and it makes no food-safety claim.

tools.name: Quilt Setting Triangle Calculator
tools.description: Size the side and corner setting triangles for a quilt whose blocks are set on point: the square to cut for four side triangles at a time and for two corner triangles at a time, how many squares the layout needs, the block count and the finished centre.
tools.method: The layout is a lattice of square blocks turned 45 degrees, so a block set on point is as wide as its diagonal, the finished block size times the square root of 2. Side setting triangles fill the gaps between the block points along the four edges and are cut as quarter-square triangles: a square of the diagonal plus five seam allowances, cut twice on the diagonal, gives four side triangles. At a quarter-inch seam that addition is 1 1/4 inches, the figure Quilter's Cache and Quiltville print. The four corner triangles are half-square triangles from a square of the diagonal divided by the root of two plus three and a half seam allowances, which is block / 1.414 + 7/8 inch at a quarter-inch seam, cut once on the diagonal for two. Both cut sizes are rounded up to the next 1/8 inch, or to the next whole millimetre in metric mode; the unrounded value is reported beside them. The layout needs two side triangles for each gap along the top and bottom and down each side, so 2 x (across - 1) + 2 x (down - 1), and always four corner triangles from two squares, so cutting whole squares can leave spares. The blocks themselves fill both grids, so the setting holds across x down + (across - 1) x (down - 1) blocks, and the finished centre measures across x block x root 2 by down x block x root 2 before any border. Ranges are 0.25 to 60 inches (0.635 to 152.4 centimetres) for the block, 0.1 to 1 inch (0.254 to 2.54 centimetres) for the seam allowance and 1 to 25 blocks each way; a missing, non-numeric, four-decimal or out-of-range value, a fractional block count and an unknown unit are each refused with a message naming the field. Conversions use exactly 2.54 centimetres per inch. Cutting the side squares twice leaves the straight grain on the long outside edge and cutting the corner squares once leaves it on the short edges at the corners, which is why the two are cut differently. Sashing, borders, backing, binding and fabric yardage are not modelled, and the top is trimmed 1/4 inch beyond the outermost points once sewn. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Wi-Fi Data Rate Calculator
tools.description: Work out the radio data rate of an 802.11n, 802.11ac or 802.11ax link from the MCS index, channel width, guard interval and spatial streams it negotiated, then the goodput that rate carries and the airtime one stream of traffic takes.
tools.method: The data rate of one spatial stream is the number of data subcarriers in the channel times the bits of the modulation times the coding rate, divided by the OFDM symbol time; the link rate multiplies that by the spatial streams. A 20 MHz 802.11n or 802.11ac channel carries 52 data subcarriers and a 40 MHz one 108; 802.11ac adds 234 at 80 MHz and 468 at 160 MHz, and 802.11ax uses 234, 468, 980 and 1960. The modulation carries 1 bit per subcarrier at BPSK, 2 at QPSK, 4 at 16-QAM, 6 at 64-QAM, 8 at 256-QAM and 10 at 1024-QAM, and the coding rate runs from 1/2 to 5/6 over MCS 0 to 11: 802.11n defines MCS 0 to 7 per stream with the stream count encoded in the index as 8 x (streams - 1) + MCS, 802.11ac MCS 0 to 9 with 256-QAM at 8 and 9, and 802.11ax adds MCS 10 and 11 at 1024-QAM. An 802.11n or 802.11ac symbol is 3.2 microseconds of data plus a 400 or 800 ns guard interval, so MCS 7 at 20 MHz gives 52 x 6 x 5/6 / 4 us = 65 Mbps and 72.2 Mbps with the short interval; an 802.11ax symbol is 12.8 microseconds plus 800, 1600 or 3200 ns, so 20 MHz MCS 11 gives 143.4, 135.4 and 121.9 Mbps and 80 MHz MCS 11 gives 600.5, 567.1 and 510.4 Mbps, the figures the vendor tables print. 802.11ac leaves a few index, width and stream combinations undefined because they would need a fractional number of coded bits per symbol: 20 MHz omits MCS 9 except with 3 or 6 streams, 80 MHz omits MCS 9 with 6 streams and also MCS 6 with 3 or 7 streams, and 160 MHz omits MCS 9 with 3 streams, so those are refused rather than given a rate the standard does not define. Goodput is the data rate times the MAC efficiency entered, the share of the air that carries payload once preambles, headers, acknowledgements, contention and retries are taken out; that efficiency is the user's own figure, between 10 and 95 percent, not a specification. Airtime is the stream demand divided by the goodput, and the streams figure is your airtime budget times the goodput divided by the demand, rounded down. Ranges are 10 to 95 percent MAC efficiency, 0.1 to 2000 Mbps of stream demand with up to two decimals and 10 to 100 percent airtime budget; an unknown standard, a width or guard interval the standard does not define, an MCS index above the standard's maximum, too many spatial streams, and every missing, non-numeric, three-decimal or out-of-range value are each refused with a message naming the field. The rate is the negotiated single-user rate: OFDMA resource units, MU-MIMO, aggregation, beamforming and vendor extensions are not modelled. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: ISO 3166 Country Code Converter
tools.description: Look up the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, alpha-3 and numeric code of any country or territory from its name, or the country from a code, one entry or a pasted list.
tools.method: The list is ISO 3166-1 as the iso-codes data set publishes it: 249 officially assigned entries, each with a two-letter alpha-2, a three-letter alpha-3, a three-digit numeric code that keeps its leading zeros, the English short name, the official name where ISO publishes one, the ISO common name where one exists, and the fuller name some tables print. The input is split on newlines, commas and semicolons and each entry is resolved on its own. A token of one to three digits is read as a numeric code, zero-padded to three places, so 4 and 004 both find Afghanistan; a two-letter token is read as alpha-2 and a three-letter token as alpha-3, either case, before any name is considered, which is why and returns Andorra. Everything else is folded to lower case with accents, punctuation and repeated spaces removed and matched against the short, official, common and alternate names, with the ISO inverted names ("Korea, Republic of") also matched the other way round ("Republic of Korea"): an exact match first, then a name that starts with the query, then a name that contains it. A stage that matches one entry resolves it, a stage that matches several is reported as ambiguous with up to four of the candidates named, and a query that matches nothing is reported as not found rather than guessed. Sixteen everyday names that ISO does not use are mapped explicitly, among them Britain and UK to GB, Holland to NL, Turkey to TR, Russia to RU, Ivory Coast to CI, Burma to MM, Swaziland to SZ, Cape Verde to CV and the UAE to AE. Up to 50 entries are converted at a time; an empty input and a longer list are refused. The tool is a reference lookup, not an authority: it prints the codes ISO assigns and never derives one. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Brass Valve Fingering Finder
tools.description: Type a written note and see every three-valve brass fingering that plays it, with how many cents each combination sits off equal temperament, on a Bb trumpet, cornet, flugelhorn or F horn.
tools.method: Valved brass is modelled as the harmonic series of the open tube plus valve tubing that lowers the whole series. The traditional just-intonation layout puts the first valve at 1/8 of the main tube, the second at 1/15 and the third at 1/5, which lowers the series by 203.9, 111.7 and 315.6 cents; a combination adds the lengths rather than the intervals, so its pitch factor is 1/(1+sum) and 1-2 comes to 303.6 cents, 2-3 to 409.2, 1-3 to 487.2 and 1-2-3 to 572.2, which is why 1-2 is not the note of 3 and why 1-3 and 1-2-3 are sharp of a true fourth and tritone. For a written note the page lists every combination and every harmonic whose pitch lands within 50 cents of that note, with the deviation in cents from 12-tone equal temperament at A4 = 440 Hz, sorted by absolute deviation so the two ways to play one pitch class sit side by side, and ties are broken by harmonic then by valve name. Harmonics run from 2 to 8, because the page works in written pitch where the pedal is C3 on all four instruments in the list (Bb trumpet, Bb cornet, Bb flugelhorn, F horn), so one fingering table covers all of them and the instrument only changes what the note sounds like: a Bb instrument sounds a major second below its written pitch and the F horn a perfect fifth below. The second table prints the open series, harmonics 2 to 8, as a written note, a sounding note and a deviation from equal temperament, which is where the 13.7 cents flat fifth harmonic and the 31.2 cents flat seventh harmonic of a just series show up. Cents are produced - target, so a negative figure is flat, and the same pitch can appear twice when a valve lands a higher harmonic on a lower one, as the third valve on the sixth harmonic is the open fifth. Only the plain three-valve layout is modelled: no fourth valve, no compensating system, no trigger, throw, slide pull or hand-stopped note, and no alternative crooks or instrument keys, and the page does not pick a fingering for the player because charts, slide pulls and the player's ear decide that. A note is read as a letter A to G, an optional sharp or flat and an octave from 0 to 8, a written range of F#3 to C6 follows from the layout and is refused outside it rather than guessed, and everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network requests.

tools.name: Audio Samples per Frame Calculator
tools.description: Turn a video frame rate and an audio sample rate into samples per frame, the exact sample where any frame starts, and the whole-sample pattern that keeps double-system sound in sync.
tools.method: Samples per frame is the audio sample rate divided by the frame rate, and the page keeps that division exact rather than rounding it. 48 kHz at 25 fps is 1,920 samples per frame with nothing left over, while 48 kHz at 29.97 fps is 1,601.6, so no whole number of samples fits every frame boundary. The fractional rates are the 1001-denominator time bases, not rounded decimals: 23.976 fps is 24000/1001, 29.97 is 30000/1001, 47.952 is 48000/1001 and 59.94 is 60000/1001, which is why 48 kHz at 23.976 fps is exactly 2,002 samples per frame and 44.1 kHz at 29.97 fps is 147,147 samples per 100 frames. The page reduces the ratio to its lowest terms and reports the exact fraction, the whole samples a frame can hold (the floor and the ceiling), how many frames take each, the frames and samples in the repeating cycle, and the start of that cycle. A frame boundary sits at floor(frame x samples per frame) and a frame carries the difference between its own boundary and the next, so every boundary is within one sample of the exact position and the rounding never accumulates: at 29.97 fps the five-frame cycle runs 1,601, 1,602, 1,601, 1,602 and 1,602. The page also prices the flat whole count that editors, cameras and DAWs usually use, because truncating costs sync: a fixed 1,601 samples per frame at 48 kHz loses three samples every five-frame cycle, which is 600 samples or 12.5 ms after 1,000 frames. Frame numbers are plain integers counted from 0 where frame 0 starts at sample 0, not timecodes, and the result is arithmetic for aligning double-system sound, building an audio-only timeline or checking a sync offset, not a converter: it does not resample, retime, shift pitch, apply a 0.1% audio pull-up or pull-down, read drop-frame timecode or model any device's own clock, buffer or converter latency. Frame rates are limited to the ten listed time bases, sample rates to 44.1, 48, 88.2 and 96 kHz, and frame numbers to 10,000,000, about 46 hours at 60 fps, with the sample position kept exact over that whole range. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Sealed Box Alignment Calculator
tools.description: Size a sealed speaker box from a driver's Fs, Qts and Vas: the net volume that lands a target system Q, or the system Q, resonance and -3 dB point of a box you already have.
tools.guidance: The volume is net internal air, after the driver, bracing, lining and any tube are taken out; loose filling can add up to about 40 % to the effective volume, while a stuffed box tunes differently again. Thiele/Small figures are small-signal averages with real tolerances (Fs around 15 %, Vas 20-30 %), so treat the volume as a starting point and measure the finished system. This page computes an alignment, not a loudspeaker: it does not choose a driver, model excursion or power handling, or design a crossover.
tools.method: A sealed box adds an air spring behind the cone. In the lumped Thiele/Small model the box compliance sits in parallel with the driver's suspension, so the stiffening factor is the same for the system Q and the resonance: Qtc = Qts x sqrt(1 + Vas/Vb) and Fc = Fs x sqrt(1 + Vas/Vb), where Vas is the volume of air with the driver's own compliance and Vb is the net box volume. Solving the Q relation for the box gives Vb = Vas / ((Qtc/Qts)^2 - 1), which is why a target only a little above Qts asks for an enormous box, and why no sealed box can pull the system Q below the driver's Qts: the air spring only ever adds stiffness, so Qtc >= Qts and Vb -> infinity as Qtc -> Qts. The page works in both directions, from a target Qtc to the volume and from a volume to the Qtc, and both paths share one ratio, Vas/Vb, which is also reported with the box size in Vas units. The response is a second-order high-pass, |H| = f^2 / sqrt((f^2 - Fc^2)^2 + (f x Fc / Qtc)^2), so the level at Fc is exactly 20 log10(Qtc) dB, the -3 dB point solves the same expression for half power, F3 = Fc x sqrt(u + sqrt(u^2 + 1)) with u = 1/(2 Qtc^2) - 1, and a peak appears only above Qtc = 1/sqrt(2), at Fc / sqrt(1 - 1/(2 Qtc^2)) and 20 log10(Qtc / sqrt(1 - 1/(4 Qtc^2))) dB. Because that peak is a ripple rather than a bump just above the Butterworth Q, the page reports one only from 0.1 dB (about Qtc 0.77) and otherwise says the response is flat into the roll-off. Above the box the response is flat and below it the slope is 12 dB per octave, half the 24 dB of a ported box. Typical targets are 0.5 (well damped, large box), 0.577 (Bessel, best group delay), 0.707 (maximally flat, F3 = Fc) and 0.9 to 1.2 (smaller boxes with a rising peak). Inputs are 5-500 Hz of Fs, 0.05-2 of Qts, 0.5-5,000 litres of Vas, a 0.1-3 target Qtc and a 0.5-5,000 litre net volume; decimal commas are accepted. A target at or below Qts is refused rather than reported as an infinite box, and so is a target that would need more than 5,000 litres. The model is the small-signal one: it ignores box and driver losses (so a real cabinet usually lands slightly flatter), takes the parameters as constant with level, and does not model cone excursion, power handling, port or passive radiator tuning, stuffing placement, a crossover or the room. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: TLS Cipher Suite Decoder
tools.description: Decode a TLS cipher-suite name or two-byte code into its key exchange, authentication, bulk cipher, key length, MAC or PRF and registry status, or read a whole ClientHello offer at once.
tools.guidance: The registry's Recommended column is IANA's own rating, not a security audit: N can mean limited applicability and D marks a suite that should not be negotiated. This page decodes names and codes; it does not say which suites a server should offer, and it does not read live traffic or certificates.
tools.method: A cipher suite is a two-byte value: 0x1301 is the bytes 0x13 and 0x01, which the registry prints as {0x13,0x01}, and this page splits and recombines those bytes. TLS 1.3 names follow TLS_AEAD_HASH (RFC 9846, Appendix B.4): the name carries only the AEAD and the hash used with HKDF, because key exchange and authentication moved into the handshake as the certificate and the signature scheme, so TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 names AES-128-GCM with the SHA-256 hash and nothing about certificates. Names of TLS 1.2 and earlier read TLS_<key exchange>_WITH_<bulk cipher>_<MAC> (RFC 5246, Appendix A.5), and the key-exchange token also names the authentication, so ECDHE_RSA is ephemeral ECDH authenticated by an RSA signature while DH_anon authenticates nobody; a trailing _EXPORT marks the 40-bit suites of the export era. In the AEAD suites (GCM, CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) the trailing hash is the PRF rather than a record MAC, and the RFC 6655 CCM suites name no hash at all because it is fixed at SHA-256, which the page reports as 'not in the name' instead of inventing one. RFC 9150's integrity-only TLS_SHA256_SHA256 and TLS_SHA384_SHA384 carry a hash and no bulk cipher. 0x00FF and 0x5600 are signalling values offered beside the suites and never selected, and the GREASE values of RFC 8701 (0x0A0A, 0x1A1A and so on, two equal bytes ending in 0xA) are deliberately unassigned. The lookup table is the IANA TLS Cipher Suites registry as fetched on 2026-11-16: all 358 named entries, with the unassigned, reserved and range rows left out, and each row keeps its registry name, Recommended flag and reference. Input is one or more names or four-digit hexadecimal codes, case-insensitive and optionally prefixed 0x, up to 32 values; a list keeps the order given, costs two bytes per suite on the wire and reports the registry status of each. Unknown names and malformed codes are refused with one message rather than being guessed at, and the whole decoder runs in the browser with no network access.

tools.name: systemd Socket Unit Builder
tools.description: Write a systemd .socket unit for socket activation from unix, TCP, IPv6 or bare-port listen addresses, with Accept= validation, SocketMode, socket ownership and the exact companion service it needs. Runs locally.
tools.method: Composes one systemd .socket unit from a base name, a description and one to eight ListenStream addresses. Addresses follow systemd.socket(5): a leading slash is an AF_UNIX file-system socket, a leading @ an AF_UNIX abstract socket, a single number a port listened on over IPv6 (dual-stack by default through BindIPv6Only=default), v.w.x.y:port an IPv4 socket, and [x]:y an IPv6 socket. File-system paths must be absolute, at most 4096 characters, free of backslashes, //, . and .. segments and a trailing slash, and fit in 107 bytes because sockaddr_un.sun_path is 108 with the terminator; abstract names need at least one character after @ and no whitespace. Ports are 1-65535 with no leading zeros; IPv4 hosts must be strict dotted quads and IPv6 hosts must be bracketed and valid, compared against a full compression-aware parser. Interface scopes (address%iface) and AF_VSOCK addresses are rejected rather than half-supported, because a literal percent would have to be doubled for unit-file specifier expansion. Addresses are emitted in input order, duplicates are refused, and spaces, double quotes and percent signs in unix names are written as \x20, \x22 and %% so the parser reads back the exact name. Accept=yes is emitted only when selected; it changes the companion unit to the template <base>@.service, where systemd starts one instance per connection and attaches the connection to the instance's standard input and output. With Accept=no the service receives every listening socket as file descriptors starting at 3 (sd_listen_fds(3)) and must not bind the address itself. MaxConnections is validated and written only with Accept=yes, and only when it differs from the default 64. SocketMode (four-digit octal), SocketUser and SocketGroup apply only to file-system unix sockets - the man page scopes the mode to file nodes - so they are ignored, not emitted, for TCP, IPv6, port-only and abstract addresses; SocketMode is written only when it differs from the default 0666, and parent directories are created with the default DirectoryMode=0755. The [Install] section with WantedBy=sockets.target is optional. The page reports the generated file name, the matching service name, the listen mix and the activation contract, warns that a bare port is an IPv6 wildcard and that a unix socket is not removed on stop, and never inspects the host or executes anything.

tools.name: Double Elimination Planner
tools.description: Plan a double-elimination draw: how many matches each winners and losers round plays, who drops into the losers bracket, the longest route to the title and the station time the whole tournament takes. Runs locally.
tools.method: Double elimination in a power-of-two draw. Every entrant starts in the winners bracket; one defeat drops them into the losers bracket and a second ends their run, so n teams play 2n-2 matches, or 2n-1 when a reset final is played. The winners bracket is a single-elimination tree: round k plays n/2^k matches and its losers drop into the matching major stage of the losers bracket. The losers bracket alternates minor and major rounds. An odd losers round pairs survivors of the previous losers round with each other, and the first one pairs the n/2 losers of winners round 1; an even losers round pairs the winners of the previous losers round with the losers of the same-numbered winners round, so each pair of losers rounds halves the bracket. That yields 2p-2 losers rounds and n-2 matches for p = log2(n) levels, which with the winners bracket's n-1 gives the published 2n-2 game count, one or two fewer than twice the teams. The page refuses any field other than 4, 8, 16 or 32 teams: a bye in a double-elimination draw leaves a losers-bracket slot that has to be settled by a walkover or a reseed, and the model does not invent one. Rounds are reported as blocks in playing order - winners round 1, losers round 1, then for each further winners round its major losers round followed by the next minor one, then the final - because a block cannot start before the matches that feed it finish, so a block costs ceil(matches / stations) match lengths. The plan reports that block time, the perfect-packing floor of ceil(total / stations) blocks, the total station time, and the longest route to the title: 2p matches for a first-round loser who wins the whole draw, one more with a reset. A single final eliminates the losers-bracket champion with one defeat, which is why the game count can land one short; a reset final replays it only when the losers-bracket side wins the first. Inputs are limited to 5-180 minute matches and 1-16 stations, and text, fractional and out-of-range values are refused with the field named. Seeding order, court assignment, walkovers, divisions and clock times are not modelled, and the page stores nothing and makes no requests.

tools.name: GitHub Actions Trigger Matcher
tools.description: Check whether a GitHub Actions workflow runs for a push, tag or pull request: evaluate the on: branch, tag and path filters and see the pattern and line that decides each one. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Reads the top-level on: block of a workflow file and evaluates it for one event. The block is accepted as a single event name, a flow list (on: [push, pull_request]), or a map of event names to filter blocks; only push and pull_request are evaluated, and the other events are listed but not modelled. Inside an event, branches, branches-ignore, tags, tags-ignore, paths and paths-ignore take a block list, a flow list, or one inline value; types, cron, inputs and any other key are reported as not evaluated. Comments, quoted scalars and blank lines are tolerated, while tabs in indentation, inline mappings, block scalars, YAML anchors and aliases are refused rather than guessed: an unquoted pattern that starts with * is a YAML alias, so it has to be quoted. Patterns are matched against the whole branch name, tag name or repository-relative path, case-sensitively. * matches any run of characters except /, ** matches any run including /, ? matches zero or one of the character before it, + matches one or more of the character before it, [...] matches one character from a set or range, and a backslash escapes the next character; a pattern is matched from the start of the path, so */README.md does not match docs/README.md but **/README.md does. Patterns are checked in order and the last matching one decides, so a later pattern prefixed with ! removes a name that an earlier pattern included, and a positive pattern after a negative one adds it back; a ! pattern needs at least one positive pattern beside it. branches with branches-ignore, tags with tags-ignore and paths with paths-ignore cannot be combined in one event, because GitHub rejects the workflow, and the page refuses them instead of picking one. For push, a ref is filtered by the branches family when it is a branch and by the tags family when it is a tag, so defining only one family means the other kind of ref never triggers the workflow; with neither family every ref does. For pull_request the base branch is matched against the branches family. Path filters run on the changed paths and are satisfied when at least one path is included, or, for paths-ignore, when at least one path is not ignored; they are not evaluated at all for tag pushes. When a branches family and a paths family are both present, both have to be satisfied. Each filter row reports its outcome, the decisive pattern and its line, and each changed path reports the pattern that included or ignored it. Activity types, schedule cron, workflow_dispatch inputs, workflow_call, merge queues, reusable workflows, protected-branch rules and the branch-protection requirement for code-owner review are outside the model, and the page stores nothing and makes no requests.

tools.name: Phase Noise to RMS Jitter Calculator
tools.description: Integrate a single-sideband phase-noise curve over a chosen offset band and report the RMS phase error and RMS jitter at a given carrier frequency, with each segment's share of the total.
tools.method: L(f) is read as a straight line in log10(offset) between the points you enter, the line-segment approximation measurement software uses. The single-sideband curve is integrated over the band you choose: A = the integral of 10^(L(f)/10) df, reported as 10 log10(A) dBc. The two sidebands double the phase variance, so the RMS phase error is sqrt(2A) radians, and dividing by 2*pi*f0 converts it to RMS time jitter. Every segment of the integrated curve is reported with its share of the total, because the close-in region and the wideband floor contribute differently and the band choice changes the answer. The band must lie inside the entered offsets: the page never extrapolates a curve, and a band start above the lowest offset simply excludes the close-in region, which is how wander is kept out of a jitter figure. The 12 kHz to 20 MHz band is offered as the telecom clock convention rather than a universal rule. Validation refuses a single point, offsets that do not increase, levels outside -250 to 30 dBc/Hz, and a band that is reversed or outside the data. Discrete spurs, residual FM, period jitter (which needs the 4 sin^2(pi f tau) weighting), amplitude noise and wander outside the band are not modelled, and the arithmetic assumes the phase noise is symmetric about the carrier. Nothing leaves the page.

tools.name: Spur Gear Geometry Calculator
tools.description: Turn a metric module, two tooth counts and a reference pressure angle into the pitch, tip, root and base diameters of both gears, the centre distance and ratio, and the contact ratio of the mesh.
tools.method: The page takes a metric module m, a pinion tooth count z1, a gear tooth count z2 and a reference pressure angle alpha, and reports the nominal geometry of a standard full-depth external involute spur gear pair. The reference (pitch) diameter is d = m z, the addendum is 1.00 m and the dedendum is 1.25 m, so the tip diameter is d + 2m, the root diameter is d - 2.5m and the whole depth is 2.25m. The base diameter is d cos alpha and the base pitch is pi m cos alpha. Both gears share the module and the pressure angle, so the centre distance is m (z1 + z2) / 2, the same as half the sum of the reference diameters, and the ratio is z2 / z1 shown as a reduced integer pair with the gear first. The contact ratio is the length of the path of contact divided by the base pitch: (sqrt(ra1^2 - rb1^2) + sqrt(ra2^2 - rb2^2) - a sin alpha) over pi m cos alpha, using the tip and base radii of both wheels. For a contact ratio between 1 and 2 the fractional part is the share of the mesh cycle with two pairs in contact; above 2 the page still reports the average pair count but shows that share as not applicable rather than inventing a three-pair split. The no-undercut limit 2 / sin^2(alpha) is printed for the chosen pressure angle and a pinion below it is flagged, because a standard cutter would undercut it without profile shift. This is nominal tooth geometry only: the page does not check bending or pitting strength, load capacity, backlash, interference between non-mating features, profile shift or addendum modification, helical overlap, manufacturing tolerance or surface finish. Validation refuses a module outside 0.1 to 100 mm, tooth counts that are not whole numbers between 3 and 400, and a pressure angle outside 12 to 30 degrees. Nothing leaves the page.

tools.name: Data Transfer Rate Converter
tools.description: Convert a data transfer rate between bit and byte units per second — bit/s through Tbit/s, B/s through TB/s, and KiB/s through TiB/s — and see every unit at once, so 100 Mbit/s reads as 12.5 MB/s. Runs in your browser.
tools.method: The page treats a transfer rate as a quantity per second expressed in a unit of data and converts every unit through bits per second. One byte is eight bits, so a byte unit is eight times its bit equivalent at the same prefix: 100 Mbit/s is 12.5 MB/s and 1 kB/s is 8 kbit/s. Decimal SI prefixes step by powers of 1,000 (kbit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s, Tbit/s and kB/s through TB/s) and binary IEC prefixes step by powers of 1,024 (KiB/s, MiB/s, GiB/s, TiB/s), so 1 MiB/s is 1,048.576 kB/s and 1 GiB/s is 1,073.741824 MB/s. The chosen pair is the headline result and every supported unit is listed in a grouped table, which keeps both families visible at once. Results are rounded to six significant digits and grouped in thousands; values below 0.0001 or at least 1e13 are printed in exponent form so that 1 bit/s does not collapse to zero in TiB/s. Input is a plain decimal number, optionally grouped with commas, from zero up to 1 Pbit/s (1e15 bit/s) in the chosen unit; text, exponent notation, a misplaced comma and negative values are refused with a specific message rather than clipped. This is nominal unit arithmetic only: it does not model protocol headers, framing, forward error correction, retransmission, duplex asymmetry or measured goodput, so a real link carries less payload than its line rate, and the decimal-versus-binary distinction reflects how a network rate is quoted against how an operating system reports file throughput. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: SMS 7-Bit Packing
tools.description: Pack a text message into the GSM 7-bit septets an SMS carries and read packed user data back, with the septet and octet counts, the extension characters that cost two septets each, and the number of message parts the text needs. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: Each character is looked up in the GSM 7-bit default alphabet of 3GPP TS 23.038, one septet per character, except the ten extension characters (form feed, ^ { } \ [ ~ ] | and the euro sign), which travel as the escape septet 0x1B plus an extension code and therefore cost two septets; a character outside both tables is refused with its position rather than replaced. The septets are packed seven bits at a time into octets, the first septet in the low bits of the first octet; when exactly seven bits are left spare in the last octet they carry the code of carriage return, because seven zero bits would read back as an @, and the septet count excludes that filler. One message part holds 160 septets in 140 octets; beyond that the text is split into parts of 153 septets, the payload left after a six-octet concatenation header. Reading hex back takes the septet count from the octet length, the largest number of septets that fits, and drops a trailing carriage return only when that derived count exactly fills the octets, since the length alone cannot tell the filler from a typed carriage return; an explicit septet count overrides both rules. Extension codes with no character and data ending on an escape septet are refused. Packed data is limited to 280 octets and text to 1,000 characters. Nothing is uploaded, stored or sent.

tools.name: Cheese Yield Calculator
tools.description: Predict how much cheese a vat of milk gives from its fat, protein and target moisture with the Van Slyke yield formula: kilograms of cheese per 100 kg of milk, the weight from the whole vat, the milk each kilogram takes and the solids behind the figure. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: The Van Slyke and Price formula predicts rennet-set cheese yield from the fat and casein of the milk and the moisture the cheese is made to: kilograms of cheese per 100 kg of milk are (0.93 × fat + casein − 0.1) × 1.09 ÷ (1 − moisture). The 0.93 keeps 93 percent of the milk fat in the cheese, the 0.1 kg per 100 kg is the casein lost in the whey as glycomacropeptide, and 1.09 adds the salt, milk salts and lactose that stay in the curd, about nine percent of its fat and casein, while the moisture fraction divides those solids up into cheese. Casein is estimated from the total protein an analyzer reports at the common casein number of 0.78, by the 0.830 × protein − 0.199 regression from the 1998 Ontario bulk-tank survey, or typed directly from a casein-calibrated test. Fat is limited to 0 to 12 percent, protein to 0.1 to 10 percent, casein to 0 to 9 percent and target cheese moisture to 20 to 60 percent, and casein has to stay above the 0.1 kg lost in the whey. The result is a theoretical target for Cheddar and Colby-style makes, not a guarantee: pasteurisation heat, whey protein in the vat, draining pH, curd fines and salt move the real yield by a few percent. Nothing is uploaded, stored or sent.

tools.name: NTP Offset Calculator
tools.description: Work out the clock offset between a server and your computer from the four NTP exchange timestamps: the offset of the server clock, the round-trip delay, the server's reading when the reply arrived and the range the true offset can occupy. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: One NTP exchange gives the offset of the server clock relative to the client clock and the round-trip delay, exactly as RFC 5905 section 8 defines them: offset = ((T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)) / 2 and delay = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2), where T1 is when the client sent the request, T2 when the server received it, T3 when the server sent the reply and T4 when the client received it. T1 and T4 come from the client clock and T2 and T3 from the server's, so only the differences inside each pair are used and any fixed origin works on each side. A positive offset means the server clock reads ahead, so adding it to a local reading gives the server's time and the local clock is that far slow. The request and the reply are assumed to take the same time on the wire, which leaves the true offset within half the delay of the estimate: a narrow delay gives a tight answer and a wide one a loose answer. A negative delay is arithmetically possible, as RFC 5905 notes when the two clocks run at different frequencies, but it cannot come from a sound exchange, so the page refuses those figures instead of clamping the delay to a precision floor. Each timestamp accepts 0 to 1,000,000,000,000 seconds with up to 12 decimal places, and the arithmetic is carried in integer picoseconds so epoch-sized readings keep every digit the input holds. Nothing is uploaded, stored or sent.

tools.name: Fiber Trunk Sizing Calculator
tools.description: Work out how many fiber strands and multifiber trunk cables a duplex circuit count needs: add the spare allowance, round up to whole 8-, 12- or 24-fiber trunks, and see the unused strands, strand utilisation and the connector counts at both ends. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: A duplex circuit needs two strands, one in each direction, so the planner first provisions pairs = ceil(circuits x (1000 + spare tenths of a percent) / 1000) and then strands = 2 x pairs. A trunk cable carries a fixed number of fibers, so trunks = ceil(strands / fibers) and the installed strand count is trunks x fibers; the difference between that and the required count is reported as unused strands, and strand utilisation is strands / installed. Connectors follow the same counts: each trunk terminates in one MPO connector at each end, giving 2 x trunks; each duplex pair is presented on one LC duplex adapter at each end, so the adapters equal the installed strand count and the LC connectors, one per strand end, are twice that. The planner also evaluates 8-, 12- and 24-fiber trunks for the same requirement and names a smaller-waste option when one exists, preferring the larger trunk on a tie because it needs fewer cables. Duplex circuits are whole numbers from 1 to 100,000, spare capacity is 0 to 100 percent with at most one decimal place, and the trunk must be 8, 12 or 24 fibers; blank, fractional, negative and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named instead of being defaulted. This is planning arithmetic: the polarity method, cassette mapping, spare policy and the parts actually ordered stay with the cabling designer, so the page states no sources for them.

tools.name: Tide Height Calculator
tools.description: Estimate the height of the tide between high and low water with the rule of twelfths: enter both water heights and the time since the reference water to get the height now, how much the water has already moved and an hour-by-hour curve. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.guidance: A planning estimate only. The rule of twelfths assumes a semi-diurnal tide that rises and falls in about six hours; wind, barometric pressure, river flow and shallow-water effects move real heights and times away from it. Use official tide tables, harmonic predictions and local knowledge for navigation, anchoring and drying heights.
tools.method: The rule of twelfths moves the water in six hourly steps of 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths of the tidal range, so the cumulative fraction of the range is 0, 1/12, 3/12, 6/12, 9/12, 11/12 and 12/12 at 0 to 6 hours after the reference water. The page takes range = high - low, and for a falling tide height = high - range x fraction, for a rising tide height = low + range x fraction. A time between whole hours interpolates linearly between the neighbouring cumulative twelfths, so 2.5 hours after high water uses 4.5/12 of the range. The change so far is the difference between the height now and the reference water, the remaining change is range minus that, and the same fraction is applied at each whole hour for the curve. Heights are given to two decimal places. Both heights must be numbers in metres with at most two decimal places between -20 and 20, high water must be higher than low water, and the elapsed time must be 0 to 6 hours written as decimal hours or h:mm; blank, malformed and out-of-range values are refused with the failing field named instead of being defaulted. The rule approximates a sine curve and assumes a semi-diurnal tide, so mixed and diurnal tides, shallow estuaries and weather depart from it; this is a planning estimate, not a harmonic prediction.

tools.name: MIDI Pitch Bend Calculator
tools.description: Convert a MIDI pitch bend value into semitones and cents for a given bend range, or turn a pitch offset back into the fourteen-bit value, its LSB and MSB and the full channel message. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.guidance: The page cannot read the receiver: the semitones it reports assume the bend range you enter matches the range the instrument or plug-in is actually set to, usually through RPN 0. Check the patch before relying on the interval.
tools.method: A pitch bend change is sent as the status byte 1110nnnn for the channel followed by the seven-bit least-significant byte and the seven-bit most-significant byte of a fourteen-bit value, so the value is MSB x 128 + LSB. Centre is 8192 (2000H) and means no pitch change. The pitch offset is (value - 8192) / 8192 x bend range, so a value of 0 is the whole range down, 16383 is 8191/8192 of the range up, and the cents are the offset x 100 with the frequency ratio 2^(semitones/12). Going the other way, the value is 8192 + (offset / range) x 8192, rounded to the nearest whole number and clamped to 0 to 16383, and the page reports how far that rounded value sits from the requested offset in cents. The bend range must be 0.01 to 127 semitones, the range RPN 0 can carry, written with at most two decimal places; the channel must be 1 to 16 and a bend value must be a whole number from 0 to 16383. Blank, malformed and out-of-range entries are refused with the failing field named instead of being defaulted. The page models the message and the arithmetic only: it does not read or send MIDI, and it cannot know whether a device honours the least-significant byte, uses a different range, or supports the resulting interval.

tools.name: Video Scan Format Timing Calculator
tools.description: Read the line and frame timing of a standard video scan format: active and blanking samples per line, line rate and duration, frame or field rate and the pixel clock, with an optional measured clock.
tools.method: A scan format fixes four counts: active samples per line, active lines, samples in a total line (active plus horizontal blanking) and total lines per frame (active plus vertical blanking). The line rate is the pixel clock divided by the samples per total line and the line period is its reciprocal, so 1080p at 25 Hz gives 74.25 MHz / 2,640 = 28.125 kHz and a 35.556 microsecond line, of which 25.859 microseconds carry the 1,920 active samples and 9.697 microseconds are blanking. The frame rate is the line rate divided by the total lines and the frame period is its reciprocal; an interlaced format carries two fields per frame, so its field rate is twice the frame rate. Fractional-rate systems use the matching integer rate divided by 1.001, which is why 59.94 and 29.97 Hz run at a 74.25/1.001 = 74.1758 MHz clock with 2,200 samples per line. The pixel clock can be overridden with a measured value: the line and frame rates then follow the clock and the page reports the deviation from the format's nominal clock. Blanking is counted per total line only; sync widths, the front and back porch split, tolerances, ancillary data and embedded audio are not modelled. The calculation runs entirely in the browser.

tools.name: API Gravity Converter
tools.description: Convert crude oil API gravity to specific gravity, density in kg/m³, lb/ft³ and kg/L and barrels per metric tonne, or back, at 60 °F with the light, medium or heavy grade.
tools.method: API gravity is a density scale for petroleum liquids: API = 141.5 / SG − 131.5, where SG is the oil's specific gravity at 60 °F (15.56 °C) relative to water at the same temperature, so SG = 141.5 / (API + 131.5). This page accepts whichever of the three measures you already have — API gravity, specific gravity or density in kg/m³ — converts it to the other two and shows the density in kg/m³, lb/ft³ and kg/L. For the volume-to-mass step it treats water at 60 °F as 999.016 kg/m³, the ASTM D1250 (2008) value, and a barrel as 42 US gallons, 0.158987294928 m³, so a metric tonne of oil occupies 1,000 / (density × 0.158987294928) barrels; at 35 °API that is 849.0 kg/m³ and 7.408 barrels per tonne. Grades follow the common cut-offs: light above 31.1 °API, medium from 22.3 to 31.1, heavy below 22.3 and extra heavy below 10. Inputs are limited to -10 to 150 °API, 0.3 to 2.5 specific gravity or 300 to 2500 kg/m³. No temperature correction is applied: a hydrometer or densimeter reading taken at another temperature must first be corrected to 60 °F with the ASTM D1250 tables. Everything is computed in the browser and nothing is uploaded.

tools.name: Speaker Crossover Calculator
tools.description: Design a passive two-way speaker crossover: enter the crossover frequency and the woofer and tweeter impedances to get the series inductor and capacitor, the second-order shunt elements, the level each branch reaches at the crossover and the resistors of a constant-impedance pad for the tweeter.
tools.guidance: Component values only: the network is designed around one impedance per driver at one frequency, and a real driver's impedance moves with frequency, so measure it at the crossover before ordering parts. The slopes are electrical, the acoustic crossover is where the two drivers' own responses meet, and this page does not model sensitivity, cone breakup, directivity, off-axis summation, power handling, part tolerances or the values you can actually buy.
tools.method: A passive two-way crossover puts a low-pass network in front of the woofer and a high-pass network in front of the tweeter, and a power amplifier's output impedance is low enough to treat as an ideal voltage source. A first-order (6 dB per octave) branch is one series reactance sized to equal the driver's impedance at the crossover frequency fc: L = Z / (2 pi fc) for the woofer's inductor and C = 1 / (2 pi fc Z) for the tweeter's capacitor, so each branch is 3 dB down at fc. A second-order (12 dB per octave) Butterworth branch adds a shunt element across the driver and scales both reactances by sqrt(2): the woofer gets L = sqrt(2) Z / (2 pi fc) in series and C = 1 / (sqrt(2) * 2 pi fc Z) across it, and the tweeter gets the mirrored pair, C = 1 / (sqrt(2) * 2 pi fc Z) in series and L = sqrt(2) Z / (2 pi fc) across it. Those values make each branch a maximally flat second-order section: 1 / sqrt(2) at fc, no peak anywhere, and 12 dB per octave beyond it, which the page's tests confirm by evaluating the exact two-element network against the analytic Butterworth magnitude. Tables that terminate the network with a source impedance equal to the driver's instead put twice the calculated capacitance in the low-pass shunt, which is why some published tables disagree on that one part while agreeing on the series elements. The tweeter pad is a constant-impedance L network: with the driver impedance Z and a voltage ratio k = 10^(-dB/20), the series resistor is Z (1 - k) and the shunt resistor is Z k / (1 - k), so the pad still presents Z to the high-pass branch and the network values above stand. Inputs are a crossover frequency from 100 to 10,000 Hz, a woofer and tweeter impedance from 1 to 32 ohms each and a tweeter level from 0 to 12 dB; decimal commas are accepted, and blank fields, text, a missing order and values outside those bounds are refused with the field named. Everything runs in the browser: no uploads, storage or network access.

tools.name: IPv6 Transition Address Decoder
tools.description: Decode an IPv6 address built by 6to4, Teredo, ISATAP or NAT64: recover the embedded IPv4 address, the Teredo server and hidden client port, the 6to4 site prefix and the NAT64 prefix length, all locally.
tools.guidance: Bits only: the page reads the address you paste and never contacts it, the Teredo server or a resolver, so it explains the layout without saying whether the tunnel works or who owns the address. A network-specific NAT64 prefix cannot be recognised from an address at all, so paste yours in the second field; without it, those addresses read as unrecognised. 6to4's relay anycast prefix was deprecated in RFC 7526, so a decodable 6to4 address is not evidence of working connectivity, and an ISATAP identifier only shows which IPv4 address the node claims, not that it is reachable. Every field shown is read straight from the 128 bits; nothing is looked up.
tools.method: The page reads the 128 bits of one address and asks which transition layout produced them, testing 6to4, then Teredo, then NAT64, then ISATAP, because a NAT64 address can end in an interface identifier that would otherwise read as ISATAP's. 6to4 (RFC 3056): the address starts with 2002::/16 and the 32 bits at positions 16 to 47 are the site's public IPv4 address, so the site holds the 2002:V4ADDR::/48 prefix and leaves through the 6to4 relay anycast address 192.88.99.1, whose anycast prefix RFC 7526 deprecated. Teredo (RFC 4380): the address starts with 2001:0::/32, bits 32 to 63 are the Teredo server's IPv4 address, bits 64 to 79 are flags whose only defined bit is 0x8000 (the client's cone-NAT belief), bits 80 to 95 are the client's mapped UDP port and bits 96 to 127 its mapped IPv4 address, both stored with every bit inverted, so the port is that 16-bit field exclusive-ORed with 0xFFFF and the address is that 32-bit field exclusive-ORed with 0xFFFFFFFF; the reserved flag bits must be zero and are reported when they are not. NAT64 (RFC 6052): the address is inside the well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96, or inside a network-specific prefix of 32, 40, 48, 56, 64 or 96 bits that you supply; the IPv4 address follows the prefix, with the first 64 - n bits in positions n to 63, the reserved octet at 64 to 71 skipped, and the remaining bits from position 72, so a /32 keeps all 32 bits at 32 to 63 and a /64 keeps all of them at 72 to 103. That reserved octet must be zero and the bits after the IPv4 address are reserved for future use, so both are reported. ISATAP (RFC 5214): the last 64 bits are the interface identifier 0000:5EFE:w.x.y.z with the four IPv4 octets in network byte order, or 0200:5EFE:w.x.y.z when the u bit marks that IPv4 address as globally unique, and the identifier can sit under a link-local, unique-local or global prefix, which is why ISATAP is matched on the identifier instead of on a prefix. A network-specific NAT64 prefix cannot be recognised from the address alone, so it is a separate field, and when it is supplied and the address falls outside it the page says so instead of guessing. The canonical form shown is RFC 5952. The page refuses rather than guesses: an empty address, spaces or control characters, brackets, a zone ID, a prefix length on the address itself, a second :: marker, groups that are not one to four hexadecimal digits, an embedded IPv4 part that is not four decimal octets, and a prefix field with no length or a length other than the six RFC 6052 allows.

tools.name: Linux Socket Table Decoder
tools.description: Decode a row of /proc/net/tcp, tcp6, udp or udp6 into the local and remote address and port, the socket state, the queue sizes, the UID and the socket inode. Runs in your browser.
tools.guidance: Use it when ss, netstat or lsof are missing - a scratch container, a chroot, a busybox or distroless image - and the kernel's own socket table is all you have. Paste the rows as /proc prints them, header and all. The inode in the last column is what ties a row to a process: it appears as socket:[N] among that process's open files, and the page shows the one-liner that finds it. In a UDP table the state reads 07 while the socket is unconnected and 01 once connect() fixed its peer.
tools.method: The /proc row has no labels, so the page locates the first token shaped like an address:port pair and then requires every column after it to match its own shape, which is what keeps a pasted header or a shifted row from being read as data. The kernel prints the address as one 32-bit word for tcp and udp, or four 32-bit words for tcp6 and udp6, with %08X straight from the socket's stored __be32 field rather than in network order, and the port as %04X; on a little-endian host the four octets of each word therefore read backwards, so 0100007F is 127.0.0.1, 3500007F is 127.0.0.53 and 00000000000000000000000001000000 is ::1. The decoder reverses the octets of each word and then formats IPv6 in RFC 5952 canonical form - lowercase, no leading zeros, the longest run of two or more zero groups collapsed, the first run winning a tie - and prints an IPv4-mapped address in mixed notation as ::ffff:a.b.c.d, which is why an IPv6 endpoint comes back bracketed with the port after the bracket. Column 4 is the low byte of the kernel's sk_state enum: the page carries the thirteen values from include/net/tcp_states.h, and because a UDP socket keeps the same enum it reads 07 (CLOSE) while unconnected and 01 (ESTABLISHED) once connect() fixed its peer, so udp mode relabels those two and flags every other code as unexpected. tx_queue:rx_queue is converted from hex to bytes, tr:tm->when to the timer state plus jiffies, retrnsmt to a count, and uid, the probes-out column and the inode are read as decimal. The page accepts the full eleven-column row, the short local/remote/state form and a lone endpoint, skips a header line and counts it, and refuses a row whose fields do not line up with the column name and the value that failed instead of shifting the rest by one. The seven debug fields after the inode - reference count, a zero pointer, retransmission timeout, delayed-ACK control word, congestion window and slow-start threshold - are counted but not interpreted. Everything is computed locally with integer arithmetic: no network access, uploads or storage.

sources.title: Linux kernel documentation, The /proc/net/tcp and /proc/net/tcp6 variables: the annotated row layout used by the column reference, including the transmit and receive queues, the timer and jiffies fields, the uid, the probe counter, the inode and the debug tail.

proc_pid_net(5) from the Linux man-pages: /proc/net/tcp and /proc/net/udp hold the kernel hash slot, the local and remote address and port, the socket status, the queue sizes, the timer fields and the effective UID of the creator.
Linux kernel include/net/tcp_states.h: the sk_state enum read by the page, TCP_ESTABLISHED = 1 through TCP_BOUND_INACTIVE = 13, with TCP_CLOSE = 7 and TCP_LISTEN = 10.

Linux kernel net/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c, tcp4_seq_show: the seq_printf that writes each row as %4d: %08X:%04X %08X:%04X %02X %08X:%08X %02X:%08lX %08X %5u %8d %llu, which fixes the column order and shows the address printed from the stored field rather than in network order.

RFC 9293, Transmission Control Protocol: the state names and transitions behind the st column and the state table, and the reason a listener, a TIME_WAIT socket and a half-open connection are distinguished.

tools.name: Hockey Goalie Stats Calculator
tools.description: Turn a goaltender's minutes played, goals against and saves into goals against average, save percentage, shots faced and shots against per 60 minutes.
tools.guidance: Use it for one game line or a whole season; ice time takes mm:ss or decimal minutes. Enter only goals charged to the goaltender and only shots the official scorer counted, because empty-net goals, shootout goals and shootout saves are not part of GAA or save percentage. Shots faced is derived as saves plus goals against, so the numbers cannot contradict each other, and a goaltender who faced no shots shows a dash instead of an invented percentage.
tools.method: Minutes played are accepted as mm:ss, where the seconds field must be below 60, or as a decimal number of minutes such as 58.2; a leading colon-free whole number counts as complete minutes. Both forms are converted to whole seconds (mm x 60 + ss, or the decimal rounded to the nearest second) and every rate is computed from that integer, so no fractional minute is rounded twice. The ice time must be at least one second and at most 100,000 minutes, which is 6,000,000 seconds. Goals against and saves must each be whole numbers from 0 to 10,000. Shots against is saves plus goals against, because a shot on goal that scores is counted as a shot and is not a save; that identity is what lets the page derive shots faced without asking for a fourth number that could disagree. Goals against average is 60 x goals against / minutes played, which is also 3,600 x goals against / seconds, and is reported to two decimals like the published statistic. Save percentage is saves / shots against, reported to three decimals in the North American decimal form where .933 means 93.3 percent, together with the same value as a true percentage to one decimal. When shots against is zero the save percentage is undefined and is shown as a dash rather than as a number. Shots against per 60 minutes scales the shot count by 3,600 / seconds. Each figure is rounded half away from zero at the precision it is displayed with. The tool computes from the counts you supply: it does not adjust for team defence, score effects, shot quality, blocked shots or the scorer's judgement, and it does not decide whether a goal should have been charged to the goaltender. Empty-net and shootout goals are excluded from official goals against average, and shootout saves are excluded from official save percentage, so leave them out of the entries. Everything is calculated in this page; nothing is uploaded, stored or fetched.

sources.title: Hockey-Reference NHL Stats Glossary: GAA is goals against divided by minutes played, then multiplied by 60; SV% is saves divided by shots against, and saves are shots against minus goals against.

Wikipedia, Goals against average: for ice hockey a goaltender's goals allowed per 60 minutes, with overtime goals and overtime ice time included but empty-net and shootout goals excluded, usually given to two decimal places.
Wikipedia, Save percentage: saves divided by shots on goal, commonly written as a decimal in North America, so .933 means 93.3 percent of shots were stopped.

tools.name: Kubernetes Resource Quantity Converter
tools.description: Convert Kubernetes CPU and memory quantities such as 250m, 1.5, 64Mi or 129e6 into exact cores and bytes, and add a list of container requests into one total.
tools.guidance: Use it when a manifest, a kubectl description or an incident note gives CPU or memory in units you want as plain numbers. CPU counts cores, memory counts bytes, and case matters: M is a million bytes while m is a thousandth, so 400m of memory is 0.4 bytes and almost always means 400Mi. The total adds the lines exactly as Kubernetes stores them, after rounding any value finer than 0.001, and the page says when it does.
tools.method: Every line is read with the Quantity grammar documented by the Kubernetes API reference: an optional plus or minus sign, a decimal number that may be written 12, 12.5 or .5, an optional decimal exponent such as 1e3, and an optional suffix, which the grammar makes an alternative to the exponent. The suffixes are m for one thousandth, k, M, G, T, P and E for 10^3 through 10^18, and Ki, Mi, Gi, Ti, Pi and Ei for 2^10 through 2^60. Parsing splits the digits into a BigInt mantissa and a decimal scale and multiplies in the suffix factor, so 250m becomes 250 with scale 3, 1.5Gi becomes 1610612736, and 129e6 becomes 129000000 without any floating-point step. The value is normalised by removing trailing zeros, and the magnitude is checked against 2^63-1, the limit the reference states for a single Quantity; anything larger is refused rather than capped silently. Kubernetes keeps at most three decimal places and rounds more precise values up in magnitude, so a parsed value with a larger scale is rounded up to the nearest 0.001 before it is displayed or summed, which is the documented 0.1m becoming 1m, and the page prints a warning naming the original value. The lines are then added by aligning their scales, so the total is the arithmetic sum of the stored lines: no per-line figure is rounded again and no fraction is dropped. For CPU the total is reported in cores and in millicores, the unit of 0.001 core that Kubernetes requires for fractions; binary and power-of-ten suffixes are refused for CPU because CPU is counted in cores, matching the documentation. For memory and storage the total is reported in bytes together with the largest exact binary multiple and, when the total is not an exact multiple, a two-decimal approximation marked with a tilde; memory quantities below one byte are flagged, and a bare m suffix on memory is called out as the 0.4-byte mistake the documentation warns about. Lines may carry a name before an equals sign for readability, a leading hash marks a comment, at most 40 quantities and 4,000 characters are accepted, and the page does no network access.

sources.title: Kubernetes API reference: Quantity — the serialization grammar (Ki to Ei, m and k to E, or a decimal exponent), the 2^63-1 magnitude limit, and the rule that values with more than three decimal places round up, so 0.1m becomes 1m.

Kubernetes documentation: Resource Management for Pods and Containers — CPU is measured in cores, where 0.1 equals 100m and precision finer than 1m is not allowed; memory is measured in bytes with the suffixes E, P, T, G, M, k or Ei, Pi, Ti, Gi, Mi, Ki, and 400m of memory means 0.4 bytes.

kubernetes/apimachinery: pkg/api/resource/quantity.go — the Quantity implementation that parses these strings, keeps three decimal places of precision, and canonicalises 1.5 as 1500m and 1.5Gi as 1536Mi.

tools.name: Lead Screw Torque Calculator
tools.description: Turn the axial load, nominal diameter, pitch, starts, thread form and thread plus collar friction into the torque needed to raise a lead screw, the torque to lower it, its efficiency, its lead angle and whether it self-locks.
tools.method: The page treats the screw as a block sliding on the unwrapped thread: one turn flattens into a right triangle with a base of the circumference at the mean thread diameter, pi dm, and a height equal to the lead, so the lead angle is lambda = arctan(l / (pi dm)) with l = starts x pitch. Resolving the axial load F along that incline against a friction angle phi = arctan(mu) gives the torque to raise the load T = (F dm / 2) tan(phi + lambda) and the torque to lower it (F dm / 2) tan(phi - lambda). A thread flank that is not square also carries the load wedged on its inclined faces, so every mu becomes mu sec(alpha) with alpha the half thread angle - 30 degrees for an ISO metric or unified 60 degree thread, 14.5 degrees for a 29 degree Acme, 0 for square or buttress - which is the published form (F dm / 2)(l + pi mu dm sec(alpha)) / (pi dm - mu l sec(alpha)). The mean diameter is the pitch diameter: dm = d - 0.649519 P for a 60 degree thread, from the 0.375 H offset of the basic ISO profile, and dm = d - 0.5 P for Acme, trapezoidal and square threads, whose thread height is half the pitch. A collar that carries the load adds Tc = F mu_c d_c / 2 at its mean radius, with mu_c and d_c entered separately and d_c = 0 for a thrust bearing, so the raising torque reported first is the thread plus the collar. The efficiency is the work delivered over the work put in, eta = F l / (2 pi T), reported once with the collar and once for the thread alone, and it is also tabulated as tan(lambda) / tan(phi + lambda) for the bare thread. The lowering torque is reported as a magnitude in the lowering direction: it is positive when friction holds the load (mu sec(alpha) >= tan(lambda), the self-locking condition, so the page prints zero and says the screw holds the load without a brake) and negative when the lead is steep enough that the load drives the screw down and a brake or a holding motor is needed. Whether the collar alone is enough to stop that run-down is reported separately. A worked default: an M30 x 3.5 single start raising 10 kN with mu = 0.15, a 40 mm collar at mu_c = 0.10 gives a mean diameter of 27.727 mm, a lead angle of 2.30 degrees, 29.79 N m in the thread, 20.00 N m in the collar, 49.79 N m total and 11.19 percent overall efficiency, and it self-locks because the 9.83 degree friction angle exceeds the lead angle. Inputs are bounded: load 0.001 to 5000 kN, nominal diameter 1 to 600 mm, pitch 0.2 to 50 mm and always under half the diameter, starts 1 to 8 whole numbers, both friction coefficients 0 to 0.5, and mean collar diameter 0 to 2000 mm. A lead so steep against the thread friction that pi dm - mu l sec(alpha) would reach zero is refused rather than returned as an unbounded torque. This is a steady uniform-load friction model of one thread: it does not check thread or nut bearing and shear stress, buckling of a long screw, wear, running-in, the critical speed, starting torque or the vibration and shock that can drop the effective friction and let a nominally self-locking screw back-drive, so it sizes a drive rather than qualifying one. Everything runs locally in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

Wikipedia, ISO metric screw thread - basic profile: effective pitch diameter D_p = D_maj - 0.649519 P from the 0.375 H offset of the 60 degree profile, and the minor diameter D_maj - 1.082532 P

Wikipedia, Trapezoidal thread form - Acme profile: the 29 degree thread angle with a thread height of half the pitch, the metric trapezoidal 30 degree angle, and the square thread as the lowest-friction, zero thread-angle form

tools.name: Cellular Frequency Reuse Planner
tools.description: Turn the cluster offsets i and j, the path-loss exponent, the sectoring and the cell radius into the cluster size, the co-channel reuse ratio and distance, the first-tier S/I, the margin against a target and the channels each cell gets.
tools.method: The plan is hexagonal: cells tile in clusters of N cells, and a cluster tessellates only when N = i² + i·j + j² for whole offsets i and j, so N can be 1, 3, 4, 7, 9, 12, 13 or 19 and never 2, 5, 6 or 8. The offsets also locate the nearest co-channel cell: move i cells along a chain of hexagons, turn 60 degrees and move j more. The nearest co-channel cells sit at the reuse distance D = R·√(3N) from the serving cell, so Q = D/R = √(3N) is the co-channel reuse ratio and 1/N is the frequency reuse factor. With equal-power base stations, a pure distance power law and the first tier of co-channel cells all at the same distance D, the cell-edge signal-to-interference ratio is S/I = (D/R)^n / i₀ = (√(3N))^n / i₀, with n the path-loss exponent (2 to 6, typically 3 to 4 in a city) and i₀ the first-tier interferers the cell or sector sees: 6 for an omnidirectional cell, 2 with 120-degree sectoring, 1 with 60-degree sectoring. Where i = j (N = 3, 12, ...) some texts count one more, 3 against 120 degrees and 2 against 60 degrees; the page uses 6/2/1 throughout and says so on the page. It reports N, 1/N, Q, D for the entered cell radius, S/I in dB, the margin against the target (18 dB is the classic AMPS figure) and the channels per cell as total/N rounded down with the remainder. A worked default: i = 2 and j = 1 give N = 7 and Q = 4.583, so at n = 3.5 with six interferers S/I = 15.36 dB and the 7-cell plan falls 2.64 dB short of 18 dB, while at n = 4 the same plan reaches 18.66 dB, the textbook AMPS result. The table lists every tessellating N from 1 to 19 at the same exponent and interferer count, so the smallest cluster that clears the target is visible without trial and error. Inputs are bounded: i 0 to 20, j 0 to 20 and not both zero, n 2 to 6, cell radius 0.1 to 100 km, 1 to 10,000 channels and a target of 0 to 40 dB. Rounding: reuse ratio 4 decimals, distance 3, S/I and margin 2, reuse factor percentage 1. This is the standard first-tier hexagonal estimate and it is optimistic against a worst-case geometry, where the nearest interferers sit at D − R rather than D; it assumes equal cell sizes and powers, a single propagation slope with no breakpoint, flat terrain, no buildings or foliage, no adjacent-channel interference and idealised sector patterns. Channels per cell is raw division before any trunking loss, so pair it with an Erlang B or C calculation for offered traffic, and remember sectoring trades trunking efficiency for interference. It plans a reuse pattern; it does not allocate channels, model real interference levels or authorise spectrum. Everything runs locally in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: T. S. Rappaport, Wireless Communications: Principles and Practice, ch. 3 The Cellular Concept — System Design Fundamentals (sample chapter): eq. 3.3 N = i² + ij + j², eq. 3.4 Q = D/R = √(3N), eq. 3.9 S/I = (√3N)^n / i₀, Table 3.1 and the 18 dB AMPS example
ECE 5325/6325 Wireless Communication Systems, lecture 2 — the hexagonal cluster geometry, the i and j cell-stepping rule, and the first-tier S/I approximation with i₀ in the denominator

ECE 5325/6325 Wireless Communication Systems, lecture 4 — sectoring: how the first-tier interferer count i₀ falls to 2 with 120° sectors and 1 with 60° sectors, and what that does to S/I and the usable N
Cellular network — frequency reuse (Wikipedia): reuse distance D = R√(3N), reuse factor 1/N, and the 3/7 and 3/4 sector reuse patterns

tools.name: Specific Energy Converter
tools.description: Convert specific energy (energy per mass) between J/kg, kJ/kg, MJ/kg, GJ/t, Wh/kg, kWh/kg, cal/g, kcal/kg and Btu/lb, see every unit at once, and turn the value into a total energy for a mass in kg. Runs in your browser.
tools.method: Specific energy is energy divided by mass, a coherent SI derived quantity whose unit is the joule per kilogram (J/kg); it is not energy density, which is energy per volume in J/m3 and needs the density as well. The page converts every unit through joules per kilogram from exact factors. A kilowatt hour is 3,600,000 J, so 1 kWh/kg is 3.6 MJ/kg and 1 Wh/kg is 3,600 J/kg; a megajoule per kilogram is a gigajoule per tonne because a tonne is 1,000 kg; a gram is a thousandth of a kilogram, so 1 cal/g is 1,000 cal per kg, which is why cal/g and kcal/kg are the same size; and 1 Btu/lb is 1055.05585262 J divided by 0.45359237 kg, exactly 2326 J/kg. The calorie is the thermochemical calorie of 4.184 J, the one used for food energy, and the BTU is the International Table BTU, not the thermochemical one, so a value copied from a table built on the other definition differs in the fourth significant digit. The chosen pair is the headline result and all nine units are listed in three groups, so the SI, fuel and imperial readings stay visible together. An optional mass in kilograms multiplies the specific energy by that mass and reports the total energy in megajoules and kilowatt hours, which is the step from a fuel's energy content to the energy in a tank or a batch. Results are rounded to six significant digits and grouped in thousands; values below 0.0001 or at least 1e13 are printed in exponent form so that 1 J/kg does not collapse to zero in MJ/kg. Input is a plain decimal number, optionally grouped with commas, from zero up to 1,000 MJ/kg (1 GJ/kg) and a mass from zero up to 1,000 tonnes; exponent notation, text, a misplaced comma and negative values are refused with a specific message rather than clipped. This is unit arithmetic only: lower and higher heating values differ for every fuel, a cell's usable energy is below its cell-level specific energy, and no combustion, efficiency, temperature or density model is applied. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

NIST Special Publication 811, 2008 edition, Appendix B conversion factors: British thermal unit (IT) 1055.05585262 J, thermochemical calorie 4.184 J and avoirdupois pound 0.45359237 kg
