tools.name: Stained Glass Materials Calculator
tools.description: Work out the glass area, lead came, copper foil and solder seam length for a stained-glass panel from the panel size and a list of cut pieces. Runs in your browser.
tools.method: A stained-glass panel is bought as flat glass, came or foil and solder, and this page turns the piece list into those four quantities. Glass area is width times height for every piece, multiplied by its count and added up. The came length follows from the seams: every piece has a perimeter, an inside edge is shared by exactly two pieces, and the panel border is an edge of one piece only. Summing the perimeters therefore counts each inside seam twice and the border once, so the came length is half the sum of the perimeters plus the panel perimeter; for a 12 by 16 inch panel cut into four pieces with perimeters 40, 24, 32 and 16 inches, that is (112 + 56) / 2 = 84 inches. Copper foil is a strip wrapped around every edge of every piece, so it is the sum of the perimeters, and solder runs down both faces of every seam, so its length is the sum of the perimeters plus the panel perimeter; a single-piece panel is the check case, where came equals the border, foil equals the border and solder equals twice the border. Glass coverage is the glass area divided by the panel area and is shown as a percentage, so a piece list that does not fit the panel is visible at once. The estimate assumes the pieces tile the panel edge to edge with no gaps or overlaps, and it is a buying figure: it makes no allowance for cutting waste, so order a little more glass, and the size each piece is cut to still comes from the pattern, because bevels, textured glass and the heart width of the came all move the cut line. Dimensions are read in inches or centimetres, the two systems are converted with the exact 2.54 cm inch rather than a rounded factor, counts are whole numbers from 1 to 200, and results are rounded to two decimals. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: COBS Encoder / Decoder
tools.description: Encode a packet with Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing (COBS) so it carries no 0x00 byte, or decode a COBS frame back to its bytes, with the code-block breakdown, frame length and overhead. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Implements Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing as described in Cheshire and Baker's paper: a zero byte is logically appended to the packet, the packet is cut at every zero into zero-terminated chunks, and each chunk becomes one or more code blocks. A code byte from 1 to 254 is followed by that many minus one non-zero data bytes and stands for those bytes plus one implied zero; a code byte of 255 is followed by 254 data bytes and implies no zero, so a run longer than 254 bytes is split into full blocks plus a final normal block. Encoding walks the input keeping one code byte open and closes it at a zero byte, at a full 254-byte block, or at the end of the packet. Decoding reads each code byte, copies that many minus one bytes and restores the implied zero except after the final block, where that zero is the phantom byte and is not part of the packet. Because zero is never a code byte and never appears in the data, a single 00 byte can delimit frames. The result gives the frame in 16-byte hex rows, its length, the overhead in bytes and as a percentage, and the code-block breakdown; decoding accepts hex with any whitespace, removes one trailing 00 delimiter, previews printable text and reports every block. This page follows the paper's reference listings without its optional trailing-block optimisation, so a packet ending in an exact run of 254 non-zero bytes costs one byte more than the published bound, and a packet of all zeros is the worst case at one code block per zero byte. Input is capped at 4,096 bytes; a 00 inside a frame or a code byte whose data runs past the end is refused with the byte position. No network access and no storage.

sources.title: Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing — Cheshire & Baker, IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking 7(2), 1999: Table 1 code values, the encoding and decoding procedure, and the reference C listings

tools.name: Flour Protein Blend Calculator
tools.description: Blend two flours with different protein levels, or boost a flour with vital wheat gluten, to reach a target protein percentage: split a batch by weight or work out how much of the second flour to add.
tools.method: Mass balance on protein by total weight: the protein in each part is its weight times its percentage, and dividing that sum by the finished weight gives the blend's percentage. Batch mode fixes the batch weight W and solves for the weight of flour A, A = W x (target - B%) / (A% - B%), with the remainder as flour B. Adjust mode fixes the amount of flour A on hand and solves for the amount of flour B to add, B = A x (target - A%) / (B% - target); that amount is positive whichever flour is stronger, so the same page dilutes a strong flour with a weak one or lifts a weak flour with vital wheat gluten. The target must lie strictly between the two percentages, and equal percentages are refused. Weights are grams, kept to one decimal, and the blend percentage is recomputed from those rounded weights, so it can differ from the target in the last decimal; protein grams are rounded to 0.1 g and read as the weight of protein, not the weight of gluten or of flour. Bag percentages are the miller's rounded figures and vary by brand and crop, and vital wheat gluten is typically about 75% protein but is not fixed; no allowance is made for moisture loss, fermentation consuming some sugars, or flour left in the bowl.

tools.name: Working Hours Between Dates Calculator
tools.description: Count the working hours between two dates and times against your own daily window — for example 09:00 to 17:00 on weekdays — skipping nights, weekends and any holidays you list. Shown as hours and minutes, decimal hours, the time outside the schedule and a per-day breakdown. Everything runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Working time is counted one minute at a time inside a repeating daily window. Every calendar day from the start date to the end date is examined: it contributes only if its weekday is one of the selected ones and it is not listed as a holiday, and then only the part of its window that falls inside the query is added. The query clips the window on the first and last day, so a start of 13:30 on a 09:00-17:00 schedule counts 210 minutes and an end of 10:15 the next morning counts 75. Outside-the-schedule time is the wall-clock span minus the counted minutes, and the scheduled day length is closing time minus opening time. Times are wall-clock readings on the device rather than absolute instants, so a daylight-saving day keeps its scheduled length instead of 23 or 25 hours; the window must end after it starts, so an overnight shift needs two ranges; seconds other than 00 are refused; and ranges longer than 3,700 days (about ten years) are refused to bound the work. Holidays match by calendar date, so one that falls on a weekend changes nothing, and no allowance is made for public holidays you did not list, lunch breaks inside the window, or time zones between the people involved.

tools.name: DHCP Classless Static Route Encoder
tools.description: Encode a list of CIDR routes and next hops into the DHCP classless static route option (121, or the Microsoft 249 form), or decode an option payload back into routes and see where each entry starts. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.guidance: Option 121 packs each route as a mask width, the significant destination octets and four router octets, and a client that supports it ignores the Router option — so include your default route here too. Data is capped at 255 bytes.
tools.method: RFC 3442 encodes each route as one octet holding the subnet-mask width, then only the significant octets of the destination — width divided by eight, rounded up, so a /8 keeps one octet, a /17 keeps three and a /32 keeps all four — then four octets of router address. A width of zero carries no destination octets and is the default route; a router of 0.0.0.0 marks another subnet on the same link, which a client whose stack cannot install such a route must ignore. Destination bits below the mask are zeroed, and the page follows the client here: it writes the network address and says so when the line had host bits set. Routes are emitted in the order typed and concatenated, the data length is their total, and the full option is code 121 (0x79) plus that length octet; the Microsoft 249 (0xF9) form carries identical data. Since the length is a single octet the data cannot exceed 255 bytes, so a longer list is refused and points at RFC 3396 concatenation instead. Decoding accepts the data with or without the code and length octets, splits it at the offsets the widths dictate, and names the byte offset when a route is truncated or a width is above 32. Addresses with a leading-zero octet are refused because some tools read them as octal. No default route in the list produces a note that clients ignore the Router option when option 121 is present.

tools.name: Lambert Conformal Conic Projection Calculator
tools.description: Convert a latitude and longitude to the easting and northing of a Lambert conformal conic map defined by two standard parallels, or read a grid position back as a latitude and longitude, with the scale factor and grid convergence at that point.
aliases: Latitude Longitude to Easting Northing Calculator
tools.method: A Lambert conformal conic map unrolls a cone that cuts the ellipsoid along two standard parallels, where the scale is exactly 1 and the map is at true scale; between them it is slightly small and outside them it grows. With the semi-major axis a, first eccentricity e, and the functions m(phi) = cos phi / sqrt(1 - e^2 sin^2 phi) and t(phi) = tan(pi/4 - phi/2) / ((1 - e sin phi) / (1 + e sin phi))^(e/2), the page computes the cone constant n = ln(m1 / m2) / ln(t1 / t2) for two parallels, or n = sin phi1 when the two are equal (the single-parallel form), then F = m1 / (n t1^n) and the radius rho = a F t^n. A point lands at x = rho sin(n dlambda) and y = rho0 - rho cos(n dlambda) east and north of the origin, where dlambda is the longitude measured from the central meridian, wrapped into -180 to 180 degrees, and rho0 is rho at the latitude of origin; the false easting and northing are then added, so the northing of the latitude of origin is the false northing. The scale factor is k = n rho / (a m), exactly 1 on each standard parallel, below 1 between them and above 1 outside; grid convergence is n dlambda, the angle between grid north and true north, positive east of the central meridian in a northern cone and negative there in a southern one, so a point on the central meridian has zero convergence and only a northing. Conformality is exact: angles and small shapes are preserved at every point even though scale varies, which is why the projection carries aeronautical charts and many State Plane zones. Scale grows steeply away from the parallels: the default Continental US grid (33 and 45 degrees north, origin 39 degrees north on 96 degrees west, WGS 84) puts Washington DC at 1,624,568.7 m east and 157,935.0 m north with k = 0.994546 and convergence 11.9572 degrees, while a point on either parallel returns k = 1 and the antimeridian cases reduce to a pure northing. The inverse solves rho from the grid, recovers t = (rho / (a F))^(1/n), iterates latitude from t in the usual way and reads longitude from theta / n, keeping the sign of rho for southern cones so that eastings still increase eastwards. Refused rather than guessed: a point exactly on either pole (the cone apex has no longitude and the opposite pole has no image), standard parallels on the equator, parallels that straddle it, a latitude of origin in the opposite hemisphere, any latitude or longitude outside its range, and a grid position exactly at the apex. Offered are WGS 84, GRS 80, Clarke 1866 and a mean-radius sphere; no datum shift, no scale factor k0, no Michigan variant, no grid rotation and no false-origin azimuth are modelled, and the page does not draw the map. Pure local arithmetic: no upload, storage or network access.

sources.title: PROJ documentation, Lambert Conformal Conic (lcc) — the lat_1, lat_2, lat_0, lon_0, x_0 and y_0 parameters, the 1SP and 2SP forms and the EPSG Guidance Note 7-2 basis.
John P. Snyder, Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS Professional Paper 1395, Lambert conformal conic, pages 104-110.

tools.name: Clef Reading Calculator
tools.description: Read a written note's staff position in nine clefs, or the note at any line, space or ledger line, with the written and sounding pitch and the position of the same pitch in every clef.
tools.method: A staff position counts diatonic steps: line 1 is step 0, the space above it step 1, line 2 step 2, with the space below the staff at -1 and ledger lines at -2, -4 and so on below and 10, 12 and up above. Each clef fixes one written letter to one staff line: the G clef marks G4 on its line, the F clef F3 and the C clef C4, so a pitch's position is the reference step plus the diatonic difference and a position's pitch is the reference pitch plus the step difference. Positions cover -6 to 14, three ledger lines below and above the staff; the comparison table runs the same pitch through all nine clefs and marks positions outside that range. An accidental is carried into the written and sounding names but never moves the note, and a clef with an octave change lowers the sounding octave by one, so a written C4 in the tenor-voice treble clef sounds C3. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Dolly Zoom Planner
tools.description: Plan a dolly zoom: read the focal length each camera position needs to keep the subject the same size, the zoom ratio, the dolly travel and how much the background grows or shrinks.
tools.method: A dolly zoom holds the subject at the same size while the camera moves toward or away and the lens zooms the other way. The thin-lens transverse magnification of an object at distance d in front of a lens is m = f / (d - f), so holding m constant across a move from d1 to d2 gives the end focal length f2 = f1 x d2 / d1 exactly, and the zoom ratio equals the dolly ratio: 50 mm at 3 m matches 25 mm at 1.5 m, and 35 mm at 2 m matches 70 mm at 4 m. The same rule is applied at each quarter step of the move for the position table, so every row keeps the subject's framing. A background plane at distance D has its own magnification f / (D - f); the page reports its size at the end as a percentage of its size at the start, relative to the subject, so a dolly-in with zoom-out shrinks the background (the classic Vertigo effect) and a dolly-out with zoom-in enlarges it. A background far behind the subject changes by almost exactly the zoom ratio, while a close one changes a little more than that ratio. Focal lengths are 4 to 1200 mm, distances 0.2 to 1000 m and the background 0.5 to 5000 m; the background must lie beyond the subject at both ends, the start and end distances must differ, and the focal length must be shorter than the start distance so that a real image forms. Distances are measured from the lens rather than the camera body, and the subject is treated as flat at its stated distance: focus, depth of field, lens zoom curves, focus breathing, rolling shutter and the framing of the subject's own edges are not modelled. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Bulk Cargo Lift Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much bulk cargo a ship lifts: tonnes from grain capacity and stowage factor, whether hold space or deadweight runs out first, and what is left over.
tools.method: The lift is the smaller of two limits: the tonnes the cargo holds can take at the cargo's stowage factor, grain capacity divided by the stowage factor, and the deadweight cargo capacity the ship may load. When the hold limit is lower the ship is space-limited and deadweight is left unused; when the deadweight is lower the ship is weight-limited and hold space is left empty; when the two agree the cargo exactly fills the holds at the deadweight. Cargo volume is the lift times the stowage factor and hold use is that volume as a percentage of grain capacity. The worked examples in the reference follow the same rule: 70,000 m3 of grain capacity and 55,000 t of deadweight lift 55,000 t of phosphate at 0.90 m3/t, because the hold limit of 77,777.8 t is above the deadweight, and 47,619 t of barley at 1.47 m3/t, because the hold limit falls below it. The reference table of typical stowage factors (iron ore 0.40, grain 1.30, coal 1.40, woodchips 2.50) supplies the comparison rows, and the cargo's own stowage factor row is dropped when it repeats one of them. The stowage factor is the volume one tonne occupies in the hold including normal stowage losses, so no separate broken-stowage percentage is applied on top of it. Grain capacity is 1 to 2,000,000 m3, deadweight cargo capacity 1 to 1,000,000 t and the stowage factor 0.05 to 20 m3/t. The page is a planning estimate, not a loading instruction: actual loading follows the ship's stability booklet, load line and cargo declaration and the terminal's measured weights, and trim, list, tank capacity, deadweight at the sailing draft, cargo density limits and segregation rules are not modelled. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Pan Law Calculator
tools.description: See how a pan position splits a mono signal between the left and right channels under the -3 dB, -4.5 dB and -6 dB pan laws, with the mono fold-down and two-speaker level change and a comparison across the three laws.
tools.method: Each law sets the left and right channel gains from the pan position: t = (pan + 100) / 200 runs from 0 at hard left through 0.5 at the centre to 1 at hard right, and the pan angle is a = t x 90 degrees. The -3 dB constant-power law uses gL = cos(a) and gR = sin(a), so gL^2 + gR^2 = 1 at every position and a centred signal sits 3.01 dB down in each channel. The -6 dB linear law uses gL = 1 - t and gR = t, so gL + gR = 1 and a centred signal sits 6.02 dB down in each channel. The -4.5 dB compromise is the geometric mean of the two, gL = sqrt((1 - t) cos(a)) and gR = sqrt(t sin(a)), which leaves each channel about 4.5 dB down at the centre. Gains are relative to the unpanned signal, reported in dB and as a percentage of amplitude, with the left-minus-right difference. The mono fold-down adds the two channels as amplitudes, 20 log10(gL + gR), the result for identical in-phase content summed to one channel. The two-speaker level adds their powers, 10 log10(gL^2 + gR^2), assuming the speakers radiate independently at the listening position. Constant power therefore holds the two-speaker level flat but folds up to 3.01 dB hot in mono, the linear law holds the mono sum flat but loses up to 3.01 dB on two speakers, and the compromise splits both errors at about 1.51 dB. Consoles and DAWs vary in detail, some compensating the taper and some not. The page models the gain taper only: it does not measure loudness and assumes one mono source panned between two channels. Pan positions must be plain decimals, optionally with a leading decimal point and a minus sign; values outside -100 to 100 percent and unknown laws are refused with the reason. Results carry two decimals. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: IPv4 Header Decoder
tools.description: Decode the hex bytes of an IPv4 header into version, header length, DS field, identification, flags, fragment offset, TTL, protocol, both addresses and a verified header checksum.
tools.method: The header is read at the offsets RFC 791 gives it. The first nibble is the version and the second is the header length in 32-bit words, so a fixed header is 20 bytes and a longer one carries options between byte 20 and the length it declares. The DS byte holds six DSCP bits and the two ECN bits that RFC 3168 names Not-ECT, ECT(1), ECT(0) and CE. Bytes 2 and 3 are the total length, which covers header and payload together, and bytes 4 and 5 are the identification. The third flag byte carries the reserved bit, DF and MF, and its remaining 13 bits are the fragment offset counted in eight-byte units, so an offset of 185 means the fragment starts 1,480 bytes into the original datagram. Byte 8 is the TTL, byte 9 the protocol number, bytes 10 and 11 the header checksum, and bytes 12 to 19 the source and destination addresses. The checksum is checked as RFC 1071 describes: the 16-bit one's-complement sum of the header, checksum field included, must come to 0xFFFF, and the value compared against it is the complement of the sum of the header with that field zeroed. A header that does not verify is still shown field by field, with the mismatch and the value expected reported. Protocol numbers are named from the IANA Protocol Numbers registry, and numbers 148 to 252 are reported as unassigned. The pasted text accepts spaces, commas, colons, 0x prefixes, contiguous hex and dump offset labels, and bytes past the declared header length are treated as payload. Options are reported but not decoded, the payload and any transport header are not read, IPv6 headers are refused, and a total length that disagrees with the number of bytes pasted is reported rather than refused. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.

IANA Protocol Numbers registry: the assigned protocol keywords and names

tools.name: meminfo Decoder
tools.description: Decode a pasted /proc/meminfo dump into the memory breakdown free reports: total, in use, available, free, buffers, page cache, buff/cache, shared memory, slab, kernel stacks, page tables and swap, with each field's share of RAM.
tools.method: Each line of the pasted dump is read as a field name, a colon, a whole number and an optional kB unit; blank lines and # comments are skipped, a field that appears twice is refused, and a value in any other unit is refused. MemTotal and MemFree are required, and MemFree or SwapFree above its total is refused as inconsistent. Total RAM is MemTotal. In use is MemTotal minus MemAvailable, the figure free(1) documents for its used column; a dump without MemAvailable takes available as MemFree plus Buffers and Cached and in use as MemTotal minus that, which is the fallback for kernels before 3.14. Buff/cache is Buffers + Cached + SReclaimable, matching the cache and buff/cache columns of free(1), and shared memory is Shmem. Kernel stacks and page tables add KernelStack, PageTables and SecPageTables when the kernel reports them. Swap in use is SwapTotal minus SwapFree. Every share is that field divided by MemTotal, or by SwapTotal for the swap rows, rounded half up to one decimal; an exact half therefore reads up, not to even. The RAM bar partitions MemTotal into in use and available and the swap bar partitions SwapTotal into in use and free, so each bar adds to exactly its total. Sizes are shown in KiB, MiB or GiB by magnitude, with GiB at two decimals. The page reads only the text pasted into it: it does not query the host, so cgroup limits, watermarks, zswap and reclaim behaviour are not modelled, and a field the dump omits is not invented. Nothing here is a diagnosis of the machine or a recommendation to change it. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.

sources.title: proc_meminfo(5) - the /proc/meminfo field list: MemTotal, MemFree, MemAvailable, Buffers, Cached, Shmem, Slab, SReclaimable, Dirty and CommitLimit
free(1) - the displayed columns: used is total minus available, cache is Cached plus SReclaimable, and buff/cache is buffers plus cache
The /proc Filesystem - the /proc/meminfo section of the kernel documentation, describing each memory counter and the CommitLimit formula

tools.name: IPF GL Points Calculator
tools.description: Score a powerlifting total with the IPF GL formula: pick sex, equipment and event, enter body weight and the result, and read the coefficient, the points and the total that would score 100 at that weight.
tools.method: The coefficient is 100 divided by A minus B times e to the power of minus C times body weight, with the A, B and C the IPF published for that combination of sex, equipment (classic or equipped) and event (three-lift powerlifting or bench press only), so eight tables in all. The coefficient is rounded half up to six decimals, multiplied by the result, and the product is rounded half up to six decimals again, which is the order the IPF document prescribes; the product is taken in integer millionths so a half at the seventh decimal rounds up the way the IPF's own worked examples do, instead of drifting with binary floating point. Score sheets print three decimals. A result of zero scores zero. The total that would score 100 at the entered body weight is the denominator itself, the reference level of an elite lifter at that weight, and the second table scales it to 50, 75, 100 and 125 points. Body weight is read as kilograms and the result as kilograms: a comma decimal separator is accepted, a value with both a comma and a point is refused, more than six decimals is refused, and the men's table is refused below 40 kg and the women's below 35 kg, which is where the IPF document defines them. A body weight above 400 kg or a result above 2000 kg is refused as outside the range these coefficients are used for, and a combination with no coefficients is refused rather than guessed. The score compares lifters of different body weights under one federation's rules: it is not a classification, a record standard, a drug-testing result or a prediction, and it does not check whether a lift counted. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.

tools.name: Debian Version Comparison
tools.description: Compare two Debian package versions the way dpkg does: epoch, upstream version and Debian revision, with the tilde and character-order rules, and see which part of the string decided the order.
tools.method: A Debian version is an optional epoch, an upstream version and an optional Debian revision, written epoch:upstream-version-debian-revision. The epoch is an unsigned whole number taken as 0 when it is absent; it is compared first, as a whole number of unbounded size by stripping leading zeros and comparing digit counts before digits, so a nineteen digit epoch stays exact instead of passing through floating point. The upstream version and the Debian revision then use the same left-to-right algorithm: the initial run of non-digit characters is compared in dpkg's character order, where a tilde sorts before everything including the end of the string, ASCII letters sort by their code before every other character, and every other character sorts after the letters by its code plus 256; then the initial run of digits is compared as a number, with an empty run counting as zero and leading zeros carrying no weight. Both steps repeat until a difference is found or both strings are exhausted. dpkg breaks the string at its first colon and its last hyphen, so a revision may contain dots and plus signs while an absent revision compares as an empty string, which is why 1.0 equals 1.0-0 and sorts before 1.0-1. The tool refuses an empty field, a version longer than 128 characters, a character outside letters, digits and . + - : ~, whitespace, a colon whose prefix is not an integer epoch, a trailing hyphen with an empty revision, and a hyphen with no upstream version, with a message naming the field instead of a result. It reports deviations from Debian Policy it can still compare, such as an upstream part that does not start with a digit or one that keeps a hyphen, as notes rather than refusals. The comparison is implemented in the browser from the published algorithm and does not call dpkg; nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.

tools.name: Pipe Offset Calculator
tools.description: Size a pipe offset: the true offset, the fitting-to-fitting travel, the run along the pipe, the roll angle of a two-plane offset, and the cut length between two elbows.
tools.method: A standard pipe offset turns the run once through the fitting angle. The calculator takes the offset as the perpendicular distance between the two pipe centre lines, then divides it by the sine of the fitting angle for the travel, the centre-to-centre distance along the diagonal, and by the tangent of that angle for the run, the distance the pipe advances along its original axis. The travel is the hypotenuse of the offset and the run, so the two legs come back exactly as offset divided by travel and run divided by travel: those are the sine and the cosine of the fitting angle. A rolling offset enters a vertical and a horizontal set instead. The true offset is their hypotenuse, and the roll angle is atan2 of the vertical leg over the horizontal one, measured from the horizontal leg towards the vertical one, so a horizontal-only set reads 0 degrees and a vertical-only set reads 90. The cut length is the travel less each fitting's centre-to-face take-out, entered per fitting because the two ends need not match. Units are labels only: no number is converted, and the page sends, stores and uploads nothing. It refuses an offset that is blank, non-numeric or not greater than zero, a rolling offset with both legs zero, a fitting angle outside 1 to 89 degrees, a negative take-out, and a pair of take-outs that adds up to more than the travel, naming the field in each message.

tools.name: Helical Antenna Designer
tools.description: Design an axial-mode helical antenna from its frequency, helix diameter, turns and turn spacing: gain in dBi, half-power beamwidth, electrical circumference, pitch angle and winding length.
tools.method: A helix radiates along its axis when the circumference is about one wavelength and the turns are spaced by roughly a quarter wavelength; this is the axial mode, and it is circularly polarised, with the winding hand setting the polarisation. The page takes the winding the user enters rather than proposing one. The wavelength is the speed of light over the frequency, expressed in the chosen length unit; the electrical circumference is the winding circumference, pi times the diameter, over that wavelength, and the electrical spacing is the centre-to-centre turn spacing over it in the same way. The classical Kraus estimate of the gain is fifteen times the square of the electrical circumference times the turns times the electrical spacing, in linear terms, reported in dBi, which reduces to 3.45 times the number of turns when the circumference is one wavelength and the spacing is 0.23 of it. The half-power beamwidth is fifty-two degrees over the electrical circumference times the square root of the turns times the electrical spacing. The pitch angle is the arctangent of the spacing over the circumference, and the winding length is the turns times the spacing. Those estimates assume a circular ground plane with a rim and an optimum pitch and read several decibels high against a flat ground plane, so the page prints them as a design target. A circumference outside 0.75 to 1.33 wavelengths, a pitch outside 12 to 15 degrees and fewer than three turns each raise a warning and still return a figure. Units are labels for the lengths the user enters. It refuses a blank, non-numeric or non-positive frequency, diameter or spacing, a frequency outside 0.1 to 300000 MHz, fewer than one or more than one thousand turns, and any unit other than millimetres or inches, naming the field in each message. Nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.

tools.name: Thermal Expansion Coefficient Converter
tools.description: Convert a coefficient of linear thermal expansion between 1/K, 1/°C, 1/°F, ppm/K, ppm/°F, µm/(m·K) and µin/(in·°F), with the 9/5 factor between the kelvin and Fahrenheit forms stated, negative coefficients accepted and a table of round values in both systems.
tools.method: The linear coefficient of thermal expansion, α, is the fractional change in length per kelvin, so its SI unit is the reciprocal kelvin; a length L changes by α L ΔT over a temperature interval ΔT. This page converts α only: it applies no temperature, length, strain or stress, and it recommends no material. Every listed unit reduces to 1/K by one exact factor. A reciprocal degree Celsius carries the same factor as 1/K, because a temperature interval of one kelvin is one degree Celsius. A reciprocal degree Fahrenheit is 9/5 per kelvin, since a Fahrenheit degree interval is 5/9 K, which is the factor behind both the ppm/°F and µin/(in·°F) forms. A part per million per kelvin is exactly 1e-6/K, and a micrometre per metre-kelvin is the same factor because a micrometre per metre is 1e-6; a micro-inch per inch-degree Fahrenheit is 1e-6/°F, so 1.8e-6/K. A conversion multiplies by the source factor and divides by the target factor, so every pair round trips, and the headline also states the change of a one-metre length per kelvin in micrometres, which is α × 1e6. Negative coefficients are accepted because some materials contract as they warm — zirconium tungstate, and water between 0 and 4 °C — so the input may carry a minus sign, while a magnitude of 10 per kelvin or more is outside the supported range and is refused. Input is trimmed and must be a plain decimal, optionally grouped in thousands; a leading decimal point is accepted, exponent form is refused. Results carry six significant digits with trailing zeros trimmed and thousands grouped, and a magnitude below 1e-6 or from 1e12 up is written in exponential form. The reference table holds round coefficients from 1 to 23 ppm/K in two systems. Coefficients vary with temperature, alloy and direction, so a handbook figure is only as good as the range it is quoted for. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Jump Ring Coil Calculator
tools.description: Plan a chainmail or wire-jewellery coil: how many whole jump rings a length of wire makes on a mandrel, the wire each ring costs including the saw kerf, the coil length, rings per metre and the ring's aspect ratio, the inner diameter divided by the wire diameter.
aliases: How Many Jump Rings From Wire
tools.method: A jump ring is a coil of wire cut into single turns, so the wire a ring consumes is the circumference measured through the middle of the wire, pi times the mandrel diameter plus one wire diameter, plus the kerf the saw removes from that turn. The ring count is the wire length in millimetres divided by that figure and rounded down to a whole ring, because a partial turn cannot be closed into a ring; the remainder is reported as leftover wire. The outer diameter is the mandrel plus two wire diameters, and the coil length is the ring count times the wire diameter, which is the coil's length while the turns still touch. The aspect ratio is the inner diameter divided by the wire diameter, the figure chainmail makers quote when comparing rings; this page reports it and does not judge which weaves a ring suits. Spring-back leaves a coiled ring slightly wider than its mandrel and hand coiling compresses the wire, so the result is a planning figure, not a measurement: cut a short test coil and measure it before a long run. The page does not model wire hardness, coil gaps, saw blade wander or metal loss from pickling, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Code 128 Barcode Generator
tools.description: Encode printable ASCII text as a Code 128 barcode: the shortest mix of set B and set C, the modulo-103 check symbol, the symbol and module count, and the bars drawn as an SVG between ten-module quiet zones.
tools.method: A Code 128 symbol is a start character, the data symbols, a check symbol and a stop pattern. Every symbol is eleven modules wide and holds three bars and three spaces, each one to four modules, so the page draws each symbol as black and white runs and wraps the whole barcode in ten-module quiet zones. Set B carries one printable ASCII character per symbol at the value of the character code minus 32; set C carries two digits per symbol at their two-digit value; 99 switches from B to C and 100 from C to B. The page chooses the shortest sequence with a dynamic program over the position in the text and the current set, so a switch is emitted only where it saves a symbol - four digits at either end of the text, or six or more in the middle - and it starts in whichever set costs less. The check symbol is the start value plus every data value multiplied by its one-based position, reduced modulo 103, and it is drawn before the stop pattern. Only printable ASCII from U+0020 to U+007E is accepted, up to 48 characters; FNC codes, Shift and GS1-128 application identifiers are not offered, so the page is not a GS1-128 label generator. The check symbol and the drawing are checked against the Code 128 specification, but a printed label still has to be test-scanned at the module width the label and scanner need. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Ganache Ratio Calculator
tools.description: Work out the chocolate and cream a ganache needs from its ratio, or the ratio behind the amounts you already have, with an optional liqueur or fruit purée counted on the liquid side.
tools.method: Ganache is a mass balance between chocolate and a liquid, so the ratio is chocolate parts to one part cream by weight and the chocolate weight is the ratio times the liquid weight. Added liquid, such as liqueur or a fruit purée standing in for some cream, counts on the liquid side and takes chocolate in the same proportion, which is the usual allowance of 100 g more chocolate for 100 g of liqueur at 1:1. Starting from chocolate C, the cream is C / ratio - extra; starting from cream D, the chocolate is ratio x (D + extra); starting from a finished weight T, the chocolate is ratio x T / (ratio + 1) and the cream is T / (ratio + 1) - extra, so an added liquid that leaves no cream is refused rather than returning a negative part. The style presets are 2:1 for a dark-chocolate truffle, 1:1 for an icing or filling and 2.5:1 for a milk or white-chocolate truffle, with a custom ratio from 0.5 to 3; these are common starting points, not a fixed law, because firmness also depends on the cocoa butter and water the chocolate brings. Weights are grams, rounded to 0.1 g, the total is the sum of the rounded parts, and the shares are recomputed from that total. The page models only the ratio: it does not predict setting temperature, shelf life, tempering or whether a particular chocolate will emulsify, and everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Swatch Internet Time Converter
tools.description: Convert a UTC date and time into Swatch Internet Time (.beat, BMT) and turn a .beat value back into a UTC instant, with the exact beat fraction, the BMT clock and a countdown to the next beat.
tools.method: The mean solar day is divided into 1,000 equal .beats, so one .beat is 86,400 / 1,000 = 86.4 seconds and an hour is 1,000 / 24 = 41 2/3 beats. Biel Mean Time is a fixed UTC+1 offset with no daylight saving, so an instant's beat is floor(((UTC milliseconds + 3,600,000) modulo 86,400,000) / 86,400), which runs 0 to 999, and the remainder of that division is how far into the current beat the instant falls. The next beat starts 86,400 minus that remainder milliseconds later. A .beat names a time of day and not a date, so the reverse panel takes the BMT date: the UTC instant of BMT midnight is that calendar date at 00:00 minus one hour, and the beat adds beat x 86,400 ms to it. Because @000 is 23:00 UTC, every beat below 41 2/3 lands on the previous UTC date, and the page says so when that happens. A watch shows whole beats, so the headline floors the fraction, while the exact quotient is reported to three decimals and clock times to 0.1 s, far finer than the 86.4 s beat. This is the fixed-offset civil scale Swatch defined, not mean solar time measured at Biel, and leap seconds are ignored.

tools.name: Clock Hand Angle Calculator
tools.description: Find the angle between the hour and minute hands at any time on a clock face, and the next times the hands form a chosen angle from 0 to 180 degrees.
aliases: Hour and Minute Hand Angle Calculator
tools.method: The hour hand turns 0.5 degrees a minute and the minute hand 6 degrees a minute, both clockwise from 12, so a time H:M:S puts the hour hand at 30 x H + 0.5 x M + S/120 degrees and the minute hand at 6 x M + 0.1 x S degrees. The angle between them is the difference taken the shorter way round, so it is never more than 180 degrees and the long way round is 360 degrees minus it. Because the minute hand gains 5.5 degrees a minute, the gap changes at 11/120 degrees a second, and the times when it equals a target A solve (11/120) x t = +/- A modulo 360, giving two moments an hour, 22 in the 12-hour cycle, except at 0 and 180 degrees where the two families coincide and there are 11. Hours are read on a 12-hour face, so 15:15 and 03:15 give the same reading and the listed times repeat twice a day. This models an ideal continuously moving face: it does not allow for a ticking movement, a stopped clock or the equation of time.

sources.title: Clock angle problem - Wikipedia: the 0.5 degree per minute hour hand and 6 degree per minute minute hand, the |0.5 x (60H - 11M)| angle between the hands, and the 11 superpositions in 12 hours

tools.name: LDAP Filter & DN Escaper
tools.description: Escape one value for an LDAP search filter (RFC 4515) or a distinguished name (RFC 4514), or read an escaped value back, with every replacement explained.
tools.method: The two string forms escape different sets of characters. RFC 4515 defines a search filter assertion value over UTF-8 and requires the five octets NUL, left bracket, right bracket, asterisk and backslash to be written as a backslash and two hex digits, because a bare asterisk is a wildcard and a bare bracket would end the assertion; every escape in a filter value is that hex pair, so a backslash before an ordinary character is not valid there. RFC 4514 defines a distinguished-name value: a backslash is required before the quotation mark, plus, comma, semicolon, the two angle brackets and the backslash itself, before a number sign that starts the value, and before a space that starts or ends it; the equals sign and the slash need no escape. This page writes those three positional cases as hex pairs, uses the two-character form for the others, and writes filter hex in lower case and DN hex in upper case, which is how the RFC examples present them. Reading is byte-based: every hex pair becomes one octet, the raw characters contribute their UTF-8 bytes, and the whole sequence is decoded strictly, so an overlong form, a surrogate encoding, a truncated sequence or a stray octet above 0x7F is refused rather than replaced. A single-character backslash escape is accepted only in a DN value and only for the characters RFC 4514 lists. The optional non-ASCII switch writes each UTF-8 byte of an accented letter or emoji as a pair, which is valid in both forms and is what some older directory clients expect; left off, non-ASCII text stays as the RFC recommends for a valid UTF-8 string. The page escapes one attribute value, not a whole filter or DN: it does not build the surrounding assertion, split a multi-valued RDN or check whether an attribute name or OID is valid. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: KML ⇄ GeoJSON Converter
tools.description: Convert KML placemarks, lines and polygons into GeoJSON, or write a GeoJSON feature collection out as a KML document, with the features, coordinates and skipped elements reported.
tools.method: KML and GeoJSON both list a position as longitude first, then latitude, with an optional altitude third, so nothing is reordered here: the conversion rewrites structure. Reading KML, the XML is parsed first, including comments, CDATA sections, the five predefined entities and numeric character references, and the root must be a kml element. Every Placemark in document order becomes a GeoJSON Feature: a name child becomes properties.name with whitespace collapsed, a description child becomes properties.description, and each ExtendedData Data or SchemaData SimpleData value becomes a string property under its name attribute. A Point, LineString, Polygon, MultiGeometry or LinearRing child inside a Placemark becomes the geometry; a MultiGeometry whose members all share one type becomes MultiPoint, MultiLineString or MultiPolygon, a mixture becomes a GeometryCollection and a single member is unwrapped. A LinearRing outside a Polygon has no GeoJSON form, so it becomes a closed LineString, and a ring whose first and last positions differ has its first position repeated at the end to make a valid GeoJSON ring; each of these is reported as a warning. A placemark with no geometry is kept with a null geometry, and a placemark holding only gx:Track, gx:MultiTrack or Model gets a null geometry and a warning. Writing KML, a Feature becomes a Placemark, name and description properties become elements, other string, number and boolean properties become ExtendedData Data values, non-scalar properties are left out with a warning, a null geometry becomes an empty Placemark, and GeometryCollection or any Multi type becomes MultiGeometry. Coordinates must hold two or three finite numbers, with longitude within -180 to 180 and latitude within -90 to 90; a KML Point must hold exactly one position, a LineString or GeoJSON line at least two, and a polygon ring at least four with the first and last positions equal - KML rings that are not closed are closed here, while a GeoJSON ring that is not closed is refused. Numbers are printed in JavaScript's shortest exact form, so coordinates keep the precision pasted. Folders, styles, styleUrl, time stamps, regions, NetworkLink, GroundOverlay, ScreenOverlay and Model are not geometry and are dropped, and a description that contains KML markup has its tags dropped and its text kept, with a warning. Input is limited to 2 MB of text, everything runs in the browser with no upload, storage or network access, and the page does not render the map.

tools.name: Ritardando & Accelerando Calculator
tools.description: Time a ritardando or accelerando: a start and end tempo across a span of beats give the total duration, the average tempo and a beat-by-beat timing table on either a time-linear or a beat-linear curve.
tools.method: Tempo is quarter-note beats per minute, so one beat lasts 60 / BPM seconds. Two curves are offered. With the curve linear in time the tempo changes by the same amount every second: the beats covered grow quadratically and the change lasts 120 x beats / (start + end) seconds, so the average tempo is the arithmetic mean of the two tempos. With the curve linear in beats the tempo changes by the same amount on every beat, so each beat lasts 60 / its own tempo and the change lasts 60 x beats x ln(end / start) / (end - start) seconds, which is the reciprocal of the logarithmic mean of the two tempos; the beat-linear ramp is always the longer of the two and both agree when the tempos are equal. The table reports the tempo and elapsed time at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of the beats: on the beat-linear curve the elapsed time is the integral of 60 / (start + (end - start) n / beats) over the beats played, and on the time-linear curve it comes from the quadratic beat count n = (start x t + (end - start) x t^2 / (2T)) / 60 for a total T. Tempos are limited to 10 to 400 BPM and the span to 0.25 to 256 beats; input is read as text, so a decimal needs a dot. Every published figure is rounded to three decimals and the page formats it for display. The page calculates in the browser with no audio engine, upload, storage or network access, and it neither plays nor records a metronome.

tools.name: Stabilization Crop Planner
tools.description: Plan the crop a stabilised shot needs: from the residual shake and roll, get the short- and long-side margin, the zoom, the field of view and pixels kept, and the shake a chosen crop budget can absorb.
tools.method: A stabiliser can only move the picture inside the recorded frame, so the crop has to be large enough that the picture never runs out of pixels. The required margin per side is the residual shake in pixels plus the roll in radians multiplied by half the frame diagonal, the distance a corner sits from the centre and therefore the farthest a turn moves any picture point, and the sum is rounded up to a whole pixel. The crop keeps the shot's shape by zooming uniformly: the scale is the short side divided by the short side less twice the margin, so a 3840 x 2160 frame with a 36 px margin scales by 2160 / 2088 = 1.0345, a 3.45 percent zoom, and the kept window is 3712 x 2088 px after both dimensions are floored to an even count. The short side keeps the margin exactly and the long side gives up the same share of its pixels, 64 px rather than 36 px at that default. The field of view kept is the kept width over the source width, and the pixels kept is the kept area over the source area. The budget table inverts the relation: a zoom of z percent gives a short-side margin of shortSide x (1 - 1 / (1 + z / 100)) / 2 and absorbs that margin less the roll margin as shake. Frame width and height must be whole numbers from 64 to 16384 pixels, the shake from 0 to 1000 px and the roll from 0 to 20 degrees, and a margin that would leave less than 64 px on the short side is refused rather than returned. Shake and roll are the residual motion you measure or expect after stabilisation, so the page plans a crop instead of predicting what a particular stabiliser will do; off-centre crops for look-room, rolling-shutter skew, parallax between near and far subjects, motion blur and resampling softening are not modelled. Calculations run entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Emergency Food Supply Planner
tools.description: Plan household emergency food: person-days, calories and meals for a chosen headcount and duration, the average meal size, how long the food on hand lasts, the shortfall, and the boxes or cases that close it.
tools.guidance: A planning count only. It does not say what your household should eat, and it is not nutrition, medical or food-safety advice. The calories per person per day figure is yours to set; the 2,000 default is a general nutrition guide, not a personal requirement. Special diets, allergies, infants, pregnancy, illness and pets are not modelled, stored food is assumed edible and in date, and package sizes are generic meal counts rather than product specifications. Ready.gov advises at least a several-day supply of non-perishable food as a starting point.
tools.method: Person-days are people x days, and the calories to store are person-days x the chosen calories per person per day. The meals to plan are person-days x meals per person per day, so the average calories per meal is the total calories divided by the total meals. Days of food on hand describe how many days this household could already eat, so the food on hand is that many days x people person-days, converted to calories at the same daily figure; days covered is the smaller of that figure and the plan length, and the shortfall is the requirement less what is on hand. Outstanding meals are the shortfall in calories divided by the average meal, and each package row divides that meal count by the package size (6, 12, 24 or 48 meals) and rounds up to a whole package, so the meals supplied exceed the shortfall except where it divides exactly. A plan that is already covered shows zero packages. Inputs are a whole headcount from 1 to 12, a whole day count from 1 to 30, a whole calorie figure from 1,000 to 4,000 per person per day, whole meals from 2 to 5 per person per day and days of food on hand from 0 to 30 with at most one decimal. Everything runs in the browser with no uploads, storage or network calls, and the page stores nothing between visits.

tools.name: DNS Message Decoder
tools.description: Decode a DNS query or response from its hex wire bytes: the header flags, opcode and response code, the question, and every answer, authority and additional record, with compressed names expanded and A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, PTR, MX, TXT, SOA, SRV, CAA and EDNS0 OPT data rendered field by field.
tools.guidance: A field reader, not a validator, resolver or security check. It makes no DNS query and trusts the bytes you paste: a message that parses is not necessarily well formed for its purpose, and the decoder does not verify DNSSEC signatures, check zone consistency or decide whether a name is safe. Names are expanded through compression pointers only when a pointer refers to an earlier byte; a forward pointer is refused rather than followed, so a crafted message cannot loop the page. Types other than A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, PTR, MX, TXT, SOA, SRV, CAA and OPT are shown as raw hex because their structure is not interpreted, and UDP or TCP framing around the message is not part of the paste.
tools.method: The message is read at the offsets RFC 1035 gives it: a 16-bit transaction ID, a 16-bit flags word (QR, opcode, AA, TC, RD, RA, Z, AD, CD and the 4-bit response code), four 16-bit counts, then the question and the answer, authority and additional records and their TTL, class and length-prefixed data. Names are read label by label; a length byte of 0xC0 is a pointer whose 14-bit offset must land earlier in the message, at most 64 pointers are followed, a label is at most 63 bytes and a whole name at most 255, so a forward pointer, a self pointer or an over-long name is refused with the byte offset rather than followed. A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, PTR, MX, TXT, SOA, SRV and CAA carry fixed or published layouts and are rendered field by field, AAAA in the RFC 5952 shortest form; the EDNS0 OPT pseudo-record (RFC 6891) reports its UDP payload size, extended response code, version and flags, and its options as code and length. Record lengths are checked against the bytes that remain, and an extended response code is combined with the header value. Type names come from the IANA DNS parameters registry, including the RFC 3597 TYPE form for unknown numbers. Everything runs in the browser with no uploads, storage or network calls.

tools.name: Critical Distance Calculator
tools.description: Find a room's critical distance from its volume and reverberation time, then see how many decibels the direct sound leads the reverberant field at any source-to-listener distance, with the equivalent absorption area and a table around the critical radius.
tools.method: Critical distance is the distance at which the direct sound from a source and the diffuse reverberant field have equal sound pressure level. The room's equivalent absorption area follows Sabine's relation A = 0.161 V / RT60 with A in square metres, V in cubic metres and RT60 in seconds, and the critical distance is dc = 0.25 sqrt(Q A / pi) with Q the source directivity factor: 1 for an omnidirectional source and about 3 for a cardioid microphone on axis. At a distance d the direct-to-reverberant ratio is 20 log10(dc / d) dB, so it reads 0 dB at dc, +6.02 dB at half of dc and -6.02 dB at twice dc. Volumes convert from cubic feet at 35.3147 per cubic metre and distances from feet at 0.3048 m per foot. Inputs are limited to 1-1000000 m3, 0.05-20 s, Q 0.5-50 and 0.01-200 m. The model takes the room constant as the absorption area, which assumes a diffuse field with absorption well below unity: small dead rooms, strong specular reflections, room modes, non-diffuse source arrays and an audience all depart from it, and a microphone's Q only holds on its axis, so the figure is a placement guide rather than a measurement. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Critical distance
Everest, F. A. and Pohlmann, K., Master Handbook of Acoustics, 6th edition, McGraw-Hill, 2015

tools.name: proc/stat CPU Utilization Decoder
tools.description: Compare two pasted /proc/stat captures and read per-CPU utilization: busy, user, system, I/O wait, steal and idle percentages, the all-CPU average and the length of the sample window.
tools.method: Only the cpu and cpuN lines of the paste are read; blank lines, comments and every other line such as intr, ctxt and btime are ignored. A line whose label already appeared in the current sample starts the second sample, so a paste of two consecutive cat /proc/stat captures is split without a separator, and a third sample is refused. Each line is read as four to ten whole-number counters in the documented order: user, nice, system, idle, iowait, irq, softirq, steal, guest and guest_nice; a missing tail column counts as zero. Because the counters are totals since boot, only the difference between the two samples is used. A counter that went backwards is clamped to zero, which the kernel allows for iowait, and the page reports how many counters were clamped. For each CPU total is the sum of the first eight differences, idle is idle plus iowait, and busy is total minus idle, so user, nice, system, irq, softirq and steal add up to busy and time waiting on I/O is reported under both iowait and idle rather than as busy. Guest and guest_nice are shown as shares of host time and are not added to total a second time. Every share is that difference divided by total, rounded half up to one decimal; an exact half therefore reads up, not to even. Idle is the exact complement of busy, so the two always add to 100. The all-CPU row is the aggregate cpu line when it is present and otherwise the sum of the per-CPU differences. The window is the all-CPU difference divided by 100 ticks per second and by the number of CPUs, which assumes USER_HZ of 100 (sysconf(_SC_CLK_TCK)) and a CPU list that did not change between the reads; it is an estimate, and no window is shown when the paste has only the aggregate line. The page reads only the pasted text: it does not query the host, and it does not model steal, CPU frequency, thermal throttling or cgroup quota, so the shares are time shares as the kernel accounts them and not a diagnosis of the machine. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.

tools.name: Throwing Sector Marking Calculator
tools.description: Work out a throwing landing sector from the event and a tape-run distance: the cross distance between the two lines, the half cross, the arc, the landing area and the effect of a 0.1 degree angle error, in metres or feet.
aliases: Track and Field Sector Layout Calculator
track and field sector layout calculator
tools.method: World Athletics Technical Rules fix the landing sector at 34.92 degrees for the shot put, discus and hammer and at 28.96 degrees for the javelin, measured between the inner edges of two lines that, if extended, meet at the centre of the throwing circle or, for the javelin, at the centre of the foul arc 8 m behind it. The tool takes the event, a distance out along one sector line and the unit, then works from that apex: the cross distance between the ends of the two equal lines is 2 x r x sin(theta / 2), half of it is r x sin(theta / 2), the arc at that distance is r x theta and the landing area inside it is 0.5 x r^2 x theta, with theta the full sector angle in radians. For 34.92 degrees the ratio 2 x sin(17.46 degrees) is 0.60008, so the rule-book shortcut of 0.60 times the line length (12 m across at 20 m, 48 m at 80 m, 60 m at 100 m) agrees to within 0.02 per cent; for 28.96 degrees the ratio 2 x sin(14.48 degrees) is 0.50008, which is 50 m across at 100 m from the arc centre. Because a javelin throw is measured from the throwing arc, the tape runs from the arc centre at the entered distance plus the 8 m arc radius, and the page reports that radial distance alongside the entered one. A sector 0.1 degrees too wide, the USATF rule 187.22 allowance, moves the cross distance by 2 x r x (sin((theta + 0.1) / 2) - sin(theta / 2)), which is 2.0 in at a 100 ft line. Distances are accepted from 1 to 120 m or 3 to 400 ft; the unit scales every length linearly and leaves the angles unchanged, and the table steps through 10 m or 25 ft from one step to ten. The core rounds its lengths and areas to five decimal places and the page shows two, so a 34.92 degree sector reads 12.00 m across at 20 m rather than the exact 12.0016 m. This is marking arithmetic only: it assumes level ground and a sector centred on the throwing direction, it does not survey a site, set competition markings or replace the competition's own field regulations, and laying a sector out still needs a tape, pegs and a second pair of hands. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.

tools.name: Makefile Build Order Planner
tools.description: Work out the order make would build a goal in: paste a Makefile, name a target, and see every recipe in dependency order, the pattern rules that fill in, the prerequisites assumed to exist as files, and any cycle. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: The planner reads the part of GNU make that decides order: explicit rules written targets: prerequisites, pattern rules with one %, recipe lines that begin with a tab, an inline recipe after a semicolon, order-only prerequisites after a pipe, .PHONY, .DEFAULT_GOAL, and the variable operators =, :=, ::=, ?= and +=. Rule lines are expanded when they are read, which is when make expands them, so a target list or prerequisite list that uses a variable reassigned further down the file keeps the earlier value; recipe lines are expanded with the values the variables hold at the end of the file, because make expands them when the recipe runs. The goal is the name in the goal field, otherwise .DEFAULT_GOAL, otherwise the first rule whose target is neither special nor a pattern. The walk is depth first, left to right: each prerequisite and everything below it is placed before its dependent, every target appears once at its first completion, and order-only prerequisites are visited after the ordinary ones. A prerequisite with no rule of its own is assumed to exist as a file, since a browser cannot stat the filesystem, and is reported separately instead of being dropped. A target whose own rule names prerequisites but no recipe takes the recipe of the first matching pattern rule and keeps its own prerequisites, which is what make's implicit rule search does. The planner refuses an empty field, more than 30,000 characters, a recipe before the first rule, a line that is neither a rule, an assignment nor a tab-indented recipe, a pattern containing more than one %, a rule that mixes pattern and ordinary targets, a goal containing whitespace, a goal with no rule and no matching pattern, a file with no default target, more than 400 rule lines or 600 steps, and any cycle, which make would resolve by dropping a prerequisite. An undefined variable expands to nothing, as in make, and is listed; functions such as $(shell ...) and $(wildcard ...), conditionals, include, target-specific variables and suffix rules are reported as not modelled rather than guessed. Nothing is executed and no file is read from disk.

sources.title: GNU Make manual, section 4.2 "Rule Syntax" - the targets: prerequisites form, the tab-indented recipe and the inline recipe after a semicolon
GNU Make manual, section 4.6 "Phony Targets" - why a .PHONY prerequisite is run every time and why phoniness is not inherited
GNU Make manual, section 10.8 "Implicit Rule Search Algorithm" - how a target with no recipe takes one from a pattern rule, and how a stem fills in the prerequisites

tools.name: O-Ring Gland Fit Calculator
tools.description: Check an O-ring in a radial gland: enter its free inside diameter and cross-section with the groove bottom diameter, gland depth and groove width to read the radial squeeze, the installed stretch and the gland fill, with warnings when a figure leaves the handbook's design window.
tools.method: An O-ring seals because its cross-section is flattened between the bottom of its groove and the mating surface, and the three figures that decide whether a gland works are all dimensional. The radial squeeze is the free cross-section minus the gland depth, reported in millimetres and as a percentage of the free cross-section; the installed stretch compares the groove bottom diameter with the free inside diameter, (D_groove − ID_free) / ID_free, and matters because a ring pulled over a larger diameter thins as it stretches, so a squeeze read on the free cord is optimistic once the stretch passes a few percent. The gland fill divides the ring's cross-section area π CS²/4 by the groove's cross-section area, depth × width, and is the share of the groove the ring occupies cold; the void that is left has to absorb thermal expansion and any fluid swell. A 24.99 mm ring with a 3.53 mm cord, stretched over a 26 mm groove bottom and sitting 2.9 mm deep in a 4.6 mm wide groove, therefore reads 0.63 mm of squeeze (17.8 %), 4.04 % of stretch and 73.4 % of fill. Parker's O-Ring Handbook (ORD 5700, §3.6 squeeze and §3.7 gland fill) puts the minimum squeeze for any cross-section at about 0.2 mm, the maximum recommended squeeze for a static seal at 30 % and for a dynamic seal at about 16 %, and asks for a gland fill between 60 % and 85 % with the optimum near 75 %, so that at least 10 % of the gland stays void; its §5.10 on stretch notes that more than a couple of percent reduces the squeeze diameter, so the page warns above 5 %. It also warns when the groove is narrower than the cord, because the ring then bulges over the side walls, and when the groove bottom is smaller than the free inside diameter, because the ring no longer grips. Inputs are bounded: free inside diameter 3 to 2000 mm, free cross-section 0.5 to 25 mm, groove bottom diameter 3 to 2400 mm, gland depth 0.2 to 15 mm and groove width 0.3 to 60 mm, and a gland deeper than the free cross-section is refused because the ring would not be compressed at all. These are the handbook's dimensional rules only: the page does not model the diametral clearance the ring may be extruded into, the surface finish of the sealing faces, the pressure, temperature or the compound and its swell in the fluid, nor the backup rings a high-pressure gland needs, so it is a fit check rather than a seal design. Everything runs locally in the browser.

tools.name: Wilkinson Power Divider Designer
tools.description: Design a two-way Wilkinson power divider, equal or with a chosen split: the quarter-wave arm impedances, the isolation resistor, the guided wavelength and the physical arm length, with the output level at each port.
tools.method: A two-way Wilkinson divider splits one input into two outputs through a quarter-wave line in each arm, with a resistor bridging the two outputs. With K squared equal to the port 3 power divided by the port 2 power, the arm to port 2 is Z0 times the square root of K times (1 + K squared), the arm to port 3 is Z0 times the square root of (1 + K squared) divided by K cubed, and the isolation resistor is Z0 times (K + 1/K). At K = 1, an equal split, both arms become Z0 times the square root of two and the resistor becomes twice Z0, which is the familiar 1.414 x Z0 arm and 2 x Z0 resistor rule. In fifty ohms at 2.45 GHz the equal-split arms are 70.711 ohms and the resistor is 100.0 ohms; a two-to-one split with two thirds of the power at port 2 gives arms of 51.494 ohms and 102.988 ohms with a 106.066 ohm resistor, so each arm must be built from its own impedance. Each arm is 90 degrees of electrical length at the design frequency, so its physical length is a quarter of the guided wavelength, which is the velocity factor times the free-space wavelength; at 2.45 GHz on 0.66 velocity factor the guided wavelength is 80.760 mm and each arm is 20.190 mm. The page also reports the output level at each port as 10 log10 of its power share, -3.01 dB each for an equal split. The system impedance is limited to 5 to 1000 ohms, the frequency to 0.1 to 40000 MHz, the velocity factor to 0.3 to 1 and the port 2 share to 5 to 95 percent; text, negative values, values outside those ranges and an empty field are refused with the field named. The model is an ideal lossless quarter-wave network with a matched source and matched loads: dispersion, junction capacitance, resistor tolerance, line loss and the layout's distance from the ground plane are not modelled, and match and isolation degrade away from the design frequency. The page stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

tools.name: Gas Compressibility Factor Calculator
tools.description: Estimate the Standing-Katz compressibility factor Z of a dry natural gas from its specific gravity, pressure and temperature, with the pseudo-critical properties, gas density and formation volume factor.
tools.method: The pseudo-critical properties come from Sutton's 1985 correlation for hydrocarbon gases, Tpc = 169.2 + 349.5 gamma_g - 74.0 gamma_g^2 in degrees Rankine and Ppc = 756.8 - 131.07 gamma_g - 3.6 gamma_g^2 in psia, where gamma_g is the gas specific gravity relative to air. The pseudo-reduced properties are Ppr = P / Ppc and Tpr = (T + 459.67) / Tpc, with the absolute temperature in Rankine. Z is the root of the Hall-Yarborough 1973 reduced-density equation: with t = 1 / Tpr, A = 0.06125 t exp(-1.2 (1 - t)^2), b = 14.76 t - 9.76 t^2 + 4.58 t^3, c = 90.7 t - 242.2 t^2 + 42.4 t^3 and d = 2.18 + 2.82 t, the reduced density Y solves -A Ppr + (Y + Y^2 + Y^3 - Y^4) / (1 - Y)^3 - b Y^2 + c Y^d = 0, and Z = A Ppr / Y. The page solves the equation by bisection over Y between 0 and 1, which converges to the single root at every reduced condition these inputs can reach (the objective is negative near Y = 0 and rises through the root to a pole at Y = 1); a grid scan of the whole accepted input envelope found one sign change every time. The published worked example is reproduced exactly: for a 0.7 gravity gas at 200 degrees F, Z is 0.922, 0.886, 1.000 and 1.254 at 1,000, 3,000, 5,000 and 8,000 psia, and the formation volume factor is 0.0172, 0.00550, 0.00373 and 0.00292 ft3/scf, while at 3,000 psia the gravities 0.6, 0.7 and 0.8 give 0.920, 0.886 and 0.851. Gas density is P M / (Z R T) with M = 28.97 gamma_g lb/lbmol and R = 10.7316 psia ft3 / (lbmol R), shown in lb/ft3 and converted to kg/m3 with 16.018463. The formation volume factor is Bg = 0.02827 Z T / P ft3/scf, the constant being p_sc / T_sc for 14.7 psia and 60 degrees F. Gas gravity is accepted from 0.56 to 1.2, pressure from 100 to 10,000 psia and temperature from 60 to 300 degrees F, which keeps Tpr at or above about 1.05. The estimate assumes a dry or lean hydrocarbon gas of typical composition: no Wichert-Aziz correction is applied for H2S or CO2 and none for N2, so sour or nitrogen-rich gases can shift Z by several percent, and the correlation is weakest near the critical point and does not describe a condensate wellstream below its dew point. It is not suitable for custody transfer, metering or equipment design, where a laboratory Z-factor or an equation of state should be used. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Scale Model Size Converter
tools.description: Convert a real dimension to the size of a scale model and back at common modelling scales, and work out the scale of a model from its real and model lengths.
tools.method: The conversion is a ratio, not an empirical model. Every length is parsed as a plain decimal number and converted to millimetres (1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 1000 mm, 1 in = 25.4 mm, 1 ft = 304.8 mm); the model length is the real length divided by the scale denominator N, and the real length is the model length multiplied by N, where the scale is written 1:N. For a model already in hand the denominator is recovered as N = real length / model length, and the page names the nearest common kit scale (1:12, 1:24, 1:32, 1:35, 1:48, 1:72, 1:76, 1:87, 1:144, 1:350) only when the recovered ratio lies within 15 % of it. The same ten scales are used for the table that repeats the real length as a model size, and the row matching the current scale is marked. Surface area scales with the square of the linear ratio and volume, and therefore mass at equal density, with the cube: a 1:72 model has 1/5184 of the surface and 1/373,248 of the volume of the object it represents. Inputs are accepted from 0.01 mm to 1,000,000 mm for a length and from 1 to 10,000 for the scale, with decimals allowed so a nominal scale such as the HO 1:87.1 can be entered; the model length is rejected when it is not shorter than the real length and the recovered ratio is rejected above 1:10,000. Results are shown to display precision and repeated in millimetres or inches, and the page only converts a length, so it says nothing about the proportions, weight or detail of a kit. Published kit scales are nominal: a moulding, a printed plan or a quoted model length is often a percent or two away from the label, and the two lengths must describe the same dimension (overall length against overall length, for example) for the ratio to mean anything. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Bed & Mattress Size Converter
tools.description: Convert a bed or mattress size between the US, UK, continental European, Australian and Japanese charts, or enter a width and length to find the closest standard size in each market.
tools.method: The chart follows one published table of nominal mattress dimensions and does not blend sources: the United States chart from 38.5 × 74.5 in to 72 × 83.5 in, the UK and Ireland chart in the National Bed Federation figures from 76 × 191 cm to 183 × 198 cm, continental Europe from 90 × 200 cm to 200 × 200 cm, Australia from 92 × 188 cm to 204 × 204 cm and Japan from 97 × 195 cm to 194 × 205 cm, 33 sizes in all. US sizes are stored in inches and converted with the exact factor 1 in = 2.54 cm, so a US queen is 152.4 × 201.9 cm; the other four charts are stored in centimetres and shown in inches by the same factor. A named size lists the closest size in each of the other four charts. Both pairs are first ordered short side first, so the shorter side of the mattress is compared with the shorter side of every listed size regardless of which field it was typed into. The gap is the sum of the two side differences in centimetres, rounded to one decimal; the closest size in each chart is the row with the smallest gap, a tie going to the earlier row, and a row counts as close when neither side differs by more than 2 cm. In measurement mode the five closest rows are shown, the single smallest gap is highlighted, and an exact match is reported only when the gap is zero. A width or length is accepted from 40 to 300 cm (15.7 to 118.1 in), which spans a crib mattress to an extra-wide double; the entered number is converted to centimetres before that range is tested, so the same limits apply in both units. Lengths and widths are treated as plain decimal numbers with no thousands separators and no unit suffixes. Results are shown to one decimal place in both centimetres and inches, and the page only compares mattress footprints: it says nothing about frame size, mattress depth, bedding drop or bed height. Published charts disagree by a centimetre or two and retailers round names differently, so the dimensions are nominal and the page says to check the shop's own figures before ordering. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Code 39 Barcode Generator
tools.description: Encode upper-case text as a Code 39 barcode: the 43-character set, three wide elements per nine-element symbol, the optional modulo-43 check character, the module count and the bars drawn as an SVG between ten-module quiet zones.
tools.method: A Code 39 symbol is a start character, the data characters, an optional check character and a stop character, each drawn as nine elements - five bars and four spaces - of which exactly three are wide. Every element is one module (narrow) or three modules (wide), so a symbol is fifteen modules across, and a single one-module space separates one symbol from the next. The page draws those modules as black and white runs and wraps the whole barcode in ten-module quiet zones, the space a scanner needs at either end. The 43 characters of the standard set are the digits, the capital letters and - . space $ / + %, with values 0 to 42 in that published order, and the asterisk is the start and stop symbol - it is added automatically and refused in the data. When the check character is enabled, the values of the data characters are summed and reduced modulo 43, and the character at that value is inserted before the stop symbol. Lower case, control characters and the full-ASCII pairs Code 39 would need for them are not offered, so the page is not an extended Code 39 encoder, and the text is limited to 40 characters to keep a printed label readable. The pattern table and the check character are checked against the symbology, but a printed label still has to be test-scanned at the module width the label and scanner need. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
