tools.name: DORI Pixel Density Planner
tools.description: Turn a camera's resolution, field of view and distance into the pixel density on a subject, classify the view against the four IEC 62676-4 DORI levels and show how far each level reaches.
tools.method: A rectilinear lens spreads the sensor's horizontal pixels across a scene that widens with distance, so the scene width at distance d is 2 x d x tan(HFOV / 2) and the pixel density is the frame width divided by that width, in pixels per metre. Doubling the distance halves the density; halving it doubles the density. Square pixels make the vertical density identical, which is why only the horizontal field of view is asked for: the vertical field of view is 2 x atan(tan(HFOV / 2) x height / width) and height / scene height gives the same number. The IEC 62676-4:2014 operational requirements are 25 px/m for detection, 62.5 px/m for observation, 125 px/m for recognition and 250 px/m for identification (published as 25, 63, 125 and 250 px/m, or 8, 20, 40 and 80 px/ft); identification works out at 40 pixels across a 0.16 m human face, and the page reports the pixels on that face. A level is met when the density is greater than or equal to its threshold, so a distance exactly at a level's limit still counts for that level. The reach of a level is width / (2 x tan(HFOV / 2) x threshold) - where that division lands on the threshold - and the pixels needed to identify a face at the entered distance is the scene width x 250, rounded up. Density in px/ft is px/m divided by 3.28084. The model assumes a rectilinear lens with square pixels and no distortion, a face square to the camera at the stated distance, even lighting and a sharp image; fisheye and panoramic lenses, tilted or receding faces, motion blur, low light, IR illumination and compression all reduce the effective density, so this is a planning guide rather than a guarantee. IEC 62676-4:2025 replaced these four names with a seven-step scale, all of which this page does not model. Inputs are whole pixels from 16 to 32,768, a field of view strictly between 0 and 180 degrees and a distance from 0 to 10,000 m; there is no storage, upload or network access.

tools.name: Map Sheet Layout Planner
tools.description: Plan how many sheets of paper a printed map of a given ground area needs at a chosen scale, with paper size, orientation, margins and sheet overlap taken into account, plus the sheet count at other common scales.
aliases: How Many Sheets to Print a Map
tools.method: A printed map draws one millimetre of paper as the scale denominator in millimetres of ground, so a sheet's ground coverage is its printable width and height (trimmed paper minus twice the margin) divided by 1,000 and multiplied by the scale denominator. The page lays that coverage in a rectangular grid and counts sheets by ceil((target - overlap) / (coverage - overlap)) on each axis, where the overlap is the paper overlap times the scale; the overlap appears on both sides of the division because every sheet after the first reuses one overlap strip, so overlap reduces the ground each extra sheet adds rather than the sheet's own coverage. A target that exactly fills the last sheet keeps that count and any part beyond it adds one. The grid extent is sheets x coverage minus (sheets - 1) overlaps, and the paper area is the sheet count times the untrimmed paper area. The same paper, margins and overlap are then reapplied at 1:10,000, 1:25,000, 1:50,000, 1:100,000, 1:250,000 and 1:500,000 to show the sheet count at other common scales. The model assumes one uniform map scale over the whole area, a rectangular grid with straight joins, uniform margins and that the entered margin is printable; it ignores projection distortion away from a map's standard parallel or central meridian, a printer's own unprintable edge, trimming and folding, and it treats the area as a rectangle rather than a shaped region. Inputs are 0.01 to 5,000 km per side, a whole scale denominator from 1,000 to 1,000,000, margins and overlaps from 0 to 100 mm with the printable size kept positive and the overlap smaller than it; there is no storage, upload or network access.

tools.name: Wind Pipe Tuning Calculator
tools.description: Find the length to cut an open or stopped tube for a chosen note, or the note and cent offset of a pipe you already have, from the bore, the air temperature and the reference pitch for A4.
tools.method: An open cylindrical pipe carries half a wavelength of its lowest note and a pipe stopped at one end a quarter, so the effective length is the speed of sound divided by twice the frequency for an open pipe and by four times it for a stopped pipe. Air just outside each open end vibrates with the column, so the page subtracts an end correction of 0.6133 times the bore radius at every open end - two for an open pipe, one for the stopped one - to give the length to cut; that is the Levine and Schwinger value for an ideal unflanged tube. The speed of sound is taken as 331.3 m/s times the square root of 1 + theta/273.15 at the air temperature entered, so cold air shortens the pipe and warm air lengthens it. Notes are placed in twelve-tone equal temperament from the reference A4 pitch, and the twelve notes of an equal-tempered octave are listed at the same bore and temperature. A pipe length can be entered instead, and the page then names the nearest note and the offset in cents. The figures describe a straight, smooth, thin-walled cylinder whose open end is cut square: a real instrument's mouth or flue, tone holes, wall thickness, foot, bell, taper and humidity all move the resonance, so the result is a cut length to start from rather than a finished tuning. Inputs are a bore from 2 to 200 mm, air from -20 to 50 degrees Celsius, a reference A4 from 392 to 466 Hz, notes from C1 to C7, and pipe lengths from 20 to 6,000 mm. Nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched; the page runs entirely in the browser.

Speed of sound - Wikipedia: dry air at 0 C carries sound at 331.3 m/s, rising with the square root of the absolute temperature

tools.name: Keyframe-Aligned Trim Planner
tools.description: Find the keyframes on either side of an in and out point from the frame rate and encoder interval, and see how many frames a stream copy must decode before the cut or re-encode after it to stay frame-accurate.
tools.method: A closed GOP starts on a keyframe and repeats at the encoder's keyframe interval, so at a constant frame rate the keyframes fall on whole multiples of the GOP length counted from frame zero of the file. The page turns the interval in seconds into a whole-frame GOP length as the interval multiplied by the frame rate, rounded, and never shorter than one frame. Both timecodes then become frame numbers: hours times 3600 plus minutes times 60 plus seconds, all times the nominal frame count round(fps) (24 for 23.976, 30 for 29.97, 60 for 59.94), plus the frame number, less two frame numbers for every minute that is not a multiple of ten when the timecode is drop-frame at 29.97 (four at 59.94). A semicolon marks drop-frame and a colon non-drop, the two notations cannot be mixed in one plan, and a drop-frame label that names a skipped frame is refused. The aligned range runs from floor(in / GOP) * GOP to ceil((out + 1) / GOP) * GOP, exclusive at the end, so it starts and ends on keyframes and contains the requested cut. Preroll is the distance from the aligned start to the in point, the tail is the distance from the last kept frame to the aligned end, and their sum is the footage outside the cut that a frame-accurate trim has to decode. The out point is inclusive, so 00:00:10:10 to 00:00:11:24 at 25 fps keeps forty frames. The model assumes a closed GOP with a keyframe exactly every interval and no keyframes from scene cuts; open GOPs, variable intervals and encoder-side scene detection move the real boundaries, so the table of five keyframes is a plan to check against the file's own keyframe list before a lossless export. Inputs allow 1 to 240 fps, intervals from 0.1 to 60 seconds and timecodes up to 23:59:59. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched.

tools.name: Referrer-Policy Resolution Simulator
tools.description: Resolve the exact Referer header a browser sends for one page and one link target under a chosen Referrer-Policy, and compare all eight policies side by side, including same-origin, cross-origin and HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade cases.
tools.method: The Referrer-Policy header and the referrerpolicy attribute both name one of eight policies, and the specification's determine-request's-referrer algorithm maps a policy, the page URL and the target URL to either no header, the origin, or the full URL. The page first strips what a referrer never carries: the fragment, any username and password, and a port that is the default for the scheme (80 for http, 443 for https). It lowercases the host and keeps an IPv6 literal in brackets. The full form is scheme, host, port, path and query, with an empty path written as a slash; the origin form is scheme, host and port followed by a slash, as the specification requires so that the value is a valid URL. A request is same-origin when scheme, host and port all match. A downgrade is a page on https and a target on http only: an http page sending to an https target is an upgrade, not a downgrade, so no-referrer-when-downgrade keeps the full URL there. no-referrer sends nothing; no-referrer-when-downgrade sends the full URL except on a downgrade; same-origin sends the full URL only within the origin; origin always sends the origin; strict-origin sends the origin but not on a downgrade; origin-when-cross-origin sends the full URL within the origin and the origin otherwise, including downgrades; strict-origin-when-cross-origin sends the full URL within the origin, the origin across origins, and nothing on a downgrade; unsafe-url always sends the full URL. An empty policy falls back to no-referrer-when-downgrade, while browsers use strict-origin-when-cross-origin as their own default when a page sets nothing. Redirects are not chained here: the header always describes the document that started the request, so one page and one target are enough. Inputs accept http and https URLs in plain ASCII without spaces; everything else is refused rather than guessed. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched.

tools.name: TCP Header Decoder
tools.description: Decode the hex bytes of a TCP segment into both ports, the sequence and acknowledgment numbers, the data offset, every control flag, the window, the urgent pointer and each option, and verify the checksum over the IPv4 or IPv6 pseudo-header.
tools.guidance: A field reader, not a validator: the bytes are trusted and a header that parses is not necessarily well formed for its purpose. The checksum cannot verify when the paste ends at the header, because the sum covers the data too, and a NIC with checksum offload can leave a placeholder. A SYN segment's own window is never scaled, and the shift negotiated in a handshake is not visible in any later segment. This page makes no capture and reads no traffic.
tools.method: The header is read at the offsets RFC 9293 Figure 1 gives it: a 16-bit source port, a 16-bit destination port, the 32-bit sequence number, the 32-bit acknowledgment number, then one byte whose high nibble is the data offset in 32-bit words and whose low nibble is the four reserved bits, one byte of control flags (CWR 0x80, ECE 0x40, URG 0x20, ACK 0x10, PSH 0x08, RST 0x04, SYN 0x02, FIN 0x01), the 16-bit window, the 16-bit checksum, the 16-bit urgent pointer and the options that fill the header out to four times the data offset. A data offset below five words, or one that reaches past the bytes pasted, is refused rather than padded. Options are walked in order: kinds 0 and 1 are one byte, every other option carries a length byte that counts its own two bytes, a length below two or one that leaves the header is refused, and the content after an end-of-list option must be zero padding. An MSS option is read as a 16-bit value, a window scale as its shift count (above the RFC 7323 cap of 14 it is reported as 14), a SACK option as 64-bit block pairs of left and right edges, and a timestamps option as TSval and TSecr; other kinds are named from the IANA TCP Option Kind Numbers registry and shown as hex. The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of a pseudo-header and the whole segment with the checksum field zeroed. The IPv4 pseudo-header is the two addresses, a zero byte, protocol 6 and the segment length; the IPv6 pseudo-header is both 128-bit addresses, a 32-bit upper-layer length, three zero bytes and 6 (RFC 8200 section 8.1). Because the sum covers the data, a segment pasted as its header alone will not verify, and a segment copied off a NIC that leaves checksum offload on can carry a placeholder instead of a real value. A window advertised in a segment with the SYN bit set is never scaled, so the window scale from the handshake is only applied to the other segments and is taken from the pseudo-header-adjacent field the user supplies. The window field is read unsigned. Payload bytes past the header are counted and shown as hex but not interpreted, port names are not looked up, and a segment is not reassembled or validated against a connection state.

RFC 2018 - TCP Selective Acknowledgment Options, section 3: the SACK option block layout

tools.name: Frequency Weighting Calculator
tools.description: Convert a measured level into dB(A), dB(C) or dB(Z): the A- and C-weighting correction at any frequency from 10 Hz to 20 kHz, the weighted reading, the C minus A difference and a table of the nominal octave-band corrections.
tools.guidance: A converter, not a meter: the level you type is taken as correct and the page only adds a curve. One band's weighted level is not an overall dB(A) reading - combine every band's energy for that - and A-weighting was derived from quiet pure tones, so it is a reporting convention rather than a prediction of how loud a sound will seem.
tools.method: Frequency weighting adds a fixed correction to a measured sound level so that a meter reads closer to the sensitivity of the ear. The corrections follow the analytic weighting functions of IEC 61672-1: R_A(f) = 12194^2 f^4 / ((f^2 + 20.6^2) sqrt((f^2 + 107.7^2)(f^2 + 737.9^2)) (f^2 + 12194^2)) with A = 20 log10(R_A), and R_C(f) = 12194^2 f^2 / ((f^2 + 20.6^2)(f^2 + 12194^2)) with C = 20 log10(R_C), each normalised to 0 dB at 1 kHz, which is what the published +2.00 dB and +0.06 dB offsets approximate; Z weighting is flat, so its correction is 0 dB at every frequency. The weighted reading is the unweighted level plus the correction, C minus A shows how much of the level falls where the A curve attenuates most, and the table lists the nominal octave-band corrections from 31.5 Hz to 16 kHz. Against the published nominal tables the analytic A curve agrees within 0.28 dB and the C curve within 0.15 dB over 10 Hz to 20 kHz, the largest A departure sitting at 16 Hz, and the page's own octave rows reproduce Arup's table within 0.14 dB. Frequency is limited to 10-20000 Hz and level to -50-194 dB, 194 dB being the largest pressure swing that air at one atmosphere allows. A weighted single band is not an overall dB(A) reading unless that band is the whole sound, and A-weighting is a measurement convention derived from pure tones at low level, so the figures are not a loudness model. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: inotify Watch Limit Planner
tools.description: Size the inotify limits for a file-watching service: watches per directory tree, per process and per user, a queue target for the drain interval, and a sysctl snippet that never lowers the limits you enter. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.guidance: A sizing aid, not a kernel rule: a watch on a directory covers that directory's entries only, so count every subdirectory, and remember that the watch and instance limits are per real user ID and shared with every other program the user runs.
tools.method: inotify holds one watch per watched path: a directory watch reports events for entries in that directory, so a recursive watcher needs one watch per directory plus one per file it watches individually. Watches and instances are counted per real user ID, and fs.inotify.max_user_watches bounds the watch total, with inotify_add_watch failing with ENOSPC once it is reached; fs.inotify.max_user_instances bounds instance creation, and because a queue belongs to an instance every watching process needs one of its own. The planner multiplies directories plus individually watched files by the number of processes of one user, adds the entered headroom percentage, and rounds the watch target up to a whole watch. The queue target is the peak rate per instance times the longest drain interval, plus headroom, rounded up to a whole event; fs.inotify.max_queued_events caps an instance's queue at creation time and events beyond it are dropped with an IN_Q_OVERFLOW event delivered instead. The instances figure is shown as a floor because the limit is shared with other programs in the session. The sysctl snippet is built only when all three current limits are entered, and each value is the larger of the current and the target, so applying it can never lower a limit. Headroom, the drain interval and the peak rate are planning assumptions supplied by the user rather than kernel defaults. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Tennis Court Marking Calculator
tools.description: Mark out a tennis court from the ITF dimensions: the painted line length, paint area and volume, the tape checks from Appendix X and the run-back footprint for club or international play.
aliases: Tennis Court Dimensions and Marking Calculator
tennis court dimensions and marking calculator
tools.guidance: Marking arithmetic only. Measure every line to its outside edge, square the court from the net line with the tapes, and check local planning rules and the space for umpires, benches and fencing before fixing the run-back.
tools.method: The ITF Rules of Tennis make the court a 23.77 m rectangle, 10.97 m wide for doubles and 8.23 m for singles, with the net across the middle, and every measurement is taken to the outside of the lines. The service lines sit 6.40 m from the net and are drawn only between the singles sidelines, so each is 8.23 m long on either kind of court and the 1.37 m doubles alleys never widen a service box; the centre service line runs 12.80 m from one service line to the other and splits each service area into boxes 6.40 m deep and 4.115 m wide (4.11 m in the rule book's table), and each baseline carries a 10 cm centre mark. The tool sums the painted length of two baselines, two doubles sidelines and two singles sidelines on a combined court (two baselines and two singles sidelines on a singles-only court), two 8.23 m service lines, the 12.80 m centre service line and two 10 cm centre marks: 146.48 m for a combined court and 93.46 m for a singles-only one. Paint area is that length times the line width, and paint per coat is the area divided by the coverage entered; the small overlaps where lines cross are not deducted. Appendix X supplies the marking-out figures the page lists: a 12.80 m net line between post centres, the inner sideline at 4.11 m, the singles sticks at 5.03 m, the outer sidelines at 5.48 m and the net posts at 6.40 m from the centre, then the 16.18 m diagonal and 11.89 m sideline tapes that meet at a baseline corner, with a 10.97 m baseline check; a singles-only court uses a 10 m net, 5.03 m to each post, a 14.46 m diagonal and an 8.23 m baseline check. The full-court diagonal is the square root of the length squared plus the width squared, 26.18 m for doubles and 25.15 m for singles. The footprint is the court plus the ITF's recommended minimum run-back, 5.48 m behind the baselines and 3.05 m beside the sidelines for club and recreational play or 6.40 m and 3.66 m for international competition; it is a planning rectangle, not a boundary, and local rules may ask for more. Net figures follow Rule 1: posts 1.07 m high, 0.914 m outside the court, and a net 0.914 m high at the centre, held by singles sticks 0.914 m outside each singles sideline when a doubles net is used for singles. Line width is accepted from 2.5 to 5 cm, the range Rule 1 sets for court lines apart from the 10 cm baseline allowance, and paint coverage from 1 to 50 square metres per litre. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: ITF Rules of Tennis 2026 - Rule 1 (court 23.77 m long, 10.97 m wide for doubles and 8.23 m for singles, service lines 6.40 m from the net, net posts 0.914 m outside the court) and Appendix X (marking out a court: 12.80 m net line, the 4.11, 5.03, 5.48 and 6.40 m points, the 16.18 m and 11.89 m tapes, and the 5.48/3.05 m club and 6.40/3.66 m international run-back minimums)

tools.name: GitHub Actions Expression Evaluator
tools.description: Evaluate a GitHub Actions ${{ }} expression against your own contexts: the value, its type and whether a step's if: condition runs, with GitHub's loose equality, object filters and status functions.
tools.guidance: Evaluation only: this page models the expression language, not your repository. Supply the contexts you want it to read, check the value and type it reports, and remember that an if: without a status function also needs the job to be succeeding, which GitHub applies as an implicit success().
tools.method: Parses and evaluates one expression from a workflow if:, env: or runs-on: against a JSON document of contexts. The outer ${{ }} wrapper is optional and stripped. Literals are true, false, null, numbers in any form the JSON grammar accepts plus hexadecimal (0xff), signs and exponents, and single-quoted strings where '' stands for a literal quote; double-quoted strings are refused because the language rejects them. The operator table is the documented one, from tightest to loosest binding: grouping, index, property dereference, !, the relational operators < <= > >=, then == and !=, then && and ||, all left-associative. There are no arithmetic operators, so + - * / and % are refused rather than guessed at. ! always yields a boolean, while && and || short-circuit and return one of their operands, so an expression can evaluate to a string or a number. Equality is loose: when the kinds differ both sides are coerced to a number, where null is 0, true is 1, false is 0, a string is read as a number (the empty string is 0, anything unparseable is NaN) and an array or object is NaN; NaN never equals anything, and arrays and objects are equal only when they are the same value. Strings compare ignoring case, ordinal rather than by locale, and the same case folding applies to < <= > >= once both sides are strings; otherwise relational comparisons coerce to numbers and are false when either side is NaN, so true > false is true and '10' < '9' is true while 10 > '9' is true. Property dereference and index access are case-insensitive for names, a property the object does not have is null, an index outside an array is null, an index on a string or number is null, and * collects the values of an object or the items of an array into an array that later dereferences map over, which is how github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name returns the label names. The functions are contains (substring or array membership, case-insensitive), startsWith and endsWith, format with {N} placeholders and {{ }} escapes, join with a comma default, toJSON with two-space indentation, fromJSON, and case(predicate, value, ..., default) whose predicates must be booleans rather than merely truthy. success(), failure(), cancelled() and always() read the earlier-steps setting on the form. An if: condition runs when the value is truthy and, unless the expression calls one of those four status functions, when earlier steps have succeeded, which is the implicit success() GitHub applies; the plain-value mode reports truthiness alone. hashFiles() needs the workflow workspace and is refused, secrets is never available inside an expression, expressions are limited to 2,000 characters and the contexts JSON to 20,000, and nesting is capped at 60 levels. Everything runs in the browser with the browser's own JSON parser: nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched.

sources.title: GitHub Docs — Evaluate expressions in workflows and actions (literals, operators, loose equality, functions and object filters)

tools.name: Worm Gear Calculator
tools.description: Size a worm and wheel pair from module, starts and teeth: reduction ratio, pitch diameters, centre distance, lead angle, sliding velocity, efficiency and whether the drive is self-locking.
tools.guidance: Geometry and a friction estimate, not a gearbox rating. The friction coefficient is an assumption you supply; check the wheel material, lubrication, power and thermal rating, and the manufacturer's data, before building or loading the drive.
tools.method: Treats a cylindrical worm and wheel with no profile shift. Inputs are the module m in millimetres, the number of worm starts z1 (1 to 4), the wheel tooth count z2 (8 to 400), the worm pitch diameter d1 (1 to 2000 mm), the worm speed n1 (0 to 60000 rpm), the coefficient of friction mu (0.01 to 0.5) and the normal pressure angle (14.5, 20 or 25 degrees). The worm diameter factor is q = d1/m, the wheel pitch diameter d2 = m z2, the centre distance a = (d1 + d2)/2, the lead L = pi m z1 and the lead angle gamma = atan(z1 m / d1). The wheel turns at n2 = n1 z1 / z2; the worm pitch-line speed is v1 = pi d1 n1 and the sliding velocity is vs = v1 / cos gamma. The friction angle is phi = atan mu, and the drive is reported as self-locking when gamma is at or below phi, because the wheel then cannot drive the worm. Efficiency is the standard estimate eta = (cos alpha_n - mu tan gamma) / (cos alpha_n + mu cot gamma), clamped to 0-100 percent, where alpha_n is the normal pressure angle; it is a friction estimate, not a gearbox rating. Tip diameters are the unshifted d1 + 2m and d2 + 2m. Values are rounded for display to three decimals, and q and efficiency to two. A warning is shown when q falls outside 5-20 or the lead angle exceeds 25 degrees. Everything is computed in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched.

sources.title: Worm gears (RoyMech): the lead angle atan(z1/q) with q = d1/m, the wheel pitch diameter from the axial pitch, the centre distance, the sliding velocity, the efficiency estimate (cos alpha_n - mu tan gamma)/(cos alpha_n + mu cot gamma) and the self-locking limit gamma = atan mu

tools.name: Directional Coupler Calculator
tools.description: Turn four measured port powers into a directional coupler's coupling, directivity, isolation and insertion loss, with a passive power-budget check.
tools.method: Converts each port power from dBm to milliwatts with P = 10^(dBm/10) and works from the four measured powers P1 (input), P2 (through), P3 (coupled) and P4 (isolated). Coupling is C = 10 log10(P1/P3), directivity is D = 10 log10(P3/P4), isolation is I = 10 log10(P1/P4), which equals C + D, and insertion loss is IL = 10 log10(P1/P2). The coupled and through fractions are P3/P1 and P2/P1, and the four-port power total is (P2 + P3 + P4)/P1, which a passive coupler cannot push above 100 percent; a total above 101 percent raises a measurement warning. Directivity assumes the through port is terminated in a matched load, so P4 is leakage through the coupler rather than a reflection from the load. Each power must be a number from -100 to 100 dBm; the coupled power must be below the input, the isolated power may not exceed the coupled power, and the through power may not exceed the input. Warnings are shown for directivity below 10 dB (or essentially zero), coupling above 30 dB, insertion loss above 1 dB and an impossible power total. Results are rounded to two decimals for the dB values and percentages, except the through fraction and the power total, which use one decimal. Power-meter accuracy, mismatch uncertainty, coupler loss and the effect of a reflective load are not modelled, and everything runs in the browser with no storage or network access.

sources.title: Microwaves101, Directional Couplers: insertion loss 10 log(P1/P2), isolation 10 log(P1/P4), coupling 10 log(P1/P3) and directivity 10 log(P3/P4), after Pozar, Microwave Engineering, 2005, p. 313
Wikipedia, Power dividers and directional couplers: the four ports, the coupled and isolated ports, and directivity as -10 log(P4/P3)

tools.name: Fuel Oil Viscosity-Temperature Calculator
tools.description: Fit the ASTM D341 Walther equation through two measured kinematic viscosities to read the viscosity at any temperature, or the temperature needed to reach a target viscosity such as a fuel's injection limit.
tools.method: Uses the ASTM D341 Walther equation log10(log10(v + 0.7)) = A - B log10(T), with v the kinematic viscosity in cSt (mm2/s) and T the absolute temperature in kelvin, so T = degrees Celsius + 273.15. The two measured points fix the line: with Y = log10(log10(v + 0.7)), B = (Y_cold - Y_hot) / (log10 T_hot - log10 T_cold) and A = Y_cold + B log10 T_cold. The viscosity at a temperature is 10^(10^(A - B log10 T)) - 0.7 cSt, and the temperature that reaches a target viscosity is 10^((A - Y_target) / B) - 273.15 degrees Celsius. The colder and hotter reference points are identified from the two temperatures, so their order in the form does not matter. Both measured viscosities must be at least 2 cSt: below that ASTM D341 adds a low-viscosity correction this page does not model, so the page refuses those readings. The hotter point must read lower than the colder one. Inputs are limited to 2 to 100,000 cSt and -50 to 300 degrees Celsius, the target temperature must fall inside that range, and the fit must give a positive viscosity at the check temperature. Warnings appear when the answer lies more than 60 degrees outside the measured span, when it exceeds 200 degrees, and when the two reference temperatures are less than 20 degrees apart. Temperatures are rounded to 0.1 degree and viscosities to 0.01 cSt. The fit is a two-point interpolation: it does not model the low-viscosity correction, wax or asphaltene behaviour, the blending of two fuels, or the measurement uncertainty of the laboratory test.

tools.name: Cutting Board Glue-Up Planner
tools.description: Plan an edge-grain or end-grain cutting board: count the strips to rip and the slices to crosscut, include the blade kerf and the trim allowance, and get the lumber width, length and board feet the glue-up needs.
tools.method: An edge-grain board is a row of strips glued face to face: the rip strip width w sets how much of the board width each strip contributes, so the strip count is ceil(finished width / w), the glued board is strips x w wide, and the stock thickness after flattening becomes the board thickness. The lumber consumed across the width is the summed strip widths plus one kerf between every neighbouring pair, strips x w + (strips - 1) x kerf, and the lumber length is the finished length plus the trim allowance at each end. An end-grain board turns that panel on edge: the strips are ripped so their width runs across the finished board length, making the board length strips x w; the panel is then crosscut into slices as thick as the finished board, each slice is rotated a quarter turn and glued face to face, so the slice count is ceil(finished width / finished thickness), the board width is slices x thickness, and the panel length is that width plus one kerf between slices plus the trim at both ends. The end-grain board thickness is the flattened panel thickness, which is why the stock must be at least as thick as the finished board in both builds. Board feet are the purchased lumber volume, stock width x stock length x stock thickness, converted at 1 board foot = 2,359,737.216 mm3 (144 in3). Lengths are entered in millimetres or inches and converted at 25.4 mm per inch. Kerf must be narrower than the strip, strips and slices are capped at 60, and the page warns when a strip is under 20 mm, when the blade removes more than 40% of a rip, when under 2 mm is left for flattening, and when rounding up leaves more than half a strip or slice over the asked size. Glue-line thickness, planing after the first glue-up, snipe, re-squaring the panel and the offcut from rounding up are not modelled, so the figures are a shopping allowance rather than a cut list.

tools.description: Convert a type size or print measurement between points, picas, twips, inches, millimetres, centimetres, quarter-millimetres and CSS pixels, with the exact absolute-length ratios shared by print workflows and browsers.
tools.method: One inch is exactly 25.4 mm, and the CSS absolute-length table fixes the rest: 1 in = 96 px = 72 pt = 6 pc, 1 mm = 1/10 cm, and 1 Q = 1/40 cm, so 1 in = 101.6 Q. A twip is one twentieth of a point, or 1/1440 in. Every entry is converted to inches and back out, so the eight units agree exactly with one another; the only rounding is in the display, to four significant digits, with a billionth added before rounding so a binary product that should sit on a decimal half rounds up rather than down. Sizes are accepted from 0.1 to 20,000 pt (about 0.035 mm to 7.06 m), which spans footnote sizes through billboard type, and the headline always reports points. The continental Didot point of about 0.376 mm and the 12-point cicero are a different system whose exact value varied by country, so they are deliberately not converted; leading, tracking, optical scaling and rasterising type at a print resolution are also out of scope. Everything runs in the browser, so nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Register Bit-Field Packer
tools.description: Pack named fields into one 8-, 16-, 32- or 64-bit hardware register and read the result as hex, decimal, binary, bit ranges and big- or little-endian bytes, with unsigned values accepted as decimal, 0x hex or 0b binary.
tools.method: Each field is written as a name, a width in bits and an unsigned value, and fields are laid out in the order listed from the most significant bit downward: the first field takes bits W-1 down to W-width, and the last field ends at bit 0. The widths must add up to no more than the word, and any bits left over are the low bits, which read as zero and are reported as unused. A value is accepted as decimal, 0x hex or 0b binary and is refused when it needs more bits than its field, so nothing is silently truncated; negative values are refused because the layout carries no sign convention. Words of 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits are supported, and the 64-bit case is calculated with BigInt so every bit survives. The register is shown as a fixed-width hex word, an unsigned decimal, binary grouped by byte, and as bytes in both big- and little-endian order, the latter being what a memory dump of the register usually shows on a little-endian CPU. Each field is read back out of the finished word and listed with its bit range, so the row values are a round-trip check rather than a second calculation. Fields cannot overlap because they are placed sequentially, and read-modify-write masks, reserved-bit rules, device-specific register maps and signed or fixed-point field interpretations are deliberately outside the page. Everything runs in the browser, so nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: High-Altitude Baking Adjuster
tools.description: Adjust a baking recipe for elevation: enter the height, leavening, sugar, liquid, flour and oven temperature, and read the reduced leavening, sugar and flour, the extra liquid, and the hotter oven the published high-altitude charts call for, interpolated between the 3,000, 5,000 and 7,000 ft bands.
tools.method: The published high-altitude charts give a per-unit adjustment for three bands, and the page holds them as pairs so both ends of each published range survive. At 3,000 ft: liquid +1 to 2 tbsp per cup, leavening -1/8 tsp per tsp, sugar 0 to 1 tbsp less per cup, flour 0 to 1 tbsp more per cup, oven 15 to 25 °F hotter. At 5,000 ft: liquid +2 to 4 tbsp, leavening -1/8 to -1/4 tsp per tsp, sugar 0 to 2 tbsp less, flour 0 to 2 tbsp more, oven 15 to 25 °F hotter. At 7,000 ft: liquid +3 to 4 tbsp, leavening -1/4 tsp per tsp, sugar 1 to 3 tbsp less, flour 2 to 4 tbsp more, oven 15 to 25 °F hotter. The page computes with the midpoint of each range and reports the resulting minimum and maximum too. An elevation between two bands is interpolated linearly; 7,000 ft and above hold the top band; below 3,000 ft nothing is changed, because that is where the published chart starts. Each adjusted amount is the entered recipe amount moved by the per-cup rate: leavening and sugar down, liquid and flour up, and the oven temperature up by the midpoint 20 °F. Amounts are US cups of 16 tablespoons, leavening is teaspoons and temperatures are Fahrenheit; the page converts feet to metres and °C at the edges. Yeast-bread proofing times, canning and pressure-cooking adjustments, and the choice of flour protein are outside the page.

tools.name: Time Clock Rounding Calculator
tools.description: Round clock-in and clock-out punches to the increment a timesheet uses - 1, 5, 6, 10 or 15 minutes, nearest, down or up - or round each shift's duration instead, and read the payable time per shift, the change against the recorded minutes and the total in decimal hours.
tools.method: Rounding runs on a grid anchored at midnight, so a clock time is moved to the nearest, the previous or the next multiple of the chosen increment and every policy lands on the same minute values whatever the date. The increments are 1, 5, 6, 10 and 15 minutes: 5 minutes, one-tenth of an hour and quarter of an hour are the steps the regulation names, and 1 minute turns rounding off. Nearest takes the closer grid line and breaks an exact tie upward, so 09:03 rounds up to 09:06 at a 6-minute increment and 09:05 to 09:10 at 10 minutes. Down floors to the line at or before the punch and up raises to the line at or after it. In punch mode each clock-in and clock-out is rounded first and the payable time is the difference between the two rounded readings, which is how a time-and-attendance system works; in duration mode the shift length is computed from the raw punches and then rounded. A clock-out earlier than the clock-in is read as the next day and 1,440 minutes are added, so an overnight shift can be entered in one row; a row whose two times are equal is refused because a 24-hour shift and a zero-length shift cannot be told apart. Times are whole minutes, HH:MM, with no seconds, and up to 30 rows are analysed at once. Totals carry the recorded minutes, the payable minutes, their signed difference and payable hours rounded to two decimals. The page rounds hours only: it does not compute pay, overtime, premiums or legal compliance, and rounding is acceptable only where it averages out over time and does not leave worked time uncompensated.

sources.title: 29 CFR 785.48 - Use of time clocks: rounding starting and stopping time to the nearest 5 minutes, one-tenth or quarter of an hour

tools.name: HAProxy Config Builder
tools.description: Build a HAProxy frontend, its backends and routing rules from weighted servers and health checks, and see the traffic split and failover time the file produces. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Builds a haproxy.cfg from a frontend, one to four backends and up to six use_backend rules. Each server keeps a name, address, port, weight, optional maxconn and a check flag, and the page writes defaults with mode and timeouts, a fe_main frontend, one acl per rule, the use_backend lines in declaration order and a default_backend naming the first backend. Weight is relative: the manual states that every server receives a load proportional to its weight over the sum of all weights, the default is 1, the maximum is 256, and a weight of 0 keeps the server out of load balancing while still accepting persistent connections. Each server therefore reports its exact weight, its share of the backend total as a percentage to one decimal, and an expected count per 1,000 requests allocated by largest remainder so the column sums to 1,000; roundrobin and static-rr follow those weights, while leastconn, source, uri and hdr do not and the page says so. Health checks use the manual's inter, fall and rise: a checked server is probed every inter milliseconds, marked down after fall consecutive failures and up again after rise successes, so the failover window is inter times fall and the recovery window is inter times rise, with defaults of 2000 ms, 3 and 2. The connection cap is the sum of the maxconn values that are set, and stays unset when none are. Routing rules offer path_beg, path_end, hdr(host) with a case-insensitive match and src; the manual evaluates use_backend rules in declaration order and the first match wins, otherwise default_backend applies, so a second rule with the same match and value is refused as unreachable, and content matches are refused in tcp mode because tcp does not parse request content. Names are limited to letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore starting with a letter, ports to 1-65535, weights to 0-256, maxconn to 1-1000000, inter to 1-60000 ms and fall and rise to 1-100; an all-numeric dotted address that is not a valid IPv4 literal is refused instead of being read as a host name. Not modelled: TLS termination, cookies and stick tables, DNS service discovery, ACL samples beyond these four, connection persistence, and whether the host runs HAProxy: the file has not been parsed by haproxy -c and the result does not deploy anything. Pure local text processing: no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: HAProxy 2.8 Configuration Manual, server and default-server options, weight: load is proportional to the weight over the sum of all weights, the default is 1, the maximum is 256, and 0 removes the server from load balancing.
HAProxy 2.8 Configuration Manual, server and default-server options, inter, fall and rise: the check interval defaults to 2000 ms, fall to 3 failures and rise to 2 successes.
HAProxy 2.8 Configuration Manual, balance: roundrobin and static-rr use each server in turns according to its weight, with a 4095-server limit for roundrobin.
HAProxy 2.8 Configuration Manual, use_backend: rules are evaluated in declaration order, the first match assigns the backend, and default_backend is used otherwise.

tools.name: Hillshade Relief Generator
tools.description: Render a shaded-relief map from a pasted elevation grid: the page computes slope and aspect over a 3 by 3 window, lights the surface from a sun azimuth and altitude you choose, and draws the relief with the slope statistics and ground area the grid covers. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Turns a rectangular elevation grid of 3 to 64 rows and columns into a shaded-relief image. Slope and aspect come from an ESRI-style 3 by 3 window labelled a to i from the north-west corner: the east gradient is ((c + 2f + i) - (a + 2d + g)) / (8 * cellsize) and the north gradient is ((g + 2h + i) - (a + 2b + c)) / (8 * cellsize). The slope is atan(z_factor * sqrt(dzdx^2 + dzdy^2)) and the aspect follows the manual's rule 10, atan2(dzdy, -dzdx) brought into 0 to 2 pi, with pi/2 for a due-north descent when the east gradient is zero and 3 pi/2 for a due-south one. The shade is 255 * (cos(zenith) * cos(slope) + sin(zenith) * sin(slope) * cos(azimuth_math - aspect)), where zenith = 90 - altitude, azimuth_math = 360 - azimuth + 90 wrapped below 360, and a negative result is clamped to 0. The manual's printed walk-through sums its window without the 1-2-1 weights and so reports 154 for its example cell; keeping the weights as the equations state gives 138 for the same window, which is what this page shows. Outer rows and columns have no full window, so they stay blank and are excluded from the statistics; a cell whose two gradients are both zero has no aspect and is counted as locally flat. Cell size is the ground distance between cell centres, the area covered is (columns - 1) * (rows - 1) * cellsize^2, and the vertical exaggeration multiplies every gradient before the slope is taken. The page reports elevation, slope and shade statistics plus the shade at the central cell; it does not resample, interpolate, smooth or reproject the grid, and it reads no file format.

tools.name: Trombone Slide Position Finder
tools.description: Enter a written note and see every slide position that plays it on a B-flat trombone, with the partial each position uses, its deviation from equal temperament and the sounding frequency. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: Lists every slide position that can play a written note on a B-flat trombone. First position is the open instrument, a B-flat1 fundamental at 58.27 Hz for A4 = 440 Hz; each position further out lowers the same partial by one semitone, so position n sounds 12 * log2(partial) - (n - 1) semitones above the fundamental. With the F attachment engaged the fundamental drops a perfect fourth to F1 at 43.65 Hz and six positions T1 to T6 are available, a semitone apart, which covers the notes between the pedal B-flat1 and the second partial of seventh position. Partial 1 is the pedal tone. A partial counts as a position for a note when its pitch is within 35 cents of that note in twelve-tone equal temperament: this keeps the seventh partial, which is 31 cents flat and is what charts print as the shortened alternates (short 2, short 3 and so on), while rejecting the eleventh partial, 49 cents flat and halfway between two notes. Positions are listed with the partial, the integer deviation in cents and the sounding frequency, fundamental * partial * 2^(-(n - 1) / 12), which is why a flat partial shows a lower frequency than the equal-tempered note. Positions within 20 cents come first, then the shortened ones; open positions precede trigger positions. The page does not model slide tuning beyond that deviation, a bass trombone's second valve, a trigger tuned down to E, alternate spellings beyond flats, or any instrument-specific position length, and it reads no file or audio input.

tools.name: Motion Blur Length Calculator
tools.description: Turn a frame rate, shutter angle, focal length, subject distance and subject speed into the length of the motion blur in pixels and as a share of the frame, with a table of blur at the common shutter angles.
tools.method: A rotary or electronic shutter is open for the shutter angle divided by 360 of each frame interval, so the exposure is angle / (360 x fps): 180 degrees at 24 fps is 1/48 s and 172.8 degrees at 24 fps is exactly 1/50 s. During that exposure a subject moving across the frame at a constant speed travels speed x exposure, and the pinhole projection onto the sensor scales that travel by the focal length divided by the subject distance, giving the smear on the sensor in millimetres. The sensor width divided by the capture width gives pixels per millimetre, and the sensor smear times that scale is the blur in pixels; the same value over the capture width is the blur as a share of the frame, which does not change with resolution. The page also reports the frame width at the subject distance (sensor width x distance / focal length), the horizontal field of view 2 x atan(sensor width / (2 x focal length)) and a table of the blur at 45, 90, 144, 172.8, 180, 270 and 360 degrees. A camera pan of one radian per second smears the image exactly like a subject moving at that many metres per second at that distance, because the image travel is the focal length times the angle swept. The model assumes a thin lens, a subject at one distance moving perpendicular to the optical axis at constant speed, and a uniform exposure with no rolling-shutter readout; depth of field, focus breathing, stabilisation, lens distortion and subjects at other distances are not modelled, and a real sensor's blur also depends on the aperture's own diffraction. Inputs allow 1 to 240 fps, 1 to 360 degrees, 1 to 2000 mm focal length, 1 to 100 mm sensor width, 64 to 16384 px capture width, 0.05 to 100000 m distance and 0 to 1000 m/s speed. Blank, non-numeric, fractional-pixel and out-of-range values are refused with an actionable message. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Emergency Shelter Space Calculator
tools.description: Check whether a covered floor shelters the people you are planning for: living space per person against the Sphere minimum, the people the floor can hold and the floor area a headcount needs.
tools.guidance: Space planning only. The Sphere figures are humanitarian minimums for covered living space, not legal occupancy limits; egress, fire separation, ventilation, structural capacity, accessibility and local building rules are not assessed, and cold climates or longer stays need more space.
tools.method: Covered living space is the floor area left after circulation, cooking, bathing, sanitation and storage are taken out, so the page first applies the non-living share: living area = floor area x (1 - share / 100). The headcount times the chosen space per person gives the living area needed, and the living area available divided by that need gives the share of the target met. Living area per person is the available living area divided by the headcount. The people the floor shelters is the whole-number floor of the available living area divided by the space per person, so capacity times the target never exceeds the living area and one more person always would. The gross floor needed for the headcount is the living area needed divided by (1 - share / 100), and its square root and the square root of the available floor give square footprints for comparison. A fixed list applies the same floor to 2, 3, 3.5, 4.5 and 5.5 square metres per person so capacity can be compared across space standards. The 3.5 m2 figure is the Sphere minimum covered living area per person in hot climates, with 4.5 m2 used in cold climates; the page lets any target from 1 to 20 m2 be entered. Inputs allow 1 to 10000 people, 1 to 1000000 square metres of floor, 1 to 20 square metres per person and a non-living share of 0 to 80 percent, with at most two decimals on areas and one on the share. Blank, non-numeric and out-of-range values are refused with an actionable message. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: UNHCR Shelter and Sustainability Overview (April 2021) - covered living area: the Sphere minimum is 3.5 m2 per person in hot climates and 4.5 m2 per person in cold climates

tools.name: Account Lockout Policy Calculator
tools.description: Model what a failed-login lockout policy costs an automated guessing attack: guesses per cycle, sustained guesses per hour and day per account, the slowdown it buys and a table of what each lockout duration leaves open.
tools.method: A lockout policy lets an account accept a fixed number of failed attempts and then refuses authentication for a period. The model treats the attacker as persistent: while the account is open it submits failures at its attempt rate, so burning the threshold costs threshold / rate minutes, and then it waits out the lockout. One cycle therefore lasts threshold / rate + lockout minutes and yields exactly the threshold in guesses, so the sustained rate is threshold x 60 / cycle guesses per hour per account: five attempts, a fifteen minute lockout and 30 attempts a minute give a 15.167 minute cycle and 19.78 guesses an hour. The slowdown is the unthrottled rate divided by that throughput, which simplifies to 1 + lockout x rate / threshold, so once the wait dominates the threshold barely moves the result and a faster attacker buys almost nothing. Guesses per day multiply the hourly figure by 24, and the fleet figure multiplies by the number of targeted accounts, which is how a password spray spreads its budget across users. The counter reading follows the counting window: when the lockout is at least as long as the window every failure has aged out by unlock and the full allowance returns, so the cycle above is exact, while a shorter lockout can leave earlier failures inside the window at unlock, giving the attacker fewer than the threshold and making the reported throughput an upper bound, which the Counter at unlock row states. The model assumes one serial attacker per account, a threshold that counts consecutive failures, and no progressive delay, CAPTCHA, bot detection, IP-level limiting or identity-provider throttling; it says nothing about offline attacks, which are not rate limited at all. Inputs allow 1 to 1000 attempts, a lockout duration from 0.1 to 10080 minutes, a counting window from 1 to 10080 minutes, 0.01 to 100000 attempts a minute and 1 to 100000 accounts; blanks, non-numeric text, fractional counts and out-of-range values are refused with an actionable message. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: ICMP Message Decoder
tools.description: Decode an ICMP message from its hex bytes into the type and code with the IANA name, a verified one's-complement checksum, the rest-of-header field for echo, redirect, parameter problem, timestamp and router discovery, and the original IPv4 datagram quoted inside an error message.
tools.guidance: A field reader, not a validator: the bytes are trusted, and a message that parses is not necessarily one a host should accept. The checksum covers the ICMP message alone, so a paste cut short of the whole message cannot verify, and a network card with checksum offload can leave a placeholder in an outbound capture. ICMPv6 is refused because its checksum covers a pseudo-header and its type registry is a different one. This page makes no capture, sends no probe and reads no traffic.
tools.method: Fields are read at the offsets RFC 792 gives them: a type octet, a code octet, a 16-bit checksum, then four bytes whose meaning depends on the type. The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the message starting at the type, with the checksum field zeroed and a final odd octet padded with a zero, so a message carrying the right value sums to 0xFFFF; the value reported as expected is the complement of the same sum. The rest-of-header field is decoded where a standard defines it: echo and information messages carry an identifier and sequence number, a fragmentation-needed message carries the next-hop MTU in the low 16 bits (RFC 1191, where zero means a router that did not report one), redirect carries a gateway address, parameter problem carries a byte pointer, timestamp carries three millisecond counters, address mask carries a mask, and router advertisement carries a count, an entry size in 32-bit words, a lifetime and a list of addresses with signed preference levels (RFC 1256). Destination unreachable, source quench, redirect, time exceeded and parameter problem quote the original datagram's IPv4 header and the first 64 bits of its data (RFC 792), so that inner header is parsed and its quoted length is compared with the original total length; source and destination ports are read when the inner protocol is TCP or UDP and at least four data bytes were quoted. Type and code names come from the IANA ICMP parameters registry, and a name the registry marks Deprecated is printed with that word. A complete IPv4 packet whose protocol field is 1 is unwrapped before decoding, a packet carrying another protocol is refused rather than read as ICMP, and an IPv6 packet is refused because ICMPv6 has its own types and a pseudo-header checksum. A non-zero unused field is called out, codes outside a type's registry are named Unassigned, and types with no code registry are named Not specified. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is sent, stored or uploaded.

tools.name: 70V Speaker Line Calculator
tools.description: Add up constant-voltage loudspeaker taps on a 25 V, 70.7 V or 100 V line and check the total against the amplifier: the line impedance and current, the headroom budget, the spare capacity and every tap against a 1 W reference.
tools.method: In a constant-voltage system every amplifier of a given line voltage produces the same maximum RMS voltage, 70.7 V being the common US standard, 100 V the common European one and 25 V used for short runs, and each loudspeaker transformer carries a primary tap marked in watts at that voltage. Because the taps share the same reference voltage their wattages add, so the total load is the sum of tap watts times the number of loudspeakers on that tap. The amplifier sees that load as an impedance Z = V squared / P and supplies a line current I = P / V, which is why a 70.7 V line works out to about 5,000 / P ohms and why the same tap is a much heavier load on a 25 V line. Each doubling of tap power adds 10 log10(2) = 3.01 dB, so every tap is also shown against a 1 W tap as 10 log10 of its wattage. The headroom allowance becomes a budget of rated power x (1 - headroom / 100), and the smallest amplifier that keeps the allowance is P / (1 - headroom / 100); the 20 percent default is a planning habit covering tap tolerance, transformer insertion loss, cable loss and program peaks, not a requirement of the standard. This is a budget rather than a measurement: cable resistance, transformer saturation, loudspeaker impedance minima with frequency and loudspeaker sensitivity are not modelled, and the figures apply only to constant-voltage outputs, never to 4, 8 or 16 ohm low-impedance loads. Counts are whole numbers from 0 to 999 per tap, amplifier power 1 to 10000 watts, headroom 0 to 50 percent, and a line with no speakers is refused. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Shell Exit Status Decoder
tools.description: Decode a shell exit code such as 139 or a raw 16-bit wait status such as 0x008b into the exit code, the fatal signal, the core-dump flag and the $? the shell reports.
tools.method: waitpid reports a child in one 16-bit integer: the exit code occupies bits 8 to 15, the terminating signal the low seven bits, and bit 7 is the core-dump flag, which is why a SIGSEGV with a core is 0x008b and a plain exit(1) is 0x0100. WIFEXITED is true when the low seven bits are zero, WEXITSTATUS is status >> 8 & 0xff, and otherwise WIFSIGNALED is true unless the low seven bits are 0x7f, which marks a stopped child with WSTOPSIG in the high byte; 0xffff is the one status WIFCONTINUED reports. Shells collapse this to eight bits: a process that exits reports its code unchanged, while a process killed by signal n appears as 128 + n, so 130 is SIGINT, 137 SIGKILL, 139 SIGSEGV and 143 SIGTERM. bash reports 127 when a command is not found and 126 when it is found but cannot be executed, and it truncates exit codes modulo 256, so exit(-1) arrives as 255. The 128 + n range covers 129 to 192 for the 64 Linux signals (129 to 159 for the named signals 1 to 31, 160 to 192 for the real-time range, with 32 and 33 reserved by the C library), while 128 itself and 193 to 255 are ordinary exit codes. Because the shell keeps only those eight bits, a program that calls exit(139) is indistinguishable from a SIGSEGV death and the core flag is lost, so the shell mode marks the core state as not visible and the raw wait status as not recoverable. Values are decimal or 0x hexadecimal, from 0 to 255 in shell mode and 0 to 65535 in raw mode; a status that encodes a stop signal of 0 or above 64, or a terminating signal above 64, is refused because the kernel never writes it. The reference table lists signals 1 to 31 with their default actions from signal(7). Everything is integer arithmetic in the browser: nothing is executed, stored or sent anywhere.

tools.name: Pickleball Court Marking Calculator
tools.description: Lay out a pickleball court from the USA Pickleball dimensions: every line with its start and end coordinates, the painted length, the paint area, the tape diagonals and the recommended playing surface.
tools.method: USA Pickleball's court specification makes the playing area a 20 by 44 ft rectangle (6.10 by 13.41 m) for both singles and doubles, measured to the outside edge of the perimeter and non-volley zone lines. The net crosses the middle, so the net line sits at half the length, and the non-volley zone lines run 7 ft (2.13 m) either side of it between the two sidelines; the centerline runs from each zone line to the baseline, which leaves a service court half the width deep and half the width wide, 10 by 15 ft on a regulation court. Painted length is therefore 2L + 4W + 2 x (L/2 - 7), which is 3L + 4W - 14: 198 ft for a 44 by 20 ft court, 60.37 m for 13.41 by 6.10 m. Paint area is that length times the 2 in (5.08 cm) line width, 33 sq ft for the regulation court, and counts each crossing once rather than subtracting it. The diagonal check is the square root of length squared plus width squared, 48.33 ft between opposite corners, and the zone diagonal is the same root across a 7 ft by 20 ft zone, 21.19 ft; both square a rectangle on site, where the two tapes meet at a corner. The recommended playing surface adds 5 ft (1.52 m) beyond each sideline and 8 ft (2.44 m) behind each baseline, which gives the rulebook's 30 by 60 ft (9.14 by 18.29 m) for a regulation court and keeps the same margin around a smaller one. Net posts stand 22 ft (6.71 m) plus or minus 1 in apart between their inside faces, about 1 ft outside each sideline on a 20 ft court; the net must be 36 in at the outer sidelines and 34 in at the center, each plus or minus 0.25 in. Lengths are accepted from 20 to 60 ft (6 to 18.3 m) and widths from 10 to 40 ft (3 to 12.2 m); a size other than 44 by 20 ft is reported as a practice court rather than refused, and the metric figures are the rulebook's rounded equivalents of dimensions that are exact in feet. This is marking arithmetic on a flat surface: it does not survey a site, square a slab, or set the rules of any competition. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Git Attributes Resolver
tools.description: Resolve the attributes a top-level .gitattributes file gives one path: every attribute named in the file with its set, unset, value or unspecified state, and the exact line that decided each one.
tools.method: Every line of a gitattributes file is a pattern followed by attribute assignments. A bare name sets the attribute to true, -name sets it to false, name=value gives it a string, and !name resets it to unspecified. When several lines match the same path, the later line wins per attribute, so a rule can override one attribute without touching the others. Patterns use the gitignore syntax: * and ? stop at a slash, ** crosses directories, a pattern without a slash matches a basename at any depth, and a pattern with a slash is anchored to the file's directory. Two differences apply here: negative patterns are forbidden and ignored with a warning, and a pattern that matches a directory does not reach the files inside, so dir/** is the way to cover a tree. [attr]name ... defines a macro; applying the macro name sets the macro itself and expands its assignments, and the built-in binary macro is -diff -merge -text unless the file redefines it. The resolver reads only the top-level file, not $GIT_DIR/info/attributes or .gitattributes files in subdirectories, and does not touch a repository. Paths are relative, use /, and a trailing slash keeps the directory path itself; basename patterns drop that slash the way git check-attr does. The page was checked against git check-attr 2.47.3 over random rule sets and paths. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Roller Chain Drive Calculator
tools.description: Size a two-sprocket roller chain drive from the pitch, both tooth counts and the centre distance: pitch diameters, ratio, the chain length the centres need, the even link count to buy, the centres that count gives and the wrap on the small sprocket.
tools.guidance: Geometry only: this sizes sprockets, the chain length and the centres, and it does not rate the chain for power. Check the manufacturer's power, wear, lubrication and alignment data before building or loading the drive, and leave room to adjust the centres by half a pitch.
tools.method: A two-sprocket roller chain drive, with the chain running on the outside of both sprockets. Inputs are the chain pitch p in millimetres (3 to 200), the driver and driven tooth counts z1 and z2 (8 to 200 each), the wanted centre distance C in millimetres and the driver speed n1 in rpm (0 to 20000). Each sprocket's pitch diameter is d = p / sin(pi / z), the circle the rollers sit on. The drive is refused when the centres fall below (d1 + d2)/2, where the sprockets would overlap. The chain length in pitches follows the usual approximation L = 2C/p + (z1 + z2)/2 + ((z2 - z1)/(2 pi))^2 * p/C; because a complete link spans two pitches the answer is rounded up to the next even number of pitches, which is the count to buy. The centres that link count gives come from the inverse form, with K = 2L - z1 - z2 and C = (p/8)(K + sqrt(K^2 - 8((z2 - z1)/pi)^2)); the page shows that value and how far it moves the centres you entered, so the mounting can allow for it. The ratio is z2/z1, the driven speed is n1 z1/z2, the chain speed is p z1 n1 / 60000 in m/s on the pitch line, the chain length in metres is the link count times the pitch, and the wrap on the small sprocket is 180 - 2 asin((d2 - d1)/(2C)) in degrees. Warnings note a driver below 19 teeth, a driven sprocket above 114 teeth, a ratio above 6:1 and a wrap below 120 degrees, which are the usual limits for a single reduction. The pitch diameters were checked against the published 25.4 mm pitch table on the source page. This is geometry, not a power rating: the chain's capacity, wear life and lubrication are the manufacturer's data. Values are shown to three decimals. Everything is computed in the browser; nothing is stored, uploaded or fetched.

sources.title: Roller chains (RoyMech): the sprocket pitch diameter p / sin(pi/z) and its table of pitch diameters for 25.4 mm pitch, the chain length counted in double pitches, the centre distance recovered from a chosen chain length, the 120 degree minimum wrap and the 19-tooth driver / 114-tooth wheel guidance

tools.name: Branch-Line Coupler Designer
tools.description: Design a single-section 3 dB branch-line hybrid: the series and shunt arm impedances, the guided wavelength and arm lengths, and the through, coupled, return-loss and isolation response at any frequency in the sweep.
tools.guidance: The layout is a ring: the two series arms of Z0 divided by the square root of two run along the through path and the two Z0 arms bridge across it. Every arm is a quarter wave at the design frequency, so shorten each one by the excess the T-junction adds in your simulator, and take the substrate, copper and etch data from the laminate datasheet.
tools.method: A single-section branch-line hybrid is a ring of four quarter-wave lines: the two series arms that join ports 1-2 and 3-4 are Z0 divided by the square root of two and the two shunt arms that join ports 2-3 and 4-1 are Z0, so a 50 ohm system uses 35.355 ohm and 50 ohm lines and a 75 ohm system uses 53.033 ohm and 75 ohm. Each arm is 90 electrical degrees at the design frequency, so its physical length is a quarter of the guided wavelength, lambda_g = c v_f / f with c = 299792458 m/s. At the design point the network is matched, the input splits equally, the through port 2 is the phase reference and the coupled port 3 lags it by 90 degrees while port 4 is isolated. Away from the design frequency the four-port response comes from the nodal admittance matrix of the four ideal lines: a line of impedance Z and electrical length theta contributes y11 = -j cot(theta)/Z and y12 = j csc(theta)/Z between its two nodes, and with every port terminated in Z0 the scattering matrix is S = (I - Z0 Y)(I + Z0 Y)^-1, evaluated by complex Gauss-Jordan elimination. Return loss is -20 log10 |S11| and isolation is -20 log10 |S41|, both capped at 60 dB because the model is lossless. The 20 dB bandwidth is the contiguous span around the design frequency over which both the return loss and the isolation stay at or above 20 dB, its edges located by bisection so the result does not depend on a scan step. Inputs are limited to a system impedance of 5 to 1000 ohms, a design frequency of 0.1 to 40000 MHz, a velocity factor of 0.3 to 1 and an analysis frequency of 0.2 to 1.8 times the design frequency; text, empty values and out-of-range numbers are refused with the field named. Warnings appear for a return loss below 10 dB at the analysis frequency, an arm shorter than 1 mm, a shunt arm above 120 ohms and a series arm below 20 ohms. The junction discontinuity, dispersion, conductor and dielectric loss and fabrication tolerance are not modelled, so a real coupler needs an electromagnetic simulation or a measured prototype.

sources.title: Microwaves101, Branchline Couplers: every transmission line is a quarter wavelength, the signal at port 1 splits into quadrature signals at ports 2 and 3, and port 4 is isolated at the centre frequency.
Microwaves101, Quadrature couplers: a signal splits into 0.707 of its voltage at 0 degrees and the same amplitude at -90 degrees.

Wikipedia, Power dividers and directional couplers, branch-line coupler: the branch lines are spaced a quarter wavelength apart, the coupling is set by the branch-line impedances, and branch-line couplers suit a 3 dB hybrid.

tools.name: Mud Weight Adjustment Calculator
tools.description: Weigh a drilling mud up with barite or cut it by dilution: the barite in pounds and 100 lb sacks, or the light fluid in barrels, with the volume change and the final specific gravity.
tools.guidance: Mix the weighting material through a hopper into the active system a little at a time and check the weight on a mud balance between additions, because a single pass rarely lands on the target and some barite always leaves with the cuttings at the shakers. Leave room in the pits for the volume the barite or the dilution fluid adds, and confirm the target weight against the drilling programme before mixing.
tools.method: A mud weight change is a mass balance. One barrel holds 42 US gallons; fresh water weighs 8.33 lb/gal and drilling-grade barite is taken at 4.2 SG, or 35.0 lb/gal, so a barrel of solid barite weighs 1,470 lb and a 100 lb sack occupies 0.068 bbl. To raise the weight, pounds of barite = 1,470 x V x (W2 - W1) / (35 - W2) for a starting volume V in barrels, which is numerically the same as the count of 100 lb sacks per 100 bbl; the barite adds V x (W2 - W1) / (35 - W2) barrels, so the treated volume grows and the final weight is W2. To cut the weight, barrels of light fluid = V x (W1 - W2) / (W2 - Dw), where Dw is the dilution fluid density, 8.33 lb/gal for fresh water and the base-oil density for an oil-based mud, and the reported volume increase is that same quantity. Both branches are solved from the same balance, pounds in divided by gallons in, and the calculator reports the material, the final volume, the volume gain and the specific gravity (weight divided by 8.33). Inputs are limited to a current and target weight of 6 to 30 lb/gal, a volume of 0.1 to 100,000 bbl and a dilution fluid of 5 to 12 lb/gal; a target within 0.005 lb/gal of the current weight is reported as no change, and a dilution fluid at or above the target is refused because the balance has no solution. Warnings appear for a target above 20 lb/gal, a volume gain over 20 percent when weighting up, a dilution fluid within 0.5 lb/gal of the target, a dilution fluid below 8.0 lb/gal (a base oil rather than water) and dilution that adds more than 50 percent to the volume. The model assumes dry weighting material, no losses to the shakers or settling, one fully mixed volume measured at one temperature, and that the target weight is already permitted by the formation pressure, the equivalent circulating density and the mud programme; it does not model those limits or the effect on rheology and filtration, so the mixed weight still has to be verified on a mud balance.

sources.title: DrillingFormulas, Increase mud weight by adding barite: sacks of barite per 100 bbl = 1,470 (W2 - W1) / (35 - W2), worked through 500 bbl of 10 ppg mud raised to 13 ppg.

Lapeyrouse, Formulas and Calculations for Drilling, Production and Workover: Increase Mud Density with barite at an average specific gravity of 4.2 and the Dilution chapter, barite sk/100 bbl = 1,470 (W2 - W1) / (35 - W2).
Wikipedia, Drilling fluid: baryte is the common weighting agent added to raise the density of the mud and hold back the formation pressure.

tools.name: Bandsaw Blade Length Calculator
tools.description: Work out the blade length a two-wheel bandsaw needs from its wheel diameters and the axle spacing, or the spacing a known blade needs, with the wrap angle and the nearest 1/8 in length.
tools.guidance: Measure each wheel across the tyre where the blade rides and take the axle spacing with the tensioner at the middle of its travel, then order a stock length near the middle of the saw's range so the tensioner can take up stretch and slacken the blade for storage. Check the number against the saw's manual before ordering.
tools.method: A band saw blade is a closed loop over two wheels: two straight runs and one arc on each wheel. With wheel diameters D1 and D2 and the axle spacing C, the exact open-belt length is 2 sqrt(C^2 - ((D1 - D2)/2)^2) + (pi + 2t) D1/2 + (pi - 2t) D2/2, where t = asin((D1 - D2)/(2C)) and D1 is the larger wheel, so the larger wheel is wrapped through 180 + 2t degrees and the smaller through 180 - 2t. For equal wheels this reduces to 2C + pi D. The shop rule 2C + pi (D1 + D2)/2 + (D1 - D2)^2/(4C) is the same geometry expanded, and differs from the exact wrap by under 0.001 in for wheels within a few inches of each other and by about 0.02 in for a 40 in wheel driving a 10 in wheel 60 in away. Given a blade length instead of a spacing, the calculator solves the same expression for C by bisection between the touching-wheel spacing, where the blade is at its shortest possible length, and the spacing at which that length fits; a blade shorter than that minimum is refused, and a required spacing above 120 in (3048 mm) is refused as outside a saw. Wheel diameters are accepted from 4 to 40 in (102 to 1016 mm), a spacing up to 120 in, and a blade from 15 to 450 in (381 to 11430 mm); a spacing no greater than the two wheel radii added together is refused because the wheels would overlap. Every length is reported in inches and millimetres, the blade length is also rounded to the nearest 1/8 in, and the report gives each straight run, the wrap on each wheel, and the blade length change per unit of wheel travel, which is twice the straight run divided by the spacing and is exactly 2 for equal wheels. Moving the upper wheel by x therefore changes the blade length by about 2x, which is why a saw accepts a band of lengths rather than one figure. The model assumes a two-wheel saw with plain tyres and coplanar wheels; it does not model three-wheel saws, crowned or stepped tyres, blade thickness, wheel tilt, or the tensioner's actual travel, so the result has to be checked against the saw's manual, and it is an ordering aid rather than a claim about the saw.

sources.title: Highland Woodworking, Bandsaw Blade Length: with no blade fitted, twice the shaft-to-shaft distance plus one wheel circumference (diameter times pi) gives the blade length, and the same sum taken at the top and bottom of the tensioner travel gives the range of lengths the saw will mount.

Wikipedia, Belt (mechanical): an open belt is two straight runs plus half the circumference of each pulley, with the difference of the radii adding a correction, so unequal bandsaw wheels need a slightly longer blade than the equal-wheel sum.

tools.name: Water Hardness Converter
tools.description: Convert water hardness between mg/L as calcium carbonate, grains per US gallon, German, English and French degrees and millimoles per litre, with the USGS hardness class and the grain figure a softener is sized from.
tools.guidance: Read the figure and its unit off the water report before converting: a US report is usually mg/L as calcium carbonate or grains per US gallon, a German one in degrees dH and a French one in degrees fH. The USGS class is a general guideline for a supply, so size a softener from its own capacity rating and the report rather than from the class alone.
tools.method: Water hardness counts the divalent calcium and magnesium in a sample as an equivalent mass of calcium carbonate, so every scale here is the same quantity in a different unit. The tool works in milligrams per litre as CaCO3. One millimole per litre of CaCO3 is 100.0869 mg/L, the molar mass of calcium carbonate. One German degree (dH, dGH) is 10 mg of calcium oxide per litre, which is 10/56.0774 mmol/L, or 17.8479922 mg/L as CaCO3. One English or Clark degree is one grain of calcium carbonate per imperial gallon and one grain per US gallon (gpg) is one grain per US gallon; with the international grain of exactly 64.79891 mg, the imperial gallon of 4.54609 L and the US gallon of 3.785411784 L those are 14.2537675 and 17.1180610 mg/L, so the same water reads about 1.2 times higher in gpg than in Clark degrees. One French degree is 10 mg/L by definition. Each converted value is rounded to six significant figures and displayed to four, so a catalog case can state the exact number the page shows. Entries are accepted from 0 to 100,000 mg/L as CaCO3, which spans distilled water to the hardest brines; a negative entry or a figure above that ceiling is refused rather than clipped. The class follows the USGS general guidelines in mg/L as CaCO3: up to 60 soft, 61 to 120 moderately hard, 121 to 180 hard and above 180 very hard. Those bands describe a water supply rather than a treatment decision: they say nothing about a softener capacity, the resin or a local utility scale, so a report in another unit should be converted before it is compared with them. The tool does not split carbonate from non-carbonate hardness, does not use alkalinity, pH or temperature, measures nothing itself, and runs entirely in the browser.

sources.title: USGS Water Science School, Hardness of Water: general guidelines classify water as soft at 0 to 60 mg/L as calcium carbonate, moderately hard at 61 to 120, hard at 121 to 180 and very hard above 180.

Wikipedia, Hard water: hardness is reported as calcium carbonate equivalents, with the conversion table between mmol/L, mg/L, German degrees, grains per US gallon, English (Clark) degrees and French degrees used to cross-check this tool's factors.
