tools.name: Motorola S-Record Inspector
tools.description: Inspect a Motorola S-record file (SREC, S19, S28, S37): verify every checksum, resolve each record’s address width, and report the data bytes, address blocks, gaps, overlaps, record count and start address.
tools.guidance: Paste the file as text: an .s19, .s28 or .s37 file from a toolchain, a bootloader or a programmer. Valid means the records are internally consistent, not that the image belongs on your board, so check the address range and the start address against the linker map before flashing. Many programmers load the data records and ignore the S0 header and the S7, S8 or S9 start address, so treat those as advisory rather than as settings the hardware will use.
tools.method: The Motorola S-record format writes binary data as ASCII lines that begin with S and a type digit. Each line is S, the type digit, a two-digit byte count, an address of 2, 3 or 4 bytes depending on the type, zero or more data bytes and a two-digit checksum. The byte count covers the address, the data and the checksum byte but not the count itself, so a 16-byte S1 record starts S113 and carries 19 bytes after the count field. The checksum is the one’s complement of the least significant byte of the sum of the byte count, the address bytes and the data, which makes a correct record sum to 0xFF; a record that does not add up is reported at its line number and left out of the image, as a loader would skip it. S0 is a header and usually holds a module name, which the tool shows as text with non-printable bytes replaced by a middle dot. S1, S2 and S3 carry data at 16-, 24- and 32-bit addresses. S5 and S6 are optional count records whose address field states how many data records precede them; the tool compares that value with the data records it has read so far and reports a disagreement. S7, S8 and S9 end the file and may carry a start address, which the tool reports but never adds to the memory image. S4 is reserved by the format and is refused. Addresses are taken at face value with no wrap: a record that would run past 0xFFFFFFFF is reported instead of folding back to zero. The result counts records, data bytes and distinct addresses, lists overlapping bytes, splits the image into contiguous blocks and measures the gap bytes between them. The tool checks structure only: it does not decode the payload, does not require the termination type to match the data width, reports only the first count record, and writes no file. Input is limited to 1,000,000 characters and 50,000 records. Everything runs in the browser.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Motorola S-record: the record layout, the S0 to S9 type table, the 2-, 3- and 4-byte address fields, the byte count that covers address, data and checksum, and the one’s complement checksum this inspector verifies.

Debian manpages, srec_motorola(5) from the srecord package: field-by-field description of the format, the S5 and S6 record counts, and the S7, S8 and S9 termination records with their start addresses.

tools.name: Laminated Dough Layer Calculator
tools.description: Count the layers a croissant, danish or puff pastry fold plan produces. Enter the dough and butter weights with the number of letter (3-fold) and book (4-fold) folds to see the layer count, the butter ratio against the dough and the whole block, and, from an optional final sheet thickness, the average layer. An optional target layer count finds the smallest plan that reaches it.
tools.guidance: Use it while planning a laminated dough: put in the weights you intend to mix and the folds you intend to make. The layer count is the number of sheets crossing a cut after the last fold, not a promise about the crumb; real pastry loses layers where the butter breaks, where a fold misses the edge, or where trimmings are pressed back in. The average layer is arithmetic from the final sheet thickness, so measure the sheet after its last rest rather than before the final roll. The form accepts up to eight folds of each kind, which is already far beyond a usual croissant or puff pastry, and weights up to 1,000,000 g per ingredient.
tools.method: A laminated dough is a block of butter enclosed in dough, rolled and folded so the two alternate in thin sheets. A letter fold brings the two outer thirds over the middle, so every sheet crossing a cut becomes three; a book fold brings both outer edges to the centre, so every sheet becomes four. The tool starts at one layer for the block before any fold and multiplies by three for each letter fold and by four for each book fold, so three letter folds give 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 layers, four give 81, and a plan of two letter folds and one book fold gives 3 x 3 x 4 = 36. The butter ratio is the butter weight as a percentage of the dough weight and, separately, of the combined block; the average layer is the final sheet thickness divided by the layer count. When a target layer count is given, the tool searches every combination of up to eight letter and eight book folds and reports the plan with the fewest folds whose count reaches the target, preferring the smaller count when two plans need the same number of folds; if no combination reaches it, the largest reachable count is 3^8 x 4^8 = 429,981,696 layers and the form refuses a larger target. Weights are limited to 1,000,000 g, the final sheet thickness to 100 mm, and folds to whole numbers from 0 to 8. The arithmetic assumes the butter stays in one unbroken sheet, that every fold spans the full width, and that the thickness is even across the sheet; it is a count and a ratio, not a prediction of rise or flake. Everything runs in the browser and nothing is uploaded or stored.

tools.name: Hijri Calendar Converter
tools.description: Convert a Gregorian date to its Hijri (Islamic) date and back with the tabular Islamic calendar, and see the weekday, the Hijri year type, the month length and the day of the Hijri year. Gregorian years 1600 to 2200 are supported.
tools.guidance: Use it to place a civil date on the Hijri calendar or to read a Hijri date in the Gregorian calendar. This is the arithmetic tabular calendar, so do not use it to fix the start of Ramadan, Eid or any other religious observance: those follow a sighted or officially announced month and can fall a day or two away, which is why the Umm al-Qura calendar exists. The page supports Gregorian 1600 to 2200 only, the window over which its epoch arithmetic was checked, and it takes no time of day or location, so a Hijri day is treated as beginning at midnight for conversion purposes.
tools.method: The tabular (arithmetic) Islamic calendar counts days from a fixed epoch: 1 Muharram 1 AH is 19 July 622 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar, a Friday, which is fixed day 227015. Years follow a 30-year cycle of 10,631 days with eleven leap years in cycle positions 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 16, 18, 21, 24, 26 and 29, so a year is leap when (11 x year + 14) mod 30 is less than 11 and is then 355 days long instead of 354. Odd-numbered months have 30 days and even-numbered months 29, except that Dhu al-Hijjah, the twelfth month, has 30 days in a leap year; the day of the year on which a month begins is therefore ceil(29.5 x (month - 1)), which gives 0, 30, 59, 89, 118, 148, 177, 207, 236, 266, 295 and 325. A Hijri date converts to a fixed day as epoch - 1 + (year - 1) x 354 + floor((3 + 11 x year) / 30) + that month offset + day, and the inverse starts from year = floor((30 x (fixed - epoch) + 10646) / 10631), steps to the year whose 1 Muharram is at or before the day, and walks the month lengths. The weekday is the fixed day modulo 7 with Sunday as zero, so the two directions share one continuous day count and cannot drift apart. The epoch reproduces 1 Muharram 1 AH as Friday 19 July 622, and the arithmetic is the four-arithmetic variant used by the Kuwaiti algorithm and by Fourmilab's converter. Because the calendar is arithmetic rather than observational, an official Umm al-Qura date can differ by a day or two; the result also treats a Hijri day as starting at midnight instead of sunset. Gregorian years 1600 to 2200 are supported, Hijri years 1008 to 1627, and a Hijri date whose civil day falls outside that window is refused. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded or stored.

tools.name: iSCSI Name Builder & Validator
tools.description: Build an iSCSI qualified name (IQN) from a domain you own and the month you owned it, or check an iqn., eui. or naa. name against the RFC 7143 structure and the 223-character limit.
tools.method: An iSCSI name is the SCSI device name of an iSCSI node, so it has to stay unique for the life of the node and must not encode an address. RFC 7143 defines three type designators. An iqn. name belongs to an authority that owns a domain: the page writes iqn., a date code yyyy-mm, a dot, the domain reversed label by label, and an optional colon-prefixed suffix. The date code is the first month in which that authority owned the domain, which is why one domain can carry different names over time; it is not the month the device was installed. DNS names are case-insensitive and an iSCSI name is compared as a normalized lower-case string, so the page lower-cases the domain and the suffix and drops one trailing dot, and it says so when it had to change what was typed. Each domain label holds 1 to 63 letters, digits or hyphens and cannot begin or end with a hyphen, and at least two labels are required because a single label is not a registered domain. The suffix is the authority's own string: letters, digits, dots, hyphens and colons, with no empty segment. The whole name is limited to 223 bytes, and the page starts warning at 200 characters. An eui. name carries exactly 16 hexadecimal digits and a naa. name an even number of hexadecimal digits up to 32, so both are checked for length and digits rather than assembled. The page checks the string form only: it does not test whether a name is unique in a fabric, whether the domain is still owned, or whether a given initiator or target will accept it, and the role, initiator or target, comes from the login and not from the name. Everything runs in the browser with no network access or storage.

tools.name: Albers Equal-Area Conic Projection Calculator
tools.description: Convert a latitude and longitude to the easting and northing of an Albers equal-area conic map defined by two standard parallels, or read a grid position back as a latitude and longitude, with the scale along the parallel and the meridian at that point.
tools.method: An Albers map unrolls a cone that cuts the ellipsoid along two standard parallels, where the scale is exactly 1, and it is equal-area: the area of every region is the same on the map as on the ellipsoid, which is why it carries thematic maps of density, land cover and population rather than navigation charts. With the semi-major axis a, first eccentricity e and the functions m(phi) = cos phi / sqrt(1 - e^2 sin^2 phi) and q(phi) = (1 - e^2)[sin phi / (1 - e^2 sin^2 phi) - ln((1 - e sin phi)/(1 + e sin phi))/(2e)], the page computes the cone constant n = (m1^2 - m2^2)/(q2 - q1) for two parallels, or n = sin phi1 when both are equal (the single-parallel form), then C = m1^2 + n q1 and the radius rho = a sqrt(C - n q)/n. A point lands at x = rho sin(n dlambda) and y = rho0 - rho cos(n dlambda) east and north of the origin, where dlambda is the longitude from the central meridian wrapped into -180 to 180 degrees and rho0 is rho at the latitude of origin; the false easting and northing are then added, so the northing of the latitude of origin is the false northing. The scale along the parallel is k = rho n/(a m) and along the meridian h = 1/k, so k is exactly 1 on both standard parallels, the area scale h k is exactly 1 everywhere, and shapes stretch north to south between the parallels and east to west outside them. Grid convergence is n dlambda, positive east of the central meridian in a northern cone and negative there in a southern one, where the radius is negative and the inverse mirrors the (x, rho0 - y) pair before dividing the angle by n; that mirror is what keeps a southern grid point in its own quarter of the world. The defaults are the US national Albers grid (EPSG:5070) on GRS 80: 29.5 and 45.5 degrees north, origin 23 degrees north on 96 degrees west, which puts Washington DC at 1,618,883.3 m east and 1,924,594.2 m north with k = 0.990448. The inverse recovers q from rho, iterates latitude in up to 60 steps and reports longitude from theta/n; the page refuses a point on a pole, standard parallels on or across the equator, a latitude of origin in the opposite hemisphere, a latitude or longitude outside its range, and a grid position at or beyond the cone apex. Offered are WGS 84, GRS 80, Clarke 1866 and a mean-radius sphere; no datum shift, no false-origin azimuth, no grid rotation and no scale factor k0 are modelled, and the page does not draw the map. Pure local arithmetic: no upload, storage or network access.

tools.name: Solfège Converter
tools.description: Convert solfège syllables to note names and back in fixed do, movable do with a major key, or la-based minor, with chromatic syllables such as di, fi, si, ra, me and te.
tools.method: A sequence of up to 32 syllables or note names is read, separated by spaces, commas or semicolons, and read as movable do in a major key, movable do in la-based minor, or fixed do. Every note is converted by its letter rather than by its pitch class alone: the letter fixes the scale degree, the key's major scale fixes that degree's expected pitch, and the difference between the two gives the alteration. An F sharp and a G flat in C major therefore read as fi and lowered sol (se) instead of collapsing onto one spelling. The natural degrees take do re mi fa sol la ti; raised degrees 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 take di ri fi si li; lowered degrees 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 take ra me se le te; an alteration with no conventional syllable is written with a sharp or flat sign after the base syllable. In fixed do the tonic is C and the key field is ignored. In movable do the tonic is the key root, and in la-based minor la is the key root while do stays on the relative major's tonic, three semitones above. Keys are offered only when their scale and, for la-major relationships, the relative major need no double accidental, so C sharp major is accepted while a syllable such as di in C sharp major is refused because it would need C double sharp. Octave numbers on note names are ignored, so results are pitch-class names rather than registers. The reference table lists the twelve chromatic steps ascending from the tonic for the chosen system and key. All of this is note-name and scale-degree bookkeeping in the browser, with no audio, storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Solfège: fixed do ties the syllables to fixed pitches while movable do assigns them to scale degrees, and la-based minor uses fi and si for the raised sixth and seventh.

tools.name: Teleprompter Scroll Planner
tools.description: Plan a teleprompter read: wrap a pasted script to a character width, turn it into a scroll height, and get the scroll speed and read time for a reading rate or a fixed slot.
tools.method: The script is trimmed, its words are the whitespace-separated tokens, and every line is wrapped greedily: words join the current line while the line plus one space plus the next word stays within the character width, otherwise the line breaks before that word, and a word longer than the width is placed alone on its own line and counted as an overlong word. A blank line becomes one empty line, which occupies one line height, and runs of spaces or tabs inside a paragraph collapse to a single space. Script height = wrapped lines x line height. Read time = 60 x words / reading rate in words per minute. Scroll speed = script height / read time, equivalently height x rate / (60 x words); one screen of text passes in screen height / speed, and the lines fully on screen are floor(screen height / line height). With a target slot of S seconds the required rate is 60 x words / S, the required speed is height / S, and the current pace over-runs the slot by read time - S. A monospaced, constant-speed scroll of the whole script height during the read is assumed: character widths, paragraph spacing beyond the empty lines, the lines that remain below the reading line, prompter speed ramps and the prompter's own font metrics are not modelled. Bounds are a script of up to 20,000 characters, 8-200 characters per line, 8-400 px line height, 120-4320 px screen height, 40-400 words per minute and a 5-7200 s slot, and the screen must be at least one line tall. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads, accounts or network access.

tools.name: Growing Degree Day Accumulator
tools.description: Add up growing degree days from a season of daily highs and lows: raise lows to the base, cap highs at an optional cutoff, and see the total, the daily average and the days left to a target.
tools.method: The daily contribution is the mean temperature minus the base temperature, floored at zero: mean = (high + low) / 2. A low below the base is raised to the base before averaging, and a high above the upper cutoff is lowered to the cutoff, so the usable maximum is min(high, cutoff) and the usable minimum is max(low, base); the cutoff is optional, and without it the high is used as entered. The season total is the sum of the daily contributions, the mean per day is that total divided by the number of days, and the warmest and coolest days are the largest and smallest contributions with their day numbers. A target is compared with the running total to find the first day it was passed; if it was not passed, the shortfall is the target minus the total and the projected days are the shortfall divided by the mean per day and rounded up, with no projection when the mean is zero. Temperatures are entered one day per line as a high and a low in the chosen unit, separated by commas or spaces; blank lines are ignored, a high below its low is refused, and up to 400 days and 20,000 characters are read. Celsius temperatures must lie within -80 to 60 °C and the base within -20 to 40 °C; Fahrenheit temperatures within -112 to 140 °F and the base within -4 to 104 °F. The arithmetic is a heat-unit sum, not a phenology model: moisture stress, day length, cultivar and any growth response beyond the cutoffs are not simulated. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads, accounts or network access.

tools.name: WebAuthn Authenticator Data Inspector
tools.description: Decode WebAuthn authenticator data from base64url or hex: read the RP ID hash, all eight flag bits, the signature counter, the AAGUID, the credential ID and the COSE key type and algorithm.
tools.method: Authenticator data is a byte string of at least 37 bytes. The first 32 bytes are the SHA-256 hash of the RP ID the credential is scoped to, the next byte is a flag field and the last four of the header are the signature counter as a 32-bit unsigned big-endian integer. In the flag byte bit 0 is User Present (0x01), bit 1 is reserved, bit 2 is User Verified (0x04), bit 3 is Backup Eligibility (0x08), bit 4 is Backup State (0x10), bit 5 is reserved, bit 6 marks attested credential data (0x40) and bit 7 marks extension data (0x80). When 0x40 is set, 16 bytes of AAGUID, a 2-byte big-endian credential ID length L that must be from 1 to 1,023, L bytes of credential ID and a COSE key follow; the page reads the CBOR item length so the key can be separated from what follows, then reads the integer parameters of the COSE key map: 1 is the key type, 3 the algorithm and -1 the curve, named from the COSE registries. When 0x80 is set a single CBOR map of extensions closes the structure; its encoded length and entry count are reported. Input is base64url with optional padding or hex with optional spaces, at most 12,288 characters and 4,096 decoded bytes. CBOR is read only in its definite-length form, to 16 levels and without indefinite-length items, and bytes left over after the structure the flags describe are refused rather than ignored. The page decodes bytes and reports what they say: it does not verify a signature, evaluate an attestation statement, compare the RP ID hash with a hostname or trust an AAGUID, so a valid parse is not proof that a registration or assertion is genuine. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads, accounts or network access.

tools.name: Reverse DNS Zone Builder
tools.description: Turn an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix into its reverse DNS zone: the in-addr.arpa or ip6.arpa apex, the RFC 2317 classless delegation CNAMEs and a PTR owner name for every address in the block. Runs entirely in your browser.
tools.method: A reverse DNS name is the address written backwards under a fixed suffix: IPv4 octets reversed below in-addr.arpa, IPv6 hex digits reversed one per label below ip6.arpa. The page masks the address to the prefix length first and reports any host bits it cleared. For IPv4 a /24 owns the three-label zone d.c.b.in-addr.arpa and the last octet is the relative owner name, so all 256 names are listed. A prefix longer than /24 covers part of one /24: the page names the RFC 2317 child zone start-end.d.c.b.in-addr.arpa and emits one CNAME per address in the parent zone so resolvers follow the delegation. A /32 is reported as one full owner name. A prefix shorter than /24 spans several /24 zones, which are listed (at most 64) rather than merged into a zone that does not exist. For IPv6 the zone is the reversed network nibbles of the prefix; a prefix that is not a multiple of 4 is rounded down to the nearest nibble boundary and the status line says so, because delegation happens on nibble boundaries. Relative IPv6 owners are the remaining address nibbles in reverse. PTR lines are listed while the block holds at most 256 addresses; larger blocks show the apex and the exact name count. The PTR target is trimmed, must be a syntactically valid DNS name of at most 253 characters, and gets a trailing dot so it is not read relative to $ORIGIN. The page emits $ORIGIN and record lines only: no SOA, no NS, no serial and no DNSSEC, because those need a server and contact it cannot know. It performs no lookup, so it cannot tell whether a zone is delegated or a PTR record answers; everything is computed locally with no network access, storage or uploads.
